11265-notes-and-queries-number-02-novemb:
The second number of Notes and Queries, dated November 10, 1849, opens with thanks to readers who have already made the new journal a literary exchange. Contributors answer earlier queries and raise new ones: Bishop Aylmer's letter and a poem on the Armada, notes on ancient libraries, a pedlar's song attributed to Shakespeare, and traditions about Hamlet. J. Payne Collier and Bolton Corney are among the correspondents.

The journal's idea was simple and new: a medium where literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists could ask and answer questions in public. This early number shows the formula working, with learning traded in short paragraphs. It is a founding document for the reference culture that later produced far larger works.
11577-notes-and-queries-number-03-novemb:
Notes and Queries number 3 is dated Saturday, 17 November 1849, priced at threepence, fourpence stamped. It calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of it.

Notes cover travelling in England, Sanuto's Doges of Venice by Sir F Madden, and letters from Lord Nelson's brother after Trafalgar. Misquotations, Herbert's and Dibdin's Ames, and notes from fly leaves follow. Queries, answers, and minor queries close the number, with a register from East Peckham church in Kent and notes on Queen Elizabeth's household.
11636-notes-and-queries-number-05-decemb:
Notes and Queries number 5 is dated Saturday, 1 December 1849. It cost threepence, fourpence stamped. Notes open with Lord Chatham and Queen Charlotte. An original letter on Pitt's resignation in 1761 follows. Public feeling and changes at court are covered there.

Ancient tapestry by Planché and travelling in England come next. Prison discipline and execution of justice follow. Queries ask about Sanuto's Doges of Venice and the manuscripts of Sir Roger Twysden. Minor queries cover a bust of Sir Walter Raleigh. Notes on books, catalogues, and sales close the issue, with notices to correspondents.
11651-notes-and-queries-number-07-decemb:
Notes and Queries number 7 is dated Saturday, 15 December 1849, priced at threepence, fourpence stamped. Notes open with a marriage contract of Mary Queen of Scots and a bill of fare from 1626. Moneta Sanctae Helenae and translations of Gray's Elegy follow.

Notes on authors and books by Bolton Corney appear as well. Queries ask about Berkeley's theory of vision and Doctor Johnson with Professor de Morgan. Suppressed passages in Cartwright's poems are queried too. Minor queries cover Christencat, hexameter verses in Scripture, and the festival of Saint Michael. Answers on lobsters in medals and straw necklaces close the round.
11652-notes-and-queries-number-08-decemb:
Notes and Queries number 8 is dated Saturday, 22 December 1849, priced at threepence, fourpence stamped. Notes open with Otloh the scribe, Cunningham's London, wives of ecclesiastics, Tower Royal, and an ancient inscribed dish by Albert Way. Barnacles, Dorne the bookseller, and sermons by Stephen follow in turn.

Queries ask about Love, the king's fool, Mare de Saham, the Advent bells, and the poets, with minor queries on Darnley, coffee, and catsup. One answer quotes Heywood on Love, prince of fools, who made king and queen merry with many good pastimes. The number is a Christmas antiquarian miscellany, brisk and crowded with small learning.
12139-the-gringos-a-story-of-the-old-cal:
B. M. Bower published The Gringos in 1913, a novel of California in the gold-rush year 1849, with help from George W. Lee, a genuine Forty-niner. The story follows American newcomers, called gringos by Californios, into a valley ruled by old Spanish families.

Vigilantes, squatters, rodeos, fiestas, and duels with riatas drive the plot, as Jerry Simpson and his neighbors clash with Don Andres household over land and honor. Bower sympathizes with both sides by turns, and her heroine, called the finest little woman in the world, steadies hot tempers. The novel mixes romance with a rough record of conquest, showing how law gave way to guns when two peoples met on one range.
13513-notes-and-queries-number-04-novemb:
Notes and Queries for November 24, 1849, its fourth number, opens with a statement of progress and prospects for the new journal. John Bruce writes on Luther and Erasmus, Hallam's Middle Ages is discussed, and notes cover writers on fly-leaves, the origin of grog, ancient alms-basins, and Dyce against Warburton and Collier.

Food of the people, bills of fare, Bishop Barnaby, trade editions, and Dibdin's Typographical Antiquities fill the notes. While queries ask about clouds or shrouds in Shakespeare and a medal of the Pretender. A note on Shakespeare manuscripts argues that none survive except his name, save one letter addressed to him. The young journal already shows its lasting pattern.
13521-notes-and-queries-number-09-decemb:
Notes and Queries for December 29, 1849, closes the journal's first year with notes on Sir E. Dering's household book, Berkeley's theory of vision, Bishop Barnaby, mathematical archaeology, and Gothic architecture. Dr. Burney's musical works, ancient alms-basins, and minor notes on Prince Madoc, St. Barnabas, Cromwell's baptism, and the Times fill the rest.

A letter on a song in the style of Suckling, and a note on the contest for the best translation of Gray's Elegy, judged by Mr. Nares of the British Critic, show the journal's literary range. The number looks back on progress made since November and forward to new questions, keeping its promise of a medium where readers answer each other's puzzles.
13550-notes-and-queries-number-06-decemb:
Notes and Queries for December 8, 1849, its sixth number, opens with a few words of explanation from the editor. Notes cover a letter from the Earl of Shaftesbury on Monmouth's ash, Drayton's poems, a passage in Goldsmith, ancient libraries, a defence of a bald head, and royal household allowances.

Adversaria notes printers' couplets, Charles Martel, Bodenham and Ling, and travelling in England, with minor notes on an ancient alms dish, a bishop that burneth, and Sussex ironworks. A royal warrant under the signet at East Hampstead in the fourteenth year of a reign orders household officers to pay allowances. The young journal already mixes documents, books, and curiosities.
16030-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number forty-nine, dated October 14, 1897, under the Great Round World Publishing Company. News, science, and stories fill the paper in words young readers could follow. This number leads with a disquieting rumour about the Seal Conference. The paper kept children abreast of diplomacy.

England, the rumour runs, refused to join the Seal Conference if Russia and Japan were admitted. At the British Foreign Office, officials would not say positively whether Britain had declined. Young readers learn how news travels: rumour, denial, and waiting. Seen now, the issue shows 1897 children meeting world politics in plain, careful words.
1936-letters-from-england-1846-1849:
Elizabeth Davis Bancroft's Letters from England, 1846 to 1849, gathers letters written during her years in London as the wife of the American minister. A portrait of Mrs. Bancroft, probably taken at Brady's National Gallery in New York after her return, fronts the volume, and the letters that follow describe a society at its height.

At a London dinner, Bancroft notes, one may meet so many people, each with a peculiar gift, that one cannot avail oneself of every opportunity. The letters move through dinners, debates, and country houses. The book is a valuable record of Anglo-American society in the 1840s, written by a woman with a sharp eye and a wide circle.
20126-the-cave-of-gold-a-tale-of-califor:
Everett McNeil wrote The Cave of Gold, a tale of California in '49. The gold rush year gives the tale its heat and risk. Bud hears fearful screams from a hill and turns pale at the sound. Yet he vows to find the cause and climbs at once.

With rifle ready, he fixes his eyes on the spot above. Boys' gold rush tales mix mines, caves, and sudden peril freely. McNeil sets greed, courage, and wild country in a fast plot. Readers get a vivid taste of how '49 looked to young readers years later.
23192-gold-seekers-of-49:
Gold Seekers of '49 is an adventure story about the California gold rush, told through a boy named Charley. Its chapter list promises a full journey west: a mysterious stranger, a call to the golden west, an unwelcome companion, and an attack by an enemy early on the road.

The route runs by Panama, up a river, and through the Golden Gate into San Francisco. Later chapters take Charley on to the diggings, where he hears a key talk, follows an enemy's trail, and makes a great discovery. Readers get the rush as a young traveller's string of risks, races, and finds.
27744-remarks-on-clarissa-1749:
Published in London in 1749, this anonymous pamphlet gathers criticisms of Samuel Richardson's novel Clarissa heard in conversation, addressed directly to its author. It reports objections to the heroine's character and conduct from the first volumes to the close.

The writer also records defenses offered by Clarissa's admirers, and adds reflections on the character of Prior's Emma. The pamphlet is a lively record of how Richardson's vast epistolary novel divided its first readers, and of the arguments they had about it. The writer insists he has neither softened objections nor added praise beyond what he heard. The talk went on.
8603-notes-and-queries-number-01-novembe:
Notes and Queries began on Saturday, November 3, 1849, as a threepenny weekly medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists to ask and answer questions. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of it. The first number prefers to show rather than promise, offering a specimen of the exchanges its prospectus had described, and leaving future numbers to prove the idea.

Inside, readers pose puzzles about books, words, customs, and family history, and other readers reply with evidence from libraries and parish records. The journal grew into a long-lived institution of British literary scholarship. This opening issue is a small treasure for historians of reading, showing how, before search engines, curious people built knowledge together, one printed query at a time.
anthem-pg1249:
Ayn Rand's novella is told by a young man known only by his council-given name, Equality 7-2521, in a city where the word I has been forgotten. Men live, work, and sleep in groups, and the Council of Vocations chooses each person's trade. Writing alone is a crime, and this journal is written in secret.

Working as a street sweeper, he finds a hidden tunnel from the old Unmentionable Times and teaches himself the lost power of light. His discoveries, and his love for a woman in the fields, drive him to flee the city. In the forest he finds books, and in them a single sacred word. The fable states Rand's case for the free individual.
arxiv-2412-00949:
Nicholas Lenzen, Amogh Raut, and Andrew Melnik present a study from twenty twenty-four on game agents in Minecraft that take goals as sound. A past agent, STEVE-1, follows goals coded as latent marks from text or sight. The team adds ears: a map from sound marks to the same goal space. That map is learned with no change to the agent's core.

They build a sound and video model for Minecraft and a prior net that turns sound into goal marks. The sound led agent plays at a par with the text and sight led ones. The team weighs what each sense gains and loses as a goal channel. Code and the sound model are open.
arxiv-2412-01149:
Joseph McGovern computes generating series for counting indices attached to compact Calabi-Yau threefolds, assuming these indices have a modular character. His examples are all quotient spaces. They include a Z7 quotient of Rødland's pfaffian threefold, a Z5 quotient of the Hosono-Takagi double quintic symmetroid, a Z3 quotient of the bicubic, and a Z5 quotient of the quintic. For each case he works out Gopakumar-Vafa invariants up to the highest genus that the boundary data allow.

For the quintic quotient alone, enough invariants emerge to give one real test of the modularity assumption. McGovern also treats five multiparameter examples in which computing a single index fixes the rest. He proposes a change to an earlier formula so that it takes torsion into account, since the examples work only because their intersection and Chern numbers stay small. An appendix discusses quotient threefolds and their Wall data.
arxiv-2412-03149:
Chuandi Zhang and co-authors study magnetic transitions in a crystal with a triangular atom layout in a 2024 paper. The compound holds manganese atoms with high spin on a triangular lattice that resists simple magnetic order. Related cobalt and nickel compounds show exotic quantum states, and this manganese version acts as their classical counterpart.

Magnet and heat measurements on powder samples showed two magnetic transitions in a row, just above one degree above absolute zero. Neutron diffraction at very low temperature revealed the ground state: manganese moments ordered in a Y-like pattern across two planes. Between the two transitions the pattern seems to shift to a simpler form held by heat-driven effects. The sequence matches theory for such triangular magnets.
arxiv-2412-04449:
Zhang and five colleagues present p-MoD in twenty twenty-four, an efficient design for multimodal language models. Such models handle text and images together but cost a lot to train and run. Most of their computation goes to processing vast numbers of vision tokens. The Mixture of Depths idea lets each layer process only key tokens.

Applying that idea to multimodal models raises stability and data problems. The authors add a gated weight normalization and a symmetric token reweighting scheme. Vision tokens grow more redundant in deeper layers, they observe. A progressive decay schedule thus cuts the kept token share layer by layer. Tests on fifteen benchmarks matched or beat baseline models. Inference used about half the compute and cache of the baselines.
arxiv-2412-04649:
Simone Borelli, Francesco Giovinazzo, Francesco Grella, and Giorgio Cannata present a robot arm controller that dodges obstacles with partial sensing, in two thousand twenty-four. Their arm carries arrays of distance sensors on only some links. Safe work beside people, though, needs the whole body to move away from sudden hazards.

The method turns sensor readings into a sparse cloud of points around the robot. It then finds the closest pair of points between that cloud and each arm link. A top-priority motion task moves the whole body away, even at links with no sensors. Tests in still and moving scenes matched established methods, with a wider safety margin in places.
arxiv-2412-05349:
Ilyasse Lamrani, Hanaa Zitane, and Delfim Torres present a 2024 mathematics paper on control of fractional systems with tempering. Fractional equations remember their past, which suits materials with memory. Tempering softens that memory at long times. Two questions matter: can inputs steer the system anywhere, and can outputs reveal its full state?

The authors first solve the system class with a Laplace transform method. They then give exact conditions for controllability and observability in terms of two Gramian matrices, the standard tests in control theory. Kalman-style rank criteria make the checks easy. Two classic chaotic circuit models, the Chua circuit and the Chua-Hartley oscillator, serve as worked examples of the theory.
arxiv-2412-05449:
Raphael Shu and four co-authors test how teams of AI agents can work as one in business settings. One agent can solve a great deal, but hard tasks with many parts call for a crew. How crews should pass work and messages, and how to grade them, is still unsettled. Their 2024 report grades a new collaboration framework on tasks drawn from three business fields. The task set is shared with the report.

Two modes are put to the test. In coordination mode, agents talk in parallel and point to shared payloads by name. In routing mode, messages are passed on with no central hand. Coordination reached 90 percent success on set goals. Crews beat single agents by up to 70 percent on those grades. Named payloads lifted code-heavy tasks by 23 percent, and routing cut wait times.
arxiv-2412-06549:
Angie Nataly Melo Castillo and co-authors tackle hidden pedestrians in road scenes in a 2024 paper. Self-driving cars must spot people on foot, yet people partly or fully hidden behind objects remain hard to detect, even for strong current systems. Human drivers use scene context to guess where a hidden person may be, and the team aimed to copy that skill.

They built OccluRoads, a data set of real and virtual road scenes with hidden pedestrians, all labeled with rich context notes. Their pipeline joins a knowledge graph, graph embeddings, and Bayesian reasoning to predict whether a hidden person is present. It reached a strong score and beat standard machine learning models by up to 42 percent.
arxiv-2412-07049:
Zizhao Hu, Xiaolin Zhou, and Mohammad Rostami test a simpler form of attention inside vision transformers. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-four. Vision transformers sort images by weighing how parts of an image relate to each other. The usual design builds both the query and the key afresh for each input. The authors ask whether the key can stay fixed instead.

Their tests show that a fixed key can match or even beat the standard design. Placed inside a Metaformer backbone, the fixed-key block also works well as a middle stage. It blends the strengths of plain convolution and self-attention. The result hints that attention can be cut from two steps to one with no loss.
arxiv-2412-07749:
Soumi Haldar and co-authors present a 2024 chemistry paper on why simulated molecular magnets relax too slowly on paper. Single-molecule magnets could store data at the molecular scale, but warmth shakes their lattices and the shaking erases the stored spin. Simulations of that spin-phonon relaxation often miss the measured rates by wide margins.

The standard simulation treats only a small active space of electrons. The authors test, for the first time systematically, what happens when correlation beyond that space is added, with two post-CASSCF methods. Cobalt and dysprosium magnets served as the case studies across temperatures. The richer treatments brought predictions to quantitative agreement with experiment. The paper tells modelers the cheap shortcut was the problem.
arxiv-2412-08149:
Han and eight co-authors fixed a flaw in twenty twenty-four in bridge tools that fill in lost parts of images. Those tools march all pixels on one noise plan, but real fix steps run out of sync across pixels. High-detail pixels get short-changed by the shared plan, they argue.

Their tool first guesses the image slope map in the lost zone. Sharp zones then get earlier, gentler noise steps than flat zones. That pixel-wise plan lets fix steps lean on each other in time. On real sets it beat top past tools, with clean-image scores up by three to fourteen percent.
arxiv-2412-08549:
Pascal Epple, Igor Shilov, Bozhidar Stevanoski, and Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye ask whether watermarked songs can be traced inside a music generator in two thousand twenty-four. AI music tools learn from vast stores of human work, much of it under copyright. If training songs carry hidden marks, the model's output may betray their use.

Two models were trained side by side, one on marked songs and one on clean ones, and their outputs compared. Marks that ears cannot hear still shifted what the model made. The size of the shift hinged on the marking method and on how much marked data was in the mix. The team also tested how well a top marking method resists removal tricks.
arxiv-2412-09449:
Suddhasattwa Brahma and co-authors present a 2024 theory paper on early universe cosmology in string theory. The setting is a heterotic string model with two moving domain walls. The authors build a duality chain to study late-time behavior. Reduced to four dimensions, the theory surprises them. It breaks no energy condition, so no bounce or ekpyrotic phase appears. Instead a passing de Sitter phase shows up: a stretch of accelerated expansion.

The phase stays inside the trans-Planckian bound, a key sanity limit. The team then builds an axion cosmology on it, with a time-varying axion coupling. Cosmologists get a string-based route to a de Sitter stretch that dodges known traps. Transient expansion phases matter because our own universe seems to sit in one. A model that yields it without breaking core rules is a notable catch.
arxiv-2412-10249:
Alessandro Perelli, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb, and Matthias Ehrhardt sketch images mid solver in a 2024 paper. Inverse imaging problems like CT involve huge images and data. Each solver step that touches the full image costs dearly. Stochastic methods already subsample the data side to save time.

Their algorithm, ImaSk, sketches the image side instead. Each iteration works on a randomly chosen resolution of the image. A saddle point view turns it into a gradient method with stored past gradients. For linear models with strong regularization, they prove linear convergence. CT simulations show the method reaches the target solution faster. More resolution levels cut the computing time further. The idea ports stochastic savings from data space into image space.
arxiv-2412-10649:
Christopher Tralie and three co-authors show in 2024 that hidden echoes can tag music made by AI tools. They hide a faint echo in training sounds, so soft that listeners cannot hear it. Later, they check if the echo shows up in sounds the model creates.

The team tried three kinds of audio models, and all of them passed the echo into their output. A single echo worked best, but longer spread-out echo patterns could carry more data. The mark even survived fine-tuning, mixing, and pitch shifts used in training. The authors say this old watermark trick could help prove where a model's training data came from, a live issue for rights and licensing.
arxiv-2412-10949:
Florian Kammüller, a solo author, extends a formal framework for security engineering with a way to prove that secret data do not leak, in a paper from 2024. The framework is built inside the Isabelle proof tool and models insiders and infrastructure. The paper's head title frames it as part two of security engineering in that framework.

The new part adds information flow security. Kammüller uses a notion called a shadow, drawn from the work of Morgan, to stand for what an observer at a lower level could see. He proves the shadow view matches the classic notion of noninterference inside the framework. That match yields conditions under which refining a design keeps it secure, solving a known paradox. A flight radar system serves as the running example.
arxiv-2412-11649:
Lecture notes from a 2024 workshop at the Institute for Advanced Study explain how gravity emerges from scattering math, in a paper edited from talks by five lecturers. Scattering amplitudes describe how particles bounce off each other. The notes show that classical gravity hides inside those quantum formulas.

A hydrogen atom example sets up how different motion regimes reveal bound and unbound behavior. Familiar results of general relativity, such as the delay of light near the Sun and Mercury's orbital drift, fall out of the amplitude view. Later sections apply worldline methods to black holes, gravitational waveforms, and three-body problems in astrophysics. The notes open a fast-growing field to students who know quantum theory but not the amplitude toolkit.
arxiv-2412-13249:
Oscar Arandes and Emil Bergholtz explore a chain of driven resonators as a quantum sensor, asking where its sensitivity truly comes from. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Open quantum systems can react sharply to tiny nudges, which tempts sensor designers. The chain here follows the squeezed Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a classic with distinct bulk phases.

The pair compare setups that differ in bulk topology and in the modes at the chain's ends. They test sensing of both plain shifts and the skin effect, where waves pile at one edge. Their study goes past tiny nudges to swings of any size. Tuning matters: the best settings boost the quantum edge without demanding fragile fine-tuning. The authors stress that practical sensors must avoid knife-edge regimes. The work maps where this platform can really deliver.
arxiv-2412-13749:
Xin Su and Zhuoran Zheng wrote a 2024 paper on merging photos taken at distinct light levels into one rich image. Phone shots keep growing in size, and old merge methods are too slow for real time use on small devices. Users also want a say in how the final image looks.

Their method leans on a color lookup grid that can grade huge images at speed. Merging shots at mixed light levels is unsure work, and that doubt strains the grid. A teacher and student network pair models that doubt to keep the grid robust. An implicit function adds an edit mode so users can tune results to the scene. Tests showed the method ranks high on both speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2412-13849:
Can Wang and co-authors present a physics paper from 2024 on reading quantum bits. In a superconductor-based quantum computer, gates are fast and sharp, but reading the bit lags behind. The strong signal used to probe the bit can also knock it out of its state.

The team designed a new layout that links the bit and its reader along the length axis. The layout kills off stray cross links that cause errors. It also adds a bend to the reader's response that trims two error kinds. In tests, reads were right 99.8 percent of the time in about two hundred nanoseconds, with no first-stage amplifier. After removing setup errors, pure read accuracy topped 99.9 percent. The design fits setups that read many bits at once.
arxiv-2412-14749:
Adel Rahman and Leonard Susskind study vector bosons in de Sitter space in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Their setting is the static patch, the region one observer can see in an expanding universe. The field is a massive vector boson described by the Proca action. They argue its true physical mass differs from the mass written in the Lagrangian.

The physical mass gains an extra term tied to the size of the de Sitter space. That shift has a striking consequence. The theory may stay well-defined even where the naive mass looks tachyonic, or unstable. They identify special features at the edge of stability, a specific mass value. Fixing a static patch also breaks the full symmetry of de Sitter space. That break explains why their modes need not fit the usual symmetry classes.
arxiv-2412-14849:
Hongling Xu, Yice Zhang, Qianlong Wang, and Ruifeng Xu build a data synthesis framework for few-shot aspect-based sentiment analysis, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Large language models can generate training samples where data is scarce. Earlier augmentation methods modified existing samples and lacked diversity. In-context learning approaches suffered labels that strayed from task requirements.

Their dual-stream framework synthesizes data from two complementary directions. One stream is key-point-driven; the other works from instances. Together they produce diverse, high-quality sentiment samples in low-resource settings. A label refinement module then cleans up the synthetic labels. Extensive experiments show the method beating previous few-shot solutions. It also outperforms other language-model data generation methods tested. The work targets sentiment tasks where annotated examples are few.
arxiv-2412-15249:
Shubham Agarwal and seven co-authors ask whether today's large language models can help write literature reviews, the survey sections that summarize prior work in a field. Their paper came out in 2024. Reviews are essential but slow to write, especially as publication volume grows.

They split the task in two: finding the relevant papers from a query abstract, then drafting the review from what was found. For retrieval, the model first extracts keywords, searches an external database, and then re-ranks the hits. Re-ranking doubled recall compared with naive search, and it exposed the model's reasons. For writing, the model first plans an outline, then drafts section by section. Their tests suggest models can assist reviews well when the job is decomposed this way. They release their evaluation protocol for future models.
arxiv-2412-15849:
Hanchun Jiang and Toshiya Namikawa study how doubt in the cosmos's second dawn affects our power to bound the waves sent out by the first burst of growth. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

That dawn, when the first stars lit gas anew, leaves a large-scale mark in the glow left from the hot early cosmos. Sky-wide probes will read that mark to test the old waves. The team asks what goes wrong if the true past of that dawn has a unlike shape from the smooth form used to fit the data. With a probe like a planned space scope, they find the bounds stay much the same. The result calms a fear for such tests.
arxiv-2412-15949:
Wei-jie Fu, Jan Pawlowski, Robert Pisarski, Fabian Rennecke, Rui Wen, and Shi Yin wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It studies the moat regime of dense quark matter, where meson links wobble in space in a wave-like way.

The team looks at how pions act in real time at set heat and density. They show the moat comes from particle-hole-like ripples near the Fermi surface. Those ripples plant a peak in the pion's spectral shape at nonzero space-like momentum. That peak reads as a new quasi-particle, which they name the moaton. Their frame also tests if the even chiral phase can hold against a wavy condensate. At the densities eyed, such a phase looks highly unlikely.
arxiv-2412-16149:
Sangmin Choi, Alok Laddha, and Andrea Puhm wrote this 2024 theoretical physics paper on a hidden symmetry of electromagnetism. Earlier work tied a universal rule about very soft photons to an endless set of phase rotations acting on matter at the edge of spacetime. Each rotation carries a conserved charge.

Here the team extend those charges to all orders in the coupling strength. They prove that keeping the charges conserved is exactly the classical rule for soft photon emission found by others in 2019. They also widen the matching memory formulas from particles to full matter fields. The result completes a three-way link among symmetry, conservation, and observable effects, known as an infrared triangle.
arxiv-2412-17949:
Where two ribbons of graphene meet, a trapped electronic state can sit at the junction, protected by topology from ordinary disturbance. Hazem Abdelsalam and co-authors classify those states across a wide family of ribbon shapes in a 2024 paper, including shapes chemists have already made. They then ask what the trapped states are good for.

Their answer is sensing and chemistry rather than computing. A modeled double junction reacts strongly to a common pollutant gas molecule settling nearby, its transport shifting in a readable way. The authors argue the pinpoint nature of junction states makes them fine probes, opening a route they call topological chemistry.
arxiv-2412-18149:
Xiao Guo, Manh Tran, Jiaxin Cheng, and Xiaoming Liu wrote this computer vision paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on making face images of a specific person from text. A user gives one reference photo and a written prompt, and the model should draw that same face doing or wearing what the text says.

Older methods either need fresh tuning for each person or drift away from the prompt. The team's model, Dense-Face, adds a pose-controlling adapter to a standard image generator, so the face can turn as asked while text editing still works. It also learns to predict dense face annotations from the generator's own inner features, which teaches it face structure. Tests show top or near-top scores on text match, identity keeping, and pose control. The authors aim at custom portraits that stay true to both the person and the prompt.
arxiv-2412-18849:
Maxence Boels, Yang Liu, Prokar Dasgupta, Alejandro Granados, and Sebastien Ourselin teach surgery video tools to see ahead. Most tools just name the phase a cut is in now. Sight ahead could tell the team what to make ready. Past work sees one near event ahead. But surgery is dense, loops a lot, and runs long. Their frame, SWAG, builds chains of phases to come, at one-minute steps, over long spans.

Two ways to build the chains vie: one pass, and step by step. Marks built from how phases tend to follow each other hone the casts. A side trick turns time-left fits into class picks. On two free surgery data sets, the top model hit F1 near a third at 20 minutes and near 41% at 30 minutes. Time-left slips stayed near a third to half a minute at short spans.
arxiv-2412-18949:
Ivanov and co-authors ask whether a metric space can be identified by its distances to the simplest possible spaces, in a 2024 paper. The test spaces are simplexes, where every pair of points sits at one same nonzero distance. The yardstick is the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, the standard way to compare shapes up to stretching. Some different spaces sit at zero distance and so can never be told apart.

The surprise: some spaces at positive distance from each other still produce identical distance lists to all simplexes. The authors exhibit such indistinguishable pairs. They then prove conditions, both sufficient and necessary, for when this blindness occurs. The paper maps a subtle limit of a widely used recognition idea.
arxiv-2412-19249:
Aryan Agarwala and Guy Even prove that two common limits on approximate membership data structures do real work. Structures that answer membership queries with false positives most often bar duplicate insertions. They also bar the deletion of items that are not members. Under those rules, known designs use close to the least space in theory.

Agarwala and Even show that if both limits are lifted, the space needed jumps. Any structure for a set under any duplicate insertions and deletions of non-members needs far more bits. The count scales with the logarithm of the number of sets that can be drawn from the universe. The bound splits the well-behaved setting from the fully general one. The rules are not mere ease of use. They are what makes near-best space possible.
arxiv-2412-20149:
Mo Zhou and co-authors design control pulses for leaky quantum systems in a 2024 paper set in circuit quantum electrodynamics. In that field, superconducting circuits are steered and read by microwave pulses. Real systems lose energy to their surroundings, so a pulse must hit its target fast and cheaply before the loss spoils the state.

Their frame rests on a classic rule of optimal control, the Pontryagin maximum principle. They cast the circuit's noisy motion as a linear control problem and derive pulses whose energy cost scales in a favorable way. The pulses beat standard shortcut methods that rush a system along a protected path. On a resonator linked to a qubit, the pulses read the qubit with a signal quality matching far costlier schemes, across a range of photon levels.
arxiv-2501-00149:
Grace Jiang, Jiangchao Qiu, and Sai Ravela (2024) hunt the rare storms that cause destructive storm tides, without simulating every storm. Climate studies produce huge catalogs of downscaled tropical cyclones. Running full water simulations on all of them is unaffordable. The authors first show that a fast surrogate model can flag the dangerous ones accurately. It even generalizes to climate scenarios it never saw. Their system, LASSE, then learns actively as it searches.

Starting from a small set of fully simulated storms, the surrogate picks which storm to simulate next. Each new result retrains it on the spot. On a large catalog, the search found every destructive storm it was tested on, with perfect precision. It needed fewer than a fifth of the full simulations as training. The authors present the method as scalable to the biggest catalogs.
arxiv-2501-00349:
Tatsuki Murakami and co-authors describe, in a 2024 paper, an architecture for spectroscopy and microwave generation based on soliton microcombs. A microcomb splits a single laser beam into many evenly spaced lines of light. In their design, the crystalline microresonators that hold the combs can be shifted in position, which gives extra control over the solitons.

Using one shared pump laser, the team produced two coherent soliton combs in separate resonators with slightly different repetition rates. This pairing supports coherent dual-comb spectroscopy. They also generated Kerr solitons directly from an ultrastable laser with a linewidth below one hertz. That approach greatly reduced phase noise in the microwaves the system produced. The authors present the design as a step toward wider use of microcombs in ranging, data links, and low-noise signals.
arxiv-2501-01149:
Yuxiang Chai and co-authors present Android Agent Arena in 2025, a test system for phone-using AI agents. Language and vision models now drive agents that tap and swipe through mobile apps on their own. Older benchmarks grade still frames or run in frozen offline apps, which misses how agents handle live, changing online services.

Their arena holds one hundred tasks drawn from twenty popular dynamic apps across twenty categories. Grading follows an essential-state method: a vision model checks step by step whether the key states of the task were reached, rather than demanding one fixed path. The package also includes tools for driving devices, resetting apps, and collecting human and agent demonstrations, all set for public release.
arxiv-2501-01549:
Vahid Nourozi builds quantum error-correcting codes from a family of geometric codes, in a 2025 paper. The codes start with Goppa codes drawn from maximal curves over finite fields, curves given by a short equation. From them he forms codes for classical and quantum use, then tweaks the designs to improve their numbers. Long runs of simulations test how the codes behave as error rates change.

The paper gives concrete examples and sets them beside known results. The new codes do not always reach the best possible minimum distance. Still, they offer orderly ways to build codes with useful trade-offs for certain tasks. Nourozi presents the graphs and tables as a guide to how these codes act in noisy settings, and as a base for later theory.
arxiv-2501-02449:
Márcio Matheus de Lima Barboza and Francisco Márcio Barboza revisit two pillars of first-semester calculus, Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem, pairing their classical proofs with computational verification. The theorems anchor much of analysis and the modeling built on it. The paper states both formally and proves them analytically, with the rigor the authors consider necessary for real understanding.

Geometric interpretations accompany the proofs, picturing the guaranteed flat tangent and the parallel secant. The second half checks the theorems computationally, an integrated theory-and-practice exercise. The goal is pedagogical as much as mathematical: to validate the results by hand and by machine in one treatment. Students meeting these theorems get both the argument and the experiment. The authors frame the dual approach as the natural modern way to teach bedrock analysis.
arxiv-2501-02649:
Haixu Liu, Penghao Jiang, Zerui Tao, Muyan Wan, and Qiuzhuang Sun present Tighnari, a model that forecasts which plant species grow at a place and time, for a LifeCLEF lab notebook. Such forecasts aid wildlife care and species ID tools. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Training drew on tens of thousands of plant surveys across Europe, plus satellite images, climate series, land cover, and soil data. A graph based feature step and a correction step shape the inputs. The team picked the best backbones for time and image data, built a fresh time cube backbone, and fused modes with layered cross attention. A threshold top pick step cleans the output.
arxiv-2501-04049:
Anica Hamer and colleagues put three bold claims to the test in a 2025 optics paper. Quantum networks need to change a photon's color without harming its fragile quantum state. Crystals do that job well, but they add noise, accept only a narrow color band, and heat unevenly under strong pump light, which hurts performance.

A hollow fiber filled with hydrogen gas offers an alternative the team had proposed earlier. New experiments back all three claims: strong pump fields do not degrade the conversion, background noise stays near zero, and the process works across a broad band at once. Fiber conversion could suit future large fiber-based quantum networks that need clean, flexible links.
arxiv-2501-04349:
Kanupriya and Shravan Kumar study spectral synthesis in multidimensional Fourier algebras in a two thousand twenty-five harmonic analysis paper. Fourier algebras encode the harmonic analysis of a locally compact group, and the multidimensional version was brought in by Todorov and Turowska.

Spectral synthesis asks which closed sets can be won back from the functions vanishing on them. The authors prove multidimensional versions of the subgroup lemma and of the injection and inverse projection theorems. The results cover both spectral sets and the stricter Ditkin sets. They also set up parallel synthesis between consecutive dimensions and prove an analogue of Malliavin's theorem, a landmark result in the classic one-dimensional theory.
arxiv-2501-06449:
Shoushuo Zhang and co-authors improve radar-like target spotting in 2025 for future 6G networks. These networks will sense their surroundings while carrying data, a dual role called integrated sensing and communication. Smart surfaces that bounce and shape radio waves, named RIS, can add extra viewpoints on a target.

Their design views the target from many angles at once, since each path has its own delay, motion, and direction signature. That variety helps pull the target's signal out of clutter. They jointly shape the sent waveform, the surface settings, and the receiver filters to boost the target signal against noise and clutter. Simulations show the multi-view plan detects targets better in hard scenes.
arxiv-2501-08249:
Junming Zhao and co-authors present Pancake, a programming language built to prove device drivers correct, in a paper from 2025. Driver bugs are the top cause of operating system breaches. Yet no fast, real driver for a nontrivial device had been fully proven before. Pancake is a plain imperative language with a clean, proof-friendly meaning.

Its compiler rests on a proven back end, so the machine code keeps the source meaning. An automatic bridge hands Pancake code to a solver front end for checking. With that chain, the team proved a fast driver for a network card. The result shows proof need not cost speed. It also gives systems builders a template for verified low-level code. More drivers could follow the same path.
arxiv-2501-08549:
Sitong Gong and co-authors present a method for cutting out objects in video based on text reasoning in a 2025 paper. Older methods lean on a single token to stand for the target, which misses shape detail and motion between frames. Their system uses large multimodal models to feed rich space and time features into layered tokens. One token type works at frame level, and another works across time.

A fusion step blends frame scores by similarity, and a selection step picks the best key frame using a segmentation model's blockage scores. That frame is cut out first, then the result spreads through the video. Scores on a known benchmark beat a prior leading method by clear margins. Readers see token design as the key to video detail.
arxiv-2501-09949:
Muñoz, Yuan, and Jain pruned large AI models without retraining in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Cutting whole blocks from a transformer shrinks it cheaply, but leaves its shape unbalanced. Their method, MultiPruner, trims along three dimensions in turn. It removes residual blocks, then narrows the feed-forward channels, then drops attention heads.

Each pass restores balance before the next cut lands. The result compresses models further than rival training-free methods. Zero-shot accuracy on downstream tasks held up better as well. Memory and compute needs fell with the size. The authors released the code and pruning settings openly. They frame balance as the missing ingredient in block pruning.
arxiv-2501-10949:
Rui Gao, Weixiao Shen, and Ruiqin Zhang present a 2025 math paper on a typical case question in ergodic optimization. The setup: a map stretches a circle, and a score function rewards each orbit. Optimization asks which invariant pattern of motion earns the highest long run average score.

The authors show that for a typical smooth score function, the answer is as simple as it can be. There is exactly one best pattern, and it rides on a repeating orbit that cycles through finitely many points. Typical is meant in two senses at once: topologically generic and full measure. The result holds for every smoothness class, from once smooth to analytic.
arxiv-2501-11849:
Nikos Kanakaris and six co-authors hunt coordinated astroturf campaigns with language models steered by network-aware prompts, no training required. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles a data curse: real campaigns are rare beside normal posts, so classifiers starve on positives. Their frame feeds the model both post text and the social graph around it. A Balanced RAG component fetches examples that offset the imbalance.

Prompt design does the rest of the work. On X data, the setup beats traditional graph-based baselines by two to three times on precision, recall, and F1. The gain comes without fine-tuning a single weight. Disinformation teams gain a detector that adapts by rewording, not retraining, when campaigns mutate.
arxiv-2501-12049:
Roberto de Almeida Capistrano-Filho, Hugo Parada, and Jandeilson Santos da Silva study when waves on a star-shaped network of channels can be steered at will. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The wave rule is the famous Korteweg-de Vries equation, used for shallow water waves. Steering such a system rests on a twin problem about watching it.

The question narrows to a spectral puzzle tied to the network. The team checks when certain functions built from that puzzle are entire, meaning smooth across the whole plane. That trait is the key that unlocks the steering proof. Star graphs join several channels at one hub, a shape met in real waterways and wires. The authors say the fine-grained check is new for this shape. The work firms up control theory for waves on networks.
arxiv-2501-12549:
Sharat Ibrahimpur and Laszlo Vegh give a faster approximation for buying a resilient network in a 2025 algorithms study. Edges of a graph are classed safe or unsafe, and the buyer wants the cheapest edge set that stays highly connected even after several unsafe edges fail. Guarantees of that kind underpin communication and transport planning.

Independent rounding turns a fractional optimum into a purchase whose cost overshoots by only a logarithmic factor in the network size. That improves the previous best guarantee. Approximation algorithms with proved factors let planners budget for resilience instead of hoping heuristics hold.
arxiv-2501-12649:
Heat flow can lag behind the warmth that drives it, tracing loops when warmth swings in waves. Renai Chen and Galen Craven study those loops in 2025 for a lone grain tied to two heat baths, each bath warming and cooling in waves. Their twist is to flip the wave's pace mid-run, fast to slow or slow to fast. Math forms for the heat in and out match lab-style simulations of the moving grain step for step.

Flipping the pace bends the loops in strong ways. Pinched loops and stacked multi-loops show up that a steady pace never makes. The pair point to heat-based brain-like gear, such as heat memory parts, as a place the trick could pay off. Pace, in their hands, becomes a knob for shaping heat itself.
arxiv-2501-13249:
D. Germani, B. Grinstein, and A. D. Polosa calculated the spectrum of tetraquarks in 2025, four-quark states whose existence tests how quantum chromodynamics binds matter. The test case is the famous X(3872) particle. A popular picture treats it as a loosely bound molecule of two normal mesons. But a recent LHCb reading of how often it decays by emitting varied photons does not fit that picture. And the authors test whether a compact tetraquark fares better.

Working in the Born-Oppenheimer estimate, borrowed from molecular physics, they compute the whole tetraquark spectrum for the three lowest spins and refine the decay ratio calculation. The compact picture agrees greatly better with the measured ratio and with the seen spectroscopy. Extending the diquark-antidiquark model so states can mix open-charm singlet and color-octet parts, they find these exotics are compact, shallow bound states in color force potentials.
arxiv-2501-14249: A large team of authors put out the paper named Humanity's Last Exam in two thousand twenty-five. Long Phan and Alice Gatti are among the first names on the list. It runs to well over a hundred names from many institutions. It sets out a benchmark exam of hard, expert-level questions. It tests how far large AI models have come. Its scale marks it as a shared yardstick for the field. It should stay hard as models grow stronger.
arxiv-2501-15149:
Zaazou, Bihlo, and Tricco teach a deep learning model to translate galaxy images between light bands in twenty twenty-five. Telescopes view galaxies in ultraviolet, visible, and infrared light, but no survey covers all bands well. A model that can fill in a missing band could save costly observing time. The team trained their model on fake galaxy views from a large simulation.

The model could guess bands inside the known range and stretch a bit beyond it. Scores on both plain image tests and star based tests showed high likeness to truth. It also worked on real survey images in a case study. The authors see uses in planning missions and probing how galaxies change.
arxiv-2501-16549:
Tina Behzad, Sílvia Casacuberta, Emily Diana, and Alexander Tolbert study what to do when equally good models disagree about a person, in a 2025 paper. Different models trained on the same data often give the same person different risk scores, a problem called predictive multiplicity. An earlier algorithm, Reconcile, uses a disagreement between two models to prove at least one of them wrong and improve it. The authors put that algorithm to work on five widely used fairness datasets.

The datasets cover criminal risk, crime rates, income, credit, and census outcomes. The study examines how reconciliation behaves in practice, where accuracy and fairness pull against each other. The work matters because a person's loan or bail outcome should not hinge on which good model a clerk happened to pick.
arxiv-2501-16649:
Chintapenta, Verma, and Majumder present a deep learning model that spots irregular heartbeats in unborn babies from belly-surface recordings, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such recordings mix the mother's and baby's signals, making them hard to read, and classic marker-based methods fail on their tangled shapes. Odd rhythms show up in both the timing and the frequency makeup of the trace.

Their model, MFConvTr, mixes convolutional layers that read several frequency bands at once with a transformer that tracks long-range patterns. Splitting the signal into channels and filtering each at a different scale captures the multi-frequency clues cheaply. The model reached top scores on its tests while using very few parameters. The authors also ran breakdown tests to show which parts carry the gains.
arxiv-2501-16949:
Ruchi and Lalit Kumar Vashisht study how to recover a hidden source from samples of a moving system in a 2025 mathematics study. The system evolves in steps over a non-uniform set of times that arises from spectral pairs, inside an infinite-dimensional space. Earlier work by Aldroubi and colleagues frames the recovery problem and its stability, which frames must guarantee.

The authors give a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for recovering the source in finitely many steps. They also derive a necessary condition for stable recovery when the source lies in a closed subspace. Stable recovery matters for sensors that watch dynamics indirectly.
arxiv-2501-17449:
Islam Oshallah and three co-authors build question answering for the Quran in twenty twenty-five. Question answering is hard in languages with scarce data. Quranic QA matters to over a billion people seeking deeper understanding of the text. It also has a special twist: questions are written in Modern Standard Arabic, while answers sit in Classical Arabic verses.

Existing data sets are small, which caps model performance. The team takes a cross-language approach to break that cap. They translate Arabic questions into English to expand the data. They paraphrase questions to add linguistic variety. Answers are retrieved from an English translation of the Quran to align with multilingual training. Readers get a recipe for sacred-text QA where data is thin and registers differ.
arxiv-2501-17549:
Wooyoung Kim, Byungyoon Park, and Wooju Kim wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It feeds graph data to large language models as a small set of learned pooling tokens, shaped by the user's query.

Node-by-node projection does not scale, while whole-graph projection washes out detail. The learned tokens strike a balance, holding both fine and broad traits of the graph. A trick called Early Query Fusion blends the question in before the graph code is built. That way the code keeps what the question needs. On the GraphQA benchmark the method gains over four percent. The language model itself is left untrained. The work suits social, citation, and knowledge graphs full of text.
arxiv-2501-18949:
Okuto Morikawa, Soma Onoda, and Hiroshi Suzuki present a 2025 talk paper on a new grid formulation of two-dimensional chiral gauge theory. Such theories are famously hard to put on a lattice, since the grid tends to break their delicate anomaly pattern. Recent constructions use a trick called bosonization to keep the pattern exact even at finite grid spacing.

Their version rests on an excision method that enforces a smoothness rule on grid fields. That rule usually bans charged objects, yet the authors show such objects can live as holes, a kind of defect in the grid. They then work out which charged objects the rules allow, extending the lattice toolkit for these theories.
arxiv-2502-00249:
Om Roy and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on reading brain networks from EEG signals over time. Standard methods track links between pairs of brain sites. Richer patterns, such as flows around triangles and loops, can hide signals that pairwise views miss.

Their framework, Hodge-FAST, joins a math tool called Hodge decomposition with a filtered connectivity method. First, the data are thinned to the most important links, and short-term links are filtered by stable long-term patterns. The signal is then split into three parts that describe flows over higher-order shapes. In patients with mild cognitive impairment tied to Alzheimer's disease, the method found time-based differences that pairwise study did not show. That opens a fresh window on noisy brain recordings.
arxiv-2502-00649:
Fabio Bresolin and a large team map how two metals spread inside the spiral galaxy NGC 6946. They use hundreds of glowing gas clouds as probes. The study belongs to a survey of roughly forty nearby galaxies with a Fourier transform spectrometer in Canada. It measures oxygen and nitrogen in well over six hundred star-forming regions. Then it examines the wiggles around the smooth radial trends. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they find a sideways pattern across one spiral arm. The leading edge runs poorer in metals than the trailing edge by a noticeable step.

Simulations explain the pattern as gas flowing along the arm. The flow dilutes one side and enriches the other. Oxygen and nitrogen vary over similar spatial scales, though stars forge them differently. Supernovae make one; aging giants make the other. The authors infer that stellar processes stir both elements into the gas over equivalent distances.
arxiv-2502-01049:
Murugaraj Odiathevar and Kim Chung Yup present a 2025 paper on simulating network traffic that behaves like real applications. Many simulators fire packets at random gaps, which misses how apps actually burst and idle. Security tools tested on such fake traffic may fail in the real world.

Their method learns the statistical shape of each application's traffic and rebuilds it from those curves. Blending the learned patterns yields dynamic traffic that scales from one machine to large networks. Behavior can be dialed up or down to stress monitoring and anomaly tools. The code is open source, so other teams can rerun and extend the tests.
arxiv-2502-02149:
Jan Kotrbatý wrote a 2025 math note on a conjecture in convex geometry. The catalog title carries a funding note, but the note itself concerns the difference body of a convex shape: the set of all gaps between pairs of its points. A known inequality bounds that set's volume, and Godbersen's conjecture claims a sharper bound using the shape and its mirror image.

Kotrbatý proposes a wider version covering higher-order difference bodies, which stack the construction further. He proves the wider claim for a well-behaved class called anti-blocking bodies. He also links the bound to a product operation on certain measures, giving a second form of the same claim. Notes like this inch a long-open problem forward in the cases that can be settled.
arxiv-2502-02349:
Vrushank Ahire, Pranav Menon, Aniruddh Muley, and Abhinandan Prasad propose a hybrid rule for deciding what a processor cache keeps. Caches are tiny, fast stores that must guess which data will be needed again. Fixed rules waste some slots and miss changing access patterns. Their rule, RAC, mixes random placement with a flexible shared-tag design.

The design spreads entries across two thousand forty-eight sets with sixteen slots each. Tags can move where demand is, so busy sets borrow room from idle ones. Storage for tags and data is trimmed for efficiency. On a standard simulator with four varied workloads, hit rates climbed as high as eighty percent. Speed per instruction rose only modestly, though. The authors stress better cache use and shorter waits as the real gains.
arxiv-2502-02549:
Ron Benchetrit, Idan Lev-Yehudi, Andrey Zhitnikov, and Vadim Indelman present a planner for robots that must act without full knowledge of the world, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The planner handles rewards that depend on what the robot believes, which suits tasks like search and mapping. Older solvers kept a fixed picture of belief, so they could not sharpen it as time went on.

The new solver refines that picture step by step and is built to improve the longer it runs. A fast update trick cuts the cost of scoring belief rewards by a large factor. Tests showed better speed and better plans than leading solvers. Readers in robotics get a tool for smarter search under doubt.
arxiv-2502-02949:
Md Hossen Mondal and Ramkrishna Joshi study the physics of sound through a homemade loudspeaker, in this 2025 paper. Sound travels as waves of squeezed and stretched air in tubes and rooms. The authors build a simple speaker from magnets and a coil driven by a wobbling signal, and ask how well basic theory predicts its behavior.

They model the setup as a driven oscillator with damping and solve it in its steady state. From that solution they pull out the frequencies where the device responds most strongly. The paper then works through how to choose the parts of the build so that theory and measured behavior line up. The aim is a low cost, hands on route into the physics of vibrating surfaces and sound.
arxiv-2502-03049:
A team led by Katsipoulaki, with Mourzidis, Jindal, Lagarde, Taniguchi, Watanabe, Kopidakis, Marie, Glazov, Stratakis, Kioseoglou, and Paradisanos, wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It steers the spin-valley polarization of excitons in single layers of WSe2 by doping them with light.

Single-shot photochlorination steps shift the layer from electron-rich to hole-rich. The polarization does not move in a straight line: it dips low near the neutral point, then climbs threefold as holes grow. A plain model of the dynamics points to exciton and carrier collisions as the main driver, while the exciton life span barely moves. The trick gives a fine knob for valley physics in such thin crystals.
arxiv-2502-04049:
Jagabandhu Mishra and co-authors build a 2025 method to both spot fake speech and name the tool that made it. Fake speech from synthesizers can fool listeners and systems. Most detectors give a bare yes-or-no answer from dense internal features that no one can read, which makes their choices hard to trust or explain.

Their method breaks a voice clip into a set of named traits, each with a chance value, that point to parts of the synthesizer that made it. Those trait scores feed simple classifiers that handle both tasks: telling real from fake, and naming the source method. They also use a game-theory tool to weigh how much each trait swayed the final call. The result is a detector whose reasoning can be inspected.
arxiv-2502-04249:
Michael Walters, Rafael Kaufmann, Justice Sefas, and Thomas Kopinski build a risk metric for multi-agent AI systems from the free energy principle, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Popular safe-AI theories often demand massive data or arbitrarily complex world models. Their alternative asks stakeholders only to state preferences over outcomes. Decision rules for risk governance then stay transparent.

The proposed Cumulative Risk Exposure metric adapts to differing contexts and needs. The framework accounts for uncertainty in both the world model and the preference model. The authors demonstrate it in a simplified autonomous vehicle setting. Gatekeeper agents evaluate risks to collective safety online and intervene in vehicle policies when needed. Even at low penetration, gatekeepers produced significant safety gains for the fleet.
arxiv-2502-05049:
Federico Cinus, Corrado Monti, Paolo Bajardi, and Gianmarco De Francisci Morales built a method in twenty twenty-five to estimate who Reddit users are. Knowing a platform's mix of age, gender, and politics matters for reading online behavior, but guessing these traits from posts risks bias and error. Their data instead rest on what users say about themselves.

They gathered over eight hundred fifty thousand self-declarations of age, gender, and party leaning. Simple probabilistic models trained on sparse activity signals beat fancier embedding methods. Their approach raised accuracy over prior work by up to nineteen percent on a standard scale, with population estimates off by under fifteen percent. Outputs are calibrated and open to inspection, down to which signals matter in each subreddit. The authors argue for grounding such work in user-provided facts.
arxiv-2502-06849:
Muhammed Öz and co-authors present a 2025 paper on Neuron Transplantation, a way to merge several trained neural networks into one without paying the cost of running them all. Ensembles predict better than single models, but they eat memory and time at every use. The authors instead move the best parts into a single body.

They first prune weak neurons from one model, freeing space. Important neurons from every ensemble member are then transplanted into the gaps. A short fine-tuning heals the small drop that follows, and the fused model ends up beating each of its donors at the same size. It also needs less healing than a rival averaging method.
arxiv-2502-07149:
Sergej Monavari builds a new moduli space in enumerative geometry, modelled on Nekrasov's gauge origami for intersecting branes. Here the branes are replaced by two affine lines crossing each other, the broken lines of the title. Monavari realises the space concretely as a Quot scheme, parametrising zero-dimensional quotients of a torsion sheaf on the two lines, and again as a space of quiver representations.

On this space he constructs a virtual fundamental class and a virtual structure sheaf, the tools needed to define K-theoretic invariants. He then computes the associated partition function at every rank. Where the space is smooth, the answer reproduces a known generating series for a refined genus. Finally, he ties his partition function to the virtual invariants of plane Quot schemes and to Nekrasov's original function.
arxiv-2502-07249:
Divyansh Agrawal and Nisha Singhal study a math transform that sums a function over flat slices of space, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. They ask a sharp question about what can be inferred from partial data. If a function is zero in one region, and its sums vanish on all slices through that region, must it be zero everywhere?

For slices whose dimension is even, the answer is no, and they give a concrete counter-case. For odd dimension, a stronger claim holds. In that case, deep flatness at one point plus a zero region around it forces the function to vanish everywhere. The split by parity is the core result.
arxiv-2502-07849:
Krunoslav Lehman Pavasovic and colleagues gave a high-dimensional theory of classifier-free guidance in 2025. Guidance is the trick that steers diffusion image generators toward a requested class or prompt, and it clearly sharpens results. Theory had suggested guidance distorts the target distribution, pushing samples toward a narrower, shifted version, which raised doubts about what generators really sample from.

In very high dimensions, the authors prove, those distortions fade away and guidance reproduces the true target faithfully. That blessing of dimensionality covers a whole family of guidance rules, including nonlinear ones. A power-law variant they study proved more robust in tests, with better fidelity and diversity on class and text image tasks. Practice and theory reconcile at scale.
arxiv-2502-07949:
Qingyuan Wu and four co-authors present a learning method for AI agents that see and read in a 2025 paper. Such vision language agents can learn from online interaction without human labels, but they learn slowly on hard tasks with rare rewards and long action chains. The authors break each big goal into subgoals to guide learning.

Their framework restates the task as a subgoal conditioned problem with a new training objective. The objective rewards reaching subgoals while staying close to a reference goal directed policy. Theory and tests both support the design. On benchmarks covering phone and web control tasks, the method beat prior leading approaches in both learning speed and final performance.
arxiv-2502-08349:
Christian Kuehn and Pascal Sedlmeier proved stability results in twenty twenty-five for wave patterns in the Barkley model of pipe flow. The model captures how smooth laminar flow breaks into turbulent puffs, and it matches experiments well. Its traveling wave solutions include fronts and backs that can stack in trains of any length.

Building on an earlier existence proof based on a twisted loop between laminar and turbulent states, the authors verify a set of abstract stability conditions drawn from classic wave theory. For an intermediate range of Reynolds numbers, every train of fronts or backs with more than one wave is stable. The work completes a full existence-and-stability account that fits the abstract framework for waves born from such loops.
arxiv-2502-08449:
Robot hands need to know exactly where an object sits against the fingers, and a single camera's point cloud is too patchy and contact-blind for that. Yankai Fu and co-authors build their control policy on correspondences instead in a 2025 paper, tying the object's known pose to the hand's own joint senses. The linked cloud carries contact maps showing where touch happens.

Trained with those signals, the policy handled six real-world dexterity tasks better than rival methods by a wide margin. It also held up when objects, viewpoints, and scenes changed. The authors credit the explicit object-hand matching for the fine control.
arxiv-2502-08849:
Dipsy Desai, Kicho Yu, and Sulyab Thottungal Valapu gauge how far geofeeds have spread on the net. A geofeed is a file that states where net number blocks sit on Earth. The young norm lets hosts post such spots for their IPv4 and IPv6 blocks. The team checks use at the big lists and at host-group scale. They test how well live feeds hew to two norms: the base one, and the proof one.

The proof route in the live norm, they find, lacks key guards. Their swap plan makes feed proof plain, and tests score its speed. The state of play is mid-spread: more feeds go up, but truth and safety lag. Spot data feeds film and song rights, law checks, and fraud tools. Sound feeds thus count far past map work. The paper gives both the count and a fix for its weak link.
arxiv-2502-10749:
Zehua Liu, Han Wu, and Yuxuan Yao lead a team merging fine-tuned language models by estimating their task vectors at low rank, no base model required. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Merging blends specialist models into one without further training. Interference between specialists is the usual failure mode.

The team noticed task vectors concentrate their energy in a few dominant directions. A low-rank estimate therefore keeps the signal and drops much of the clash. They cast merging as an optimization problem built on that estimate. Wide experiments showed less interference and better preservation of each skill. The method advances merging benchmarks without touching training data. Not needing the base model widens where it can be applied. The authors frame low rank as the natural geometry of fine-tuning. That idea may guide merging theory generally.
arxiv-2502-13449:
Dongki Kim, Wonbin Lee, and Sung Ju Hwang present a 2025 paper on a language model built to understand molecules in depth. Knowing molecules is key to knowing living things and to finding new drugs. Past models could shift between tasks, but they often read molecular features poorly.

The new model, called Mol-LLaMA, is trained on data types that cover the core features of molecules. The data aim at the skills needed to reason about structure and behavior. A special module blends input from several molecule encoders, each strong in a different way. Tests reported by the authors show gains in grasp and in the model's power to explain its answers.
arxiv-2502-13849:
Hou, Tang, and Toh tackle in twenty twenty-five a class of hard optimisation problems used to relax mixed yes-no quadratic programs. These relaxed problems carry huge numbers of constraints and variables, which makes them slow to solve at scale. Their method bets that good solutions have low rank, a compact hidden structure, and builds that bet into an augmented Lagrangian scheme on curved spaces.

A key rewrite turns most awkward squared constraints into simpler straight ones after the low-rank split. They also show a hard projection step can be recast as an easy convex problem under mild conditions. Tests confirmed the speed gains. The method also fits general problems of the same family, serving as a prototype solver.
arxiv-2502-14049: Christine Breiner and Ben Dees study the bad points of energy minimizing maps into branching spaces, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The target spaces include complexes that model tree-like buildings. At bad points the map fails to be smooth, and those points group into layers by type. The authors sort those layers in a natural way and prove they can be measured in a well behaved way. Their result extends classic facts to a far rougher setting.
arxiv-2502-14449:
Robert Helling wrote this physics paper in 2025 on Bohmian mechanics, a view of quantum theory in which particles follow real paths steered by a wave. The view is said to match all tests of standard quantum theory. Helling tests that claim with a setup built on the GHZ state, a linked state of three parts. Here the qubits are read as positions in space.

He finds a clash: for links between positions at unlike times, the path view gives answers that standard theory does not. The clash turns on the fact that such positions cannot be jointly fixed. To erase the gap, the path view would need an added account of how the wave collapses when watched. The paper thus marks a spot where the two views split, at least in their plain forms.
arxiv-2502-17649:
Yuhao Wang and co-authors show, in a 2025 optics paper, how two protected light states living at separate interfaces can merge and reshape the light they shed. Such interface states are prized for their toughness, and here they sit in a gain medium that feeds them energy. Bringing the interfaces closer couples the states into a bonded pair and an anti-bonded pair.

The bonded mode glows dimly and evenly in all directions, while its partner glows brightly in a tight beam. Changing the gap between the interfaces tunes the energy split, the quality factor, and the beam shape all at once. The authors pitch the pair as a design platform for beam shaping, nonlinear optics, and quantum devices.
arxiv-2502-18349:
Meredith Shea studies a tiling model from statistical mechanics in this two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. The Aztec diamond dimer model places domino-like pairs on a lattice region, with weights that vary periodically. Recent work clarified its statistics under general periodic weights. Shea defines a variant that breaks periodicity in one direction by stitching together two different two-periodic weightings, and computes its correlation kernel.

The computation extends methods of Berggren and Duits, using the Eynard-Mehta theorem and a Wiener-Hopf factorization. From a form of the kernel suited to asymptotic analysis, she derives local behavior in the model's different macroscopic regions. The leading-order local statistics agree with the ordinary two-periodic model, as expected. The sub-leading terms, however, are changed by the seam between the two weightings, which is the paper's main finding.
arxiv-2502-18949:
Moritz Winterott and Samir Lounis propose a new way to read swirling magnetic patterns inside materials, in a 2025 paper. These three-dimensional spin textures could store data in future devices, but spotting them is hard. Tools that sense the stray magnetic field fail for a class of magnets whose field cancels out. The authors use scattering theory to show the textures carry a hidden electric charge pattern instead.

That charge arises when neighboring magnetic moments point in mixed directions and electrons scatter among them. It leaves marks in phase images made by electron holography, a microscope method. The team computed how much each known and new effect adds to those images under varied settings. Their results open a path to finding textures that older methods miss.
arxiv-2502-19249:
Michael Hu and co-authors study how training on formal languages shapes language models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Formal languages are rule-built toy languages, simpler than natural speech. Earlier work showed that a first phase on such languages can help models learn real language later.

The team asks which features of the toy language carry the benefit. They argue two conditions matter: the toy language should mirror the dependency structures of natural language, and it should stay within the model's computing limits. Experiments support the first condition strongly and the second modestly. Strikingly, the pre-phase cut the needed natural language data by about a third. Attention patterns learned early stayed important later.
arxiv-2502-20049:
Suffa and co-authors push fluid simulation to huge scales in this 2025 computing paper. Their method lets solid objects move through a simulated fluid on a regular grid, with cells partly filled by solid where the two meet. The hard parts are mapping complex shapes onto the grid cheaply and keeping the physics right.

Their mapping is both accurate and efficient, and the solver code is generated automatically for both normal and graphics processors, reaching most of each chip's peak speed. The coupling adds only modest cost. A spinning rotor test used up to 4.3 billion grid cells and scaled well across tens of thousands of processor cores on two supercomputers.
arxiv-2502-20349:
Wilka Carvalho and Andrew Lampinen argue that cognitive science should study people in richer, more natural settings, in this 2025 paper. Lab tasks are tidy, but real behavior is messy and wide-ranging. Theories built only on tidy tasks may fail to explain how minds work in daily life.

The authors review work from brain science, mind science, and artificial intelligence. Natural tasks often stir different behavior and brain processes than stripped-down ones. Models trained on natural data also learn in new ways. The pair urge the field to join these strands, using modern AI tools to build theories that hold up across the full range of human behavior.
arxiv-2502-21049:
Jingru Fu and co-authors present a framework that simulates how an individual brain will age, in work from 2025. Predicting a person's future brain scans is hard because ageing and disease follow shared patterns yet each brain differs. Generative models can make realistic average templates, but they miss personal variation over time.

Their framework learns population ageing paths with a generative network, then adapts those paths to one person using a parallel transport method from geometry. Because the simulation warps the original scan smoothly, the anatomy stays consistent by design. Tests used scans from a public dataset covering Alzheimer's disease and healthy ageing. Starting from a single baseline scan, the system produced realistic three-dimensional scan sequences. It could also model the shift from normal ageing into disease.
arxiv-2503-00049:
Judging the mood of a video takes more than reading faces; a slumped posture, a bleak backdrop, or a tense action can carry the feeling. Jiamin Luo and co-authors set a new task in a 2025 paper that asks systems to find a video's sentiment, locate where it sits, and say what drives it. Their setup uses both the plain scene cues and the hidden ones.

Their model mixes specialist parts that take turns by scene type, with a causal block that lifts the hidden cues above the plain ones. On new test sets built for plain and hidden cues, the model beat leading video language systems by wide margins. The authors argue that mood in video is a whole-scene property, and systems that read only faces will keep missing it.
arxiv-2503-02249:
Changhe Chen and colleagues ask whether large language models can learn how to design soft robots, in a paper released in twenty twenty-five. Designing such robots mixes materials, mechanics, and control, and often depends on trial and error. The authors built a test set using a simulator that creates soft robot challenges.
