The tasks cover moving across the ground, handling objects, and balancing. Models must link a plain task description to choices about body shape and materials.

Tested models showed they could pick up useful design patterns, but they often missed small differences between designs that perform quite differently. The authors also show that model choices can serve as a starting point for a real design search. They offer the test set to help other researchers compare models on equal terms.
arxiv-2503-02949:
Elena Cáceres, Brian Kent, and Harita Balaji unify two analogy programs between gravity and electromagnetism in a 2025 paper. Both programs turn certain spacetime shapes into electromagnetic potentials. One, gravito-electromagnetism, compares tidal forces across the theories. The other, the double copy, builds gravity solutions from electromagnetic ones in reverse. The authors show the resulting potentials usually match the spacetime's own symmetry vectors.

Those vectors, called Killing vectors, were long known to behave like electromagnetic potentials. Using them, the team links two forms of the double copy without leaning on special coordinates. They spell out the hidden assumptions in one form and the role symmetry vectors play. A key claim: matching tidal tensors across theories needs the same source rules as the double copy. Special spacetimes with an extra symmetry tensor make the correspondence vivid. The paper gathers these threads into one perspective.
arxiv-2503-03149:
YiQiu Guo and seven co-authors present DSVD, a 2025 decoding method that helps large language models catch their own errors while writing. Models often state false facts with confidence, and checking only after the full answer costs time. DSVD checks the text as it forms. One part grades the draft continuously, in parallel with writing. Another part rolls back to the error point and rewrites just that stretch when a problem appears.

Across five benchmarks, the method raised truthfulness in question answering and factual accuracy in scored summaries. It also stacked well with older faithful-decoding methods, lifting them further. The authors argue that live self-checking is a practical route to more trustworthy models, since it needs no separate verifier model and fits real deployment.
arxiv-2503-03649:
Andrei Ermolaev and seven colleagues simulate a learning machine made of light traveling through optical fiber, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In an extreme learning machine, only the final readout is trained, while the middle layer scrambles inputs in rich, fixed ways.

Here the scrambling comes from the fiber itself, as pulses spread and mix under nonlinear and dispersive effects. The team models the process with a generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation. They test it on the standard handwritten digit task and vary how the data is encoded, read out, and noised. Accuracy topped ninety-one percent in one dispersion regime and ninety-three percent in the other. A key finding is a built-in penalty: quantum noise on the input pulses caps how well the machine can do. The study maps where such photonic learners can shine and where physics holds them back.
arxiv-2503-04349:
Steinacker and co-authors compare in 2025 two ways to design bike networks that hold up well as conditions change. Good bike networks lift cycling, but growth over long horizons is hard to plan. Network effects and shifts in travel choice make the task complex.

One path uses direct welfare optimization, the other a simple network heuristic. Both were tried on plans for cycle superhighways in Copenhagen. The complex models gave better welfare, but only by small margins. They also proved more fragile when inputs were off. The result is a warning that fancy long term plans can rest on shaky ground, despite high benefit to cost ratios.
arxiv-2503-05949:
Maggio and Carlone introduced a mapping method in twenty twenty-five that lets robots build three-dimensional maps labeled by meaning, ready for whatever task is at hand. A robot may need the scene split into chairs and tables for one job, or into safe and unsafe zones for another.

Their system, Bayesian Fields, builds the scene from soft three-dimensional blobs. Instead of fixing object boundaries in advance, it clusters the blobs according to the current task. When several camera views label the same spot, it merges the labels with a proper probability update rather than a plain average. That respects how the underlying vision-language model actually behaves. The result is a detailed map that uses little memory and yields clean object shapes on demand. The code is open source. The authors argue task-shaped maps beat one-size maps for real robots.
arxiv-2503-07449:
Donát Takács and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on the piston effect in fluids near their critical point. There, a fluid is both gas and liquid at once in a sense. A sudden heat jolt sends a pressure pulse through it, a thermoacoustic quirk. Models of the effect need codes that are fast and free of fake waves.

Their code splits the field into parts that reverse and parts that do not. That split parts the sums into a wave form and a heat form, each with its own time step plan. The grid is staggered in space and time and runs in full explicit steps. They then run the piston case on the new code.
arxiv-2503-08649: Marta Calanchi and Massimo Grossi study a degenerate Poisson problem in a 2025 mathematics paper. The equation models diffusion where the conductivity fades near the boundary of a smooth bounded domain, at a rate set by distance to the edge and an exponent below one. They describe how the solution behaves near the boundary and discuss its regularity properties, that is, how smooth the solution can be expected to be under a continuous source term.
arxiv-2503-09549:
Fabio Cassini and Chiara Segala present a 2025 study of the turnpike effect in control problems where many agents interact and noise shakes the system. The turnpike effect says that the best long-run plan spends most of its time near one steady state, like a highway between two cities. Earlier proofs covered calm, deterministic systems. The authors show the effect survives in discrete time with random noise, under the right conditions on stability and control.

Stiff systems, whose parts move at very different speeds, are handled with exponential integrators, a time-stepping method that copes with stiffness. Computer tests confirmed the theory. The exponential method beat standard explicit schemes, and the turnpike control stayed effective under noise. The work extends a planning shortcut to realistic, uncertain swarms.
arxiv-2503-09749:
Yuan and Bowyer built a new test in twenty twenty-five that tells if two eye photos come from the same kind of twin. The iris is the colored ring in the eye, and its marks are used to check who a person is. Folks once thought left and right iris marks were as unlike as those of strangers.

Their twin-net tool learns from pairs of photos and sorts them as twin-type or not. It trains on real twin pairs, same-person pairs, and pairs of strangers. Both the iris marks and the skin and lids near the eye help the tool decide. Its scores beat the scores past work found for human judges.
arxiv-2503-10549:
Youngjin Kwon and Xiao Zhang build MASQUE in this 2025 paper, a text-guided makeup generator that shields faces from recognition systems. Face recognition now sits inside government and business services, and misuse worries are growing. Makeup-based defenses are popular, but older ones mostly impersonate a chosen identity, which dodges poorly and invites abuse. They also smear artifacts across the whole face.

MASQUE uses a diffusion model steered by the user's own text prompt, so the makeup stays local and personal. It needs no outside identity: a pairwise trick compares two shots of the same person to guide the attack. Tests on open models and commercial services showed stronger dodging than all baselines. Image quality and prompt flexibility also improved, and the effect survived image transforms.
arxiv-2503-10849:
Thévenet and five co-authors showed that water turns into a superacid deep inside planets in twenty twenty-five. At crushing pressure and heat, the chemistry of water shapes the insides of planets and the deep carbon cycle. Tests had found hydrocarbons in hot, ionized water turning into heavy hydrocarbons and nanodiamonds. No clear path explained the change.

The team ran quantum simulations of molecules, with boosted sampling and machine-learned force laws. They watched hot, squeezed water ionize into a bath like a superacid. That bath adds protons to hydrocarbons, making short-lived five-way carbonium ions. These forms shed hydrogen and yield reactive carbocations. The carbocations grow chains that end as nanodiamonds. Pressure also shifts charge in methane, feeding the same web. The authors claim the first proof of a superacid water regime. It ties the odd changes seen in tests into one story.
arxiv-2503-11149:
Michael Brannan, Daniel Gromada, Junichiro Matsuda, Adam Skalski, and Mateusz Wasilewski prove a quantum version of a classic graph theorem in a paper from 2025. Frucht's theorem says every finite group is the symmetry group of some graph. The quantum version replaces groups and graphs with their quantum counterparts. The authors first build several quantum Cayley graphs for a given quantum group.

They then give a systematic way to merge those graphs into one with exactly the right symmetries. They also show the dual of any non-abelian finite group is quantum rigid, meaning a Cayley graph exists whose symmetries are exactly that dual. The result anchors quantum symmetry theory.
arxiv-2503-12549:
Alexander Koebler, Ralf Gross, Florian Buettner, and Ingo Thon help robots grasp hidden objects in two thousand twenty-five. Flexible factories need robots to grip items in random poses. Parts often hide each other or sit behind structures. Missing depth data then breaks grasp point math.

Their autoencoder based inpainting rebuilds the missing point cloud parts. Robust object matching can then compute grip points as usual. The method plugs into a live industrial grasping system. Far fewer objects get discarded by the process now. Real world occlusion, not just lab cases, is the target.
arxiv-2503-12649:
Hao Chen and four co-authors scale up the merging of trained models in a 2025 paper. Merging several fine-tuned models into one multi-skill model avoids costly joint training. Older merging recipes assume tidy in-house models and break down as the pool of candidates grows.

Their method recasts merging as a constrained optimization problem. A classic Frank-Wolfe routine repeatedly picks the single most useful model from the pool. Each pick triggers a small local merge that improves the combined objective. The objective encodes the behavior the final model should show. Candidate models themselves mark out the space of allowed solutions. The design suits the messy open ecosystem, where models arrive with partial documentation and varied origins.
arxiv-2503-12849: Ankur Pandey, Nijjwal Karak, and Debarati Mondal connect two ways of calling a set negligibly small in function spaces whose growth rule varies from point to point. One is Sobolev capacity, defined through the energy of functions covering the set. The other is a generalized Hausdorff measure built from a gauge function. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they prove that sets of zero capacity also have zero generalized Hausdorff measure, for suitable gauges, in both variable-exponent Sobolev spaces and a class of Musielak-Orlicz-Sobolev spaces.
arxiv-2503-13049:
Stikuts and co-authors wrote this 2025 physics paper on making a dragged particle lock into fractional speeds. Shapiro steps are plateaus where a driven system holds its velocity steady while the driving force grows, long known for particles crossing wavy landscapes, but only at whole-number speeds. The team drive one colloidal particle across an optical landscape whose shape and rhythm they can sculpt.

In the non-sinusoidal, time-modulated landscape, fractional steps appear beside the integer ones. Tracking the single particle reveals the microscopic dance behind each kind of lock-in. Tuning the shape of the landscape and the driving protocol moves and widens the steps at will. The authors present the setup as a flexible bench for studying synchronization in soft matter, one particle at a time.
arxiv-2503-13249:
Ziming Li and co-authors report tests of a prototype veto tank for a neutrino observatory in a 2025 paper. The observatory, TAO, will sit about thirty meters from a reactor core in Taishan, China, and measure its antineutrinos with record sharpness. Around its central detector sits a water tank that must veto, or flag, stray particles that could fake a signal.

The tank holds a thick shell of pure water watched by hundreds of small light sensors, sharing electronics with its big sister experiment, JUNO. The prototype departs from the usual cyclic design, as its title states. The team checks how the water Cherenkov light system performs with those sensors and electronics, including a software trigger that decides what counts as an event. Long stability runs round out the test.
arxiv-2503-13349:
Otger Ballester and a large team of co-authors lay out, in a 2025 preprint, the technical design of a laser radar for watching the sky over a gamma-ray observatory. Cherenkov telescopes read gamma rays through air showers, so air quality bends their data. The pathfinder Barcelona Raman LIDAR will monitor the air above the northern site of the Cherenkov Telescope Array. It pairs a steerable 1.8-meter mirror with a pulsed laser firing ultraviolet and green light. Two elastic and Raman channels read how aerosols scatter and absorb that light.

The instrument is rebuilt on a retired telescope frame. Parts include a coaxial laser path, a near-range system, a liquid light guide, and a custom polychromator. A year of tests at the mountain site checked stability and semi-remote running. The design leads to the final observatory LIDAR. Real-time air data should keep the gamma-ray science accurate.
arxiv-2503-15149:
Zhaoxiang Shen and four co-authors train a machine learning stand-in for a costly physics calculation, in a 2025 paper. Many-body dispersion forces are the subtle attractions that hold liquids and soft matter together, and computing them exactly is slow. Polymer melts need those forces described well, which blocks large simulations. The team builds a surrogate model on a trimmed neural network that keeps only the most relevant atomic links.

The model was checked on melts of polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyvinyl chloride. It predicted the forces with high accuracy and held up on new structures. A fast surrogate lets researchers run melt simulations at sizes and lengths that the exact method cannot reach, which serves plastics design and recycling research.
arxiv-2503-17049:
Giulia Cavalleri and Alain Miranville study best control of a brain tumor growth model that joins lactate use, spring like tissue traits, and tissue harm. Control here means picking drug doses that steer the tumor best. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The model links a spread equation for tumor cell density with one for lactate, a force balance for tissue shift, and a rule for harm growth. Two controls stand for chemo and a lactate targeted drug. The authors set a cost score for care, prove that best controls exist, and show how the state shifts when controls shift. They end with a first order rule that any best care plan must meet.
arxiv-2503-17149:
Guchuan Li, Sarah Petersen, and Elizabeth Tatum lift a classic splitting result, in a 2025 preprint, into the equivariant world of stable homotopy theory. In the nineteen eighties, Mahowald and Kane broke a certain product of spectra into simpler pieces. That split powered much progress on the stable homotopy groups of spheres. The present paper works with the real form of connective K-theory, which carries an action of a two-element group. The authors build the matching split for the cooperations algebra at the level of spectra, not just algebra.

They describe the split pieces as equivariant Adams covers. A parallel split for ordinary cohomology with its equivariant upgrade is recorded too. Along the way they compute the full operations and cooperations algebras for both theories. Such computations are the raw fuel for spectral sequence work. Specialists gain a sharper tool for periodic phenomena in equivariant homotopy.
arxiv-2503-17549:
Andrzej Rostworowski goes back to a classic numerical relativity test: whether ripples in empty spacetime can focus and collapse into a black hole. The result from the early 1990s by Abrahams and Evans has led to decades of attempts to verify it. The threshold behavior is a trap for numeric work. The work reports first steps toward a check of his own.

Rostworowski sets up Einstein's equations for a vacuum, axisymmetric spacetime with vanishing twist in spherical-polar coordinates. A linear version of the system is derived alongside the full one. The author finds concrete blocks to stable evolution exactly at the collapse threshold, where the key physics lives. The work is openly a first step, aimed at a setup that can survive the critical regime.
arxiv-2503-18049:
Matthäus Schulik and co-authors model how moons of young giant planets can lose their air. Their 2025 paper deals with satellites heated above their normal temperature by light from the planet. Low gravity makes such moons prone to heavy loss of gas into space.

The team finds that some gases, such as ammonia and methane, can form layers that trap heat under planet light. Those hot profiles drive escape at rates well above simple model estimates. A moon can lose most of its air this way unless its interior cools fast. Escape rates also rank by gas type, since upper layers decouple by heat. The result helps explain why some moons may be bare while others keep thick air.
arxiv-2503-18449: Oscar Kivinen, Alexei Oblomkov, and Dimitri Wyss present a 2025 arXiv paper in algebraic geometry, on invariants of a plane curve singularity. Using motivic integration over symmetric powers of a deformed curve, they study two kinds of discriminant integrals. One recovers the motivic classes of the principal Hilbert schemes of points on the curve. The other gives the plethystic exponential of the motivic Igusa zeta function, a result that also holds in higher dimensions. Combined with work of Gorsky and Némethi, the integrals gain an interpretation through knot Floer homology.
arxiv-2503-18649:
Jin and Zhou build in 2025 a Ginzburg-Landau theory for triple Q magnetic orders on hexagonal lattices. The head title frames the work as a phenomenological theory of these states. Models with two and three spin components are covered through symmetry allowed terms in the free energy.

Full phase diagrams emerge from competing interaction parameters. Single, double, and triple Q states each carry their own symmetry breaking patterns and collective excitations. Real materials such as a sodium cobalt telluride show the same interplay of frustration and multiple ordering vectors. The frame links microscopic couplings to observable traits, a tool for predicting new phases in frustrated magnets.
arxiv-2503-19549:
Zubair Shaban, Nazreen Shah, and Ranjitha Prasad tackle, in a 2025 paper, the messy reality of training AI models across many phones and sensors at once. In federated learning, devices train locally and send updates to a server, keeping raw data private. Sending updates over the air, all at once, is fast. But real wireless channels add noise, signals fade, and devices differ in data and stamina, which can wreck convergence.

Their framework, RoCo-FL, builds the mess into the math. Local updates are treated as deliberately inexact, within structured limits that act like a stabilizer. The team proves the method still converges for the hard, non-convex objectives used in practice. On three image and handwriting datasets, it beat rival methods in accuracy and stability, especially when slow stragglers joined. The authors frame noise-proof design as a condition for real-world deployment.
arxiv-2503-20449:
Laura Gardini and co-authors analyze jagged one-dimensional maps whose pieces are straight lines sharing one fixed point. Their paper appeared in 2025. Such piecewise maps appear in economics, engineering, and ecology. The team shows their motion can be read through the well-known piecewise linear circle map. Away from the shared fixed point, bounded behavior narrows to two options: stiff cycles that are not hyperbolic, or quasiperiodic orbits that densely fill line segments, and both can coexist.

A financial market model illustrates the theory. Its price paths look chaotic at a glance, with irregular swings that suggest randomness. The analysis proves they are quasiperiodic instead, following a hidden regular order. The authors say the distinction matters before anyone labels market motion as chaos.
arxiv-2503-21249:
Yufei Bo and Meixia Tao design a joint code for sending matched images from two senders over wireless links, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Each sender holds one of a pair of linked images, such as two views of one scene. Each codes and sends its own image, and the receiver rebuilds both.

Older learned methods pick up the link between the images only by feel from data. The new design states the link in plain math through a shared chance model of the coded forms. That model sets how many symbols each sender may spend. At the receiver, each rebuilt image helps restore the other, and a shift block lines the codes up for best use of their link. One loss trains the whole chain, and tests show crisper rebuilds for the bits spent.
arxiv-2503-21749:
Shitian Zhao and a team of co-authors build a suite for text in images in twenty twenty-five. Image generators often garble the words they are asked to render. Prompt richness and rendering fidelity pull against each other. Their suite, LeX-Art, attacks the problem from the data side.

A synthesis pipeline built on Deepseek-R1 curates a data set of ten thousand images. Each is high-resolution, refined for aesthetics, and rich in rendered text. A prompt enrichment model, LeX-Enhancer, strengthens weak prompts. Two text-to-image models trained on the data reach state-of-the-art text rendering. A new benchmark, LeX-Bench, grades fidelity, aesthetics, and alignment. A new metric measures text accuracy more robustly than edit distance alone.
arxiv-2503-21849:
Zsofia Talyigas, Francesco Paparella, Bastien Mallein, and Emmanuel Schertzer ask whether evolution selects the fittest or merely the luckiest in a 2025 mathematical biology study. Selection judges phenotypes, the traits an organism shows, and chance events blur the link between a good genotype and reproductive success. The authors model that blur and its long-run consequences.

Their analysis shows a Goodhart-like effect emerging inside evolution itself: once a trait becomes the target of selection, luck in expressing it can swamp the underlying quality. The result reframes how biologists should read adaptation, since winners may owe their place partly to fortune.
arxiv-2503-22549:
Anja Beck, Michele Atzeni, and Eluned Smith extract decay amplitudes from B meson data without a fixed model. Such decays, nicknamed electroweak penguins, can hint at new physics. Amplitudes vary with the masses of the decay products in a smooth way. Past fits forced those shapes into set forms, which can bias the hunt.

Their trick rewrites the angular decay rate so a sPlot method can run on the angles. Weight functions then pull out each wave's size as a smooth curve. Fake data with both S and P waves check the method's power. The curves come out unbiased and can face theory head-on. Hadron shape factors, above all in the S wave, stand to gain.
arxiv-2503-22749:
Kanishka Ranaweera and co-authors add adaptive clipping to private few-shot learning to protect its accuracy. Their 2025 paper works where two scarcities meet: few labeled examples, and a formal privacy guarantee that usually costs model quality. Clipping, which caps how much any one example can sway training, is where much of that cost is decided.

Their method adjusts the clipping threshold as training proceeds instead of fixing it once. It fits several private meta-learning algorithms that learn how to learn from small data. Dynamic control limits how much sensitive information leaks while curbing overfitting on tiny sets. Tests show better generalization under the same privacy promise. Privacy tools that forget less could serve medicine and other fields where data are both scarce and sensitive.
arxiv-2503-23549:
Van Higgs and Doug Pickrell wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on a round version of a classic quantum system. The classic system is the harmonic oscillator, a particle held by a spring-like pull. In flat space it splits into separate one-way motions and can be solved with standard raising and lowering tools.

The spherical version does not split that way, which makes it harder. The two-dimensional case turns out to be the critical one. For it, the authors compute the full set of energy levels and a key counting function called the partition function. They note the system may matter for chiral models in two-dimensional field theory.
arxiv-2503-24349:
Shafin, Rabbi, Hasan, and Zibran studied release speed and security in the Maven software ecosystem in twenty twenty-five. Modern apps rest on chains of libraries, and how often each library releases shapes both freshness and risk. The team traced ten thousand Maven artifacts across more than two hundred thousand releases and one point seven million dependencies.

Faster-releasing artifacts spent far less time outdated. They also carried fewer known vulnerabilities, the CVEs tracked in security databases, in their dependency chains. The link was a strong negative correlation in both cases. The authors argue that quicker release cycles are a practical security strategy, not just a convenience. Their findings speak to developers, maintainers, and the people who run shared software ecosystems.
arxiv-2504-00249:
Five researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on neural networks that solve physics problems and can adapt to new conditions. Standard physics-informed networks learn one solution for one set of boundary conditions, so a change at the edge forces retraining. The authors want a network that, once trained, answers for any boundary setup.

Their network learns the shape of a wave decomposition rather than one fixed solution. Training uses a spread of randomly chosen boundary conditions. On a test system of two linked oscillators, the trained network predicted solutions for new conditions correctly. The trick cuts the ratio between training effort and later use.
arxiv-2504-00849:
Sunjung Kang, Vishrant Tripathi, and Christopher Brinton study remote tracking systems in a 2025 paper. Such systems must keep a live view fresh while also rebuilding past paths accurately later. Freshness alone, measured by the age of information, misses that second goal. With a finite buffer, a system must choose which packets to keep or drop.

They compare three policies: keep old, keep fresh, and their own policy that drops packets based on gaps between arrivals. Keeping the freshest data minimizes age but not rebuilding error. Their policy adjusts retention using generation times and balances both goals. Analysis and simulation of queue behavior back the comparison.
arxiv-2504-00949:
Bernat Capdevila and four colleagues present a model-independent way to analyze a rare B meson decay without binning the data. The four-body decay's dynamics depend on two invariant masses, and standard analyses either bin in those masses or assume a model for the amplitudes. Their moments-based method extracts continuous observables unbinned in both variables.

The approach needs no statistical fit, avoiding bias and poor uncertainty estimates with small samples. The team gives Standard Model predictions for the unbinned observables and derives new geometrical bounds on their values. They study zero-crossing points of key observables as new physics contributions vary. The method can also test the amplitude models that experimental analyses rely on.
arxiv-2504-01649:
Nuno Crokidakis models a siege with differential equations in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The Siege of Syracuse, from two hundred fourteen to two hundred twelve BC, ended with Rome taking the city despite strong defenses and Archimedes' war machines. The model tracks how fast Syracuse's stores drained, how its people fell, and how long the Roman army held out. Strategy and supply enter as settings that steer how these amounts change.

The study finds a sharp line for how strong Syracuse's defenses had to be. Above it, the city holds off the attack in the model; below it, collapse comes. Since history records the fall, the author holds that the defense strength sat below that line. Tests vary siege length, supply limits, and defense strength to show which points mattered. It shows math modeling can shape claims about old battles, not just retell them.
arxiv-2504-01849:
Rohin Shah and a large team of co-authors set out a technical plan for keeping future general-purpose AI safe and secure. Their paper appeared in 2025. They sort the risks into misuse, misalignment, mistakes, and structural harms, then focus on the first two, where engineering can bite. For misuse, the plan is to spot dangerous capabilities early and wall them off with security, access limits, monitoring, and built-in safeguards.

For misalignment, they propose two lines of defense. The first builds an aligned model through stronger oversight and robust training. The second assumes failure and contains harm through system-level monitoring and access control. Interpretability and uncertainty tools feed both. The authors frame the approach as defense in depth for systems whose power is still growing.
arxiv-2504-01949:
Tristan Fauvel and four co-authors compare Bayesian methods for borrowing treatment effects across trials, in a simulation study from 2025. When a new trial cannot recruit enough patients, borrowing results from related studies can help. Borrowing whole treatment effects, not just control data, is less understood, so the team simulated six trial settings with varied endpoints.

They varied trial size and how far the borrowed effect drifted from the truth. At matched error rates, power gains over a plain analysis were usually small, and some adaptive methods lost more. Borrowing cut estimation error when effects agreed but hurt coverage as drift grew. Matched prior designs balanced gains and robustness best.
arxiv-2504-02649:
Mahmoud Khabou, Edward Cohen, and Almut Veraart wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a model for counts that repeat in time with a seasonal beat, where past counts can sway the present across a web of linked series.

The model is a Poisson autoregression with many series, a seasonal cycle, and memory that may stretch far back. The authors prove the process settles into a steady seasonal state, and bound how fast it gets there. They then give a fast Markov stand-in and prove its fitted values hold up as data grows. A test on weekly rotavirus case counts in Berlin beats the prior PNAR model at forecasting.
arxiv-2504-02749:
Sohaib Alam, Jun Zen, and Thomas Scruby find a fault-tolerant measurement schedule for the Bacon-Shor quantum error-correcting code through a coloring game, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The schedule has period four and covers spacetime with constant-weight detectors.

Earlier approaches leaned on code concatenation to reach a noise threshold. Here the schedule emerges as the solution to a coloring game played on a square grid. Under a uniform circuit-level noise model, simulations show a threshold near zero point three percent when decoding with minimum weight perfect matching. The authors conjecture a decoder tailored to the scheme could push the threshold higher, making the code more practical.
arxiv-2504-03449:
Michele Botti and Lorenzo Mascotto prove a family of inequalities for functions that jump between mesh cells in a 2025 paper. Modern simulation methods chop a domain into many-sided cells and let the solution behave separately in each. Analysis of such methods needs Sobolev-Poincare inequalities: bounds that tie a function's size to its slope, cell by cell, over very general meshes.

Their result covers shape-regular meshes of polygons and polyhedra in any dimension, including plain triangles and grids as special cases. The constants in the bounds depend openly on the geometry, so users can see the price of a bad mesh. Key tools are new trace inequalities and stable ways to undo the divergence operator under mixed boundary conditions. The estimates serve error analysis for nonconforming methods on nonlinear problems.
arxiv-2504-03549:
Kumar and Rajesh analyse in twenty twenty-five the splash thrown off when energy hits the edge of a one-dimensional uneven gas. The gas thins out with distance by a power rule, and the blast sits at its border with empty space. Energy input flings fast spatters into the vacuum, and the gas left behind loses energy by a power law over time.

The pair solved the flow equations exactly with a self-similar method, finding the decay exponent for each thinning rate. Computer simulations of colliding particles matched the exact answers. Knowing the exponents also fixed how density, speed, and temperature evolve in space and time. The work gives a clean benchmark for blast physics in graded media.
arxiv-2504-03849:
Valerii Chuiko, Giovanni Da Rosa, and Paul Ayers predict molecule energies with deep learning, in two thousand twenty-five. Their input is not the molecule's shape, but its one- and two-electron integrals, a compact record of its electronic structure. The descriptor they build stays unchanged when the molecule moves, turns, or is reframed.

An attention-based network learns from that descriptor and keeps a key property: energy scales cleanly with system size. Training on small, few-electron systems can thus guide calls on larger ones. They test the method on hydrogen clusters, a hard case where electrons are strongly linked. Results beat geometry-based learning models on accuracy, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-04149:
Wei and six colleagues build a light amplifier on a chip with a mirror designed by computer search in twenty twenty-five. The amplifier is a channel in lithium niobate glass, spiked with the metal erbium. Such amplifiers boost weak light signals in fiber networks. At the channel's end they placed a tiny mirror shaped by an inverse design search.

The mirror bounced light back through the channel for a second pass of gain. Net gain rose by a large margin over a twin device with no mirror. The design also removed the need to pump light in from both ends. The team says the trick can pack stronger amplifiers into dense photonic chips.
arxiv-2504-04649:
Jingtao Lin and Jingtao Shi prove a maximum principle for a hard control problem in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A decision maker steers a system tracked only through noisy observations, while caring about risk. Random jumps, tangled forward-backward dynamics, and non-round control sets make the problem thorny.

The team first recasts it as a full-information problem with a special generator. New variation techniques handle the way costs blow up with risk. The result is a global principle that any optimal control must obey. They apply it to risk-sensitive investing under a factor model. A filtering chapter derives a corrected equation for tracking the hidden state amid jumps and linked noise.
arxiv-2504-05349:
Eugen Barbulescu, Antonio Alexoaie, and Lucian Busoniu present a 2025 computing paper on pruning neural networks. Pruning cuts weights to make a network faster and lighter at run time. Most methods chase scores on benchmarks and leave the pruning process itself poorly understood.

Their method, Hyperflux, treats pruning as a system that evolves in a continuous way. Two forces drive it: flux, the response of the loss gradient when a weight is removed, and pressure, a global push toward cutting weights. That model makes behavior readable at both the single-weight and whole-network levels. A new pressure schedule targets a chosen sparsity with care. Tests on standard image sets with several known networks gave competitive results.
arxiv-2504-06349:
Lorenzo Bertassi and co-authors propose a new test for pairs of giant black holes in a 2025 paper. Two such black holes bound close together should make their shared gas glow in shifting ways. Orbital motion boosts the light aimed at us, like a lighthouse beam sweeping past. The surrounding gas then re-emits that light in broad spectral lines.

The team model how a disc of this gas answers the sweeping beam. The blue and red sides of the lines answer half an orbit out of step with each other. A single black hole with pulsing brightness cannot mimic that pattern. The lag split offers a fresh signature for hunting true black hole pairs in survey data.
arxiv-2504-06949:
Zhixuan Lin and co-authors prune wasted work inside a transformer that forgets, in a 2025 paper. The model type adds a forget gate to attention, and many heads forget so fast that they lean on nearby words only. Far links then cost computing time for near zero gain.

Their method drops those decayed links on the fly, with a threshold that proves the dropped weights are trivial. In training runs, attention cost fell by about seventy percent across model sizes. End to end training sped up as well, more so for long texts. Scores did not drop. Code is shared in public for teams that train such models.
arxiv-2504-07849:
Francesca Dilisante, Pablo Valganon, David Soriano-Panos, and Jesus Gomez-Gardenes present 2025 work on infections picked up while people travel between places. Models of linked local groups tend to count spread that takes place inside each place alone. Spread during the trip itself, on shared transport, is left out of most such models.

The team extends a known movement model so that agents can catch the disease in transit as they move and return. Adding that route lowers the bar for an outbreak to take off by a marked amount. It also spreads the path of the outbreak across places, most of all in the early stage. Local control that looks sound on paper may thus fall short in fact.
arxiv-2504-08149:
Danielle Sullivan-Pao, Nicole Tian, and Pooya Khorrami present LoRAX, a system that learns to name which AI generator made an image, and keeps learning as new generators appear. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Attribution guards media trust by tracing synthetic pictures to their source model. Old models fade as new generators launch, and retraining from scratch is impractical.

LoRAX adds a tiny, cheap feature extractor for each new task. Each extractor is trained with a low-rank adapter, using a sliver of the base model's parameters. The extractors stack without erasing old skills. On a continual deepfake detection bench, LoRAX matched or beat top rivals in every setting. It did so with a fraction of the trainable parameters of full methods. The code is shared in public.
arxiv-2504-08449:
Jian Wang, Rishabh Dabral, Diogo Luvizon, and co-authors present a framework for tracking human motion from wearable devices in this 2025 paper. Headsets, smart glasses, phones, and watches each give different signals, and those signals come and go. The goal is one system that captures and describes body motion from any mix of them.

Their method, called Ego4o, turns sensor readings, camera views from the wearer's side, and optional written motion notes into a shared code. A decoder then rebuilds the motion from that code. When no written notes exist, a large multi-modal model can draft them, and those drafts in turn sharpen the tracking. Tests showed the system holds up when inputs drop out and improves when more signals combine. The authors see it serving virtual and augmented reality, where body tracking must work on consumer gear.
arxiv-2504-08649:
Charamaras and co-authors find vast sum sets in dense parts of swap groups. A swap group here is a count-able set where sums swap free. Two group traits frame the work: a thin twin set and a thin twin map. The team sets low bounds on how dense a part must be. Past that bound, the part holds a sum set of a set form. The form sums two picks from one vast set B in the group.

A shift t may lead the sum set in one of the two forms. Both group traits prove a must for the claims to hold. The team also marks which spread chains let the claim run. Their low bounds prove best in a strong sense in the work. No less dense part can dodge the sum set by their proof.
arxiv-2504-08849:
Mallika Mainali and Rosina Weber explore cognitive attributes in financial choices in two thousand twenty-five. Such traits shape how people take in facts, weigh options, and decide. AI that aims to think like humans must count these traits. Past alignment work stressed values and skipped the traits that set people apart.

The pair first survey the literature on these traits. They then set five rules for what counts as such a trait. Last they sort a set of traits tied to finance choices. The three parts form a base for AI that mirrors human choice. Finance is a high stakes test ground for that aim.
arxiv-2504-09049:
Adrianna Romanowski, Pedro Valois, and Kazuhiro Fukui test whether language models can spot the funny lines in stand-up comedy. They propose a humor detection metric with three scoring options: fuzzy string matching, sentence embedding similarity, and subspace similarity. Models received transcripts under various prompts and had to extract the humorous quotes.

Leading models, including ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek, scored at most fifty-one percent regardless of prompt engineering. Human evaluators scored forty-one percent on the same task, so the models actually won. Agreement varied widely for both groups. The authors read the result as evidence of humor's subjectivity and the difficulty of mining punchlines from live performance transcripts.
arxiv-2504-09649:
Bruno Souza and co-authors add galaxy mergers to a universe model with a fractal spread of galaxies, in a 2025 paper. The base model is an uneven cosmos that starts with a shared big bang. Its galaxies sit in two stacked fractal patterns with set dimensions.

The authors let merger gain follow a decaying power law with distance in time. They solve the model for small merger rates and test which settings stay sound. Patterns drawn from recent surveys fit for a range of merger strengths and starting scales. The results show mergers can join such a cosmos without breaking it. The work speaks to critics of the standard smooth model.
arxiv-2504-11049:
Giovannetti, Lloyd, and Maccone present a quantum algorithm that estimates the determinant of a matrix. The method rests on quantum spectral sampling, which reads off information from a matrix's eigenvalues. It estimates the logarithm of the determinant for positive sparse matrices.

The running time grows only with the logarithm of the matrix size, far faster than earlier methods that grew in direct proportion to it. The same approach estimates any sum built from a function of the eigenvalues. Examples include the partition function of a physical system and the entropy of a density matrix. The authors frame the result as a broad speedup for eigenvalue-based quantities.
arxiv-2504-11149:
Alejandro Luque-Cerpa, David Orellana-Martín, and Miguel Á Gutiérrez-Naranjo apply a formal computing model to disaster relief. Their 2025 paper starts from a real problem: after quakes, storms, or refugee crises, aid groups compete for funds while help is duplicated in some places and missing in others.

The authors frame relief as a shared equilibrium problem where each group's best plan depends on what others do. They then show that membrane computing, a model based on cell-like compartments, can capture that problem. A family of such systems computes the balance points for relief work. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 serves as the test case. The paper speaks to both computing theory and planners who want aid efforts that fit together.
arxiv-2504-11249:
Luke Evans and co-authors show that cryo-electron microscopy images hide a simple inner structure in a 2025 paper. Cryo-EM photographs frozen molecules from many angles, and neural methods now infer molecular shapes from learned internal representations. What those representations look like geometrically was unclear.

The team applied manifold learning to representations of the hemagglutinin protein, from both simulated and real data. The high-dimensional codes turned out to lie on smooth, low-dimensional surfaces. Simulated data covered the real data's surface well. Reading the surface's main directions linked them to physical parameters of the molecule. A simple hidden geometry strengthens trust in these inference tools and may guide better ones.
arxiv-2504-11349:
Yang and co-authors review in 2025 how AI methods rebuild 3D medical images from radiology scans. Clear 3D images aid diagnosis, but scans cost time and expose patients to radiation. AI promises sharper rebuilds with less scan time and lower dose.

The review sorts methods into four families by how they encode the target image. Those are grid forms, basis expansions, basic shape units, and neural implicit forms. Links among the families are drawn, with radiance field methods set as a subtype of the last group. Shared test sets and scoring metrics are summed up. The authors close with open problems and likely next steps for the field.
arxiv-2504-11649:
Alan Panuco Linan, Daniela Perez, Carlos Luna, and Gustavo Romero test gauges of the pull force's own heat count. The work came out in 2025. They check if the gauges heed the second law when a black hole shifts form. The thought that heat count ties to pull itself has some weight. Still, each gauge must match the known Hawking-Bekenstein count at a hole's rim.

The test case is a shift of form. A plain Schwarzschild hole eats a charged test speck. It then turns into a charged Reissner-Nordstrom hole. The team also runs the shift in reverse. They check two gauges of the count. One is built from the Weyl form. One is built from the Bel-Robinson form. Both pass the second law test. The fine points hinge on if the shift can be run back or not.
arxiv-2504-11949:
Jie Wang, Chen Ye Gan, Caoqi Wei, Jiangtao Wen, and Yuxing Han wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It matches features across videos by motion alone, a tack the authors call Flow Intelligence.

Classic matchers read how a scene looks, and break on noise, shift, or a change of sensor kind. This method pulls motion marks from pixel blocks across frames and pairs those marks between clips. Motion is by nature free of shift, turn, and scale woes, and it needs no training data at all. Tests show it beats look-based rivals in the hard cases where they fail. Uses run from robots to scans.
arxiv-2504-12149:
Zi-Zhao Zhang, Rong Li, and Bo-Chao Liu study charmonium like mesons in a 2025 physics paper. These heavy particles contain a charm quark and antiquark, and some states do not fit the conventional picture. A diabatic approach can describe ordinary and exotic states in one framework.

Using a more realistic potential with spin dependent forces, they compute the spectrum below a set energy. Masses align well with experimental data. They also give the probability that each state is a simple quark pair versus a meson pair. Several famous states show significant molecular components, and two states are matched to expected conventional levels.
arxiv-2504-12749:
Weijia Li, Guanglei Chu, Jiong Chen, and three co-authors set a check in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Logical anomalies are not scratches or dents. They are wrong links: too many objects, wrong counts, or set-ups that can not be. Past detectors bolt on reasoning modules. That hurts their use and clarity. The team sets out Reasoning Logical Anomaly Detection as a task. Systems must find flaws and explain them. They put forth LAD-Reasoner.

The reasoner is a multimodal model on a three-billion-parameter vision-language backbone. It is trained in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning builds grasp. Group relative policy optimization sharpens detection and reasoning. Rewards back how exact the output is and its shape. No hand-written data is used. On the MVTec LOCO data set, it matched a seventy-two-billion-parameter sibling on accuracy and F1, with shorter reasons.
arxiv-2504-13049:
Wenmin Zhao, Ana Solaguren-Beascoa, and colleagues join two kinds of foundation models for single-cell biology in a 2025 study. One model family reads DNA sequence, while another reads single-cell measurements. Each alone misses what the other sees, and gene regulation depends on both sequence and cell context.

Dynamic token adaptation bridges the two, translating DNA embeddings into the token space of the single-cell model. Training an adapter on that bridge lets the combined system predict regulation in varied genetic settings. The authors probe how DNA changes ripple into the learned regulatory networks. The method is general, with the single-cell case as the worked example.
arxiv-2504-13749:
Lion Frangoulis, Zahra Khatibi, Lorenzo Mariano, and Alessandro Lunghi speed up the hunt for magnetic molecules in this 2025 paper. Designing compounds with target traits usually takes years of back-and-forth between theory and lab work. Single-molecule magnets show the cost: big gains came slowly and at great expense.

The team's pipeline mixes three tools. Genetic search breeds new candidate structures from old ones, machine learning screens them cheaply, and accurate quantum calculations check the best ones. The system can invent fresh building blocks rather than only reuse known ones. As a test, it produced new cobalt compounds with record magnetic traits in a small fraction of the usual time.
arxiv-2504-14449:
Sridharan and co-authors present an imaging strategy in two thousand twenty-five for a next-generation radio telescope array, the ngVLA. The facility spans a wide frequency range with sharp sensitivity and resolution, opening new discovery space. Its science goals demand images with very high dynamic range, the contrast between bright and faint features.

The baseline plan leans on the array's own sensitivity. Frequent self-calibration, where the instrument corrects itself using the sky signal, counters air-driven delays on short timescales. Pointing self-calibration fixes aim errors. Using these tricks routinely can simplify several subsystems and improve reliability. In some cases the approach may even reach the thermal noise limit. The paper lays out the reasoning and shows examples in parallel.
arxiv-2504-14649:
Eugene Tang KangJie and four co-authors survey what older adults want from lessons about artificial intelligence. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Most past work on AI teaching looks at students and children. This team asked one hundred three adults aged fifty and up about their drive. They also asked about struggles and how these adults like to learn.

The adults said learning about AI matters to them. They want its benefits and hope to avoid its risks. They also see it as needed for the years ahead. Many found the topic hard to grasp and did not know where to start. Above all, they favored learning by doing, with hands-on practice. The authors close with design ideas to build AI lessons that fit older learners.
arxiv-2504-15149:
Chen Su and co-authors build a machine learning route to cosmology from the universe's emptiest places in this 2025 paper. Cosmic voids bend light, and that bending carries clues about matter and gravity. The trouble is that no tidy formula predicts the signal, so classic analysis stalls.

Their framework learns from simulations instead. A forward pipeline grows fake universes across many settings, complete with the messy link between galaxies and their dark matter homes. A neural estimator then studies the mock data until it can read real void lensing backward, returning the odds for two key cosmic parameters. Tests on held-out settings showed honest answers: the estimates landed on the truth with error bars of the right size. The authors offer the method as the first step toward running void lensing on real survey data.
arxiv-2504-15949:
Firas Ben Ramdhane and three co-authors map the rules that make non-linear cell grids act in clean ways. In such a grid, one local rule is used at each cell, all at once. Three traits shape much of what the grid can do. Does each state have a prior state? Can the rule run in reverse? Does it permute in each axis?

The paper shows how these traits — surjectivity, reversibility, and permutivity — push on and bound each other. It gives tests for when a rule is permutive in one sense or in both. Worked cases show where each claim holds and where it stops. Non-linear rules lack the neat tools that settle such points for linear rules. The authors fill that gap. They make clear which acts non-linear grids can and cannot do.
arxiv-2504-20449:
Naoto Nakatsuji and his four co-authors, publishing in 2025, map the electronic landscape of a three-layer crystal sandwich with a twist. Each layer of the material WSe2 is rotated slightly against its neighbors. The misalignment prints two overlapping moiré patterns, like two window screens overlaid. The team models how the atoms settle and what energy bands result, for the two natural twist styles.

The middle layer feels both patterns at once, doubling the depth of the energy landscape. In the helical twist style, the settling creates domains where the combined pattern forms a Kagome lattice, famous for hosting flat energy bands. In the alternating style, deep triangular wells appear instead. A modest electric field can flip which layer holds the electrons at the band edge. The authors present trilayers as a wider design space than the much-studied bilayers.
arxiv-2504-20549: Evgeny Feigin wrote a paper from 2025 on an algebraic form of a known geometric equality about symmetry spaces. The original claim, since proved, says two spaces of sections have the same size. Feigin recasts both sides as sizes of algebraic modules named for Demazure, then builds an explicit bridge between them. The bridge works in type A only, but covers a far wider class of cases than the geometric claim.
arxiv-2504-20849:
Anum Afzal, Alexandre Mercier, and Florian Matthes study machine-made ad text for the music trade, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Shops want text made from data, but plain methods tend to repeat the same phrases again and again. A set of near-twin ads is of little use, so range matters as much as quality.

The authors test several large language models, with fine-tuning and with few-shot or zero-shot prompts. They set a base line for text that is both good and varied. They also add a new score, JaccDiv, that gauges how much a set of texts spreads out. The lessons reach past music, to any field where the same kind of text is made at scale.
arxiv-2504-21049:
Sneha Baskota trains a deep network to sort web addresses into four risk classes in a paper from 2025. Phishing pages steal credentials and money, and older detectors miss new attack types. The model reads an address as a sequence of characters. A bidirectional memory network then judges context from both directions. Classes cover benign, phishing, defacement, and malware addresses.

Training used more than six hundred fifty thousand labeled addresses. The system reached ninety-seven percent accuracy overall. The author reports clear gains over traditional techniques. False positives, a pain point for older systems, were a design target throughout. The paper is a compact applied study in security machine learning.
arxiv-2504-21649:
Dahal and Hymas show that separate regions of spacetime share quantum entanglement in twenty twenty-five. The vacuum of a quantum field is not empty of correlations. They demonstrate entanglement between the future and left Rindler wedges of flat spacetime. The past and right wedges are likewise entangled.

That pattern underlies the Unruh effect, where acceleration creates particles. The authors propose extracting the entanglement with two simple detectors. The detectors sit in the past and right wedges. Tuning their frequencies in step with time transfers the entanglement to them. Teleportation through the vacuum might then be possible. They suggest current superconducting qubit technology could implement the protocol.
arxiv-2505-00649:
Marco Braga, Pranav Kasela, Alessandro Raganato, and Gabriella Pasi adapt search rankers to new domains by adding and subtracting model weights. Language models re-rank documents well until vocabulary and style shift under them. Task arithmetic merges models trained on different tasks through simple weight operations. No extra fine-tuning is required.

The team synthesizes diverse task and domain knowledge into a single retriever this way. Experiments span scientific, biomedical, and multilingual collections. Re-ranking quality rose by up to eighteen percent on one standard measure and fifteen on another. Both gains came at zero-shot, on tasks the merged model never trained for. The analysis also maps where the trick strains. Code is public. For search teams facing a new domain with no labeled data, weight arithmetic offers a cheap first adaptation.
arxiv-2505-00949:
A large team at NVIDIA presents a family of reasoning language models in a 2025 technical report. The models, named Llama-Nemotron, aim to think step by step without wasting effort. Long chains of thought raise cost and slow replies. The team tunes the models to switch deep reasoning on for hard tasks and off for easy ones.

The report describes how the models were trained and tested across math, code, and science tasks. Careful data mixing and staged training kept quality high while trimming size and compute. The models are released for other builders to use and study. Efficient reasoning matters because these models are now used at huge scale every day.
arxiv-2505-01049:
Nishant Jain, Xunpeng Huang, Yian Ma, and Tong Zhang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It puts multi-step consistency models on firm theory ground, a class of fast generators that rival diffusion models.

Consistency models map a noisy input to any point on the reverse path, so samples come in a few steps. The authors prove a tight bound on the gap to the true spread, reached in a step count that grows only with the log of size over error. A like bound holds when the data are rough, with a step count that grows with dimension. They also show the models can be learned well with small steps, in both smooth and rough cases. The rough-case rates lead the field.
arxiv-2505-01449:
Jiayu Wang, Aws Albarghouthi, and Frederic Sala forecast which way to adapt a language model before paying for the trial in this 2025 paper. Fine-tuning and in-context tricks each shine in different settings, and picking wrong burns compute. Their framework, COSMOS, predicts both score and cost for each candidate plan.

Two predictors do the work. Small proxy models fed with embeddings guess fine-tuning outcomes, while scaling laws fitted on few samples forecast retrieval-based in-context learning. Across eight benchmarks the framework's predictions tracked reality closely. The savings were large: about ninety-three percent less compute on average, and near ninety-nine percent in the heaviest cases. The authors argue that choosing an adaptation strategy should start with a forecast, not a fleet of trial runs, and that deployment budgets can shrink without giving up quality.
arxiv-2505-01849:
Bandyopadhyay and a co-author applied Markov models to Twenty20 cricket chases in a 2025 paper. In a chase, the second team must reach a set target with balls and wickets running out. A past gauge, the Pressure Index, scores how hard that squeeze feels ball by ball.

Higher-order Markov models track how each ball's outcome leans on the last few, not just the last one. Joined with the pressure gauge, they chart how a chase tips toward win or loss. Teams can read the charts to pick when to attack and when to hold. The work turns raw score feeds into chase plans.
arxiv-2505-02349:
Hakam Alomari, Christopher Vendome, and Hilal Gyawali introduce srcVul, a tool for finding and patching vulnerable code clones. Copying code is common in software development, but clones propagate vulnerabilities across every copied segment. Fixing one copy leaves the others exposed.

The tool combines program slicing with locality-sensitive hashing. It first builds a database of vulnerability-related slices from known vulnerable programs and their patches, indexing each slice's structural characteristics as a vector. When scanning a target program, it matches slicing vectors against the database and recommends a patch when it finds a similarity. Evaluated against three state-of-the-art detectors, srcVul reached ninety-one percent precision and seventy-five percent recall on established vulnerability databases and open-source repositories. The authors argue the approach scales while staying precise. For security teams, it offers a way to hunt down every copy of a known flaw, not just the original.
arxiv-2505-02549:
Yongxiang Li and co-authors tackle person matching across normal and heat-sensing cameras in a 2025 paper. The task, called person re-identification, must match the same person in day images and night thermal images without hand-labeled training data. The gap between the two image types makes the job hard.

Common methods group images by computer and trust the group labels, but those labels carry errors that pile up as training goes on. The authors build a learning scheme that expects label noise and resists it, guarding against overfitting and drift. Their method aims for steadier matching where no labels exist at all. Surveillance and search teams get a more robust tool for cross-camera tracking.
arxiv-2505-03049:
Thirty-four hackathon teams spent a weekend pointing large language models at chemistry and materials problems, and Yoel Zimmermann and co-authors catalog what they built. The projects span the full research cycle: they predict molecular traits, design new materials, automate lab work, manage data, draft papers, and mine past papers for new ideas.

Patterns emerged across the projects. Models handled low-data problems better than expected, with added reasoning switched on. They served as quick test-build platforms as much as tools that predict. The review is candid about weak points too: trust in the outputs, clear logic, and results others can repeat all lag behind raw power. The authors frame the set as a snapshot of a field mid-change.
arxiv-2505-03249:
Owen Moulding and a large team report multilayer crystal field states in a cerium compound in two thousand twenty-five. Crystal field states set how f electrons act in such solids. In the local view those states stay locked on one site. Polarized Raman spectra of CeCoSi break that simple picture.

More excitations show than the local model allows for. The team reads that as entanglement of states across cerium layers. Spin, orbital, and sublattice traits join in that composite. Such mixing could seed new quantum orders past this one case. Any system with local but not global symmetry loss may host them.
arxiv-2505-03349:
Scheduling random jobs on parallel machines admits a near perfect scheme when the job sizes come in few flavors, prove Antonios Antoniadis and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Each job's length is a coin flip between short and long, and the goal is to minimize the average finishing time in expectation.

The key move reshapes any optimal policy into a stratified one that decides only at set moments, at negligible cost. Two traps, keeping the new policy informed and stopping delays from piling up, are disarmed in turn. Dynamic programming then finds the best stratified policy. A looser version gives a strong guarantee for the general case.
arxiv-2505-03749:
Cut a triangle by its longest side, again and again, and the angles of the shards could in drift run wild. Amalia Adlerteg and Linus Carlsson bound that drift in 2025 for a three-way cut. Their method splits the longest side in thirds and joins the cuts to the far corner, then repeats on each shard. The work is drawn from Adlerteg's thesis work.

For a general start, the top angle of any later shard stays under a fixed multiple of the start's top angle, part proved and part shown by number runs. Two clean starts, the equal-sided and the right isoceles, earn full two-sided bounds. Mesh builders need such bounds: shard angles gone wild spoil the sums that ride on the mesh.
arxiv-2505-04149:
Omer Avci proves, in a 2025 number theory paper, that the torsion points of an elliptic curve stop growing in a certain tower of number fields. Torsion points are the finitely many points on the curve that return to the start after repeated addition, and they form a tidy group.

Starting from a curve over the rational numbers and a square-root number field, the tower adds layer upon layer of p-power roots of unity style extensions. For primes above five, Avci shows the torsion group over the whole tower equals the one over the base field. That equality lets him list every group that can occur, borrowing the known list for square-root fields.
arxiv-2505-05149:
Mansour Naslcheraghi and Gunes Karabulut-Kurt present a 2025 scheme to analyse the web that links ground stations and satellite groups for space awareness. Keeping watch over all actors in space needs a network that stays aware at all times. When objects can be seen and steered rests on real orbits, which tangle the web in ways a static view misses.

Their scheme treats the time pattern of each satellite, its temporal spectrum, as the key design element. It folds in real dynamics to map how the ground-space web is built, which stations sit alone, and which rule the web. Sims of the full system measure how each satellite's time pattern shapes links within and between constellations. The counts show how ground stations and groups act on each other in practice.
arxiv-2505-05949:
Max Glockner and colleagues built a question-answering benchmark out of invented news in a 2025 paper. Retrieval benchmarks rot quickly: questions that once forced a model to look facts up become answerable from memory as newer models train on fresher data. NeoQA sidesteps the rot by generating fictional news events, entities, timelines, and articles, so no correct answer can exist in any model's training data.

Questions must then be answered purely from retrieved evidence, and only when that evidence suffices. Variants include missing and misleading details to test caution. The authors found models often miss subtle mismatches between question and evidence and rush to answer on thin support. Controlled fiction gives retrieval research a stable yardstick.
arxiv-2505-06649:
Dimitris Korobilis studies how central bank rate shocks spread through the United States economy, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. He builds a large Bayesian model that tracks many series at once and treats shocks as hidden factors. The design keeps the math fast even as the data set grows, and it lets policy effects shift over time.

Shocks are picked out with high-speed market surprises plus sign rules on the results. The method held up across many model choices. A key result is that the Federal Reserve sway over single consumer prices shifted a lot in the high price-rise years from two thousand twenty-two to two thousand twenty-four. Readers get new detail on how policy reaches prices.
arxiv-2505-06849:
Subramani and Bartscher pair learn tools with slim sums for a heat twin of a lamp sink. Twin tools mock real gear live and guess its next states. Their twin tracks a car head lamp heat sink in the work. Flow sums give a base of true heat paths for the sink. Slim forms, built by mode splits, hold those paths at low cost. Learn tools then pick the best slim form for each new state.

Four learn tools take the pick task in the test runs. Tree, near-peer, curve, and nerve tools all get a shot. The nerve tool wins with a mean miss of 54.240. Guess and true marks sit close in the count checks. The frame scales, reads plain, and suits car heat work. It backs firm builds and care that plans in front.
arxiv-2505-07649:
Dominique Fourdrinier, William Strawderman, and Martin Wells construct special estimators in a 2025 paper. Their target is the mean of a multi-dimensional bell-shaped distribution, judged by squared error. Bayes minimax estimators are prized because they are admissible like Bayesian rules yet carry the cautious risk guarantees of frequentist ones. Building them has been a live problem.

The authors show such estimators can be built through integral transforms, using two classic transforms, as long as the prior is chosen with the right spherical shape. Several worked examples show the method in action. The paper is technical and aimed at mathematical statisticians.
arxiv-2505-07849:
Revanth Gangi Reddy and nine co-authors present SweRank, in a 2025 preprint, a fast way to find the code behind a bug report. Given a plain-language issue, developers must locate the files and functions to change. That hunt eats time on every project. AI agent systems can do it, but they are slow, pricey, and often closed. Classic ranking models are cheap but trip on the wordy, failure-focused style of issue text. SweRank pairs a retriever with a reranker trained for this exact job.

To train it, the team built SweLoc, a large dataset from public GitHub projects. It pairs real issue reports with the code edits that fixed them. On two standard test sets, SweRank topped both older rankers and costly agent systems. The dataset also lifted other retrievers and rerankers when they trained on it. The authors offer both as resources for cheaper, open issue localization.
arxiv-2505-09149:
Ichiro Oda presents a fully covariant quantization of quadratic gravity in this 2025 paper. Quadratic gravity adds higher-derivative terms to Einstein's theory, which may help quantize gravity. The challenge is doing so while respecting general coordinate invariance at every step.

Working in the de Donder gauge with BRST symmetry, Oda computes the equal-time commutation relations in detail. The relations between the metric and its time derivatives vanish identically. He then reads off the theory's physical content: a massless graviton, a massive scalar, and a massive ghost. The ghost makes the theory non-unitary as it stands. Oda closes by discussing whether confining the ghost could restore a unitary scattering matrix.
arxiv-2505-09649:
Abisha Thapa Magar and Anup Shakya built a next-word tool in a 2025 project paper. Guessing the next word is a core task for language software, but the best tools today are huge nets trained with vast data and costly machines. The pair asked whether a leaner design could still do the job well.

Their design joins a graph net with a memory net. The graph part codes the sense of the words so far, and the memory part uses that code to pick the next word. They trained it on a Wikipedia text set with modest gear. The project shows a graph-based route to word guessing that small teams can afford to try.
arxiv-2505-10149:
Mirai Ikebuchi extends a counting argument about axioms to higher-order logic in a 2025 paper. Familiar theories, like that of groups, can often be stated with far fewer axioms than first written down. For first-order theories, a homology-based method already gives hard lower bounds on how few axioms can suffice, by turning the theory into algebraic objects.

Ikebuchi carries the method into the typed lambda calculus with product and unit types, where equations run between lambda terms rather than simple symbols. Homology groups are defined for such a theory, and the count of its independent cycles yields a floor on the number of equations any presentation must contain. The result gives logicians a new measuring tool for higher-order systems.
arxiv-2505-10549:
Zachary Bare and seven co-authors hunt for new battery materials by computer screening, then make one in the lab. Their twenty twenty-five paper targets Wadsley-Roth niobates, a family prized for fast lithium storage. Fewer than thirty such structures were known, which limits the search for better or cheaper mixes.

The team swapped elements into ten known templates, across forty-eight elements, and tested thousands of candidates with quantum calculations. Over a thousand looked stable enough to exist. They then synthesized one predicted mix and confirmed its structure by X-ray. The new material stored charge fast and beat a recent benchmark of the family.
arxiv-2505-11649:
Chu and four colleagues study how people bond with AI companion chatbots in twenty twenty-five. The bots offer steady empathy and praise, which can feel like closeness. Over seventeen thousand user shared chats from Reddit forums were analyzed. The team tracked how feeling flows between user and bot.

The bots mirror user mood and pump up good feelings. That held even when users shared explicit or rule breaking content. Such mirroring may drive the intimacy illusion the title names. An anonymized data set of charged chats is released for study. The authors urge treating social bots as high risk for tender users.
arxiv-2505-12849:
Ben Liu and Zhen Qin speed up a state of the art image generator called TarFlow, in this 2025 paper. The model marries transformer blocks with a flow method and tops several benchmarks. Its weakness is sampling: the step by step design forces slow, sequential drawing of each image.

The authors recast sampling as an iteration problem and attack it with a blended solver method. They first rank blocks by how fast each settles and score how good a starting guess each receives. Difficult blocks then get more iterations and careful starts, while easy ones finish quickly. Across four model variants the trick sped sampling up to about five times. Image quality scores did not slip. Code and trained models are public.
arxiv-2505-13249:
Le Vu Anh, Dinh Duc Nha Nguyen, and Phi Long Nguyen present a 2025 study on a hidden flaw in large language models. Test data can leak into the data a model trains on, which makes test scores look better than they are. Past tools for spotting such leaks have been weak or slow. The team set out to build a faster and surer check.

Their method, called RN-F, reads faint leftover patterns in the model's own signals to flag leaked items. It needs one pass, uses no gradient work, and adds no extra math load. The method works across models and needs no change to the model itself. On several models and leaked data sets, RN-F beat the best prior tools, with gains of up to 10.5 percent on detection scores. The work gives testers a light way to guard the honesty of model scores.
arxiv-2505-14749:
Ding-fang Zeng presents a 2025 physics paper on the complementarity of gravitational collapse, the second in a series. The catalog title differs, but the text itself develops an exact one body method, called XOB, for two body gravity problems such as merging black holes.

Zeng shows that the method, expanded for weak fields and low speeds, matches the standard post Newtonian series to all orders for the conservative part of the motion. With a modulated formula, it yields merger waveforms that agree closely with large numerical simulations. Zeng argues the match supports inner structure in black holes.
arxiv-2505-15249:
Yerin Hwang and five co-authors ask whether doctored images can fool the vision-language models now used to grade text-to-image output. These model judges are popular for scoring how well a picture matches its prompt. Their reliability on the visual side had barely been tested.

The team defines several image-induced biases and adds them to FRAME, a new benchmark built with varied score distributions across domains. Every tested judge inflated scores for manipulated images, in every domain. Stacking multiple biases made the effect stronger, and pairwise judging was fooled too. Prompt-based defenses did not remove the bias. The authors call for sturdier model judges before evaluation pipelines lean on them further.
arxiv-2505-16449:
Gianmarco Del Sarto, Matthias Hieber, and Tarek Zöchling analyze a climate model with noisy boundaries. Their 2025 paper couples an energy balance model to geophysical flow equations. The link runs through a dynamic boundary condition, with and without random noise. Such models mimic how surface energy and ocean motion interact.

The team proves the full system is well-posed in a strong global sense. The proof covers the plain deterministic case for large starting data. It also covers the noisy case in a standard function space. Well-posedness means solutions exist, are unique, and behave stably. That groundwork lets later studies trust simulations built on the model.
arxiv-2505-16849:
Böckling, Paulheim, and Iana introduced a simple method in twenty twenty-five for grounding language model answers in a knowledge graph. Models often invent facts or rely on stale memory, and fetching facts from a structured graph can fix that, but many fetching schemes are heavy and brittle.

Their method, Walk&Retrieve, wanders the graph along short paths from the question's key terms. It then turns what it finds into plain sentences, building a small text the model can read before answering. No training on special data is needed, so the method adapts at once when the graph changes. Despite its simplicity, it matched or beat more complex systems on answer accuracy and cut made-up facts. It also answered faster and scaled to large graphs. The authors offer it as a strong, light baseline for future work.
arxiv-2505-17149:
Qin Chen and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on how well large language models can forecast from data. Forecasting guides choices in fields from health to trade. Models shine at talk and code, yet skill at forecasts from real data was untested. The team built a test set, named PredictiQ, to fill that gap.

The set holds over a thousand queries drawn from dozens of real data sets in eight fields. Their checks weigh text insight, code craft, and how well the two line up. Twelve known models took the test. All faced steep hurdles in this kind of work. The team shares the test in public for later use.
arxiv-2505-17349:
David Porlles and Wei Chen trace the Meissner effect, the expulsion of magnetic fields by superconductors, to the quantum geometry of momentum space. Their paper appeared in 2025. Recent work defines a quantum metric from how filled states overlap at neighboring momenta. For superconductors with several bands and mixed pairing, the team shows the superfluid weight, the stiffness behind the Meissner effect, equals a weighted sum of that metric's parts.

Summing the metric also gives the spread of the state's localized wave packets, a stability marker for superconductivity. Their marker can be drawn site by site on a lattice, even with disorder included.
