In test cases, the diamagnetic current turned turbulent around impurities, and the field penetration depth grew, matching experiments.
arxiv-2505-17749:
Ghada Sokar and Pablo Samuel Castro wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on why deep reinforcement learning agents trained on raw pixels fail to scale. Larger networks often perform worse in such settings, and the cause was unclear. Earlier fixes patched the issue indirectly through new designs or training tricks.

The authors trace the problem to one junction: where the image encoder, a stack of layers that read the pixels, hands its output to the dense layers that decide actions. They call this junction the bottleneck. Their analysis shows earlier remedies were all easing pressure at that same point. They propose global average pooling as a simple, direct fix for the bottleneck. The method avoids the complexity of the earlier workarounds.
arxiv-2505-17949:
Mieke Wessel and Svenja zur Verth write, in twenty twenty-five, a math paper on counting solutions to a quadratic equation with restricted variables. A quadratic form is an expression built from squared terms and cross terms. They study a non-singular form, meaning a well-behaved one, with many mixed terms. They fix a target integer and ask how many weighted solutions land on it. The weights come from a chosen sequence, which limits which variables count.

Their tool is the circle method, a classic way to count number theory solutions by splitting an integral into parts. They give conditions on both the weights and the form that let the method work. Only solutions up to a set height are counted.
arxiv-2505-18049:
Gaole Dai and co-authors build a vision system inspired by how the human eye splits its sensing work. Their 2025 paper notes that cone cells handle color while rod cells track motion and light change. Modern cameras echo that split: normal cameras capture color, while spike cameras record rapid brightness changes.

Their system, SpikeGen, feeds both streams into a generative model that works in a compressed latent space. The team test it on several joint tasks: sharpening blurred images and video, rebuilding dense frames from spike streams, and synthesizing new views of fast scenes. Experiments show the split design handles these tasks well. Borrowing the eye's division of labor may help machines see fast, messy scenes more reliably.
arxiv-2505-20849:
Rosendahl and Kirkeby present a 2025 framework for checking data flow inside custom hardware designs. Chips built on programmable arrays speed up heavy computing, but their parallel layout is hard to design well. Data must move between parts at the right time and rate. The framework studies that traffic without running the chip, a static check done from the design text.

The check maps how parts of the datapath talk to each other. Those maps show jams, dead ends, and waste that a designer can fix early. Static checks cost far less than building and testing a flawed chip. The authors aim the tool at design and tuning stages of hardware work. Clear views of data traffic are a base need for fast, sound accelerators.
arxiv-2505-20949:
Andrea Giovanni Nuzzolese, writing alone in 2025, presents PyRML, a Python library for building knowledge graphs. Knowledge graphs weave mixed data into linked facts for many fields. Mapping languages like RML state how to turn tables into graph form. Python users lacked a native way to write and run those mappings.

PyRML supports the core of RML inside plain Python code. Mappings can be authored, run, and tested in one place. It plugs into Pandas for data and RDFlib for graph handling. Workflows stay modular and open to inspection. Shared, repeatable mappings help teams trust their graphs. The library lowers the entry bar for careful data integration.
arxiv-2505-21249:
Mohamed Benzaghta and co-authors propose data-driven ways in 2025 to manage handovers in cellular networks. As networks grow denser and users move at varied speeds, fixed handover settings often fail. Settings that are too slow cause dropped links, while fast ones cause wasteful back-and-forth switches.

One approach tunes handover settings with a smart search method. The other lets a learning agent pick the serving cell from live network data. Both beat standard benchmark settings in a real-world scenario modeled with ray tracing. Transfer learning helps both adapt to new user speeds, including drone users.
arxiv-2505-21549:
Daniel Csizmadia and seven co-authors improve image-text search by teaching a small model from a bigger one, in a 2025 paper. The base model, CLIP, matches pictures with captions but is locked to fixed image sizes and short text, which blurs fine detail. Search tasks often hinge on exactly that detail.

Their method first fine-tunes a cross-modal transformer teacher that lets image regions and text spans attend to each other both ways. Object boxes from a detector ground the regions. A light student model then learns from the teacher's enriched embeddings through a mixed loss. Trained on a modest set of about sixty-seven thousand pairs, the student raised search scores clearly. It also kept nearly all of the original model's zero-shot sorting skill.
arxiv-2505-21649:
Nazia Tasnim and co-authors introduce, in twenty twenty-five, a benchmark that tests whether vision-language models truly understand object orientation. Humans learn orientation in stages, from which way an object faces to relations among several objects. Existing benchmarks blur orientation into general spatial reasoning. Their benchmark, DORI, makes orientation the primary target. It splits the skill into four dimensions, each tested at coarse and fine levels. The set holds over thirty-three thousand multiple-choice questions over nearly fourteen thousand images, real and synthetic, from fourteen sources.

The design isolates orientation with single objects, standard reference frames, and structured prompts. Twenty-six top models were tested. Models strong on general spatial tests stayed near random here. The best scored about sixty-four percent on coarse and forty-three percent on fine judgments.
arxiv-2505-21749:
Ebrahimi and Roland Memisevic revisit a richer way for recurrent networks to update their state, in work from 2025. Hidden units are often cast as passive memory stores, with gates to guard what they hold. The pair casts them as active parts of the math. Their update multiplies hidden state with input codes, a step called bilinear.

Proofs and tests show that step fits state-tracking tasks in a natural way. Such tasks are the simplest ones where hidden units must truly compute. The steps form a ladder of rising task depth. Known lean models, Mamba among them, sit at the ladder's low rung.
arxiv-2505-23949:
Xiang Meng, Mehdi Makni, and Rahul Mazumder tackle a gap in neural network pruning: sparse patterns that survive matrix transposition. Keeping only N of every M weights speeds up forward computation, but the pattern breaks when matrices are transposed during training. Earlier fixes either failed to scale or allowed only one small pattern size.

Their algorithm TSENOR recasts mask-finding as an optimal transport problem, solved with entropy regularization and Dykstra's algorithm. A rounding step finishes the mask, and a tensor implementation uses GPU parallelism for large speedups. Plugged into standard pruning frameworks, it sparsified an eight-billion-parameter model at a sixteen-of-thirty-two pattern. Performance stayed close to ordinary sparsity at that setting.
arxiv-2505-24549:
Linda Greggio, Rémi Robin, Mazyar Mirrahimi, and Alexandru Petrescu showed in twenty twenty-five that a strongly driven superconducting qubit can pollute its neighbors with noise. Fast, high-fidelity control needs strong drives, but a hard-driven transmon turns chaotic: its computational states mix with the rest of its spectrum, spoiling readout and charge sensitivity. The authors ask whether that chaos leaks outward.

Modeling a driven transmon coupled to a spectator two-level system, with both full quantum simulation and semiclassical analysis, they performed noise spectroscopy of the interaction. In a certain limit the driven qubit acts on its neighbor exactly like a stochastic diffusive noise process. The finding matters for multi-qubit processors: one qubit's aggressive control pulse can become another's decoherence, even without direct crosstalk.
arxiv-2506-00949:
Tanmoy Chakraborty and Punyabrata Pradhan study how particles move and bunch up in a simple ring model, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The model holds particles that hop over gaps of mixed lengths while the total count stays fixed. Two cases get close study, one with short hops and one with hops of any length.

In the long-hop case the flow becomes wild near a key density and the particles start to clump. The team works out the spread of the total flow and shows that ease of flow grows without bound at that point. The drag stays finite, which breaks the usual pattern for calm systems. Readers get a clear test for telling when such clumping starts.
arxiv-2506-01149:
Maclean Rouble and seven co-authors tune sensitive detectors in place in a 2025 physics paper. Kinetic inductance detectors sense faint light for astronomy. Each one rings at its own frequency, which lets many share one wire. Built frequencies often drift from their design targets, though.

The team shows the readout signal itself can shift that frequency. A steady tone near the ring point can move it by several widths. The device then settles at a new stable point set by the tone. That effect rests on a known quirk where the response folds over. Learning to control the shift could fix crowded detector arrays. The authors frame this study as a first step toward a full control method.
arxiv-2506-01549:
Paul Chote and eleven co-authors report a fourteen-week watching campaign on six geostationary satellites, timed around a docking in orbit, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A servicing craft, Mission Extension Vehicle 2, approached and docked with the aging Intelsat 10-02 satellite. The team tracked brightness changes with telescopes to read the satellites' behavior from the ground.

Fast single-color readings were backed by color measurements, sharp imaging, and radio positioning from partner sites. The light curves caught rapid glints on one satellite, a brightening of the weather satellite, and clear changes in Intelsat's signature after docking. Glints even let the team pin down the docked pair's position. The paper also details the care needed to reach sub-percent brightness accuracy.
arxiv-2506-02049:
Beichen Huang, Ran Cheng, and Kay Chen Tan present EvoGit, a frame where many coding agents evolve one codebase with no central boss. Their paper from twenty twenty-five casts each agent as an independent editor. Agents never pass messages or share memory. All coordination flows through a Git-based family tree of versions.

Agents read and write the shared repository out of sync with each other. The tree tracks full lineage, which supports fine branching and parallel work. A steady history keeps the record straight. Humans set the goals, scan the tree now and then, and nudge or prune lines with light feedback. Tests built a web app from scratch and bred a solver for bin packing. The authors see a path to continual, decentralized software growth. Code is open.
arxiv-2506-02449:
Bo Peng and three co-authors evaluate a subtle social skill in twenty twenty-five. Good dialogue systems infer user backgrounds implicitly from conversation. They then personalize help without being told the facts outright. Data to test that skill is scarce, and building it by hand is costly and privacy-sensitive.

Their benchmark, IP-Dialog, uses automatic synthetic data instead. It covers ten tasks and twelve types of user attributes. An evaluation framework with four metrics scores attribute awareness and reasoning. Five causal graphs map how models reason their way to personalization. Extensive experiments yield observations about where models succeed and fail. Readers get a privacy-safe way to grade a capability that matters for helpful assistants.
arxiv-2506-02549:
Akie Kowaguchi and five co-authors bring a path-finding trick from computer games into a well-known way of running models of matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The model method runs many copies of a system at once and swaps them, to beat slow settling. Its yield rests on how many copies are used and how apt swaps are. The team treats copies and swap odds as a graph, and uses a famed shortest-path rule to pick the best swap path. The path keeps change in a key term low. Tests on a change between solid and liquid show faster sampling. The plan gives a clear way to tune such runs.
arxiv-2506-02749:
Changyi Xiao and Yixin Cao improve knowledge graph completion in a twenty twenty-five paper. A knowledge graph stores facts as triples, like subject, relation, object. Completion fills in missing facts, and tensor models, which treat the graph as a three-way array, do this well but tend to overfit.

Past fixes just shrink the embedding vectors, which helps little. The pair instead shrinks the intermediate variables that arise in the several ways of computing the predicted tensor. They prove this pushes the tensor toward low trace norm, a known guard against overfitting. The fix fits most tensor models and stays cheap to compute. Tests confirm the gains, and code is shared.
arxiv-2506-03149:
Language models read text chopped into subword pieces, and the chopping itself can tilt what the model believes. Pietro Lesci and co-authors define this tokenisation bias and measure it as a causal effect. The question: how much does adding one subword to the vocabulary change the odds the model gives its characters?

Each model trains with only one tokenizer, so no direct comparison exists. The authors exploit the sharp cutoff where tokenizer builders stop adding ranked subwords. Pieces just inside and just outside the line are near twins, which allows a clean causal estimate. Across model sizes and tokenizers, the effect is real and sometimes huge: one piece's presence raised its characters' odds up to 17-fold in a small model. Tokenizer choice, they argue, is a first-class design decision.
arxiv-2506-06049:
Yonah Weiner and Noam Soker model how jets from an infalling companion star reshape a giant star's envelope in a 2025 astronomy study. In common envelope evolution, a small star spirals inside a red giant or asymptotic giant branch star, the birth route of many planetary nebulae. The companion's jets push back on the envelope, a negative feedback that throttles their own fuel supply.

Using a stellar evolution code, the authors deposit jet energy into the outer envelope, which inflates it and lowers its density. The jets' power falls by a factor tied to the companion's mass. The mimic captures feedback without a full three-dimensional simulation.
arxiv-2506-06249:
J. Myles and co-authors measured a known flaw of optical galaxy group catalogs in 2025. Methods such as redMaPPer find groups from images, but galaxies sitting in front of or behind a group get mistaken for members because their distances are uncertain. These projection effects must be measured before the catalogs can support cosmology. The team used spectroscopy from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument to check true membership.

They proved that the share of false members depends on group richness, more than doubling for poor groups weighed with rich ones. They also found the first spectroscopic evidence that projection effects grow with redshift over the range studied, and hints that fainter galaxies are more often interlopers far behind the group. Speed spread readings accompany the membership study, sharpening how optical catalogs can be corrected.
arxiv-2506-06349:
Thien Nhan Vo, writing alone in 2025, compares two ways to sort heartbeats from ECG data, the tracings of the heart's electric signal. Sorting beats well helps doctors spot rhythm problems early. One way feeds the machine hand-picked measures, like beat spacing and signal spread. The other turns each beat into a picture and lets a vision model read it.

Vo cleaned the data first, then trained many models of both kinds. A fast tree-based model using hand-picked measures won, with accuracy near ninety-nine percent. The picture-based models scored clearly lower. The author suggests future work should add signals from more chest leads and use the flow of beats over time.
arxiv-2506-06449:
Salvador Centelles Chuliá, Tim Herbermann, Antonio Herrero-Brocal, and Avelino Vicente look at two theories of neutrino masses in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Both stretch the standard model with a chiral symmetry that breaks on its own and is anomaly-free. The break makes Dirac neutrino masses, through a seesaw mechanism, and leaves a massless Goldstone boson called the Diracon. The two models share particle content and scalar potential but break the symmetry in distinct ways.

That split flips the phenomenology. In the first model the Diracon couples weakly to leptons, but right-handed neutrinos flood the universe, so cosmology, through the effective number of relativistic species, bounds it. In the second, right-handed production is held down and flavor-violating decays turn into a probe, as when a muon turns into an electron plus a Diracon. The pair shows how cosmology and flavor add to each other.
arxiv-2506-07549:
Zhangchi Zhao and co-authors slim down a hungry neural network design in a 2025 paper. Kolmogorov-Arnold networks replace fixed weights with learnable curves, which makes them expressive and readable but far heavier to train than standard networks. Their fix, MetaKAN, lets a small side network generate the big network's weights.

Both parts train together in one smooth process. Across tasks from symbolic formula fitting to physics equations and image sorting, the slim version matched or beat the original while using far fewer trainable parameters and less memory. Interpretability, the design's selling point, survived the diet. The authors offer the method as a way to scale these networks toward real workloads without the training bill that has held them back.
arxiv-2506-08049:
Tengfei Lyu, Weijia Zhang, and Hao Liu build TelePiT, a transformer for world climate forecasts weeks to months ahead. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Such forecasts guide farms, energy plans, and storm prep, but air chaos and cross-scale play make them hard.

Three parts carry the design. A sphere-wise embedding lays world data on the globe's true shape. A physics-led neural step tracks air processes across bands that the model learns. The transformer itself wears far-flung climate links, teleconnections, in its attention. Tests beat top data models and live weather systems at all lead times.
arxiv-2506-08349:
Yuxuan Zhou and co-authors grade language models on medical thinking at three levels in a 2025 computing paper. Most medical benches test recall, which flatters the models. Borrowing a classic teaching ladder, the team built tasks for raw knowledge, for applied knowledge, and for solving fresh clinical scenarios. Models from six leading families, both general and medical, sat the same ladder.

Scores fell steeply as the tasks climbed the ladder. At the top level, bigger models pulled ahead clearly, while small ones faded. Medical tuning helped most at the lower rungs. The results argue that passing a fact exam is a weak promise of bedside reasoning, and they point training effort at the top rung.
arxiv-2506-08749:
Viktoria Patapovich and Maniraman Periyasamy lead a team packing exponentially many quantum sub-models into one circuit, so quantum learners gain the depth classical networks enjoy. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum circuits are usually linear and share parameters across outputs. That caps what they can express.

Superposition is the lever: a flip-flop memory plus repeat-until-success steps embed many parameter sets at once. Amplitude transformations then supply polynomial activation functions, the missing nonlinearity. The architecture is described analytically, including parallel training of the packed models. On a step-function fit, a two-qubit version cut error a thousandfold against a matched baseline. A two-dimensional classification task gained accuracy and steadier runs. The authors pitch the design as hardware-efficient depth. Quantum machine learning needs such structural ideas, not just more qubits.
arxiv-2506-08849:
Qu and a team including Han tune vision language models for medical ultrasound in twenty twenty-five. Ultrasound's speckle and shadows clash with models trained on photos. Their hybrid tuning freezes the image backbone and adds a small adapter. The adapter filters frequency artifacts and gauges noise to recalibrate features.

Six multi center sets tested the tuned models on outlining and classing. They beat past adapters and medical vision language models by clear margins. Few shot cases held up with striking data thrift. Cross set spread was strong as well. Keeping old knowledge while modeling the noise is the key, they argue.
arxiv-2506-09149:
Daniel Caballero and Nicolás Yunes study the stability of neutron stars under small radial pulses, in two thousand twenty-five. Neutron stars are dense dead stars, and their matter can flow in ways that strain simple physics. Models of thick, fast-moving fluid must also respect the speed limit set by relativity.

The pair test three such fluid models on a neutron star background. For small thickness of flow, all three share the same stability pattern. They stay stable against some effects, but heat flow can unsettle them if certain heat conditions fail. The authors derive a rule for that case. Two models also add fast-moving pulse types that the third lacks.
arxiv-2506-09649:
Ankitha Bangera proves errors in a standard noise formula for staircase light sensors in a 2025 paper. The sensors, solid-state cousins of photomultiplier tubes, amplify light signals in steps. Each step's ionization is random, and that randomness is the main source of internal noise in the devices.

Recent groups estimated total noise with a formula by Capasso, itself built on a classic cascade noise formula. Bangera's proof shows where that reasoning breaks for an n-step multiplier. Wrong noise numbers mislead the design of sensitive cameras and detectors that rely on these sensors. The paper gives device physicists a corrected footing and a warning to recheck published estimates that used the faulty formula.
arxiv-2506-10449:
Ezequiel Smucler, Ludovico Lanni, and David Masip study a confidence set for treatment effects in this 2025 paper. The target is the local average treatment effect in instrument based studies. Their set comes from inverting a score test built on an influence function estimate. It stays valid even when the instrument is very weak.

Weak instruments can make the set stretch to infinity at some data laws. The authors list all six shapes the set can take, from a single point to the whole real line. At any fixed law it nearly matches the standard Wald interval from a doubly robust estimator. The gap shrinks at a known rate. In efficient cases the score set is optimal in width, in the sense made precise in the paper.
arxiv-2506-10549:
Takayuki Hayashi, Yoshiaki Hagiwara, and Masatoshi Imanishi wrote an astronomy paper in 2025. They studied three nearby galaxies that glow brightly in infrared light. Each galaxy seems to hide a bright active core deep inside dust and gas. The team asked where the radio waves from these galaxies come from.

They used a chain of radio dishes spread far apart to get very sharp views. Two galaxies showed tight, bright radio spots at their centers. In one galaxy, the spot was hot enough to prove the core is the source. In the third galaxy, no tight spot was seen. The authors also explain why the radio signal fades at high pitch in all three. Old particles from galaxy mergers, and in one case a young core jet, can account for the fade.
arxiv-2506-11149:
Igor Kuzmenko, Y. B. Band, and Yshai Avishai revisited a subtle quantum effect in 2025, the Aharonov-Casher phase. In this effect, proposed in 1984, a particle carrying a magnetic moment picks up a quantum phase while moving through an electric field, even where it feels no ordinary force. The authors ask how the phase relates to force, to fields that change in time, and to the better-known Berry phase.

They derive the general Hamiltonian for the effect using the Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation of the Dirac equation. For special geometries they obtain exact expressions for the phase. For a uniform electric field of any direction, they find the phase grows quadratically with field strength when the field is weak and linearly when it is strong. The work clarifies when the phase is a purely geometric quantity and when time dependence changes the picture.
arxiv-2506-11649:
Michal Šmíd and a large team of colleagues wrote a 2025 physics paper on a test of how light bends in empty space. Quantum rules say even a vacuum seethes with brief particle pairs. These make light passing near strong fields shift its polarization, an effect called vacuum birefringence.

Their darkfield method tries to catch that faint shift while blocking the main beam. The paper reports a proof-of-principle run of the setup. It also targets light-by-light coupling, where two light beams affect each other through the vacuum. Spotting either effect would confirm a long-standing quantum prediction. The team lays out the method so bigger tests can follow.
arxiv-2506-11949:
Tobias Oketch and Mohammad Sepehrifar present a 2025 study on predicting how long things last before they fail. Engineers model failure times with the Weibull curve, but a Bayesian take on the curve lacks neat prior rules. The pair build a flexible sampling method to fill that gap, using modern chain sampling in a standard stats tool.

They test 24 mixes of prior choices across 72 made-up data sets of varied shape. Their sampler adapts as it runs and handles curves that rise or fall in risk over time. The tests sort which priors keep the results steady and fair. As a real case, they predict the remaining life span of prostate cancer patients from past data. The work gives engineers and doctors a surer way to plan around failure and survival times.
arxiv-2506-13749:
Ari Shnidman and Artane Siad compute average sizes of class groups for a family of number fields in a 2025 paper. Class groups measure how badly unique factorization fails in a number system. Heuristics predict their average sizes, but some families misbehave.

For cubic fields built from cube roots, the authors find the average is 3/2 for wildly ramified fields and 2 for tamely ramified ones, a split older heuristics miss. Their proof rests on a new reciprocity law for relative class groups. They propose updated heuristics for families with a fixed symmetry group, which explain the odd split and predict similar surprises elsewhere in number theory.
arxiv-2506-14749:
Shiyu Cheng, Luyao Niu, Bhaskar Ramasubramanian, Andrew Clark, and Radha Poovendran plan motion for whole swarms at once with Swarm-STL, a two-stage framework for signal temporal logic tasks. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that per-agent planning collapses computationally as fleets grow. Swarm specifications instead state goals for cooperating teams collectively. Stage one abstracts each swarm into a reduced state space whose size ignores the agent count.

Planning happens at swarm level with safety and specification guarantees attached. Stage two derives low-level controls that keep individual agents on the synthesized paths. Single and multi-swarm trials complete every task safely. Compute time scales with swarm count, not agent count, so thousand-agent futures stay plannable.
arxiv-2506-15249:
Lucas Schulze, Jan Peters, and Oleg Arenz present context-aware physics models for robot control in this 2025 paper. Robots that learn their own physics can act in ways that generalize better. But a single global model fails when a scene holds many objects with unknown traits. Their answer is to identify a local model on the fly. Each local model covers only the objects that matter right now. The model style they build on keeps energy rules built in.

Energy rules may not hold across different contexts, they note. Still, each single local model should stay physically plausible. That plausibility matters when the model drives predictive control. The controller looks ahead over a short horizon to choose moves. Online identification keeps the model matched to the scene at hand. The work targets robots that handle varied objects.
arxiv-2506-15649:
Ankan Deria and co-authors present ViMaR, a two-stage method that makes image captions faster and more faithful. Their paper appeared in 2025. Search-based captioning scores many drafts, which is slow, and low-confidence text often slips through, causing made-up details. ViMaR first makes one pass to pick the best full caption from a set of drafts, using a learned value model. Then it repairs only the weak or poorly grounded segments.

A margin-based penalty, tuned to the model's confidence, discourages shaky continuations while keeping rich detail. Across several vision-language models, captions came out more accurate and detailed. Speed rose more than fourfold over older value-guided methods. The authors trained the system on one mid-size model and showed it transfers to others.
arxiv-2506-16249:
Arun Kumar and three co-authors turn a silica gel into a water-based lubricant in a 2025 paper. Oil and grease pollute; a gel of silica nanoparticles in salted water might replace them. The team measured the gel's flow behavior and tested it on steel sliding against steel, against dry and plain-water comparisons.

Tuning the gel's thickness optimized performance. At best, the friction coefficient fell by about 97 percent against both dry sliding and water, reaching 0.016, while wear dropped by up to 99.6 percent. The authors credit a self-repairing gel that forms a renewing film, with the particles acting as nano-bearings. The gel rebuilds itself at rest and slips into the contact zone under motion, they report.
arxiv-2506-16349:
Nikola Jovanović and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on marking images made by a class of AI image tools. These tools build a picture piece by piece, much like a text model builds a sentence word by word. A hidden mark in the output can show where a picture came from. That matters as fake images spread. No one had yet marked this kind of tool at the level of its building pieces.

The team hit a snag. When a marked picture is turned back into pieces, the piece order shifts, and the mark is wiped out. They fixed this in two ways. They retrained the piece maker so the round trip stays stable. They also added a layer that keeps the mark in sync. The mark then survives common edits, squeezing, and attacks meant to strip it. Tests give sound odds that a found mark is real.
arxiv-2506-16449:
Ixandra Achitouv and David Chavalarias map who sways whom in online debate during the 2022 French presidential vote, in a 2025 paper. They gathered daily posts on key topics from candidates and their close circles. Simple links can show who posts together, yet not who drives whom.

A causal method that reads how patterns rebuild each other let them sort drivers from followers. Some parties tended to start shifts in activity, while others tended to react. Health and foreign policy acted as sparks for cross party sway, above all at tense points in the race. The frame can help campaigns and analysts watch influence move in real time.
arxiv-2506-16749:
Ping Yang and co-authors predict unusually strong light responses in a flat, two-dimensional magnet, in a 2025 physics paper. The material is a single layer of a ruthenium compound whose electrons move in nearly flat bands, which concentrates their optical action. Its magnetism cancels out overall, a pattern called antiferromagnetism.

Computer calculations, checked against symmetry rules, point to a record twist of light polarization, reaching twenty-eight degrees. The material also absorbs light very unevenly by direction, with contrast up to fifty percent, far above other two-dimensional magnets. The two effects peak at different light energies, tracing a switch between flat and normal bands. Thicker films strengthen both effects. The authors see promise for tiny optical and spin-based devices.
arxiv-2506-18349:
Zichong Li and six co-authors shrink very large language models in twenty twenty-five. They work with mixture-of-experts models, where only some parts fire for each input. Such models are strong but huge, so fine-tuning or running them costs too much for many users. Retraining a small model from scratch is also dear.

Their framework, SlimMoE, compresses a big model in stages. It slims the experts and passes knowledge down through middle stages by distillation. That staged path limits the quality drop common in one-shot pruning. As a demo, they cut a model with about forty-two billion parameters down to under eight billion. Readers get a route to small, capable models without a full retrain.
arxiv-2506-18549:
Paolo Ferro wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It rebuilds quantum theory from a single intuition: a physical system can carry only a bounded amount of information.

Ferro formalizes that bound and adds a second hypothesis. If a measurement is nearly ideal, the information it yields should not depend on how it was performed or which quantity was probed. He expresses this through the geometry of a space whose points are system states. The description leans on statistics: systems are captured by parameters, and measurements by estimators of them. A divide-and-conquer construction then splits the space of two conjugate variables into a binary tree of nested sets. From these modest bricks, the paper claims, the linear and probabilistic skeleton of quantum mechanics rises.
arxiv-2506-18849:
Danilo Gambacurta and Marcella Grasso compute, in 2025, how long four atomic nuclei take to undergo beta decay, using an advanced many-body method. Beta decay half-lives test how well theory captures weak forces inside nuclei. Their method adds correlations beyond the standard approximation, including couplings to more complex excited states.

Those added correlations naturally weaken the effective strength of the decay, with no hand-tuned fudge factor. The resulting spectra are richer and more spread out, and half-lives come out shorter than the standard method gives, matching experiments better. Extra terms tied to angular momentum were also checked. Four nuclei from oxygen to tin anchor the test.
arxiv-2506-19849:
Shahar Hod studies edge cases that join a Schwarzschild black hole with a massive Proca field. The field is coupled in a non-minimal way. Past work showed that such fields in curved black-hole space can grow fast and turn unstable. Computer work showed that the start of the monopole instability rests on one unit-free value. That value joins the mass of the field and the place of a pole in its equations.

Hod uses math by hand to probe the critical cases at the edge of stability. He finds a short, compact formula for the set of Proca field masses that mark those cases. The formula holds when the pole sits close to the horizon of the black hole. Such hand results let teams check computer work. They also show just where stability gives way.
arxiv-2506-20849:
Ziyang Lu, Cenk Gursoy, Chilukuri Mohan, and Pramod Varshney wrote a 2025 paper on how a dual-job system should split its time. Part of the time goes to tracking targets in the sky. The rest goes to communicating with them. Such systems wed a radar eye to a communication set in one box. Time spent on one job is time lost to the other.

Their way is a learning tool with hard limits built in. It weighs the communication value of the position of each target, and feeds time to the communication side when value runs high. It must still keep the targets tracked within their span. Simulation runs show the tool lifts communication quality in fast-changing scenes, the team says. It holds the time limit while it does so.
arxiv-2506-21149:
Jaser and Toran link pebble games to algebraic proof systems in twenty twenty-five. Pebble games model the cost of computations on directed graphs. Algebraic proof systems refute formulas by polynomial reasoning. The authors study refutations of pebbling formulas, which encode pebble games as formulas.

They show a parallel between three game variants and three proof systems. A refutation with set degree and size yields a pebbling strategy with matching space and time. A pebbling strategy can likewise be turned back into a refutation. The space needed in each game variant matches variable space in its proof system. Using known pebbling bounds, they prove separations between the proof systems. Strong trade offs between degree and size are also shown for one system.
arxiv-2506-21649:
Andrés Macho-Ortiz and co-authors build an information theory for light-based computers in a 2025 paper. Digital electronics strain at real-time matrix work for tasks like AI and drug design. Programmable photonics, chips that steer light, promise fast, low-power analog computing. A companion theory already matches the math of computing to what the chips natively do.

What was missing was the information side: how much information such a chip can generate, transform, and recover. The new framework, API, supplies it. It also shows the computing scheme tolerates noise and hardware flaws well. That robustness avoids the heavy error correction quantum machines need. Together the two theories found a full foundation for on-chip photonic computing. The authors position photonics as a complement to digital, quantum, and brain-like machines.
arxiv-2506-21949:
Takuma Nishibuchi and Tetsuo Hyodo study hidden states in multi-channel particle scattering in a 2025 physics paper. Resonances show up as poles of the scattering amplitude in the complex energy plane. With several channels open, the math surface gains many sheets, and poles of different kinds appear.

The pair trace how poles on different sheets shape the spectra that experiments see. They follow one path in detail: a bound state turning into a resonance through a virtual state as a decay channel opens. The pole below threshold does not slide smoothly into the one above; instead the poles swap roles. Worked examples use meson-baryon models for two known Xi resonances. The authors show how the pole pattern prints onto measured mass distributions.
arxiv-2506-23049:
Leander Melroy Maben and co-authors introduce AURA in 2025, an open-source voice assistant that can act, not just chat. Speech systems have advanced fast, yet no open system offered full speech-to-speech talk over several turns with tool use and step-by-step reasoning. AURA joins open speech recognition, speech synthesis, and language models in one pipeline.

The assistant books calendar events, looks up contacts, searches the web, and sends email, and new tools plug in through plain prompts. On standard voice benchmarks it beat all open-weight rivals on one knowledge test, nearly matching a leading closed system, and scored well on a chat quality test. Human judges gave it ninety percent success on complex multi-turn speech tasks.
arxiv-2506-23349:
Naggita and LaChance argue that the scores used to price and select training data can quietly mislead. Data valuation methods rate how much each data point helps a model. Buyers in data markets might pay by those scores, so fairness matters.

Testing nine datasets and six valuation methods, the authors show simple preprocessing choices swing the scores wildly. Selecting data by score can deepen class imbalance. Data from underrepresented groups tends to be undervalued. They propose Data Valuation Cards, standard reports that disclose how scores were produced. Wider disclosure, they argue, would curb misuse and build trust in data markets.
arxiv-2506-23549:
Huai-Chih Wang and co-authors teach AI agents to coordinate with partners they have never met. Working with strangers is hard for multi-agent systems: training against diverse partners helps, but adaptation to a truly new partner is slow, and fine-tuning costs too many interactions. Their framework, CooT, uses in-context learning instead. Trained on recordings of agents with strong behavior preferences, it infers a partner's intent from a short history of play and aligns its own actions, with no parameter updates.

On two benchmarks, a cooking game and a football game, CooT beat population-based training, fine-tuning, and meta-learning rivals. Human judges also preferred it as a collaborator. Stress tests showed it adapts quickly and stays stable when a partner suddenly changes style. The authors aim the method at human-AI teamwork, where habits are unknown and retraining is costly.
arxiv-2506-24049:
Kévin Le Balc'h, Jingrui Niu, and Chenmin Sun revisit a basic question in control theory: from which regions can one observe a quantum particle's state on a donut-shaped surface? For the plain Schrödinger equation, any open patch, however small, suffices. Adding a magnetic field changes the story.

The authors study operators that combine electric and magnetic effects on the two-dimensional torus. They prove a geometric condition that is both sufficient and nearly necessary for observability, meaning some regions work and others provably cannot. The condition folds the magnetic potential into the geometry of paths across the surface. It can also be restated as a control condition on the magnetic field itself. The result closes a gap left by the classical theory, where magnetism was an afterthought.
arxiv-2507-00349:
Lü, You, and Zhao (2025) introduce a broad family of infinite-dimensional Lie superalgebras and settle their basic structure. A Lie superalgebra mixes ordinary symmetry rules with sign rules borrowed from physics. The family built here twists the known affine-Virasoro type. The twist uses a chosen derivation and a finite-order symmetry that commute. The class is wide. It contains many named algebras at once, from twisted Heisenberg-Virasoro algebras to the W-algebra W(2,2) and the N=1 BMS superalgebra.

The authors determine the universal central extension of the new algebras. That is the standard way of adding the central terms physics applications need. They then classify the well-behaved modules over them, cuspidal ones first, through a weighting method. Then they classify all simple modules with finite-dimensional weight spaces. The results gather many findings from math and physics into one frame, and add new examples.
arxiv-2507-00549:
Vijay Yadav and co-authors simulate how two tiny particles interact when a charged polymer floats between them in a 2025 paper. Charged polymers let engineers tune the surface charge of nanoparticles, a skill at the heart of many nanotech designs. The polymer here carries the opposite charge to the particles, so it is drawn to their surfaces.

A subtlety drives the study: particle charge is not fixed. It shifts with acidity, salt, and chain length, an effect called charge regulation. Their hybrid simulation lets charge adjust as the system runs, and they compare it with runs where charge is frozen. Regulation pulled more polymer onto the surfaces. With frozen charge, the polymer instead bridged the gap between particles across a wide range of spacings. The contrast matters for anyone designing particle assemblies.
arxiv-2507-01249:
The Belle and Belle II Collaborations published a 2025 paper reporting a search for a hypothetical particle in decays of B mesons. Axion-like particles are candidates in theories that extend the Standard Model, possibly tied to dark matter. If they exist with the right properties, a B meson could decay into a kaon plus the new particle, which would then turn into two photons. That signature is what the search targets.

The data come from electron-positron collisions recorded by the Belle detector, analyzed with its successor collaboration. Physicists sifted the collisions for the telltale kaon-and-two-photon pattern above noise. Searches of this kind either find the particle or fence off where it could still hide, narrowing the masses and coupling strengths allowed. The paper adds a checked corner in the hunt for physics beyond the particle list.
arxiv-2507-01449:
Tianyu Liu and co-authors speed up text generation by guessing ahead. In speculative decoding, draft tokens are proposed and the model checks several at once. Retrieval-based versions fetch drafts from a reference text instead of running a small model, but they often fail to find a match. The model's output scores for the last token hint at the next token and the one after. LogitSpec uses that hint twice over.

It first speculates the next-next token, then retrieves references matching the next and next-next tokens, widening the pool of drafts. The method needs no training and plugs into existing inference frameworks. On benchmarks it reached up to two and a half times speedup, with more accepted tokens per step. The authors release the code. The trick is a reminder that model outputs carry more information than the next word.
arxiv-2507-01549:
Jacob Elford and Timothy Davis lead a team checking whether dense gas line ratios can flag an active galactic nucleus, by comparing them against the classic optical verdict. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A tight link between dense gas and star formation anchors galaxy studies. Some claim the same lines betray a feeding black hole.

Five nearby unobscured nuclei were observed with a submillimeter array for three dense gas lines. Three targets yielded the needed detections. Even with the nucleus's influence, the galaxies obeyed the known gas-star formation relation. Optical spectra gave the standard excitation classification for comparison. Where both verdicts existed, submillimeter and optical agreed overall. The authors infer that nuclei excite dense molecular gas and thin ionized gas together. A new diagnostic survives its first cross-check. The survey's reference data set grows in value.
arxiv-2507-02549:
Yue Wu builds a controller that steadies a nonlinear system by a deadline the user picks, in this 2025 paper. Model-based control needs exact models, while pure data methods lack safety proofs. Wu's framework joins both: a data method first lifts the system into a high-dimensional linear model, called a Koopman model, and measures its error bound. A new adaptive backstepping design then works on that model.

The design dodges the complexity blow-up that plagues classic backstepping. Tests on the classic Van der Pol oscillator show the states settling near zero within the chosen time, from any start. All signals stay bounded. The author presents the pairing as a way to keep data-driven flexibility with proof-grade rigor for safety-critical control.
arxiv-2507-02749:
Hamza Boumaza and David Langlois study how neutron stars ring when nudged sideways, under a modified gravity theory, in a research paper from 2025. The theory adds a scalar field with higher-order terms while avoiding known instabilities. Star shapes under the theory were computed in earlier work.

The authors derive the equations for axial wobbles of such stars. They then compute the ringing tones, the quasi-normal modes, for several theory settings and matter recipes. Both tone pitch and fade time shift away from standard gravity's values. They also test how the tones track star compactness, probing whether the usual universal links survive the modification.
arxiv-2507-02849:
Talath, Govindaraja, Divyamani, and three colleagues demonstrate a leaner way to reconstruct quantum states in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Quantum state tomography normally needs many measurement settings; for three qubits the conventional Pauli approach uses sixty-three. Their scheme needs only seventeen settings for full three-qubit tomography. They ran it on IBM's one hundred twenty-seven qubit open-access processor in Osaka, preparing the entangled three-qubit W state.

They also implemented a two-qubit protocol with seven settings to reconstruct two-qubit marginals of the W state. Theory says any two of a three-qubit pure state's two-qubit reductions determine most such states uniquely. Strikingly, the W state rebuilt from its marginals had consistently higher fidelity than the one from full tomography. The authors present this as proof of principle that subsystem-based tomography is not just cheaper but practically better on today's noisy hardware.
arxiv-2507-03149:
Six authors, listed by first name in the record, study how accent strength shows up in the movements of speech in 2025. A strong accent means a speaker's sounds stray far from a standard pattern. The team wanted a measure based on how the tongue and lips actually move, not just how speech sounds.

They scored accent by comparing what speakers said with dictionary forms, sound by sound. A learned tool then guessed the hidden mouth movements behind the recordings. In read speech from American and British speakers, tongue position split the two groups best. The sounds most affected were the r-like vowels and low back vowels. The work aids tools that analyze accents on their own.
arxiv-2507-04749:
Chengyu Wang and co-authors present, in twenty twenty-five, a framework to rebuild three-dimensional shapes and their materials from photos taken from many angles. The core problem, inverse rendering, is to untangle shape, surface material, and lighting from flat images. Their method, MatDecompSDF, trains three neural parts jointly. One represents shape as a signed distance field, which gives the distance to the surface at each point. One predicts material traits such as base color, roughness, and metal content. One models the unknown scene lighting.

A rendering layer that follows physics links these parts back to the input photos, so training can proceed end to end. Extra rules enforce smooth materials and valid shape fields. Tests on synthetic and real data beat prior methods, and outputs can be edited and relit.
arxiv-2507-05549:
Khatiwada and four colleagues weigh the ethics of AI made art in twenty twenty-five. Image generators now flood creative fields, and public doubt is rising. Their study walks through five trouble spots. Each gets a history, a cause, and a set of views.

The spots are carbon emissions, false media, copyright breach, star likeness misuse, and artist job loss. Their research ties the tools to real harm in each area. Fixes are proposed case by case. The core claim is that the field needs proper laws and rules. Without them, the same harms will keep scaling, they argue.
arxiv-2507-05649:
Kaixiang Zhao and co-authors present in 2025 DESIGN, a framework for running graph neural networks on encrypted data without huge slowdowns. Fully homomorphic encryption lets servers compute on sealed data, but graph models under it are usually too slow for real time use. Their insight is that input graphs carry much redundancy that uniform processing wastes effort on every node.

The server scores node importance from encrypted degree data, then prunes unimportant parts of the graph. It also varies activation complexity by node importance. Tests show large speedups over prior encrypted methods with competitive accuracy. Code is public for secure graph analytics work.
arxiv-2507-05949:
Damianos Michaelides, Simon Bate, and Marion Chatfield describe a software package for the R language in a 2025 paper. The package, called hassediagrams, helps researchers map the structure of an experiment before they model its data. Getting that structure wrong can lead to the wrong model and misleading results.

The tool works out the layout structure of a design and draws it as a Hasse diagram. It then folds in how items were randomized, which yields a second, restricted structure that can also be drawn. The terms in that structure tell the analyst which terms belong in the model. The authors say this steady route keeps model choice consistent across studies.
arxiv-2507-06649:
Quantum circuits too big for today's machines can be cut into smaller pieces, run separately, and stitched back together. Friedrich Wagner and co-authors apply that trick to a sampling job: drawing candidate solutions from a trained optimization circuit called QAOA. Cutting distorts the results, broadening the spread of answers and shifting it toward worse ones. The team attacks the distortion by choosing cut points with integer programming, keeping the number of cuts as small as possible.

Cutting also shrinks each piece, which reduces the noise that corrupts real quantum hardware. In experiments on actual quantum processors, the trade favored cutting for large circuits: the noise saved outweighed the distortion added. Small circuits gained less, since their noise was already low. The authors read this as evidence that optimized cutting can stretch problem size and tame noise on near-term quantum machines.
arxiv-2507-07449: Takuma Byakuno proves an embedding theorem in metric geometry in this two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. The Gromov-Hausdorff space collects all compact metric spaces, with a distance measuring how nearly isometric two spaces are. Starting from a convergent series with positive terms, he takes for each term the spaces whose diameter stays below it. He proves the supremum-metric product of these subspaces embeds isometrically into the Gromov-Hausdorff space itself, a self-similarity result about the space of spaces.
arxiv-2507-08249:
Bill Marino and Ari Juels present a 2025 position paper on a new risk in artificial intelligence. Interest is growing in letting AI agents hold cryptocurrency and use smart contracts on their own. The authors argue that this step could open wholly new kinds of AI harm, not just faster versions of old ones. Money that moves on its own, with no human in the loop, changes what a rogue agent can do.

The paper first sets out the traits of crypto systems that make the pairing risky. It then lays out three new harm paths in detail, in what the authors call a first taxonomy of its kind. Traits such as instant, final payments and code-run deals leave little room to undo damage. The authors close with a call for more study of guards and limits, and offer first ideas as a start.
arxiv-2507-09049:
App reviews hide useful complaints about privacy and security inside a flood of everyday feedback. Aakash Sorathiya and Gouri Ginde present CMER, a method that mines those ethics-related reviews without hand-labeled training data. It pairs a language inference model, fed with domain-tuned test statements, with a large language model that does the final sorting.

The team tests the pipeline on more than 382,000 reviews of mobile investment apps. They compare several inference models and three language models, then combine the best of each. The combined system found 2,178 privacy and security reviews that a keyword search had missed. Those reviews can be turned into concrete requirements for app teams. The authors show the approach scales to a problem where ethical language is rare and specialized.
arxiv-2507-09349:
Ramos, Moriggi, and Machado present a paper from twenty twenty-five on dynamical entropy in high-energy nuclear collisions. The entropy notion extends earlier work on proton collisions to heavy ions. It can estimate the starting entropy density of the fireball. A gluon distribution function supplies the key probability input. Realistic models are built with scaling behavior and a classic collision approach. Normalization and scaling make the entropy nearly independent of nucleus size. Results are given as entropy density across rapidity.

The work ties entropy estimates to measurable gluon structure. It offers a bridge between theory and collision data. Heavy-ion programs gain a new diagnostic from the frame.
arxiv-2507-09749:
Beau Leighton-Trudel develops, in a 2025 paper, a test for when shared information between distant parts of a quantum chain can act like a distance. The recipe builds a number from mutual information, the amount two sites reveal about each other, and asks whether it obeys the triangle rule that real distances must follow. The test is tuned so a standard decay pattern gives back ordinary distance.

Under broad conditions, the author proves that slow, power-law decay of mutual information yields distance-like behavior, while fast exponential decay breaks it. An exact solution of the transverse-field Ising chain checks the claim. At the chain's critical point the decay sits near the benchmark power and the triangle defect stays harmless. In gapped phases the defect turns strongly positive, marking the failure of distance.
arxiv-2507-10049:
Yao Ma and Yong-Liang Ma study what scalar mesons are made of and how that makeup changes dense matter, in a 2025 physics paper. Mesons with spin zero come in several flavors, and their internal mix is disputed. The authors extend a linear sigma model with baryons. They add flavor structures built from antisymmetric tensors of the chiral groups. They tune the model to reproduce nuclear matter at its normal saturation density, while keeping known vacuum facts.

With those anchors, the model predicts a plateau in the symmetry energy at middle densities. That feature is needed to match both a famous neutron star merger signal and lab data on lead nuclei. Neutron star structures are then computed for several parameter sets. The work links a particle's inner recipe to the size of the densest objects in the universe.
arxiv-2507-10349:
Zhiyuan Zhao and co-authors present, in a 2025 forecasting paper, a transformer model built to predict demand peaks across many future weeks at once. Retailers need such forecasts for buying and stocking, and holiday or promotion peaks are the hardest and the most costly to miss. Their model leans on context known ahead of time, like sale events.

A new attention scheme aligns each future week with the context that shapes it, inside both the reading and the writing halves of the model. On two large in-house retail data sets, peak accuracy rose by up to thirty percent. Overall accuracy stayed level with the best rivals. The authors aim the tool at smoother shopping during big events.
arxiv-2507-10449:
Han and four co-authors built a question-answering dataset for coral reefs in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Reef photos hold vital health clues, but reading them takes expert eyes. Vision-language models could let anyone query reef images, if trained on the right data. No large dataset existed for that purpose.

CoralVQA gathers nearly thirteen thousand real reef images from three oceans and sixty-seven coral genera. Over two hundred seventy-seven thousand question-answer pairs probe ecology and health. Marine biologists helped build a semi-automatic labeling pipeline for quality. Benchmarks of leading models exposed clear weaknesses in reef reasoning. The authors offer the set as a foundation for conservation tools.
arxiv-2507-13349:
Adam Smercina leads a team reading the life story of a wispy galaxy being torn by its giant neighbor. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. F8D1 is an ultra-diffuse satellite of the M81 galaxy. It is among the nearest of its kind beyond the Local Group. Tides are visibly disrupting it. Deep Hubble images resolve its individual stars.

Two deep fields cover the center and a spot along its long axis. Eight shallower fields trace the rest. Star formation histories are computed field by field. Those histories reveal what made the galaxy so diffuse. Tidal processing, bursty feedback, and spin are rival explanations. The evidence weighs them for this one clear case.
arxiv-2507-13549:
Jim O'Connor and three co-authors train racing controllers in a game in twenty twenty-five. The game is Xpilot-AI, which now has a new racing mode. Its physics includes inertia, friction, and gravity, making driving a hard control task. The team used NEAT, a method that evolves both the shape and the weights of neural networks.

The racing mode allows flexible track designs and tests many agents in parallel. That makes it fast to improve controllers over generations. Evolved controllers cut lap times by up to about a third compared with their starting point. They also learned sound racing tactics, such as better lines through corners. Readers see neuroevolution produce skill from scratch in a tough physics setting.
arxiv-2507-14049:
Paweł Budzianowski and co-authors present EdgeVLA in 2025, a leaner design for robot control models that see, read, and act. Big models of this kind can guide many robot tasks, but they run too slowly on small robots with tight power and memory. The team wanted real-time speed without losing skill.

Their first change drops the step-by-step guessing of the robot hand's target spot, which sped up responses about sevenfold. Their second change swaps the big language core for a small one, which trained just as well in early tests. The result matched a leading open model in training behavior while using far less memory. The team released the model and code for others to build on.
arxiv-2507-14349:
Anthony Badea, Austin Baty, and a large team measure the shape of particle collisions using archived data in a 2025 particle physics analysis note. Thrust shows how pencil-like or spherical the debris of an electron-positron annihilation is, a classic probe of the strong force. The data were recorded decades ago by a detector at the European laboratory's former collider, at the energy of the Z boson peak.

Using archives again with modern methods squeezes new precision from old collisions. Event shape measurements test quantum chromodynamics calculations and help tune the simulations every collider study depends on.
arxiv-2507-14749:
Wai Keen Vong and Brenden M. Lake tested whether a computer model can learn words from the kind of input a small child actually receives. A child learns language from limited daily experience, while large models train on enormous datasets. An earlier study trained a network on sixty-one hours of video and speech from one child's head camera and found it could link words to the things they name. The open question was whether that success depended on that one child.

The pair used automatic transcription across the full SAYCam collection, over five hundred hours from three children, and trained networks on each child's data. Models learned word meanings that carried across videos, children, and image sets, though each child's input left its own pattern in what was learned.
arxiv-2507-14849:
Yifei Wang and co-authors present a 2025 study of a trade-off in training smaller language models to reason. Copying the long reasoning chains of a top model can lift a small model's reasoning sharply. What that heavy diet does to the model's other skills, such as finding and using facts inside a long document, was largely unexplored.

The team tested a family of open models distilled from a leading reasoning system across long-context tasks. These tasks matter for search-augmented systems that must pull the right facts from long inputs and reason over them. Their checks bridge two skills often studied apart: step-by-step reasoning and long-context understanding.
arxiv-2507-14949:
Philippe Balbiani and Olivier Gasquet settled the complexity in twenty twenty-five of deciding satisfiability for a bimodal logic combining transitivity with weak density. Modal logics extend reasoning about necessity and possibility; adding axioms changes how hard it is to test whether a formula can be true somewhere. The authors' prior work introduced windows as a device for polynomial algorithms in a related logic.

After revisiting the folklore bimodal K4 case, they show windows, mixed with standard bimodal algorithms, decide the transitive weak-density case in polynomial space. Both satisfiability and validity come out PSPACE-complete. The paper is a technical completeness result: it pins this logic's difficulty exactly and showcases the windows method as a reusable proof technology.
arxiv-2507-16249:
Srivatsan Krishnan and co-authors use many learning agents to map neural networks onto chips, in a 2025 paper. Mapping decides where each part of a network runs, and it shapes speed and energy use. The space of choices is vast, and single agent search wastes many trials.

Their team of agents splits the search, and a clustering step gives like choices to the same agent. That keeps parallel training from stepping on itself. Trials showed the method needs far fewer samples than a single agent to reach a good map. Delays and energy delay scores fell by large factors at equal sample counts. The work targets accelerator design.
arxiv-2507-18249:
Cyber ranges let power grid defenders practice against attacks without risking the real grid, but building one by hand is slow and costly. Muhammad Roomi and co-authors present a 2025 framework that generates such ranges on its own.

The team first defines a modeling language for smart grids, written in a format both people and machines can read. The language folds in standard configuration files used by real grid equipment. A tool chain then reads a model and builds a working cyber range from it. Models can be shared and rebuilt elsewhere, unlike one-off custom ranges. The authors aim to close the gap between lab research and live grid defense training.
arxiv-2507-18949:
Yongjie Li, Ruilin Nong, Jianan Liu, and Lucas Evans present a framework for adaptive learning in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large language models can tailor study paths to each student. Their system uses model-powered analytics on live learning data to shape a personal curriculum.

The framework keeps assessing each learner and adjusts pathways and resource picks to match progress. Teaching strategies shift with the data, keeping material relevant and engaging. Trials across varied school settings showed clear gains in engagement and knowledge retention. The authors argue the approach can move standard teaching toward a more student-centered model.
arxiv-2507-20449:
Noor and co-authors build a network for matching researchers with collaborators, based on what people write about rather than whom they cite. Their topic-based network uses a topic model with a science-tuned language model to link researchers across fields by shared interests. A distortion worries them: prolific authors publish across many topics, so their minor interests drown under their main ones and the network misses links.

Their fix is cloning. Each author's publications are clustered by topic, and every cluster becomes its own node, letting one person belong to several communities at once. Judged on the resulting groups, the cloned network produced more meaningful communities than the plain one. It also surfaced a wider range of possible collaborations, which the authors offer as the practical payoff for interdisciplinary teams.
arxiv-2507-20849:
Yilun Qiu and co-authors personalize large language model output by comparing users with each other in a 2025 paper. Most personalization leans on a user's own history alone. Yet how a user differs from peers who liked similar things carries strong signals. Writing those differences into text prompts, though, often fails to capture them well.

Their framework works in the model's hidden space instead. It builds soft prompts from the gap between a user's embedding and peers' embeddings. A sparse filter then keeps only features relevant to the task before feeding them into a frozen model. On review-writing tests, the method beat baselines across several measures. The authors share their code for others to try.
arxiv-2507-21049:
Zedong Wang, Siyuan Li, and Dan Xu rebalance multi task learning at the representation level in a 2025 paper. One network learning many tasks can suffer when tasks fight. Standard fixes rescale losses or massage gradients in the optimizer. The shared representation space, where tasks actually meet, was largely left alone.

Their method, Rep-MTL, scores how salient each task is inside that shared space. Entropy penalties steer those saliencies away from domination. Sample wise alignment across tasks encourages sharing of useful features. The goal shifts from pure conflict removal to protecting each task's training. Four benchmarks covering task and domain shifts tested the idea. Even with plain equal loss weighting, gains were competitive. Power law checks confirmed better balance among tasks.
arxiv-2507-21349:
Amirmohammad Shamaei and co-authors use a patient's earlier brain scans to rebuild new ones faster, in a 2025 paper. MRI is a mainstay of brain care, but long scan times raise costs and tire patients. A previous scan of the same person carries much of the needed detail. Earlier methods aligned that old scan with slow classic tools. Their pipeline pairs a first reconstruction network with a learned alignment model and a transformer that polishes the result.

They tested it on 2,808 images from 18 people, speeding scans by factors of five to twenty. The method beat rivals on quality scores at every speed. Brain segmentation run on the rebuilt images also matched reference results more closely. Total rebuild time fell sharply against classic alignment, which the authors say suits live clinical use.
arxiv-2507-21449:
Rohan Hitchcock and Jesse Hoogland propose a benchmark for local sampling in neural networks in a 2025 paper. Network loss landscapes have flat, degenerate regions, and common sampling algorithms carry global guarantees that rest on shaky assumptions there. The authors argue evaluation should shift from the whole posterior to local regions. Their benchmark tests how faithfully samplers reproduce local posterior shape, and it scales to very large models.

Several popular algorithms were compared on it. A preconditioned variant of Langevin sampling represented local geometry best. The authors note global guarantees are still missing, but useful local information can be extracted even in huge models.
arxiv-2507-21749:
Veerababu Dharanalakota, Ashwin Raikar, and Prasanta Ghosh present a dynamic learning rate scheduler in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The learning rate strongly shapes neural network training, yet it is usually fixed in advance. Complex problems often need the rate to adapt as training unfolds.

Their scheduler adjusts the rate from the loss values seen during training itself. They test it on physics-informed neural networks and on image classification with plain and convolutional networks. In these tests, the scheduler sped up training and made it more stable. The authors pitch it as a simple fix for a common tuning headache. Adapting the rate to the loss curve replaces guesswork with feedback.
arxiv-2507-22749:
Luca Biferale and co-authors release a large data set on how pollution spreads in churning air, in a 2025 paper. Finding a leak or smoke source from a few sensor hits is hard, since gusts scatter the traces. The team built clean test data that search methods can be graded against.

The data come from direct simulations of full three dimensional flow. They track hundreds of millions of tracer particles released from five point sources, with and without a mean wind. Each record holds a particle path and the local flow speed along it. The set also gives smoothed density maps for quick tests of source finding methods.
arxiv-2507-23049:
Shih-Yu Chang published a research paper in 2025 extending a mathematical tool for tracking how operators change when perturbed, into the harder world of continuous spectra. Many of them in quantum theory and geometry have smeared-out spectra and no tidy basis, and the non-self-adjoint ones are unstable to analyze. Multiple operator integrals organize such questions.

Chang builds the generalized theory for them. It covers their algebraic rules, continuity, size bounds, and a perturbation formula that extends classic results. As an application, a spectral shift formula of Krein type is derived and pushed to arbitrary accuracy orders. The framework is meant to serve spectral theory, operator algebras, and noncommutative geometry alike.
arxiv-2507-23449:
Shervin Rahimzadeh Arashloo presents a method for spotting odd patterns in streams of data that change over time, in a paper from 2025. The catalog title differs from the title printed in the text; the text's version names signature-kernel one-class learning. The method learns what normal data looks like and flags what strays. Older tools compare data point by point and miss the shape of the whole path.

His method reads each series as a path, using a kernel built for that view. It also adds a penalty that respects how normal data clusters in space. The math keeps the same form as the base method, so old solvers still run. Tests on five known benchmark sets place the method near the top of the field. It also handles unevenly spaced samples, which real sensors often produce.
arxiv-2508-00349:
Yuga Kanaya and Kenjiro Takazawa study popular matchings in a 2025 mathematics paper. A popular matching pairs people or items by preference in a way that would win a majority vote against any rival pairing. Checking popularity directly takes far too long, so researchers use two kinds of shortcuts to test it.

One shortcut describes the graph structure of such matchings, tailored to each problem variant. The other uses best weight matchings and works the same way for all variants. The authors prove each shortcut can be derived from the other, for three variants of the problem. Their proofs give a unified view, rather than relying on both describing the same matchings.
arxiv-2508-01449:
Mohamed Belfkir, Mohamed Amin Loualidi, and Salah Nasri use machine learning to sharpen a search for double Higgs boson events, in a paper from 2025. The target decay leaves two bottom quarks and two photons, a rare and faint signal at the Large Hadron Collider's current energy. The team trained two classifiers on simulated events: a boosted tree model and a graph neural network that uses event geometry.

The graph model beat the tree model clearly. It tightened the expected upper limit on double Higgs production by about twenty-eight percent. Both beat the latest published experimental results on limits and on the Higgs self-coupling constraint, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-01949:
Nasir Sohail, Aftab Shah, and Kristo Väljako study a question in abstract algebra in a 2025 paper. Semigroups are sets with a rule for combining pairs of items. Some semigroups sit inside richer ones that also allow undoing moves. Whether a given ample semigroup fits that way is known to be undecidable in general.

The authors narrow the question to special classes of ample semigroups. For those classes, they give answers on when the embedding works. They seek fits that keep all three operations of the host intact. Examples in the paper split the left and right versions of the ample property. Some semigroups hold one side but not the other. The work maps parts of a boundary that no general method can cross.
arxiv-2508-02449:
Zhibing Zhang and Qian Zu proved Liouville-type theorems for a complex fluid system in two thousand twenty-five. The equations describe magneto-micropolar fluids, which carry magnetic fields and tiny rotating particles. Liouville theorems say that under set growth limits, the only steady solution is the trivial one.

Using an iteration method, the special structure of the equations, and new mixes of interpolation tools, they prove such results when solution size grows slowly on ring-shaped regions. An energy method plus careful analysis of a linked equation then relaxes the limits by logarithmic factors. The loosest limit falls on angular velocity, which may grow at any polynomial rate in their result.
arxiv-2508-02749:
Road crews plan repairs from forecasts of how pavement will decay, and most forecasts treat each road stretch as if it stood alone. Lu Gao, Ke Yu, and Pan Lu argue the network matters in a 2025 paper. A stretch's neighbors share traffic, weather, and ground, so their decay should rhyme.

The team feeds a graph neural network the road map itself, letting each stretch learn from its neighbors' state. Their test bed is a Texas data set with over half a million pavement readings, one of the largest in the field. Models that used the network layout beat those that ignored it. For agencies that must stretch repair budgets, sharper decay forecasts mean fixing the right mile at the right time.
arxiv-2508-02949:
Jakub Karnowski and Przemysław Szufel wrote a 2025 paper on oligarchic economies, with Ukraine as the case in point. There, a few rich owners rule key sectors and join mines, mills, and power plants under one roof. They also grip key networks, which blocks rivals and locks in waste.

Past work praised the gains of breaking such rule, but proof by model was scarce. The authors build a computer model where firms with mixed skills trade inside a value chain. Some firms sit under oligarch grip and some do not. Runs of the model score how distinct break-up plans change total output growth. Results show the best plan depends on where the oligarch sits in the chain. At times the fix is raw access; at times it is grip on deals.
arxiv-2508-03049:
Jun Zhang, Chao Yi, Mingxi Ma, Mengling He, and Chao Wang tackle sharper hyperspectral images, a key task in remote sensing. Their paper from two thousand twenty-five notes that these images have a huge number of spectral bands. That size makes methods that mix low-rank and smooth priors hard to apply head-on.

Their method, called JLRST, works on a smaller subspace form of the image instead. It checks gradients of grouped coefficient tensors in all three modes to use spectral links and shared patterns. A log-based norm cuts bias from the standard tensor norm. In tests, the method beat top model-based rivals on both speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2508-03249:
Pritha Paul and Chris Clarkson draw pictures of how relativity bends the apparent shapes of cosmic structures, in this 2025 paper. Astronomers map galaxies by redshift, and motion along the line of sight squashes round clusters into ellipsoids, a famous distortion. On the largest scales, subtler effects from the Doppler shift and from gravity's own redshift join in.

Those higher order effects break the symmetry of the squashing, turning spheres into egg or bean like forms. The authors work out how over dense regions, clusters and superclusters with matter falling in, and under dense voids with matter flowing out, should look once the full relativistic treatment is applied. The pictures matter practically: stacking voids to measure them assumes they stay radially symmetric, and they do not.
arxiv-2508-03749:
Fiorista and five co-authors counted platform crowds from security cameras in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Transit agencies need live crowding estimates, but fare data and staff reports are blunt tools. The team tested three computer vision routes on station footage from Washington's metro. Over six hundred hours of privacy-protected video fed the study.

One route detects and counts each person with modern object detectors. A second classifies the whole scene's crowd level with a vision transformer.
