Codes from the smaller, sign-alternating states are spectrally stable but carry eigenvalues of negative Krein signature, a warning sign for stability. Computer work then identifies which stacked mixtures of the two kinds remain spectrally stable.
arxiv-2511-12749:
Zong-Han Bai and Po-Yen Chu ask when pooling information across many sparse demand series actually helps a forecast. Retailers must predict intermittent demand, where most periods sell nothing. A forecaster decides how much of each item's past to keep and how much to borrow from related items. In their hierarchical Bayesian hurdle model, one forgetting rule applied at both levels turns those two choices into a single decision with two opposing effects.

Forgetting keeps a shared prior influential, but raises the noise that fine differences must rise above. The authors turn that trade-off into a diagnostic that screens, in advance, for cases where refining pools cannot pay. On five public panels with over nineteen thousand series, the diagnostic was right both ways. One panel with room to improve resisted, which they flag as an open problem.
arxiv-2511-13049:
Antoine Ledent, Mun Chong Soo, and Nong Minh Hieu bound the error of recommender systems that learn from clicks as well as ratings. In their matrix completion setting, both the true preference matrix and the distribution deciding which entries get observed are low rank and share a subspace. Abundant unlabeled data, the implicit feedback of clicks and purchases, comes from that distribution, while labeled explicit ratings are scarce and noisy. Combining low-rank subspace recovery with classic generalization theory, they prove an error bound with two terms, one shrinking with the unlabeled sample size and one with the labeled.

Synthetic experiments confirm the error really splits that way, and on Douban and MovieLens, with most ratings removed, their method beat baselines using explicit ratings alone. The theory formalizes the intuition that implicit feedback carries real information about preferences.
arxiv-2511-13549:
Rayirth Bhat, Justin R. David, and Semanti Dutta test holographic entanglement formulas with vector excitations in three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. They quantize a massive Chern-Simons field and compute its single-particle states' effect on entanglement entropy across a Ryu-Takayanagi surface. The correction is evaluated at the first sub-leading order in Newton's constant.

The lowest state matches a spin-one primary operator in the dual field theory, with the rest forming its descendant tower. Their entropy from the Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena formula agrees exactly with a replica-trick calculation in the dual theory at leading and sub-leading order. A careful check shows the edge mode adds nothing after vacuum subtraction, which the match requires.
arxiv-2511-13849:
Duncan Farrah and 25 co-authors ask how well astronomers can measure the brightness of dusty, infrared-bright galaxies. Such galaxies build stars and black holes, but their power is usually estimated by fitting model curves to infrared data points. The team used simulated observations of a well-studied nearby sample to test how each choice in the data affects the answer.

They find that covering the peak of a galaxy's infrared output, with dense sampling, matters most, keeping bias under about twenty percent for starburst and active nucleus power. Host galaxy light is harder and usually comes out too low. Their tables of bias and error can guide work with JWST and future far-infrared missions.
arxiv-2511-14249:
Rui Liu, Yuan Zhao, and Zhenqi Jia argue that automatic movie dubbing sounds fake because it skips the director. Real dubbing starts with directors feeding actors reference footage so they absorb a scene's emotion before performing. Their system, Authentic-Dubber, rebuilds that director-actor loop around a multimodal reference footage library.

Language models help the system grasp emotional content across the library's signals. At dub time, an emotion-similarity retrieval step pulls the reference material closest to the target silent clip. The generated voice then matches both the speaker's timbre and the intended feeling, while keeping lip sync. A progressive learning scheme ties the pieces together toward more authentic dubbed performances.
arxiv-2511-14349:
Junfu Pu, Teng Wang, Yixiao Ge, and three co-authors cut hour-long videos into navigable chapters with summaries at several levels. Lectures, podcasts, and documentaries are hard to browse, and earlier chaptering tools trained on small sets with short, coarse labels that missed subtle transitions. ARC-Chapter is a model trained on more than a million long-video chapters with bilingual, time-grounded, hierarchical annotations.

The training data were built by unifying speech transcripts, on-screen text, and visual captions into multi-level labels from short titles to long summaries. A new metric, GRACE, rewards flexible many-to-one segment matching plus semantic similarity. Experiments show large gains over the previous best and strong transfer to new domains.
arxiv-2511-14549:
Su Yang, Sathyanarayanan Chandramouli, and Panayotis Kevrekidis study dispersive shock waves in periodic lattices. Such waves appear in optical waveguide arrays and in superfluids held in optical lattices. The model is a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a periodic potential. Initial data join two distinct nonlinear periodic modes in a piecewise smooth way.

A tight binding approximation reduces the system to a discrete model with a Riemann problem. Each constant state stands for a Floquet-Bloch mode of the full system. The reduction works best for deeper potentials. The authors then apply Whitham modulation theory to interpret the wave dynamics. The framework links lattice physics to classic shock wave analysis.
arxiv-2511-14749:
Alexander Vedernikov, Puneet Kumar, and three co-authors use vision-language models to clean up noisy labels in student engagement videos. Judging engagement from video is subjective, so training labels often disagree, and that noise caps how well detectors can learn. The team lets a large vision model do the first pass at quality control.

A questionnaire draws behavioral cues from each clip, and clips are split into high- and low-reliability groups. Training then follows a curriculum: clean clips first, doubtful clips later with softened labels that reflect the doubt. Classic vision models trained this way improve on the raw data. The lesson is that strong models can serve as noise handlers for weaker ones.
arxiv-2511-14849:
Adeel Mahmood and Aaron B. Wagner refine the theory of sending information over a noisy Gaussian channel under detailed power limits. Real transmitters face more than a simple average power cap: peaks and other traits of the power pattern can each be limited. The authors model this with a general setup where any finite set of power statistics can be constrained at once.

Through a careful higher-order analysis, they characterize the best possible error rate as a function of the main coding rates. Older limits, from the plain maximum power rule to recent mean-and-variance rules, fall out as special cases. Sharper limits tell engineers how close practical codes can come to perfect on power-limited links.
arxiv-2511-15049:
Antonio Enea Romano shows how dark energy perturbations can be encoded as an effective coupling between matter and gravity. Dark energy is expected to perturb and thus alter how cosmic structures evolve. Romano finds that effect can be written as a coupling that depends on momentum, position, and polarization. That compact encoding clarifies several observational consequences at once.

For scalar perturbations the effective coupling can turn locally negative where dark energy is underdense. With phantom dark energy it can also explain suppressed structure growth at low redshift. For gravitational waves the coupling makes emitted radiation depend on polarization and frequency. The framework ties evolving dark energy hints to concrete, testable signatures in structure and wave data.
arxiv-2511-15749:
S. Preethi, Ankush Kamboj, Ramkarn Patne, P. A. L. Narayana, and Kirti Chandra Sahu find a new instability in a thin liquid layer driven by wind at its top and rotation at its base. The setup mimics ocean surface flows shaped by wind stress and Earth rotation. Stability analysis asks which small disturbances grow instead of fading, and the linearized problem is solved both numerically and with a long-wave approximation.

New long-wave unstable modes appear whenever the rotation measure is nonzero. The most unstable mode uses disturbances that vary across the flow but not along it, and it becomes unstable at the lowest parameter values. The approximation matches the numerics well and confirms the mode analytically, showing a combined wind and rotation effect not reported before.
arxiv-2511-15849:
Batya Kenig extends a key tool of parameterized algorithms to problems that must cut some links while keeping others intact. Important separators are minimal vertex cuts with a maximality property that keeps the set of useful cuts small enough to list. Cut-uncut problems add a demand: a chosen terminal set must stay linked to the source side. Standard separators ignore that demand.

Kenig defines connectivity-preserving important separators and bounds how many of bounded size can exist. A listing algorithm enumerates them in terms of a min-cut subroutine. Uses include better bounds for mixed multiway cut-uncut problems and a faster method for an annotated odd cycle problem with protected terminals.
arxiv-2511-16249:
Zihao Liu and six co-authors present controllable layer decomposition for reversible multi layer image creation. Designers build images layer by layer, but once layers are flattened into one raster, layer level editing is lost. Matting and inpainting methods recover layers only with limited control and precision. Their method separates a raster image into distinct editable layers with fine grained control.

A dedicated decomposition transformer decouples elements into layers. A multi layer conditional adapter injects target image information into layer tokens for precise conditional creation. A new benchmark and tailored metrics support comprehensive evaluation. Reversible decomposition would let editors revise finished artwork structurally. The work targets design workflows where layer structure is creative capital, not disposable metadata.
arxiv-2511-16749:
Shivani Harer and a large LISA test-bench team report validation of an optical interferometer demonstrator built for the LISA gravitational wave observatory. LISA is a European Space Agency mission set to launch in the mid-2030s with arms millions of kilometers long. The space detector needs picometer path length stability, and ground demonstrators must prove the technology first.

The Zerodur interferometer, called ZIFO, reduced bench noise enough to hold the needed stability specification across the millihertz to one hertz band. The team also identified and characterized the dominant remaining noise sources, including phasemeter noise and beam tilt leaking into the path length readout. The results validate critical technology for the test setup of LISA's interferometric core.
arxiv-2511-17149:
Marius Ghergu and Zhe Yu analyze what can happen at a single singular point of an elliptic equation set in a punctured ball, a domain with its center removed. Their first question is integrability. For a differential inequality with a nonnegative, radially symmetric potential, they find optimal conditions under which any smooth solution, and the terms built from it, remain integrable up to the missing point. That extends a 1982 result of Brezis and Lions, which covered only constant potentials.

Their second question concerns a nonlinear equation whose right-hand side involves a convolution, a weighted average of the solution's powers with a singular kernel. For dimensions three and up, they give sharp conditions on the exponents for singular solutions to exist, and describe exactly how those solutions blow up near the origin. The two-dimensional case is classified separately.
arxiv-2511-17249:
Riccardo Tedoldi and five co-authors present FlexiFlow, a generative model for drug discovery that designs a molecule and its shapes together. A molecule's three-dimensional conformations govern its properties and how tightly it can bind a protein target, yet leading design models produce only a single conformation. FlexiFlow extends flow matching so it samples a molecule jointly with an ensemble of its low-energy shapes, while respecting the symmetries the physics demands.

On the QM9 and GEOM Drugs benchmarks, the model generated valid, unstrained, novel molecules that matched the training distribution closely. Its conformational ensembles covered the relevant shapes about as well as established physics-based methods, at a fraction of the computing time. The model also transferred to designing ligands for a given protein pocket, even when training data lacked conformations for that task.
arxiv-2511-17349:
Christoph L. Schröder and Harvey B. Meyer develop coordinate-space perturbation theory for quantum field theories that contain a single mass scale. Working in Euclidean space of general dimension, they expand in Gegenbauer polynomials and derive analytic expressions for several three-point correlation functions in theories mixing one massive and one massless field. The technical core is a systematic study of antiderivatives of products of Bessel functions times powers of their argument.

Such results serve calculations with high-degree vertices, at finite temperature or in finite volume, and auxiliary computations for lattice treatments of hadronic effects in precision observables. As an illustration, the authors compute the one-loop propagator of a massive particle coupled to a massless one, in vacuum and at finite temperature. The paper is a toolkit contribution for perturbative quantum field theory.
arxiv-2511-17449:
Machine-learned interatomic potentials have become the default tool for atomistic simulations that do not track electrons explicitly. Standard guidance warns that these models need exhaustive training sets and must not be used beyond the training space. That confines them to interpolation and rules out finding new phenomena by luck. Iñigo Robredo-Magro and three co-authors take a more sanguine view and test two widely used approaches with minimalist training sets.

Their training sets rest on little prior knowledge of the materials, and the models use modest default settings. Even so, the models predict non-trivial structural effects correctly, in quality and nearly in quantity. The effects include competing polymorphs, energy barriers for structural changes, and non-trivial topologies. The authors argue that such cheap, easy models can serve as tools for finding novel and complex physical phenomena, not just for filling in known ground.
arxiv-2511-17649:
Juntao Cheng and nine co-authors introduce SWITCH, a benchmark for agents that must operate physical control panels over long stretches. Panels, remotes, lifts, and built-in screens fill daily life, and using them takes more than spotting a button: an agent must act. Watch the state change, and check whether the goal was reached. Older tests mostly grade single steps or passive looking, missing that loop.

SWITCH holds over a thousand interactive videos shot from a first-person view across many kinds of device. Each is labelled with instructions, actions, state changes, outcomes, and recovery moves when things go wrong. The set also probes whether models can picture how a scene evolves. For builders of household and workplace agents, it offers a far sterner test than one-step benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-17849:
Shuyuan Fan and Zhao Zhang present Pier, a training method that cuts the global communication slowing down pretraining of large language models. Synchronizing many processors often dominates cost, so Pier builds on an approach that syncs less often, with local training steps in between.

Two fixes to the outer update, warming up its momentum and then decaying it, keep training stable and preserve model quality. Across GPT models of several sizes, Pier speeds training several fold on large graphics clusters, with no loss on validation or on a suite of downstream tasks. The design also supports mixing data and tensor parallelism.
arxiv-2511-17949:
Ali Jafari, Mohamed Mousa, and Mostafa Nouh build logic gates out of sound waves traveling in a solid, so computation happens mechanically without converting signals to electronics. Earlier mechanical logic relied on slow shape changes or active materials, limiting speed.

Using topology optimization to search a huge design space, they carve voids into a uniform plate so waves interfere and concentrate energy at readouts that encode a logic function. Experiments confirm the gates work and tolerate uneven loading. By combining gates into a mechanical adder, they show the approach can scale toward larger signal processing circuits with very low power needs.
arxiv-2511-18149:
Kingshuk Adhikary, Darren Moore, and Radim Filip show how to create quantum states of an oscillator that carry coherence, a genuinely quantum feature, using only absorption of single quanta. Linear absorption through a saturable system can make non Gaussian states, but they merely approach simple number states and show no coherence.

Adding a minimal nonlinear absorption process changes the picture. The two individually passive processes together are not passive, so coherence emerges and grows in phase space with no external drive. The resulting states develop a complex asymmetric pattern, unlike the symmetric patterns from either process alone. Extensions cover other absorbers and switching schemes.
arxiv-2511-18249:
Mostafijur Rahman Akhond and Gias Uddin use a test trick to make code writing by large language models more sound. Vague user specs lead models to give mixed or wrong code. Their agent, CodeMetaAgent, uses paired rules that say when two inputs should count as the same task in new words.

Those rules guide the agent to sharpen the spec and build test cases that stay true to the task sense. Trials run on three code test sets with four large models. Scores rise by up to about a sixth, and test cover nears full in the best runs. The work shows a classic test idea can curb model drift when it steers the prompt, not just the check at the end.
arxiv-2511-18549:
Kerr Maxwell loosens a core rule in geometric quantization and tracks what changes. Quantization turns a classic phase space into a quantum system, guided by a symplectic form and a curvature rule on a line bundle. Maxwell weakens that curvature rule and calls the result geometric pseudo-quantisation.

Such a structure, he shows, arises in a natural way from plain shifts of the symplectic form and from pulling back the quantum data by maps that do not preserve the form. The main result derives motion equations for some simple cases. Worked cases from symplectic and near symplectic geometry follow, plus the general shape of the bent commutator that sets quantum order. The study maps how far the classic rule can bend.
arxiv-2511-18649:
Goun Pyeon and nine co-authors grade large language models on a fresh national math exam with no chance of leaked answers. Past test sets may sit inside model training data, which inflates scores. The team digitized all questions of the 2026 Korean College Scholastic Ability Test math section within two hours of its public release.

Twenty four top models took the test in text only, image only, and mixed forms, with prompts in Korean and in English. The GPT-5 family hit perfect scores in a limited set of setups. Three rival models also scored near the top, and a small open model scored high as well. The clean set gives a rare leak free read of model math skill.
arxiv-2511-18749:
Matthew R. DeVerna, Kai-Cheng Yang, Harry Yaojun Yan, and Filippo Menczer test large language models as end to end fact checkers of political claims. Hopes run high for auto checks, and chatbots now ship with reasoning and web search that users trust for verification. Past studies gave mixed grades, so a hard test was due.

Fifteen recent models from four makers faced over six thousand claims checked by PolitiFact. Base models did poorly; reasoning helped little; web search helped a fair bit, though the checks sit on the open web. A curated search system fed with PolitiFact summaries more than tripled the score on average. The lesson is plain: curated context, not raw access, makes model fact checks reliable.
arxiv-2511-19149:
Moazzam Umer Gondal, Hamad Ul Qudous, Daniya Siddiqui, and Asma Ahmad Farhan build a system that writes fashion captions and hashtags from product photos. Plain image captioners often miss details such as fabric or fit and struggle on new styles. Their pipeline grounds the text in detected facts before any writing happens.

A YOLO detector finds each garment, color clustering extracts dominant shades, and a CLIP-FAISS search infers fabric and gender from a product index. Those facts, plus style examples, guide a language model to write the caption. Compared with a fine-tuned BLIP baseline, the retrieval pipeline covers attributes better and generalizes more broadly.
arxiv-2511-19449:
Adeline Guéret asks how many individual electric car profiles a power system model really needs. Adding dozens of separate battery electric vehicle profiles, instead of one averaged profile, keeps real variety but slows the model down. Too few profiles can distort the optimal plan the model produces.

Tests show accuracy rises with profile count only up to a threshold, after which extra profiles add little robustness. For fleets of five to twenty million vehicles, the rule of thumb is one profile per two hundred thousand to two hundred fifty thousand vehicles. The study also checks whether the choice of specific profiles skews results, guiding modelers on time versus accuracy.
arxiv-2511-19549:
Axel Petzold, Joachim Pum, and David P Crabb review whether lab tests for brain disease biomarkers actually measure what they claim. These blood and spinal fluid tests guide diagnosis and trials for neurodegenerative diseases. A key validity check is parallelism: diluted samples should track the test's standard curve, or reported amounts can be biased.

The registered systematic review gathers studies from late 2010 to mid 2024 and grades how often partial parallelism appears and how well it is reported. The check was rare and unevenly reported in most assays, with narrow dilution ranges limiting reach. The authors call for transparent protocols, with stakes for trial design and approvals.
arxiv-2511-19649:
Angelo Gaspar Diniz Nogueira and four co-authors fight Android malware with synthetic training data. Attackers now use AI to spin endless malware variants, while defenders struggle to gather and label fresh real samples. Machine learning detectors starve without current data. Their method, MalSynGen, fills the gap artificially.

A conditional generative adversarial network learns the statistical shape of real malware data and produces synthetic tabular samples that preserve it. Classifiers trained with that data are then tested for detection quality, data fidelity, and computing cost across several data sets. The aim is stronger Android malware detection that keeps pace with fast-changing threats.
arxiv-2511-20249:
Bonte, Devillez, Dusollier, Hertz, Mélot, and Schindl ship a web tool for extreme molecule graphs. Their 2025 paper presents ChemicHull for chemical graph theory. Topological indices summarize molecular structure as numbers. Degree-based ones add edge weights from endpoint degrees. Chemists use them to predict physical properties.

The tool studies graphs where vertices have degree at most three. Such graphs model conjugated molecular systems. Each graph maps to a point in three-dimensional space. Extremal index values become linear optimization over a polyhedron. Only a small family of graphs can ever be extreme. Some graphs provably never win for any index. ChemicHull finds and displays the extremal graphs interactively. Known results for trees and unicyclic graphs were recovered easily. A published Randić index result fell to a counterexample. The tool exposed that error directly. Anyone can now test extremal hunches online. Mathematical chemistry gains a shared proving ground.
arxiv-2511-20349:
Kherchouche, Galpin, Dumas, and colleagues speed up video encoding by guessing block splits. Their 2025 paper attacks VVC intra partitioning complexity. The Versatile Video Codec gains about fifty percent efficiency over HEVC. Its encoder pays with a far heavier search. Trying every block split is the main cost.

Two learning methods estimate split costs cheaply. A regression network predicts normalized rate-distortion costs per block. Neighboring blocks' costs feed in as features. The design works for any block size uniformly. A second method frames splitting as a decision process. A deep Q-network agent learns from split trajectories. It sees two depths of decisions before choosing. Fixed thresholds turn estimates into split decisions. Both methods skip most of the exhaustive search. Quality losses stay controlled by the thresholds. Future work aims at rate control reuse. Encoder designers get size-independent acceleration tools. Real-time VVC encoding moves closer.
arxiv-2511-20449:
Rigutto, Ratz, and Mendez rebuild smooth flow fields from scattered measurements. Their 2025 paper improves radial basis function regression for fluid data. Such meshless methods reconstruct velocity fields from particle tracking. Round, identical kernels struggle near sharp gradients, though. They produce spurious wiggles where flows turn anisotropic. The new method adapts kernels to the flow itself.

Local polynomial fits estimate gradients at the data points. Those gradients guide smarter resampling of the measurements. Dense sampling lands near steep gradients; smooth regions thin out. Each basis function stretches along the local flow direction. Observed gradients enter the fit as soft extra constraints. Tests included simulated turbulent channel flow data. A measured turbulent jet provided the experimental case. The method beat isotropic versions on accuracy and smoothness. It used ten times fewer basis functions overall. Computation time dropped by about half on average.
arxiv-2511-20649:
Hidir Yesiltepe and colleagues at Virginia Tech describe in 2025 a way to let video-generating models run without a built-in time limit. Today's autoregressive video models hit a wall because their position code, called 3D RoPE, fails past 1024 latent frames. Long videos also react slowly when the prompt changes, and they cannot jump between scenes like edited film.

Their fix, named Infinity-RoPE, works at run time and needs no retraining, so an already trained model can use it directly. One part recodes each new block of frames against a moving reference point, removing the 1024-frame ceiling so generation can continue indefinitely. A second part keeps only two frames in memory, the first and the newest, so fresh prompts take effect at once. A third part deliberately breaks the position code to create clean scene cuts inside one stream, and the system beat earlier models on overall VBench scores.
arxiv-2511-20849:
Dong Dong and Weijie Su redesign in 2025 the tokenizer, the component that chops text into the tokens a language model actually reads. Standard Byte Pair Encoding builds its vocabulary by frequency alone. Length-MAX instead optimises average token length, choosing a vocabulary that covers text with as few, long tokens as possible, cast as a graph partitioning problem with a greedy solver.

On FineWeb and other domains it produced 14 to 18 percent fewer tokens than BPE for vocabularies of 10,000 to 50,000, and 13.0 percent fewer at 64,000. GPT-2 models trained from scratch at three sizes reached a fixed validation loss in up to 18.5 percent fewer steps, with inference latency down as much as 13.7 percent and throughput up 16 percent at the smallest size. Downstream quality rose too: LAMBADA perplexity fell 11.7 percent and HellaSwag accuracy gained 4.3 points. Coverage hit 99.62 percent of vocabulary with only 0.12 percent out-of-vocabulary rate, and inference memory dropped 18 percent.
arxiv-2511-21349:
Dario Corona, Stefano Nardulli, Ramon Oliver-Bonafoux, and Giandomenico Orlandi count the many ways a superfluid-like system can swirl on a curved surface, in 2025. Their equation is the time-independent Gross-Pitaevskii equation, a Schrödinger-type model of superfluidity and nonlinear optics, posed on a closed Riemannian manifold. Solutions arise as critical points of the Ginzburg-Landau energy that carry a prescribed momentum set by a background velocity field.

Corona and his coauthors prove lower bounds on how many distinct solutions must exist. The count is governed by the topology, the hole-and-handle structure, of the set where the velocity reaches its maximum. Their regime assumes small momentum and tiny vortex cores. The proof blends critical point theory with Gamma-convergence for Ginzburg-Landau energies, plus new results on codimension-two isoperimetric problems in the small-flux regime that may interest geometers independently.
arxiv-2511-21449:
Steffen Tillmann, Felipe González, and Stefanie Elgeti ask what shape a 3D printer nozzle should be, and answer with simulations in 2025. In fused deposition modeling, molten plastic is squeezed through the nozzle, and pressure loss inside it caps printing speed. Most printers still ship standard nozzle shapes. The authors built an optimization framework that tunes the nozzle two ways: by a single cone angle, or by a flexible spline curve describing the whole profile.

Tillmann and his coauthors compared two melt models. Under a shear-thinning viscous model, the best half-opening angle depends strongly on feed rate: fast feeding favors angles near 30 degrees, while slow feeding prefers wider cones. A viscoelastic model showed a much weaker dependence. Surprisingly, the fancy spline profiles bought only marginal pressure savings over the single-angle designs, a useful reality check for nozzle engineering.
arxiv-2511-21549:
Jason Yik and ten coauthors give brain-inspired chips their first proper performance manual, in 2025. Neuromorphic accelerators compute with event-driven, brain-like architectures that exploit sparse activity, promising efficient machine learning at the edge. Yet engineers optimizing workloads for them relied on crude network-wide sparsity counts whose link to real speed was never checked. The team set out to find what actually limits these chips.

Yik and his coauthors combine analytic modeling with measurements on three real accelerators: BrainChip's AKD1000, SynSense's Speck, and Intel's Loihi 2. They identify three bottleneck states, memory-bound, compute-bound, and traffic-bound, and which workload settings trigger each. Their floorline model, modeled on the classic roofline chart, shows at a glance where a workload sits and how to improve it. Applying the method yielded up to 3.86 times faster runtimes and 3.38 times lower energy at equal accuracy compared with hand-tuned configurations.
arxiv-2511-21649:
Mohamed El Jbari, Fernando García, Hugerles Silva, and Felipe de Figueiredo work out exactly how to detect bits sent as modulated noise, in 2025. Thermal noise communication powers ultra-low-energy wireless links for Internet of Things devices by varying the noise level itself instead of transmitting a carrier. Real channels fade, though, and earlier analyses leaned on Gaussian approximations that ignore fading and inflate errors.

Working under Rician fading, the team derives the optimal detection threshold from chi-squared statistics, plus a bit error probability formula evaluated by Gauss–Laguerre quadrature. The model eliminates approximation error and stays accurate even at small sample counts. Simulations by Monte Carlo confirm the analysis and show significant error-rate improvements over Gaussian-based detectors. The study also quantifies how sample size, resistance ratio, and the Rician K-factor each move performance, giving receiver designers a rigorous foundation.
arxiv-2511-21749:
Svitlana Volkova and six coauthors build BRIES, a compound AI system that detects influence attacks and tests whether defenses against them work, in 2025. As language models generate convincing content at scale, reactive takedowns lag behind. BRIES instead borrows inoculation theory from psychology: exposing audiences to weakened attacks works like a vaccine.

Four dedicated agents divide the labor. A Twister generates adversarial content using targeted tactics. A Detector identifies attack types with tunable settings. A Defender crafts resistance-building content, and an Assessor uses causal inference to measure whether it worked. Experiments used the SemEval 2023 Task 3 technique taxonomy on a synthetic dataset. Skill varied sharply by model. GPT-4 excelled on complex techniques like Appeal to Fear and Whataboutism. Open models such as Llama3 and Mistral struggled with subtle tricks, including Equivocation and Red Herring, suggesting architectures differ in the speech patterns they encode.
arxiv-2511-21849:
Saberi asks a practical question about networks: with eleven published measures of centralization, the extent to which a network is dominated by a few hub nodes, which ones can actually be trusted? Saberi normalizes all eleven onto a common scale, then tests them against six basic postulates any sound measure should obey.

The second test runs them on textbook graphs, stars, rings, and complete networks, plus disturbed versions with known answers. The measures disagreed sharply despite sharing the same goal. Three came out as most reliable: normalized betweenness centralization, which captures dominance over paths, normalized closeness centralization, which captures ease of reach, and normalized degree centralization, which captures raw hub connectivity. Applied together to real networks from different fields, the three gave complementary views that no single measure provided, so Saberi recommends reporting them jointly rather than picking one favourite.
arxiv-2511-22049:
Richland, Kiiskinen, Wang, and colleagues, including Hastie and Tibshirani, adapt uniLasso, a two-stage sparse regression method, to computing polygenic risk scores at biobank scale. The method first fits each genetic variant alone, then uses those univariate coefficients and their sizes to guide a second. Penalized fit, which stabilizes feature selection when predictors are heavily correlated, as neighboring variants in the genome typically are.

Applied to the UK Biobank, with over a million variants measured on hundreds of thousands of people. The adapted method matches the standard Lasso's predictive accuracy while selecting substantially fewer variants, giving sparser and more interpretable risk scores. Standard multivariate methods tend to smear one causal signal across its whole correlated neighborhood. It also outperforms the widely used PRS-CS competitor, and folding in external summary statistics improves prediction further while keeping the model sparse, a practical combination for large genomic studies.
arxiv-2511-22249:
Lai, Wang, Rambhatla, and colleagues diagnose why bigger latent spaces make worse pictures. Latent diffusion generates images inside an autoencoder's compressed space, and raising that space's dimensionality keeps improving reconstruction while generation quality deteriorates. Through controlled perturbations in both pixel and latent domains, the team traces the mismatch to frequency: decoders lean heavily on high-frequency latent components to restore fine detail. Encoders under-represent those bands, so diffusion training barely sees them and underfits them.

Their fix, FreqWarm, is a warm-up curriculum that front-loads exposure to high-frequency latent signals during diffusion or flow-matching training, with no autoencoder changes or retraining. Across high-dimensional autoencoders it cuts generation FID, by 14.11 points on Wan2.2-VAE, 6.13 on LTX-VAE, and 4.42 on DC-AE, with gains growing at higher dimensionality. The authors argue autoencoders and diffusion models should be co-designed around frequency budgets.
arxiv-2511-22549:
Feng and colleagues design one image codec serving both human viewers and machine vision systems. Compression is tuned for one audience: pictures that look good to people, or pictures algorithms read well. The authors argue the two goals share a foundation, because preserving a scene's semantic content matters for both, and quality even helps machines extract features. Their Diff-ICMH framework builds compression on a pre-trained diffusion model, whose generative prior supplies realistic detail.

Two additions keep meaning intact at low bit rates. A Semantic Consistency loss penalises reconstructions whose semantics drift from the original. A Tag Guidance Module feeds the diffusion model tags, nudging generation toward the right content for very few extra bits. Across diverse machine tasks, a single bitstream from this one codec supported analysis with no task-specific retraining, while humans still saw high-quality images, a route to versatile compression.
arxiv-2511-22849:
Al Asif and colleagues profile the Mamba architecture to find where its time goes. Selective state space models promise Transformer-level quality with linear scaling. Nobody had mapped Mamba's runtime behaviour in detail: which components dominate, and how costs grow from 64 to over 16 thousand tokens. They profiled computation, memory access, and I/O across that range for Mamba-1 and Mamba-2.

The state space module is the bottleneck, accounting for more than half of total computation and memory. Acting on that, the authors prune low-activity states inside the module, removing redundancy while leaving expressive power intact. Within a moderate pruning regime the result was a 1.14 times speedup and 11.50 percent lower memory usage across sequence lengths, with accuracy maintained. The study doubles as a design guide: optimise the update rule first; dynamic cache allocation and hardware-optimised sparse-state computation are next steps.
arxiv-2511-22949:
Zhao and colleagues propose a new way to get rid of axion domain walls. These sheet-like defects formed in the early universe. They would otherwise grow to dominate its energy and wreck standard cosmology. Axions are hypothetical particles invented to solve a puzzle in the strong force and are also a dark matter candidate, so their leftover walls are a real problem to clear away.

Instead of adding a bias term that breaks the underlying symmetry, as earlier fixes do, they couple the axion to a twisted primordial magnetic field. They run three-dimensional lattice simulations of the wall network. The coupling drives the walls to collapse. The decay speed depends strongly on the field's correlation length, with both very short and very long lengths slowing the collapse. The process also yields a gravitational wave signal that future pulsar timing experiments could detect.
arxiv-2511-23149:
Del Vecchio and colleagues project how precisely the FCC-ee electron-positron collider could measure the Higgs boson's decays into quarks and gluons. These hadronic modes probe how the Higgs gives fermions their mass. Their combined fit is the first to cover all hadronic decays at once, using both Higgs-strahlung and vector-boson-fusion production and treating interference effects in the neutrino final state.

Assuming four detectors of the IDEA design collecting data at 240 and 365 giga-electronvolts, the study reaches percent-to-per-mil precision for the modes, with expected uncertainties of 0.21 percent for bottom-quark decays and 1.75 percent for charm decays in Higgs-strahlung at the lower energy, both stated alongside the gluon and strange results. It also establishes first sensitivity to the rare decay into strange quarks, opening a path to evidence for the strange-quark Yukawa coupling that the LHC cannot reach.
arxiv-2512-00449:
Turbulence is usually studied in three dimensions, but its character changes with the number of dimensions available. Richard Ho and co-authors measure that effect with direct numerical simulation in 2025. They solve the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with forcing at different spatial dimensions.

The team measures turbulent and chaotic properties, including Lyapunov exponents, which quantify how fast nearby flows diverge. Those exponents fell with dimension in their runs, turning negative in six dimensions at modest Reynolds numbers. Such results test basic theories of chaos and turbulence in a clean, controlled setting. Direct numerical simulation resolves every scale, which is why dimension studies use it. Lyapunov exponents turn the vague word chaos into a measurable number. For folks who study storms in air or sea, the gain is a clean lab. The spin of chaos can be weighed as the room it plays in gains new sides.
arxiv-2512-00649:
Mutual information measures how much two parts of a quantum system know about each other. Beau Leighton-Trudel introduces a geometric scaling relation for correlations in one-dimensional quantum spin chains in 2025. The construction defines an informational distance from the mutual information between regions.

A geometric conversion factor quantifies the local scale behavior of that distance. Turning information into geometry echoes ideas from holography, where distances emerge from entanglement. A clean scaling relation in spin chains could give physicists a new ruler for criticality and correlation, tested in systems simple enough to compute exactly. One-dimensional chains are the systems where such informational geometry can be computed exactly. Mutual information is zero for independent regions, so the distance responds to correlation alone.
arxiv-2512-00749:
G Bande and G Franzoni present a physical model of the Reeb foliation in a 2025 math paper. A foliation slices a space into surfaces stacked like pages in a book. The Reeb foliation is a famous example on a solid torus, often shown only in drawings and proofs.

The paper first explains basic ideas from the modern theory of foliations, in order to describe the Reeb example clearly. Then the authors build what they call the first full physical model of it. They use geometric methods tied to 3D printing. Holding a model in hand can make an abstract shape far easier to grasp.
arxiv-2512-00849:
Yunbo Long, Jiaquan Zhang, Xi Chen, and Alexandra Brintrup tackle private clustering across sites in a 2025 paper. Federated clustering groups data held by many owners without pooling it. Local differential privacy adds noise at each site to protect individual records before anything is shared.

The challenge is keeping clusters accurate under strong noise and uneven data, without many rounds of communication. Older one-shot methods lean on unstable pairwise distances or rankings and degrade badly. The team's topological method uses gravitational potential fields to guide cluster centers. A steadier method could let hospitals or banks cluster jointly without exposing raw data.
arxiv-2512-01049:
Heman Shakeri and four coauthors give a fast algorithm for finding light cycles in graphs in a 2025 paper. Cycles are basic features of networks, shaping robustness, information flow, community structure, and dynamics. Tools that probe cyclic structure are in demand across graph mining, network optimization, bioinformatics, and social network analysis.

Their algorithm finds minimum weight cycles, the cheapest loops under edge costs, in cyclic graph topologies used in mining. Faster cycle finding helps analysts spot feedback loops and redundant paths in huge networks. The paper aims for efficiency without losing exactness about which cycle is lightest.
arxiv-2512-01849:
Klaas De Kinder and Christophe Caloz build a framework for dispersive space-time varying media. Space-time media can steer waves in unmatched ways. Most studies assume ideal, nondispersive matter. Real platforms disperse, with response shifting by frequency. That gap limits design claims.

Their framework finds which frequency transitions are physically allowed. Waves scattered at moving boundaries are the test case. Allowed-transition rules guide real device design. Dispersive honesty brings space-time optics closer to lab-ready filters and switches. Moving boundaries model Doppler and lens effects together, so allowed transitions guide both communication links and exotic lens designs.
arxiv-2512-01949:
Multimodal language models turn images and video into long streams of visual tokens, and processing all of them is slow and memory-hungry. Zhongyu Yang's 2025 paper, called Script, prunes those tokens, discarding the redundant ones, while keeping the ones that matter for the user's actual question.

Earlier pruning methods often ignored the query, cutting tokens by generic importance, or leaned on attention scores with known limits. Script instead builds a graph over the tokens and conditions its choices on the query's meaning. Smarter pruning promises faster, lighter multimodal models that still answer with the visual detail the question needs.
arxiv-2512-02049:
Waves bouncing off several objects at once, multiple scattering, are costly to simulate across a whole volume. Rémi Marsal and Stéphanie Chaillat work in 2025 with the boundary element method, which needs values only on the objects' surfaces, and build a physics-inspired network around it, called PIBNet.

In the boundary approach, one first solves an integral equation for the wave's trace on each boundary. The full solution everywhere else then follows cheaply from a boundary integral formula. A network designed around that structure inherits the method's efficiency. Faster scattering simulations serve acoustics, electromagnetics, and any field where waves meet cluttered geometry.
arxiv-2512-02449:
Brendon McBain, Yi Hong, and Emanuele Viterbo study how users switch between satellites in low Earth orbit networks. Their 2025 study tackles handover, the moment a link passes from one fast moving satellite to the next. Older theory often assumed short serving times, or grew too hard to compute for real plans.

The authors build a general math framework that works for any handover rule a network might use. It measures long term average capacity, meaning the data rate users can expect over time. People who design or run large satellite fleets get a cleaner way to compare switching rules first. It also gives teams a fair way to test new rules side by side.
arxiv-2512-02949:
G. Q. Garcia and three co-authors study fermions living on a spacetime where time and space scale differently. Lifshitz spacetimes break the usual balance between space and time scaling. The authors examine two dimensional Weyl fermions in such a background, in two space and one time dimensions.

Using the Dirac phase method, they show how geometric phases arise from coupling to the Lifshitz geometry. They also check for well behaved fermionic zero modes. Zero modes and phases of this kind matter for topological matter, where geometry leaves fingerprints on quantum states. Odd space time is more than a game. Such back drops test if our rules for spin and phase hold when the stage is bent out of shape.
arxiv-2512-03549:
Long coding tasks need agents that check their own work. Yuki Orimo and co-authors introduce PARC in this 2025 work. PARC is a coding agent built for autonomous, robust execution of long-horizon computational tasks.

Its design is hierarchical, with planning, execution, and self-assessment layers. A separate mechanism evaluates actions and outcomes from an independent context and feeds back. Self-reflection could cut the silent errors that plague long agent runs. That matters as firms delegate longer software tasks to AI. Independent feedback contexts reduce self-deception, a known risk when agents grade themselves.
arxiv-2512-03749:
Image generators trained on web-scale data absorb the stereotypes present in that data and reproduce them in their pictures. Korada Sri Vardhana, Shrikrishna Lolla, and Soma Biswas introduce SelfDebias in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Their method reduces biased outputs from text-to-image diffusion models without any human-labelled training data.

SelfDebias works at test time and fits any diffusion model that uses a UNet to predict noise. It finds clusters of meaning inside an image encoder's representation space, then steers generation so the output distribution spreads more evenly across those clusters. No external classifiers or concept-by-concept annotation are needed. Experiments across prompts and model designs show the method generalises to both conditional and unconditional models. It softens demographic stereotypes while keeping images sharp, and it also helps with subtler, abstract biases that are harder to name.
arxiv-2512-03849:
Spacecraft can ride halo orbits around a planet-moon pair, but the highly tilted versions of those orbits behave in complicated ways. Chankyu Joung, Dayung Koh, and Otto van Koert chart that behaviour in a 2025 dynamical systems preprint. Their setting is the circular restricted three-body problem, where a small craft moves under two larger bodies, sometimes passing dangerously close to the lighter one.

Using a Hamiltonian formulation with Moser regularisation, the team built tools that trace periodic orbits and their stability even near collision. They describe vertical collision orbits and the families budding from them through pitchfork, period-doubling, and period-tripling bifurcations, including halo and butterfly families. Those families are then continued into real systems such as Saturn-Enceladus, Earth-Moon, and an equal-mass pair. The resulting maps give mission designers groundwork for polar orbits, including future flights through the plumes of Enceladus.
arxiv-2512-03949:
Jets at the Large Hadron Collider start either from quarks or from gluons, and telling the two apart sharpens nearly every analysis. The ATLAS Collaboration reports a transformer-based tagger for that job in a 2025 experimental preprint. The algorithm reads properties of a jet's constituents, gathered by the detector's tracker and calorimeter, and classifies the jet's origin.

Performance is measured on dijet data from proton-proton collisions across the collider's second and third runs. Two routes estimate what pure samples look like in data. One is a simulation-heavy matrix method. The other, jet topics, leans less on modelling the underlying physics. Efficiencies in data differ from simulation by factors the paper tabulates. The jet topics method carries notably smaller systematic uncertainties in places. The collaboration presents the tagger as a robust instrument for precision measurements and searches for new physics.
arxiv-2512-04049:
TT Arietis is a nova-like binary whose brightness flickers on many timescales, including puzzling quasi-periodic oscillations. I. Vega-Manubens and colleagues reanalyse those oscillations in a 2025 preprint, using far more complete data than earlier studies. The MOST space telescope watched the star continuously for hundreds of hours during its bright state in October 2012.

Their method searches short stretches of data for frequencies, then groups neighbouring detections into frequency groups: episodes of steady or slowly drifting oscillation. They catalogue about one hundred sixty groups with periods between roughly fourteen and fifty-three minutes, lasting a few hours each and often wandering in frequency. Sometimes two groups run at once. Tests on randomised data show chance explains only a fraction of the groups. Their appearance shows no link to the superhump phase, leaving the oscillations' origin open.
arxiv-2512-04249:
An underactuated robot that must repeat a motion forever, a walking cycle or a flapping wing, needs its periodic trajectory stabilised against disturbances. Maksim Surov and Leonid Freidovich present a control design for that job in a 2025 robotics preprint. Their systems have one degree of underactuation, and the standard optimal control design for such cycles is computationally heavy.

The method combines partial feedback linearisation with subspace stabilisation. Studying motion across the reference orbit yields a linear time-varying system possessing a stable subspace. Sliding-mode control then drives trajectories toward that subspace. The design avoids solving costly regulator problems, the expensive step, and improves robustness to matched shocks. Experiments on the Butterfly robot validate the methodology.
arxiv-2512-04449:
Suyeon Lee, Kangkyu Park, Kwangsik Shin, and Ada Gavrilovska present AXLE, a system that moves work into smart memory chips and streams results back without stalling the host. New CXL links let computers add far-off memory that can also compute in place. That near-memory work can cut the cost of hauling data back and forth. Yet older offload schemes ignore trade-offs between distinct CXL routes. Their 2025 arXiv paper maps those trade-offs first.

AXLE pairs two CXL protocols so results flow back while new work flows in, a scheme the team calls Asynchronous Back-Streaming. Light host-side control keeps the pipeline full across both sides. In tests, end-to-end run time fell by as much as half on fitting workloads. Gains hinge on data size and compute weight, which the study charts. The design points toward data centers that treat memory as an active partner.
arxiv-2512-04649:
Yarden Sheffer, Ruihua Fan, and Ady Stern devise new ways to detect the chirality of exotic quantum phases straight from their ground-state wavefunctions. Two-dimensional chiral topological phases are famous for the gapless modes that run along their edges. How that edge anomaly hides inside the bulk wavefunction was only partly understood. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds entanglement measures that expose it without touching an edge.

The trick is to take several copies of the wavefunction in neighboring regions and permute how they join. The seams left behind are called permutation defects. The measures built on those seams stay robust under small changes. Standard topological field theory misses the chiral piece, yet the authors' field-theory frame recovers it exactly. Reading chirality from the bulk could help identify new topological materials, where edge access is hard and bulk data is what experiments give.
arxiv-2512-04849:
The PandaX Collaboration, with Zhe Yuan, Zihao Bo, and many co-authors, reports the most precise measurement yet of double beta decay in xenon-136, from deep underground in China. In this rare decay, a nucleus sheds two electrons at once. Its smooth energy spectrum tests the Standard Model and may hide signs of new physics. Their 2025 arXiv paper analyzes the full spectrum recorded by the PandaX-4T detector over a large exposure.

The team measured the two-neutrino half-life with an uncertainty half that of their prior result, the tightest value to date. They also extracted a ratio that compares the subleading and leading parts of the nuclear matrix element, and it agrees with theory. A search for Majoron-emitting decays, a channel beyond the Standard Model, accompanies the main result. Precision spectra like these discipline the nuclear theory that any future discovery claim must use.
arxiv-2512-05749:
Dexuan Zhou, Huajie Chen, Cheuk Hin Ho, Xin Liu, and Christoph Ortner speed up a trusted method for finding the ground state of quantum systems. Variational Monte Carlo guesses a wave function and tunes it to lower the energy. The best tuning method, stochastic reconfiguration, corrects the gradient with a large covariance matrix. Inverting it again and again is unaffordable for large networks.

Their 2025 fix is to warm start the linear algebra. A singular value decomposition from the previous step gives a head start, and a low rank picture of the matrix is refined as iterations proceed. The costly inversion shrinks to updating a compact approximation. Tests on typical atomic and molecular systems show the method works well inside real variational Monte Carlo runs. The advance matters because the method is prized for steadiness where plain gradient methods stall. Making it cheap lets deep wave functions use it in practice.
arxiv-2512-06049:
Laura Rinaldi, Alvise Sommariva, and Marco Vianello release ORTHOCUB, a software package for computing integrals and derivative values over polynomial spaces in several variables. Cubatures sit underneath much of computational physics. It computes its rules from orthogonal polynomial moments, with near minimal cubature inside a bounding box. The design avoids the usual numerical trap: no matrix inversion or factorization is ever needed, so conditioning problems do not arise.

It all reduces to moments and matrix vector products. Matlab and Python codes are free, as building blocks for larger solvers. The value is the combination: a clean construction, no standard failure modes, liftable code. Cubature in many variables is a quiet bottleneck across applied mathematics; a stable, ready made tool for it is infrastructure, and infrastructure compounds.
arxiv-2512-06249:
Matthew Prest and four co authors study how disorder changes the way light matter hybrids push on each other inside a tiny cavity. The hybrids, called polaritons, form when light trapped in a cavity mixes with excited states in a thin semiconductor layer. Random flaws in that layer are usually seen as a nuisance, something engineers try to smooth away.

The team works out the energy patterns of both the bare excitations and the hybrids, this time with disorder built into the math. Their sums show that the flaws do not weaken the hybrids. Instead, disorder makes the push between two polaritons stronger than it would be in a clean layer. That result matters for devices that rely on these particles bumping into each other, such as low power switches and simulators built from light. It hints that a bit of mess can be a feature, not only a flaw.
arxiv-2512-06649:
Camellia Zakaria and five co authors estimate a harmful soot pollutant from traffic cameras that cities already run. Black carbon pours from traffic, gathers near big roads, and falls hardest on nearby marginalized neighborhoods. Measuring it takes pricey specialist gear, so most streets have no readings at all, and policy flies blind on local sources. Traffic video, by contrast, is everywhere.

Their system reads vehicle behavior and conditions from the video and blends those features with weather data. The model then estimates black carbon at street level, matching held out readings with solid accuracy. The point is leverage: no new sensor network, just new value from infrastructure cities already pay for. Estimates at this grain can guide pollution cuts, street planning, and health work where the burden actually falls, block by block rather than city by city.
arxiv-2512-06749:
Ming Ma and eight co authors debug teams of AI agents by intervening, not just by reading logs. When a multi agent system fails, the trace of who said what is long and branching. The usual fix is to have a language model read the log and blame one agent at one step. That blame is an untested guess, and it may be ill posed: the authors find several distinct fixes can each rescue the same failed task.

Their framework, DoVer, pairs each failure hypothesis with a targeted intervention, such as editing a message or altering a plan, and runs the system again to see whether the fix works. Success is then graded by outcome: did the task get solved, or measurably closer? Inside a known agent framework, on two benchmark suites, DoVer turned a solid share of failures into successes and settled many of its hypotheses by direct test.
arxiv-2512-07049:
T Nagao and co-authors report that a massive star spent its last decades throwing off giant clumps of itself before exploding as the supernova called 2024qiw. Theory says some stars shed mass heavily near death, but the mechanism is unknown. Light curves, spectra, and polarization measures for this event all point the same way: the blast wave is plowing into clumpy material the star had already expelled, at a furious rate.

The bumpy brightness, the broad hydrogen signature, and the shifting polarization fit several major eruptions rather than a steady wind. Such eruptions resemble those of luminous blue variables, rare unstable giants. That raises a dilemma: either those giants can explode directly, against standard expectations, or some other late stage of stellar life erupts the same way. Oddly, despite the heavy shedding, the explosion registered as an ordinary Type II supernova rather than the interacting kind.
arxiv-2512-07449:
Mukta Debnath, Krishnendu Guha, Debasri Saha, Amlan Chakrabarti, and Susmita Sur-Kolay wrote this 2025 computing paper. It concerns deep neural networks split across small edge chips and cloud machines. Splitting saves time and energy, but faults in the hardware can quietly spoil the results.

Their tool, AFarePart, chooses how to split a network with faults in mind from the start. It weighs accuracy loss under faults alongside energy use and delay. During the search it injects fake faults at runtime to test each candidate split. A feedback loop then favors splits that survive faults best. The team tried it on three well-known image networks running on accelerators. Fault tolerance rose clearly, with only a small cost in speed. Safety-critical edge systems, they argue, should plan for faults at partition time.
arxiv-2512-07549:
Miles Gould wrote this 2025 mathematics note on operator algebras, the algebra of quantum observables. It lifts a classic result, the Kadison transitivity theorem, into an infinite setting. The stage is a class of very large algebras that includes the Calkin algebra.

The infinite version grows out of a saturation property of pure states. Massive algebras inherit that countable saturation from their states through excision. Gould shows the saturation matches several order-based traits of a linked filter. One of those traits earns the state the name quantum P-point. Such states cannot be proved to exist from the usual axioms alone. Under mild extra assumptions from set theory, they exist in abundance. The note ends with a cautionary example on the other side. One representation of the Calkin algebra fails the infinite transitivity property. The result maps both the reach and the limits of the theorem.
arxiv-2512-08149:
Milan Rosko, a researcher in logic and the foundations of computing, posted a short paper on arXiv in December 2025. His subject is uniform separation, a hoped for principle in constructive arithmetic, the system known as HA. He argues that a strong structural barrier blocks any such principle from working as intended.

The barrier, he shows, does not depend on what the separated classes mean. It appears whenever two distinct evaluator predicates run in parallel and inference stays uniformly representable in an extension of HA. Under those conditions, any uniform separation principle turns into a special case of a fixed point construction, the kind that breeds paradox. Rosko argues this limit is stricter than classic barriers in complexity theory, because it constrains the logical form of uniform separation itself. Those older results only restricted particular proof techniques.
arxiv-2512-08249:
Sagnick Mukherjee, Jonathan J Fortney, Theron W Carmichael, and colleagues, planetary scientists, posted a modeling study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is transiting brown dwarfs, whose sizes can be measured directly when they cross their host stars. Because those sizes are direct, these objects test theories of brown dwarf and giant planet interiors.

The team built atmospheric and evolution models for this population. Intense host star light, they show, can inflate a brown dwarf radius at all masses, especially past a high flux threshold. Irradiation also changes burning rates, lowering the minimum masses for deuterium and hydrogen burning. That shift moves the boundaries between planets, brown dwarfs, and stars more than metal content or clouds do. Fitting the known sizes of dozens of transiting brown dwarfs, the irradiated models matched better than star ignoring ones. A stubborn set of objects still disagreed, pointing to gaps for future work.
arxiv-2512-08549:
J J Gomez Cadenas and a team of nine colleagues, particle physicists, posted a detector proposal on arXiv in December 2025. They work on xenon time projection chambers hunting for neutrinoless double beta decay, a rare process that would rewrite particle physics. These detectors can image particle tracks, telling a lone electron from the paired electrons of a true decay, but drifting electrons blur as they travel, softening the picture.

Their concept, ITACA, images the mirror track of ions as well. A trace of ammonia converts xenon ions into ammonium ions, which drift slowly toward the cathode without disturbing the electron signal. A sensor there captures them, and laser probing reveals an ion image with sub millimeter sharpness. The electron image still gives the event energy and center. Combining both views improves background rejection by about tenfold. Sharper topology could push these detectors toward much longer decay lifetimes.
arxiv-2512-08649:
Soumitra Ghara, Surjit Kumar, and Shailesh Trivedi introduce a new notion for tuples of bounded operators that commute with each other. The notion weakens a known homogeneity property tied to the unitary group, giving a broader class to study. The authors ask when such a weakly homogeneous tuple is in fact similar to a fully homogeneous one.

They give a sufficient condition for that similarity to hold in general. They then focus on multishifts, a concrete and important class, and fully characterize the weakly homogeneous cases. For multishifts, weak homogeneity holds exactly when the tuple is similar to a homogeneous one. The results are sharpened further for spherically balanced multishifts, giving a clear picture for that subclass of operators.
arxiv-2512-08849: Srijan Ghosh studies rational curves on low degree surfaces inside orthogonal Grassmannians, spaces that collect isotropic subspaces of a fixed dimension under a symmetric bilinear form. The author studies moduli spaces for rational curves in a general surface of low degree. Under a stated numeric condition linking the ambient size, the subspace size, and the degree, the surface is proved to be rationally simply connected. That property is a strong form of rational connectedness for the variety.
arxiv-2512-09049:
Gandham Sai Santhosh and coauthors introduce EMMap, a systematic method for mapping where electromagnetic fault injection affects a microcontroller and for classifying the resulting faults. Fault injection with electromagnetic pulses can flip bits and perturb instructions, making it a powerful security testing tool. Past literature lacks a unified method to map spatial sensitivity and classify fault behavior in a repeatable way.

Building on earlier insights, the method is designed to be platform agnostic, so the same workflow can be applied across embedded architectures. Pilot tests on three representative targets, including an ESP32 class chip and two research boards, are presented as illustrations rather than final reviews. Those early observations motivate a generalized, reproducible workflow for future studies. Researchers can adopt the method to analyze susceptibility of diverse devices in a consistent manner. The work aims to move fault injection testing from ad hoc probing toward a shared, comparable practice.
arxiv-2512-09149:
Anton Vasiliuk and coauthors introduce MindShift, a benchmark for how large language models react to mind based prompts. Language models can absorb and reflect traits and attitudes set by users, but measuring that ability needs robust test based tools. The study adapts the most studied test in mind literature, a major personality inventory, to examine model behavior.

Personality based prompts create detailed roles that vary in trait strength, letting the team measure how closely models follow each role. Results show a consistent improvement in role reading across models, credited to better training data and alignment methods. Responses to the test based assessment also differ greatly across model types and families. That variation suggests models differ in how well they can emulate human like personality traits. MindShift prompts and review code will be released publicly. The benchmark gives researchers a shared way to test role skill,.
arxiv-2512-09349:
Lin Li and four co-authors present COVLM-RL, a self-driving framework that pairs vision-language models with reinforcement learning. End-to-end driving systems struggle to generalize, train efficiently, and explain their decisions. Vision-language models reason well when supervised on big datasets but can be brittle in new scenes, while reinforcement learning adapts yet learns slowly and opaquely.

COVLM-RL uses the vision-language model as a critical-object reasoner. A chain-of-thought prompting strategy makes it pick out key traffic elements and produce semantic decisions, turning multi-view camera input into guidance for the learning loop. That guidance speeds training and makes the policy easier to interpret. A consistency loss keeps the model's semantic plans aligned with the controller's actual outputs. In the CARLA simulator, the system raised success rates substantially in trained and unseen environments alike.
arxiv-2512-09649:
Angiraben D. Mahida leads a team reporting the deepest radio search yet for accretion onto the intermediate-mass black hole in Omega Centauri, the Milky Way's most massive globular cluster. Fast-moving stars in the cluster's core gave the strongest evidence that such a black hole, between stellar and supermassive in size, sits there. How efficiently it feeds would show up as radio and X-ray emission.

With one hundred seventy hours of Australia Telescope Compact Array observations, the team produced the most sensitive radio image of the cluster to date, reaching noise near one microjansky. They detected no radio emission at any of the proposed center positions. That silence imposes limits: through the fundamental plane relation linking black hole activity across scales, the accretion efficiency around this black hole must be low. The result constrains how intermediate-mass black holes grow, or fail to grow, inside star clusters.
arxiv-2512-09749:
Katsuhiko Matsuzaki studies the Teichmüller space of smooth reshaping maps of a circle. The maps he allows have a mild regularity condition, called Zygmund continuity of their derivatives. The space collects all such maps up to a natural notion of sameness. Matsuzaki brings two tools to bear on it: simultaneous uniformization, a method from surface geometry, and composition operators acting on Besov spaces, a scale of function spaces.

From these tools he draws two main results. First, he gives a new proof of a known match between distortions inside the unit disk, fading at a steady rate, and boundary maps on the circle. The maps land in exactly the regularity class he studies. Second, he shows the whole space is real analytically equivalent to a standard Banach space of Zygmund continuous functions on the circle. The result gives the space a clean coordinate description for further work.
arxiv-2512-09849:
Naman Jain, Jin Zhang, Marcus Culemann, and Philipp M. Preiss demonstrate control over fermionic atoms held in optical tweezers. Their array holds lithium atoms in an eight by eight grid of light traps. The team prepares chosen product states with two internal components, atom by atom, in a fully programmable way. The atoms sit in their motional ground states with fidelity above ninety-eight percent. Large differences in magnetic moment between the components help them resolve spin at each site.

The setup also reads out spin, site, and atom number in a single short exposure, and experiments cycle in a few seconds. Low entropy state preparation has been a key hurdle for simulating fermions, the particle family that includes electrons. By combining deterministic assembly, high ground state fidelity, and fast detailed readout, the work establishes a scalable platform for fermionic quantum simulation. The results appeared in Physical Review Letters.
arxiv-2512-09949:
Yuma Sato and Shuichi Matsukiyo model a plasma probe called collective Thomson scattering inside a beam plasma system. The technique shines waves into a plasma and reads the scattered spectrum to infer conditions inside. Their tool is a particle in cell code on a flat grid. They formulate the shape of the scattered spectrum in wave number space for general setups, where the beam and wave paths can point any way.

In this flat setup, they find, the spectrum becomes lopsided. Looking along a fixed direction, the electron and ion signatures in the spectrum grow and distort when instabilities strike: the Buneman instability for electrons and the ion acoustic instability for ions. A second run, with a weak hot beam that stays linearly stable, still showed a lopsided spectrum. The findings should help interpret radar observations of ionospheric plasmas and laboratory measurements.
arxiv-2512-10049:
Jocelyn Nembe builds a unified theory of adaptive estimation that exploits symmetry. The setting is nonparametric functional estimation: recovering an unknown function from noisy data without assuming a formula. When the target function has structure along the orbits of a group action, a symmetry group moving points around the input space, estimation should be easier. Nembe builds a hierarchy of kernels transported along those orbits, calling the resulting setup Twin Spaces. A penalized model selection scheme, obeying a Kraft type inequality, picks among the transported kernels automatically.

Three contributions follow. Non asymptotic oracle inequalities with explicit constants bound the estimator's risk against the best choice in hindsight. New regularity classes capture smoothness along group orbits, and the estimator adapts to them without being told which class holds. Finally, the setup recovers the classic optimal rates in ordinary Euclidean problems, while improving on them when orbital structure is present.
arxiv-2512-10249:
Ellen C. C. Lin and colleagues compare the rhythm of repeating fast radio bursts with the pulses of a magnetar, hunting for a shared engine. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of unknown origin; some repeat, irregularly. Magnetars, fiercely magnetized neutron stars and a leading suspect for the burst sources, emit similar but far fainter pulses. The team analyzed burst sequences from three repeating sources and from the galactic magnetar SGR J1935+2154. For arrival times, energies, and peak frequencies, they measured two diagnostics: an index of randomness and the largest Lyapunov exponent, a gauge of chaos.

Waiting times in every repeater show high randomness and low chaos, matching the magnetar pulses closely. Energies tell a messier story: bursts and magnetar pulses occupy the same region of the diagnostic plane but scatter far more widely than timings or frequencies. Beaming or varying emission efficiency may explain the scatter.
arxiv-2512-10349:
Quan Yuan, Zhenting Du, Daqian Cao, and Weibang Bai build a robot finger that bends all its joints in lockstep from a single motor. Tendon driven underactuated fingers promise dexterous hands with few actuators and simple mechanics. Their hard tradeoff is getting high load capacity and adaptive compliance together in a compact shape. The authors' answer is synchronous tendon routing: one tendon path mechanically couples every joint at fixed angular velocity ratios, so one actuator drives the whole finger. Their models cover the kinematics and statics, including tendon elasticity, which lets them predict the finger's stiffness before building it.

A prototype matched the models closely under static loading. Five such fingers were then integrated into a complete robotic hand, which manipulated objects across diverse scenarios.
arxiv-2512-10649:
Sisi Huang and Xiaohua Yao prove boundedness results for the wave operators of a fourth-order Schrödinger operator, the biharmonic operator plus a potential, on the integer lattice. Wave operators compare the perturbed dynamics with the free one. And their boundedness on sequence spaces is the backbone of scattering theory: it transfers decay and Strichartz-type estimates from the free equation to the real one.

The authors assume the potential decays. How fast it must decay depends on the type of zero resonance at the thresholds. Under those assumptions, the wave operators are bounded for every exponent strictly between one and infinity. If both thresholds are regular points, the result is sharp: boundedness fails at both endpoint spaces. The proof leans on asymptotic expansions of the resolvent near the two thresholds and on singular integral theory. Decay estimates follow for the beam equation, in a sixty-page analysis.
arxiv-2512-10749:
Merve Ipek Bal and Diogo Pacheco measure how bots bent political conversation in Brazil. Working with more than three hundred and fifteen million tweets from August 2018 to June 2022, spanning one presidential election and the run-up to the next, they compare the behaviour, sentiment. And topics of bot posts against human ones.

Bots leaned heavily on retweets and replies, and their reply activity spiked after the 2018 election, a pattern the authors read as conversational infiltration and amplification. Their emotional tone stayed narrow, while human sentiment swung with events. Topic modelling found bots repeating a tight, Bolsonaro-centred message set, while humans ranged across candidates, civic concerns, and personal reflections. The authors conclude that bots acted as amplifiers of narrow agendas, with a real potential to distort the online debate citizens saw.
arxiv-2512-10849:
Geoffrey Bomarito and Patrick Leser let a computer rediscover physical laws, and ask it to admit how unsure it is. Symbolic regression searches for a formula, written in symbols, that explains data, and it can surface real governing laws. Noise is its weakness: a formula that fits noisy data perfectly usually fits the noise too, and a single best answer hides that risk.

Their Bayesian version samples from the posterior spread over expressions instead of naming one winner. A sequential Monte Carlo engine does the sampling, combining random selection, adaptive tempering that slowly sharpens the target, and scaled marginal likelihood to score candidates. The result favours short expressions that generalise, with an honest spread of options. Against standard genetic programming baselines, the method handled noisy benchmark problems better, overfitting less and recovering accurate, readable equations more often.
arxiv-2512-11249:
Chandra Raskoti and Weizi Li present a model run setup that lets traffic flow and detailed vehicle physics run jointly on lifelike hilly terrain. Testing self driving systems needs both large scale traffic and faithful 3D perception, yet current tools rarely include real elevation.
