Current spotters adapt poorly to in-the-wild deepfakes, though audio deepfakes pose a grave safety threat. The framework lets audio language models generalize training-free to unseen deepfakes and give textual rationales for spotting outcomes. Pairwise contrast reasoning guides the model to spot and filter fakes and off-topic sound traits. A routing mechanism sends odd samples to the language model, and ICLAD lifts macro F1 by up to 2 times.
arxiv-2604-17149: Dai and five colleagues propose FlowRefiner, a refiner for 3D turbulent flows. It swaps noisy steps for ODE correction, uses one training goal across all stages, and fixes the noise range at any depth via a sigma schedule. On large-scale 3D turbulence, it achieves top autoregressive accuracy with strong physics consistency.
arxiv-2604-17349: Mukherjee and Sain model how a dividing cell pinches itself in two, focusing on the thin actomyosin cortex beneath its surface. Using three-dimensional simulations of a deformable shell, they show a ring of aligned filaments forms on its own at the equator and drives a sharp inward furrow. Counter-rotating flows appear near the furrow, arising not from built-in twist but from bias in the starting alignment, a kind of memory in the system. A simpler flat-interface model then isolates the ingredients behind the surface instability.
arxiv-2604-17449: Gang and three colleagues introduce a refined 3D index, building on the Dimofte-Gaiotto-Gukov and Gang-Yonekura T[M] gauge theory. The refined index counts as a superconformal index of T[M] with extra gradings for enhanced flavor symmetries. Built from a Dehn surgery presentation via an ideally triangulated link complement, it yields an explicit infinite-sum formula. Example checks support invariance under triangulation and presentation changes, and as a stronger invariant it distinguishes 3-manifolds and gauge phases more finely. A Refined Index Calculator tool accompanies it.
arxiv-2604-17549: Duque and four colleagues present an energy-based deep learning framework for transmission problems in heterogeneous media with discontinuous materials. They introduce a weighted First-Order System Least-Squares formulation tied to an energy-norm Poincaré constant, proved equivalent to a natural energy norm with constants independent of material parameters. The landscape thus tracks a useful error measure even under material contrast, where losses degrade. It also shows passive variance reduction: gradient variance falls as loss falls. Its solution space comes from a neural network plus a least-squares solver.
arxiv-2604-17749: Ge and nine colleagues define Egocentric Instructed Visual State Transition: making middle frames showing object changes between start and target states under an instruction, from an egocentric view. Grasping real-world change matters for human thinking and AI systems, and the first-person view bridges humans and machines. The task poses two hurdles: grasping start and target scenes and thinking about change steps egocentrically, and making a steady middle step matching the order while keeping look. Their EgoIn system infers the multi-step transition process between states using TransitionVLM.
arxiv-2604-17849: Gonzalez-Pumariega and four colleagues ask why a computer-use agent that succeeds once may fail the same task on a repeat run. They trace the fault to three sources: chance during runs, vague task wording, and shifts in how the agent acts. Studying repeats on OSWorld with paired tests, they find success hinges on both task wording and shifts in action. They urge tests under repeats, letting agents clear up vague wording by asking, and favoring plans that stay stable across runs.
arxiv-2604-18249: Herron, Hjuler, Rossato, Allauzen, and Portet run a layer-by-layer fairness analysis of self-supervised speech encoders. Such models serve some speaker groups worse than others, but the technical source of the gap was unclear. Probing each layer for speaker identification and speech recognition, they find bias against certain groups from the very first layers. Speaker-identification bias shrinks where overall error shrinks, yet recognition bias grows where recognition error shrinks, and fine-tuning for recognition leaves the pattern in place.
arxiv-2604-18349: Cao, He, and Tan present HiGMem, a two-level memory system for long-term conversational agents. Pure vector retrieval returns bloated evidence sets, adding similar turns without improving recall. HiGMem lets the model read event summaries first as semantic anchors, then open only the turns worth reading. On the LoCoMo10 benchmark it tops four of five question categories, and adversarial F1 reaches 0.78, up from A-Mem, while retrieving ten times fewer turns.
arxiv-2604-18649: Utsunomiya and three colleagues say after-the-fact fixes cannot wipe away liability from unlawful capture and training, since compliance turns on data history, not outputs. First, copying and intake without leave can break the law, and weights can act as fixed copies holding training value. Second, contract, tort, and unfair-competition rules can curb access and use. Third, since guarded-input value can linger in weights, stripping gains may reach the model itself. They urge a move from after-the-fact cleanup to upfront checked compliance.
arxiv-2604-18749: Riedo and seven colleagues review laser ionization mass spectrometry as a way to search for signs of life within our solar system. The method maps microstructures in complex rock hosts by chemical depth scans, reads sulphur isotope signatures, and finds varied organic molecules. The spectra can feed network and machine-learning routines for unbiased biosignature search. The authors call the technique novel and promising for future missions devoted to life detection.
arxiv-2604-19049: Agarwal presents Refute-or-Promote, an adversarial review method for LLM defect discovery. Plausible but wrong reports overwhelm maintainers, so agents try to disprove candidates at each gate. Cold start reviewers limit anchoring, and cross family review catches shared blind spots. Over 31 days across 7 targets, it killed roughly 79 percent of 171 candidates before disclosure. Outcomes: 4 CVEs, a C++ paper item, editorial fixes, compiler bugs, and security fixes without CVEs. Ten reviewers unanimously backed a nonexistent OpenSSL padding oracle, killed only by one empirical test.
arxiv-2604-19149: Chen and five colleagues study how answers read traces. Prior steering shapes traces, but how answers read and integrate them is less understood. Answer-to-reasoning attention shows a benign self-reading pattern tied to correctness: focus drifts forward, staying on anchors. Incorrect solutions show diffuse, irregular attention. They read this as certainty: the model commits to a branch and integrates evidence. They build a training-free steering method using Self-Reading Quality scores and geometric and semantic metrics to select steering data. Experiments show accuracy gains.
arxiv-2604-19649: Mandl, Sexty, and Unterhuber present lattice simulations at the continuum limit of quantum chromodynamics above the crossover temperature and at newly high baryon levels at physical masses, using the complex Langevin method. They pin down the QCD equation of state from baryon density and pressure as functions of baryon chemical potential and temperature. Wrong turns of complex dynamics are under control. Results agree with previous lattice studies at smaller values and with hard-thermal-loop results at high heat.
arxiv-2604-19749: Zeng and 11 colleagues reveal tool overuse in language models: the unnecessary use of external tools during reasoning, found across diverse models. They trace the habit to a knowledge epistemic illusion, where models misjudge the bounds of their own internal knowledge and fail to sense what they actually know. The study first maps tool-use behavior across regions of differing internal knowledge availability. To counter it, they propose a knowledge-aware boundary alignment strategy built on direct preference optimization.
arxiv-2604-19949: Girish and three colleagues introduce Indic-CodecFake, the first large benchmark of real and neural-codec-synthesized speech across Indic languages. Detectors trained on English data fail on it, tripped by Indic phonetic diversity and prosodic variety, and current audio language models also perform poorly in zero-shot tests. Their SATYAM model fuses Whisper semantic features with TRILLsson prosodic features through two-stage hyperbolic alignment. It beats rival end-to-end and audio-model baselines across the benchmark.
arxiv-2604-20249: Das and Agarwal show layered matter can host an intrinsic magnetoelectric Hall effect from mixed layer-orbital quantum geometry. Out-of-plane electric and magnetic fields couple layer polarization to orbital moment, giving a Hall response scaling with both fields at once. The response needs no scattering time, no magnetism, and no spin-orbit coupling, staying finite and unquantized inside the band gap. Its coefficient flips sign under gate reversal and tracks layer polarization, shown in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene with conductivity near 0.05 in units of e squared over h.
arxiv-2604-20349: Ammad and five colleagues present HYMN, a hybrid multi-tech navigation data set for indoor-outdoor positioning research. Five systems feed it in a factory hall: ultra-wideband, Bluetooth Low Energy, WiFi, 5G, and satellite navigation, all time-synced. Unlike single-tech sets, HYMN covers indoor-outdoor shifts, backing multi-sensor fusion for seamless positioning. Each record carries a unique measurement id with time-stamped notes and ground truth, aiding fingerprinting, cross-tech fusion, and seamless positioning.
arxiv-2604-20549: Turki, Sabolčec, Messmer, and Jaggi study quality filtering for multilingual data, where data is scarce for many languages. They test cross-lingual transfer, third-quartile sampling, and retention tuning, asking whether quality markers stay consistent across languages. Multilingual pooling beats monolingual baselines in stability and accuracy for a 1B model trained on 103B tokens. It lifts French accuracy by 1.2 percent and matches or beats monolingual baselines for low-resource languages. Yet scale does not ensure stability. French needs boundary refining through sampling or tuning to fully use the signal.
arxiv-2604-20849: Rainey, Acar, and Sezer present a structure-aware search pipeline over tree-structured files. Search tools often chop files into fixed-size chunks, which obscures section structure, lists, and tables. The core idea is to treat picks as subdocuments: exact, addressable selections that keep their structural identity. They define primitives: path sets, pruning-based subdocument extraction, and two contextualization mechanisms. Across tests on HTML benchmarks, keeping structure while adding context to selections yields better, more diverse quotes than strong passage-based rivals.
arxiv-2604-21749: Schütz and three colleagues present CuRast, a CUDA software rasterizer that draws massive triangle meshes without building acceleration structures first. A three-stage pipeline draws small triangles directly, storing the closest fragments, and forwards larger ones to later stages. It renders models with hundreds of millions of triangles up to 2 to 5 times faster than Vulkan for unique geometry. For instanced geometry, it is up to 12 times faster. Vulkan stays far faster for low-poly meshes.
arxiv-2604-21849: Wu, Liang, and Yang replace density-based divergences in Bayesian optimal experimental design with integral probability metrics. Old design by expected information gain, usually via Kullback-Leibler divergence, suffers nested expectations, mismatched support, thin tails, and rare-event sensitivity. Their plug-and-play framework uses Wasserstein distance, Maximum Mean Discrepancy, and Energy Distance, with stronger geometry-aware stability under surrogate error and wrong priors. Designs yield tight credible sets and accurate designs where nested Monte Carlo and variational methods break down.
arxiv-2604-21949: Cushman and O'Regan show a sum-product bound for fractal sets, using recent advances in incidence geometry for balls and tubes and sum-product theory in the discrete setting. For s between 0 and 1/2, take any set A in the reals with Hausdorff dimension s. Then either the upper-box dimension of AA, or the lower-box dimension of A plus A, must be at least 29s/23. A slightly better bound of 33s/26 is obtained when the sum-set is replaced with the smoother difference-set.
arxiv-2604-23449: Kleiman and six colleagues build ArguAgent, a system that groups STEM students for classroom argumentation by mixing differing stances while keeping argumentation skill within one level. It scores arguments on a short rubric, then clusters positions, and in simulations nearly all groups satisfy both design rules, over three times the rate of random grouping. Prompt design, rather than model upgrades, drives most of the scoring gains, the team finds.
arxiv-2604-23749: Chang and eight colleagues build StateScribe, a system that helps blind and low-vision people track how real places change between visits. A dual-layer memory of scenes and objects lets it report live scenes plus what changed, when, and where, such as a shop newly closed. Across many revisits it stays accurate above 83 percent, fast under two seconds, and light under 54 megabytes, and a user study confirms better change awareness.
arxiv-2604-23849: Yang and colleagues trace a fresh vector current in accelerating relativistic fluids to the Weyl trace anomaly. The anomaly pins down the second-order transport coefficient linking the electromagnetic field to fluid acceleration. They derive it by extending anomaly matching to the trace anomaly and confirm it independently in boundary field theory using the Rindler horizon. In the rest frame, electric fields add charge density while magnetic fields drive a transverse current with a Nernst-like tensor form.
arxiv-2604-24249: Godet and colleagues describe ECLAIRs, the high-energy transient trigger camera at the core of the SVOM gamma-ray burst mission launched in June 2024. The 4-150 keV coded mask camera autonomously triggers and localizes transients in its field of view. French labs built the flight model under CNES supervision, with partner institutes supplying data reduction and analysis software. The paper outlines science goals, instrument subsystems and characteristics, configuration and operation, in-flight measured performance, and science performance through March 2025.
arxiv-2604-24749: Pabbaraju settles the best sample complexity for multiclass and list learning. Binary learning complexity is well known, but multiclass learning had a gap tied to the DS dimension. Building on a recent algebraic account of multiclass classes by DS dimension, he shows the max hypergraph density of any multiclass class is at most its DS dimension. This proves a long-held conjecture of Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz and fixes the best DS dependence of sample complexity.
arxiv-2604-24849: Fukuda and Harigaya solve the strong CP problem with a chiral U(1) symmetry. It gives an accidental Peccei-Quinn symmetry, broken by mirror QCD dynamics. The model has no massless fermions or a light QCD axion. It allows a high reheating temperature for baryon asymmetry via leptogenesis. Metastable domain walls and a mirror QCD phase transition generate gravitational waves. One pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson is a viable WIMP dark matter candidate. Its gauge boson links dark matter to the Standard Model.
arxiv-2604-25249: Cacioli tests whether symptom validity testing from malingering work can identify sandbagging through below-chance performance on forced-choice items. In a pilot, the gate failed: zero of 12 model-domain cells showed below-chance performance under sandbagging instruction. Analyses found three modes: two models ignored the instruction, and one complied but collapsed responses onto middle options. An anti-task instruction drove two of three models below chance. Cacioli proposes positional shift as a better marker than below-chance accuracy for prompted underperformance.
arxiv-2604-25349: Urbano argues the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, oft sold as a safe swap for the t-test, rests on a false tale. Texts paint Wilcoxon as the right swap since scores are not normal. A close look shows gaps and slips in test rules, sowing IR confusion. Wilcoxon has been misused for decades, giving false safety from a nonexistent threat, while adding a flaw that ensures breakdown. Text review and TREC data show Wilcoxon loses grip on its Type I error rate in IR work. Its use is not justified.
arxiv-2604-25449: Kaur and Kumar study the J/psi mass shift in asymmetric nuclear matter at zero and finite temperatures, with D D and D D-star meson loops. They find rising baryonic density gives a negative J/psi mass shift. This suggests attraction to nuclear mean fields and possible bound states. They work out J/psi binding energy and decay width in ground and excited states of oxygen-16, calcium-40, zirconium-90, and lead-208. The results should aid upcoming Jefferson Lab and antiproton-ion facility studies of low-momentum charmed mesons inside nuclei.
arxiv-2604-25549: Gogacz and four colleagues open the study of partially finite models, where a formula marks a part of the model that must stay finite. They focus on partially finite query entailment: does a query hold in all models where a distinguished concept takes a finite set? In the logic S, an extension of ALC with transitive roles, partially finite conjunctive query entailment sits in 2-exptime. The proof uses infinite model surgery far beyond combining the finite and infinite arguments. Query containment with closed predicates reduces to partially finite query entailment.
arxiv-2604-25649: Venturelli and five colleagues propose a quantum anneal method for interpreting convolutional neural networks in image classification. Deep learning models serve in critical applications where mistakes carry serious consequences, so knowing their outputs matters. The approach selects key feature maps behind each prediction, framing that choice as a quantum constrained optimisation problem solved by quantum anneal. Against GradCAM and GradCAM++, the method shows improved class separation, with more distinct decision boundaries and clearer reasoning. The team also studies the minimum energy gap and success probability of the anneal computation.
arxiv-2604-25949: Miao, Shen, and Mitra present FalconApp, an iPhone app for rapid perception deployment. FalconApp converts brief handheld video of a rigid object into a deployable perception unit for mask and pose estimation. From user video it rebuilds an editable GSplat asset. It composites that asset with diverse backgrounds, renders synthetic images with true masks and poses, then trains and deploys the module. Across five objects, models need about 20 minutes each and beat a PnP baseline on four of five. On-device latency is around 30 milliseconds.
arxiv-2604-26049: Bloch, Ferraro, Martín de Diego, and Bharadwaj adapt discrete variational integrators to systems with double-bracket dissipation. Such integrators are numerical methods prized for mechanical systems. In the dissipative case, energy falls while certain orbits stay fixed. Working with forced Euler-Poincaré and Lie-Poisson systems, they construct a geometric integrator that preserves those coadjoint orbits exactly. Comparisons with general-purpose methods, including higher-order ones, show the advantage of that exact preservation across simulations drawn from satellites with dampers, geophysical fluids, plasmas, and stellar dynamics.
arxiv-2604-26149: Hussein, Abdullah, and Gudmundsson study a thin carbon-nitrogen-oxygen structure. Density functional theory and molecular dynamics show it stable to heat and energy in air, though weaker in motion. Its electronic structure is semiconducting, with a mid-size indirect gap from mixed p-states. Its optics show strong visible and ultraviolet absorption, with anisotropy across directions. Heat capacity at room temperature nears the classical limit, while lattice thermal conductivity is very low. It is thus a good candidate for tiny optical and thermal-control devices.
arxiv-2604-26349: Hsieh and Liang designed a learning-augmented online algorithm for preemptive FIFO buffer management, where packets arrive over time and some buffered packets may be dropped to make room. With perfect predictions it achieves the optimal competitive ratio of 1. It degrades smoothly as prediction error grows. It stays asymptotically robust at the square root of 3 under wild predictions. A new error metric scores predictions on transmitted schedules rather than raw arrivals, and a buffer-clearing fallback bounds the cost of switching.
arxiv-2604-26649: Guo, Wu, and Yiu tackle a mismatch between retrieval-augmented generation and large reasoning models, which need evidence injected during long chains of thought rather than only before reasoning starts. Their framework, ReaLM-Retrieve, spots knowledge gaps at the reasoning-step level, learns when external evidence helps most, and streamlines integration. Tests on three multi-hop question sets show about ten points of F1 gain over standard retrieval while cutting retrieval calls by nearly half. On MuSiQue, it reaches about 71 percent F1 with under two calls per question.
arxiv-2604-26749: Meijer, Miltzow, Ockenfels, and Stojaković show the Nesting Bird Box Problem ER-complete, sharpening hardness results for the Hidden Set Problem. Given a polygonal domain and a number k, the question is whether k points can sit inside it so no two see each other. Each point stands for a birdhouse that birds use only when no occupied neighbor lies nearby. The proof builds on the Art Gallery problem's ER-completeness techniques but runs shorter, using newer tools and hole-punched polygonal domains instead of simple polygons.
arxiv-2604-26949: Tamang and three colleagues study anomaly-driven transport in a five-dimensional holographic Einstein-Maxwell model with Chern-Simons terms, with broken symmetry. Including the full backreaction of scalar and gauge fields on the metric, they compute transport coefficients from Kubo formulas over charge and energy current correlators. They find anomaly-driven transport reaches beyond anomalous currents into the ordinary sector, with coefficients tracking the mass parameter. The work maps how quantum anomalies interplay with broken symmetry in holographic systems.
arxiv-2604-27049: Iannotti and four colleagues give a closed-form expression for the non-local entropies of fermionic Gaussian states under local unitaries, proved at Rényi index 2 for any subsystem. The formula computes in polynomial time from the reduced covariance matrix. They apply it to non-local magic across regimes: a Page-like curve for typical states, log scaling at the XY critical point, and a quasiparticle picture for magic in quantum quenches. Needing only two-point correlations, it offers a scalable lab route via shadow tomography.
arxiv-2604-27249: Cacioli maps when language models told to underperform on choice tests engage with content versus falling back on spot shortcuts. Using a six-condition scale of adversarial instruction detail, he tests two tuned models, Llama-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B, on 2,000 MMLU-Pro items. Response-position entropy and a difficulty-accuracy check jointly classify each condition. Three regimes emerge, not a smooth transition. Vague instructions preserve content engagement, while standard deliberate underplaying collapses position entropy.
arxiv-2604-27449: Xu and Chu study extended thermodynamics of anti-de Sitter holes under linked contractions of time generation and Newton coupling. Starting from the Carroll Hamiltonian action, they derive an edge identity with a cosmological constant and find energy, horizon, and pressure terms for Schwarzschild-anti-de Sitter shapes. They verify the spatial and lapse equations while keeping the boost link, and compare edge workings with Lorentzian contractions. On the finite Carroll branch picked by scaling of work terms, temperature fades and entropy soars while conjugate product stays finite.
arxiv-2604-27649: Le Bihan, Dmytriiev, and Zech interpret blazar 3C 279's 2013 orphan gamma-ray flare with a two-zone model. The EMBLEM code computes a stationary quiescent region plus a second zone accelerating inside the broad-line region. A region outside the torus plus an accelerating blob reproduces the short, intense flare with no optical match. The flare comes from the changing external photon field as the blob crosses the broad-line region toward its terminal Lorentz factor. The model predicts delayed EUV/X-ray brightening after the blob exits.
arxiv-2604-27849: Youssefi and four colleagues present a tunable grid-aware Agent-Based Model for EV charging under varying conditions. The model combines mixed EV behavior, charging column limits, and a shared Energy Sandbox regulating power. Built in Python using SimPy, the approach supports scalable simulations across sizes and strategies. A workplace scenario shows how setup and coordination affect energy delivery, use, and total load. The results highlight context-dependence of suitability and show how strategies and charger types reshape outcomes and grid behavior.
arxiv-2604-27949: Rohleder and colleagues present MyoKin3X, a rig that records three-dimensional forces from all five fingers at once for studies of hand control. Five sensors, in-place cross-calibration and software joining muscle signals to force readings give standardised measures across hand sizes and tasks. Validation shows tiny calibration drift and very low crosstalk between axes, supporting reliable studies of grip, coordination and human-machine interfaces.
arxiv-2604-28049: Arif and Singh tackle judging text-to-SQL systems in live use, where gold queries and database plans are mostly missing. Their STEF tool works only from the user question, a fuller restatement and the SQL it produced, scoring it from zero to 100 on filter match, meaning verdict and judge confidence. It also checks question quality and copes with grouping, ordering and limit quirks, so live monitoring can run with no schema in hand.
arxiv-2604-28149: Hertel's team makes time series foundation models open to inspection for day-ahead power load forecasting. Grid teams need a clear view, not black boxes. Their fast SHAP method exploits flexible context lengths and side inputs through temporal and covariate masking, scaling readouts for these models. On grid data both tested models match a specially trained Transformer zero-shot. Their readouts align with domain knowledge, notably weather and calendar effects.
arxiv-2605-00349:
Yuan Wang and 7 co-authors report that galactic disks slowly swivel, like a coin settling, and that this precession is everywhere. Disk precession on scales above a kiloparsec had barely been studied, since observations lack the dynamical detail to measure it. The team instead traces spin directions through cosmic time inside the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations, where gravity is modeled in full.

Precession turns out to be driven by tidal torque from the lopsided matter around each galaxy. It runs violently in the young universe and more gently today, once disks settle. The swivel can warp cold gas, heat stellar orbits, and even tip satellite galaxies toward their hosts, matching known alignments. Based on its observed warp, the authors predict the Milky Way itself precesses at a few degrees per billion years right now.
arxiv-2605-00549:
Jordan Gué and David d'Enterria recycle decades of axion hunting into limits on a different unseen particle: a massive spin-2 graviton-like particle coupling alike to all matter. Axion-like particles and these gravitons are made and found by similar means, photon swapping in magnetic fields among them. That analogy lets the authors reuse axion bounds with little model input.

Constraints drawn in the axion's mass-versus-coupling plane are carried, across a huge mass range, into the graviton-like particle's own space of mass and coupling. The sources span small cavity detectors, helioscopes, magnetometers, interferometers, beam dumps, colliders, and sky observations, with dark-matter and non-dark-matter cases both covered. Today's axion searches do not yet beat fifth-force tests for these particles. Future versions of those magnetic and light-based devices, however, could probe far deeper for light gravitons than for axions themselves.
arxiv-2605-00649:
Michael Helcig and Dan Alistarh solve a recurring allocation problem in efficient AI: assign one of several options to each of many groups, under one exact budget. Mixed-precision quantization, pruning, and expert selection all take this shape. The objective depends on all assignments jointly, so combinatorial solvers chase proxies, evolutionary search has no gradients, and penalty methods enforce the budget approximately, after heavy tuning.

Their insight is geometric. Under a softmax relaxation, the budget constraint carves out a Riemannian manifold in the model's logit space, with clean structure. The normal direction is known in closed form. Moving along the cost vector changes expected cost monotonically. Their algorithm wraps projection, retraction, and momentum transport around a standard optimizer step. It optimizes the loss, holds the budget exactly at every step, and adds no constraint hyperparameters. On synthetic and compression tasks it matched or beat leading methods, often faster.
arxiv-2605-01149:
Tina Oberoi and two co-authors propose adaptive window decoding for practical fault-tolerant quantum computation. Window decoding cuts decoding complexity for real-time operation and is essential for scalable universal fault tolerance. Prior methods improve throughput by parallelization or cut reaction time by speculation, but use a fixed window size and pay a fixed time overhead for every window.

Average-case errors in quantum error correction are sparse, so that fixed overhead is often unnecessary. Their technique adapts window size based on decoder confidence, reducing decode time and reaction time without harming logical error rates. Benchmarks across different codes and hardware-inspired noise models reach target error rates while keeping decoding time overhead low.
arxiv-2605-01449:
Pang Liu and Yingjie Lao argue that headline scores for picture-based attacks on vision-language models mix up two very different events. Reports claim success rates well over half for sneaky image tweaks that try to smuggle a prompt past the model's guardrails.

The authors split the grade in two: whether the output merely drifted, and whether the attacker's chosen concept actually appeared. They build attacks from two known methods under a tight tweak budget and test over 6,600 pairs across four open models. Drift is common, found in about two thirds of pairs by a strict text score. True injection is rare: under one percent reach any real tier, and only two cases match word for word. The few hits ride on screenshots and documents, carriers that invite text copying anyway. All data and grading caches are public, so anyone can re-derive the numbers exactly.
arxiv-2605-02049:
Constantia Alexandrou and colleagues compute the strange electromagnetic form factors of the nucleon in lattice quantum chromodynamics. Form factors describe how a particle responds to an electromagnetic probe, and the strange quark part is hard because it comes only from disconnected quark loops. The team uses twisted-mass fermions with two plus one plus one flavours, tuned to physical quark masses.

Four lattice spacings let them take the continuum limit directly at the physical pion mass. High-statistics methods and noise reduction tools, such as spin-colour dilution and hierarchical probing, handle the loop estimates. From the momentum pattern they extract the strange electric and magnetic radii and the strange magnetic moment in that limit.
arxiv-2605-02749:
Kyle Foster and four co-authors demonstrate a flexible light source that makes two colors of ultrafast pulses with a programmable delay between them. Such sources serve studies of multiphoton ionization, where atoms lose electrons under intense light. Their design rests on a noncollinear optical parametric amplifier whose seed pulse is deliberately chirped, or spread in time by color.

Controlled spread in the seed lets the pump-seed delay select which colors are amplified, yielding two pulse parts that can each be tuned, with adjustable relative timing, at a high repetition rate. Cross-correlation and dispersion-scan measurements characterize the pulses in time and spectrum. As a benchmark, the source drives an ionization experiment on trapped lithium atoms in a reaction microscope setup, revealing delay-dependent pathways.
arxiv-2605-02849:
Amirhosein Javadi, Shirin Saeedi Bidokhti, and Tara Javidi present a video compression method for extremely low bit rates, built on diffusion generation. At such rates, sending every frame is impossible, so the decoder must rebuild most frames from very compact clues, guided by a strong generative prior. Control of that generation from tiny signals is the core design problem.

Their system splits video into segments of varied length, sends keyframes only when needed, and sums up motion with a compact set of tracked point paths. Two mechanisms pick keyframes by content and choose paths under a budget. The diffusion decoder then synthesizes the missing frames from those signals. Encoding is fast, decoding slower, a profile suited to cloud rebuilding and archival storage.
arxiv-2605-03049:
Santiago J. Benavides and Miguel D. Bustamante look for a rule that sets which way energy and other conserved quantities cascade in two-dimensional turbulence. No single predictive rule has settled that question, despite its central place in turbulence theory.

They show the answer sits in the phases of the velocity field's Fourier modes, grouped in triples called triads. A simple stochastic model of triad phase, checked against many simulations, yields a phase distribution with no fitted parameters. From it they close the energy equation and prove the cascade directions follow from the energy spectrum alone.
arxiv-2605-03149:
Katharine Kowalyshyn and Matthias Scheutz offer a framework for spotting when teammates' mental models drift apart during spoken teamwork. Gaps form when updates go unsaid, and those gaps hurt team performance, yet standard checks rely on slow expert coding after the fact.

Their scheme sorts gaps in dialogue into four types: unsupported beliefs, false beliefs, contradictions, and omissions. In talks from twenty pairs doing joint object tasks, past gap counts predicted later gaps with useful accuracy. Different gap types predicted with different strength, suggesting live dialogue carries early warning signals for coordination trouble.
arxiv-2605-03249:
Jia Choon Lee and Ana Peón-Nieto describe a spectral match for cyclic Higgs bundles. They view these bundles through quiver bundles. A Higgs bundle pairs a vector bundle with a special map on it. Spectral methods turn such pairs into sheaves on another space, which are easier to study.

For the cyclic case, they prove a one-to-one match. The partners are sheaves on a noncommutative surface. That surface comes from the path algebra of the cyclic quiver. The result extends a known match for one family of Higgs bundles. It also links a second family's data to modules over even Clifford algebras.
arxiv-2605-03349:
Kevin Ford and Maksym Radziwiłł prove that the Liouville function takes both signs inside any reduced residue class modulo a large prime, at modest size. The Liouville function tracks the parity of prime factor counts, and its sign changes in arithmetic progressions connect to deep results on small primes in those progressions.

For any small tolerance, they find two integers below a stated power of the modulus, both in the target class, where the function equals minus one and plus one respectively. The exponent echoes Heath-Brown's bound in Linnik's theorem on the least prime in a progression.
arxiv-2605-03649:
Yannick Mvondo-She studies the rank-two logarithmic sector of critical topologically massive gravity, a theory where the usual rules of conformal symmetry are extended by a nilpotent mixing term. He works through the action of the Virasoro zero mode, which splits into a semisimple grading part and a nilpotent part that mixes a logarithmic pair of operators.

Applied to two-point functions, the semisimple part gives the ordinary conformal power law, while the mixing gives the characteristic logarithmic dependence on distance. For the critical weights, the result is a holomorphic power law plus a logarithm of the full distance. Applied to the one-loop partition function, the same action re-expresses its known grading exactly, tying both calculations together.
arxiv-2605-04049:
Shuwen Kan and seven co-authors present FTPrimitiveBench, a benchmark for fault-tolerant quantum computing. It studies how logical operations behave in realistic noise. Performance is usually scored with the uniform depolarizing noise model. Its homogeneous assumptions miss the heterogeneity, asymmetries, and correlations of real devices. Those same structured features create opportunities for joint code-hardware co-design.

The benchmark supports custom settings and representative structured noise families. They include Pauli bias, measurement bias, and spatial or spatio-temporal non-uniformity. It ships with code that builds core surface-code Clifford primitives. Those include logical memory, lattice surgery, a transversal logical Hadamard gate, and the logical phase gate via lattice surgery. The aim is to compare how logical primitives behave under noise that resembles target hardware.
arxiv-2605-04149:
G. Mantovan and eighteen co-authors confirm TOI-159 b, a giant planet orbiting a young, pulsating gamma Doradus star, and give a preliminary look at its atmosphere. Fast-rotating hot stars are hard exoplanet targets because rotation broadens spectral lines and pulsations add scatter, so their planetary systems remain relatively unexplored. The host star is about one hundred fifty million years old.

Joint modeling of radial velocities, TESS transits, and spectro-photometry pins the planet down. Its orbital period is near three point seven days. Its radius is near one point six Jupiter radii. Its mass is near three point five Jupiter masses. It is the hottest hot Jupiter known with a significant eccentricity, about a quarter, and sits in a close binary system. The team disentangled stellar rotation and pulsation signals and produced a low-resolution transmission spectrum.
arxiv-2605-04749:
Dongheon Lee and six co-authors improve speech enhancement with many channels, by inventing extra microphones in software. More microphones sharpen a system's spatial hearing, but real devices at the edge have no room for large microphone arrays.

Their neural network generates virtual microphone signals from the few real microphones a device has. It estimates what extra sensors at other positions would have captured. A learning framework then conditions the enhancement system that follows on those virtual signals and their features. Across several separation systems, the approach beat existing spatial upsampling baselines. Those systems include end-to-end enhancement and neural beamforming. The approach nearly matched the oracle result of having all microphones actually present.
arxiv-2605-04949:
K Andrew Edmonds releases AllSERP, a detailed enrichment of the AdSERP dataset of Google search results pages gathered for commercial searches before AI Overviews appeared. The original corpus holds thousands of trials with screenshots, page code, eye tracking at high rate, mouse data, and pupil signals. Its boxes, however, covered only advertisements, a small share of attributed clicks.

AllSERP adds pixel-accurate boxes for organic results and widgets, semantic types across thirteen element kinds, and click attribution covering more than ninety percent of the corpus. Edmonds ships the pipeline, per-trial files, a corpus table, and a browser replay viewer. Everything is reproducible from the original public data volume.
arxiv-2605-05049:
Sajal Dash and Feiyi Wang tackle the cost of training mixture-of-experts models on high-performance computing clusters. These models promise large-model quality at lower running cost, but training brings huge memory use, heavy communication, and uneven workloads. The authors first build a mathematical model of memory, compute, and communication needs under different parallel schemes.

Measurements then pinpoint the bottlenecks, including slow all-to-all communication, poor overlap between compute and communication, and idle graphics processors from imbalanced work. Their framework, Piper, uses the resource model to pick training strategies and applies pipelined hybrid parallelism. It achieved several times higher hardware utilisation than leading frameworks, plus a faster all-to-all algorithm.
arxiv-2605-05549:
Naming tree species from satellite records supports forest management across whole provinces. Motasem Alkayid and nine co-authors present GDS-Mamba, a classifier for MODIS time series over Canada. Species look subtly alike, and their spatial, spectral, and seasonal signals are tangled together, which makes the task hard.

A mini-batch graph method adds large-scale context between images. A disentangling Mamba design then separates spatial patterns, spectral signatures, and seasonal behavior, while sparse tokens keep the model efficient. Accuracy reached about ninety-four percent inside Alberta and about eighty percent when tested across provinces, beating twelve rival models.
arxiv-2605-05649:
A time crystal is a material whose properties repeat in time, driven by an external clock. Minwook Kyung and five co-authors show a photonic version where one clock produces two response rhythms. In their lattice of nonlinear dipoles, the pump locks the sum of the two frequencies while the leftover phase keeps winding.

The result is a discrete time quasicrystal: quasiperiodic order the medium selects for itself rather than receiving fully formed. Measurements across lattice sites showed locked-phase coherence over a finite range of settings. The work demonstrates self-organized temporal order in a guided-wave photonic system.
arxiv-2605-05749:
Rebuilding a 3D scene from a streaming camera means remembering past views without drowning in duplicates. Feifei Li, Qi Song, Chi Zhang, and Rui Huang propose a memory that stores each observation with its viewing ray. Appearance-only memory updates accumulate redundant views and destabilize geometry when viewpoints swing.

Each pointer in their memory holds a 3D position, a ray direction, and a feature embedding. Updates adapt using that geometric information, not just visual similarity. The design targets dense reconstruction that stays accurate and stable over long streams, treating long-term memory management as a first-class goal alongside geometric accuracy.
arxiv-2605-06049:
Weijian Su and five co-authors make infrared and visible image fusion adapt to different users' demands. Fusion helps both human viewers and machine vision, but each side wants different emphases from the merged image. Fixed methods cannot flex across those heterogeneous preferences, which the authors treat as the core open problem.

Their framework, DPOFusion, first trains a latent diffusion model that produces varied candidate fusions with different properties. A second model is then fine tuned with direct preference optimization on individual cases, steering output toward the stated preference. Experiments show precise alignment with signals from humans, vision language models, and task networks. The authors report a new benchmark for adaptive fusion quality and task transfer.
arxiv-2605-06349:
Michael Multerer, Paul Schneider, and Chiara Segala price American options with a low rank kernel method for optimal stopping. Pricing such options means solving a recursive Monte Carlo problem: at each exercise date, the holder compares exercising now against a continuation value that must be estimated. Standard regression approaches rebuild their models at every date in the backward pass, which wastes effort and limits how large the problem can grow in practice, the authors note.

Their reformulation learns the conditional expectation once, as a linear operator in a kernel space acting on future payoffs. That operator is fitted offline from simulated data and reused at all exercise dates. Convergence guarantees and explicit error bounds across dates support the construction. Numerical experiments show speed and accuracy gains over existing methods for this classic finance problem.
arxiv-2605-06449:
Weisen Huang and seven co-authors investigate the Multistar Turbulence Monitor, an instrument that profiles atmospheric turbulence for astronomy. Turbulence blurs telescope images, so sites need its strength at different heights. The monitor infers that profile from small image motions measured between many star pairs in short exposures.

The study combines theory, instrument checks, simulations, and three nights of on-sky data at the Daocheng Astronomical Site. A Monte Carlo inversion with thirteen height nodes recovers both seeing and the vertical profile with reliable error bars. Its seeing values closely track a standard monitor, supporting the device as a simple, portable option for site testing.
arxiv-2605-06549:
Chengchang Liu, Zongqi Wan, Haishan Ye, and John C. S. Lui study zeroth-order optimization when the data distribution itself shifts with the current decision and only noisy function values are observable. The setting covers non-smooth, non-convex objectives where gradients are unavailable. Their goal is a Goldstein stationary point, a generalized stopping notion for rough landscapes.

They prove an explicit oracle complexity for reaching such a point, achievable with just one noisy evaluation per iteration. Extensions cover smooth objectives and those with Lipschitz Hessians, where their bound improves the best known dependence on accuracy for decision-dependent zeroth-order methods. The guarantees suit black-box problems where sampling reacts to choices.
arxiv-2605-06749:
Claudio Battiloro and five co-authors build the first statistical framework for algorithmic collective action when several groups act at once. Collective action means users coordinating data changes to steer a learning system's behavior, offering a lever beside regulation and corporate design. Real efforts are fragmented into multiple collectives with different sizes, strategies, and sub-goals, while prior theory treated only one collective.

Focusing on classification, the authors bound each collective's chance of success as a function of group sizes and how aligned their goals are. Each group can compute its bound knowing only part of the others' plans. Simulations inspired by climate adaptation in smart cities illustrate how the bounds guide strategy.
arxiv-2605-07049:
Yi He and Xingyu Zhou give the first theoretical guarantees for private reinforcement learning with general function approximation. Earlier private learning results covered only simple table-based or linear settings. Their method updates policies in batches and chooses among them with a privacy-preserving selection mechanism, backed by a new regret analysis.

Even in the general setting, their regret matches the best known rate for the linear case. The work also yields a new regret bound for batched online learning based on a standard complexity measure. Finally, the authors uncover real gaps in recent linear-case results, clarifying where the field's privacy guarantees actually stand.
arxiv-2605-07249:
Youngjoon Jang and three co-authors argue that multilingual search should be judged on language as well as meaning. Standard evaluations treat a relevant passage as equally good in any language. Yet users may prefer results in their query language, and mismatches complicate later answer checking. Their MLAIRE protocol separates those two dimensions.

Controlled pools of parallel passages across languages let the protocol measure semantic accuracy and query-language preference independently. New metrics and a four-way failure breakdown expose trade-offs that standard scores hide. Across thirty-one retrievers, some semantically strong systems returned correct content in the wrong language, while language-loyal systems sometimes retrieved weaker content.
arxiv-2605-07449:
G. Sharvan Prakash and R. Muthuganesan analyze a hybrid quantum battery built from one qubit and one qutrit, a two-level and a three-level quantum system coupled together. An anisotropic exchange interaction and a uniform magnetic field govern the device. The authors track quantum coherence and entanglement alongside energy performance measures like ergotropy, power, and capacity.

Both usable energy and power oscillate over time, while capacity stays constant, and nonclassical effects prove central to storage efficiency. The model connects to a real nickel-radical molecular complex, where coherence, entanglement, and efficient storage persist even at room temperature. That link gives the design a realistic experimental pathway.
arxiv-2605-07549:
Christopher Ries and three co-authors bring conformal prediction to object detection, the vision task of drawing boxes around objects and naming them. Conformal methods wrap a model's guesses in intervals with a guaranteed coverage rate, which matters for safety-critical uses like driving. Detection is harder than simple prediction because each answer has several parts.

The team conformalizes each box corner separately, corrects for the multiple parts, and scales interval widths using uncertainty estimates from a probabilistic detector. A second stage adds class prediction sets and conditions the boxes on them. Across three driving datasets, scaled intervals were sharper than fixed-width ones, with up to 19 percent better overlap scores, while coverage held. Class-wise calibration improved coverage further.
arxiv-2605-07649:
Berkehan Ünal and three co-authors ask whether vision-language models can serve as zero-shot sensors for the operational design domain of an autonomous system. That domain is the set of conditions the system is certified to handle. Safety rules hinge on that domain, above all for self-driving cars. So perception must spot its defining elements as definitions evolve.

They tested four vision-language models on a custom dataset and on Mapillary Vistas, for both labeling and detection of domain elements, and logged the failures. An ablation compared zero-shot tuning strategies with their costs, and the team released reusable prompting templates with usage guidance. Definition-anchored chain-of-thought prompting with persona decomposition worked best, while several other methods lost recall.
arxiv-2605-07749:
Hartmut Häntze and nine co-authors benchmark medical foundation models on a hard, data-scarce task: sorting kidney lesions in CT scans into six classes, from common cysts to rare cancer subtypes. Foundation models promise transferable representations, but clinical fields with little training data need proof, not promises.

Using frozen feature probing, they compared three foundation models against a handcrafted radiomics classifier and a 3D ResNet trained from scratch, on external test data. The foundation models roughly matched the from-scratch network and ran cheaply after feature extraction. But radiomics beat every deep learning approach clearly, suggesting current generalist embeddings miss the fine texture and shape differences that separate these subtypes. Radiomics remains the state of the art here.
arxiv-2605-08049:
Saikat Banerjee, Tara Steinhöfel, Florian Lange, Matthias Eschrig, and coauthors show how light can control hidden magnetic order. Some spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulators hide multipolar order that is hard to detect or steer with normal probes. The study focuses on systems with edge-sharing octahedra and two electrons in the relevant shells.

Using a Floquet Schrieffer-Wolff expansion of a driven Hubbard-Kanamori model, the authors derive a low-energy Hamiltonian with two new light-driven terms. One acts like a static field coupled to the magnetic octupole, an octupolar inverse Faraday effect. The other is a bond-dependent exchange absent in equilibrium, which reshapes the multipolar landscape and can stabilize new states.
arxiv-2605-08149:
Harshavardhan studies how interpretable features inside a language model compete when the model is unsure. Sparse autoencoders split the model's internal activity into readable features, and the author defines feature rivalry as pairs of features that move in opposite directions.

Working with Gemma-2-2B and Gemma Scope autoencoders on PopQA questions split by answer entropy, the study finds much stronger rivalry for high-uncertainty questions at two specific layers. Steering activations along a rivalry direction changed outputs more than random steering did, which suggests rivalry sits upstream of the answer. The pattern could serve as a readable signal of model uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-08249:
Izaldein Al-Zyoud and Abdulmotaleb El Saddik ask a pointed question. Does a frozen vision foundation model describe one image in a self-consistent way? A model builds a coordinate system for images. The same feature dimensions should switch on together across the parts of a single picture. That holds only if the system is coherent.

Their tool, Dimensional Coactivation, compares regions dimension by dimension. It skips centering and normalization on purpose. It also skips full Gram coupling. Raw size carries meaning when the coordinate system is fixed. Deepfake detection serves as the test task. Fake content should break the natural pattern. The measure gives a per-dimension view of coherence inside one sample.
arxiv-2605-08549:
Xiao Xiao, Hayoun Noh, and Mar Gonzalez-Franco probe whether language models can sense human developmental stage from writing. They draw on Robert Kegan's theory of how people build meaning, where expert interviews are deep but hard to scale. Their new twenty item sentence completion test aims to draw out stage like patterns through short self written answers.

Leading models recover intended labels well for invented personas, but agree only fairly with human judges on real people's answers. Models answering with no persona also show stable family level patterns. The results warn that clean synthetic signal is easier than real human signal, a key limit for stage aware chat systems.
arxiv-2605-08649: Frederick Goodman and Hans Wenzl prove a criterion for when a large class of algebras is semisimple, meaning it splits cleanly into simple building blocks with no tangled remainder. Their new method applies to several algebras central to representation theory and low dimensional topology: the Brauer algebra, the Birman-Murakami-Wenzl algebra, and a q-deformed Brauer variant. These algebras encode diagram based multiplication rules, and semisimplicity decides when their representation theory stays orderly. The criterion gives researchers a unified check across families that were previously handled case by case.
arxiv-2605-08749:
Mikhail Parakhin, André Carvalho, and Patrick Haluptzok present a loss function that reshapes point embeddings into a perfect Gaussian without any random sampling. Each point splits into a direction on a sphere and a transformed radius, forming a wristband shape. They prove, with machine checked verification, that matching the uniform wristband target happens exactly when the source is a standard Gaussian, and they compute the matching energy two efficient ways.

Extra terms speed finite sample learning, and calibration turns the pieces into one standardized score. On tricky impostor data with correct margins but wrong dependence, the method leads at higher dimensions. Representation learning gains a deterministic route to clean latent spaces.
arxiv-2605-08849:
Eman Bagheri, Riccardo Casali, Stefan Becker, and Philipp Schlatter hunt the origin of swirl switching, a puzzling flip in the swirling flow inside bent pipes. Three direct numerical simulations cover a half circle bend at two speeds and two curvatures. Standard modal decompositions blur distinct instabilities together, so the team introduces a filtered Hilbert decomposition that separates them into clean modes.

Seven modes in four families emerge, with the switching and breathing modes living in the curved section as the wavy and pulsing instabilities of the bend's twin vortices. Local stability analysis of the mean flow independently finds the same modes, with switching the most unstable. The agreement supports swirl switching as an intrinsic instability of the bent pipe flow itself.
arxiv-2605-08949:
Binghang Lu and eight coauthors fight the loss of old skills as models learn task on task. Guard plans steer new steps clear of old task paths. They tend to gauge all with the plain Frobenius gauge. The Muon plan's wins hint at a next gauge. Muon uses square, set right steps with a spectral air. That air may fit matrix weights more.

Muon-OGD casts each step as a task with a spectral cap and line guards. Dual loops and matrix sign near forms solve it fast. On stock suites, and on code, math, and care sets, it beats plain tuned runs and strong guard base lines. It stays lean at scale.
arxiv-2605-09449:
Gu and five colleagues build SpaceMind++, a video model building a voxel map from RGB videos. That gives video models a lasting world-centred picture for 3D reasoning. Following the mammalian dual-stream system, where meaning and spatial cues are processed and integrated into an allocentric map, the map reorganises scattered observations into a shared picture. That keeps object permanence and topology across viewpoints.

To use the allocentric picture in a video model without breaking its interface, the team adds Coordinate-Guided Deep Iterative Fusion. It relays map-level spatial knowledge into original 2D traits. The fusion leans on coordinate embeddings and 3D Rotary Positional Encoding, grounding interactions in metric space, like entorhinal binding of sensory traits to metric space. Experiments show SpaceMind++ reaching new best performance on VSI-Bench, with stronger generalisation on SPBench, SITE-Bench, and SPAR-Bench, showing toughness in unseen environments.
arxiv-2605-09649:
Bui and three colleagues tackle the key value cache bottleneck in long context inference. The cache stores past keys and values so the model need not recompute them, but it grows with sequence length, as does attention over it. Existing eviction methods cut cost but usually degrade performance against full cache use. The authors argue full cache attention is not always best: irrelevant tokens can water down attention to useful evidence, so a selective, learnable eviction policy can improve generation, not merely approximate it.

Their global retention method learns each token's utility under one budget. Retention gates score cached entries, and a shared final projection calibrates scores across layers and heads. Tokens from layers, heads, and modalities then compete for space. Theory shows keeping useful tokens reduces attention dilution. Across long context language, vision language, and dialogue benchmarks, the method cuts memory while matching or beating full cache use.
arxiv-2605-09749:
Tomasi and three colleagues fixed a practical headache for discrete diffusion models, which build sequences by slowly unmasking tokens. Forcing global property rules during generation, like topic, molecule, or playlist rules, was still an open challenge. Their primal-dual guided decoding frames constrained generation as a KL-regularised optimisation problem, solved live with adaptive Lagrangian multipliers.

At each denoising step, token scores shift by an added bias tied to the constraint, with multipliers updated by mirror descent from constraint violation. The bias is the optimal KL-regularised projection of the constraint, keeping output as close as possible to the free distribution. No retraining or extra model runs are needed, several constraints can run at once, and formal violation bounds hold. Tests on topical text, molecules, and playlists showed better rule satisfaction with quality kept.
arxiv-2605-09849:
Guo, Shpitser and Ogburn work on causal inference, the statistics of cause and effect, when the outcome itself is partly hidden. Proxy methods handle unseen variables by using stand-in measurements, and one influential line rebuilds the hidden distribution from eigenvalue patterns in the observed data. This paper first shows the full data law can be identified in the hidden-outcome setting, then builds estimators for causal effects from it.

The estimators rest on influence functions, tools that describe how each observation nudges an estimate. The authors claim they are the first such estimators here that need neither unbiased proxy measurements nor partial observation of the outcome. They also achieve multiple robustness, staying valid when some but not all model parts are right, plus good efficiency properties. Simulation studies back the performance claims.
arxiv-2605-09949:
Li and four colleagues ask how chemical language models learn meaning from SMILES strings, the text codes for molecules, rather than just string patterns. Chirality is the hard test: mirror-image molecules, called enantiomers, can differ sharply in drug effect and toxicity, yet models often fail to tell them apart. Their Pan-CORE family translates SMILES with encoder-decoder transformers, tracked checkpoint by checkpoint.

Across every variant, chiral-token accuracy jumps abruptly after a long plateau, so the stall is not a matter of model size alone. Attention, residual-stream and latent-space analyses point to the encoder, where chiral representations first destabilise and then rebuild, tracing a V-shaped dip and recovery. Removing a handful of chiral-sensitive attention heads proves their role in the transition.
arxiv-2605-10049:
Ouyang and four colleagues built Janus, a compiler safety tool that blocks transient attacks like Spectre and control-flow seizure on ARM64 platforms. Janus joins speculative runs and control flow links with PA tags, using PA and BTI chip parts to stop control-flow guessing attacks. It secures both control flow and speculative runs through existing control-flow checks.

To trim costs, Janus merges defense steps across other defense layers, called modifier fusion, and reuses slots of guarded values, called carrier reuse. SPEC CPU2017 mean extra cost is 3.85 percent, with real-world apps at 2.97 to 7.80 percent.
arxiv-2605-10149:
Yeo and four co-authors improve temporal action segmentation, the task of splitting raw videos into tagged action segments. Fully supervised methods have grown, but action spread, fuzzy edges and costly tagging persist, above all in fresh or low-resource domains. Grammar-based methods add structural priors yet depend on complex parsing that limits scalability. The authors propose a lightweight, constraint-based polish system instead.

Stats shape priors, including shift trust, action edge sets and per-class length, are drawn straight from tagged data and folded into a tweaked Viterbi reading method. That allows run-time polish with no retrain and no added model bulk. The approach lifts both fully and semi-trained splitting models by fixing shape guess errors while staying lean, with code released publicly.
arxiv-2605-10649:
Diego Portero-Rodríguez and co-authors give a formal account of a built-in light-chip wave front sensor for astronomy, tackling solar wave front sensing, where low Sun-sky contrast limits tunable optics. Night-time sensing tracks a point object's shift, but solar fixing needs wide images, limiting spatial detail and rebuild quality. Their method measures phase differences across the wave front directly by interferometry, without forming images, using built-in light chips for a low-power, tiny solution.

A mathematical model characterises the proposed sensor's response, and Python-based tunable-optics test runs verify it. The test runs show the sensor's real response and highlight factors essential to its correct functioning, showing how light chips can shrink and simplify star instruments.
arxiv-2605-10949:
Usman Nazir, I-Han Cheng, and Sara Khalid test whether satellite data can help predict child health risks tied to climate. Malaria, childhood lung infection, and poor nutrition together kill over two million children under five each year, mostly where climate swings drive spread, exposure, and food.

Three studies use AlphaEarth satellite embeddings as predictors, covering infection and stunted growth in poor settings where health tracking stays sparse and reactive. Satellite views offer a cheap, wide-area complement to ground data, and the synthesis shows where they truly predict child health. Global-health teams get a grounded read on a promising but poorly tested data source.
arxiv-2605-11149:
Karthik Sreedhar, Aryan Kaul, and Lydia B. Chilton probe chat-based reshaping of work systems through an email system that users reshape in natural language. End-user tweaks have historically stayed rare and confined to setup or breakdown moments, but generative AI now makes such reshaping technically feasible.

Participants reshaped inbox categories, added interface elements, and authored new workflow behaviors by talking to the system over several days in their own workflows. Changes mostly adapted and narrowed existing patterns rather than inventing entirely novel features, and reshaping changed how users engaged with their inboxes. Design teams learn what people actually reshape, when they choose to, and how reshaping changes everyday tool use.
arxiv-2605-11449: Alexander Caviedes Castro and Juan Sebastián Cortés-Cruz extend the Kostant game. The game is a counting tool that builds positive roots in Lie algebras. By adding any multi-vertex change, they prove game setups match shortest representatives of parabolic quotients. This gives a dynamic, step-by-step view of reduced words. The framework yields a new root counting identity. It gives a Coxeter base for combinatorial work on the Mukai conjecture, regularity of reduced word sets via finite automata, and a build of Standard Young Tableaux.
arxiv-2605-11649: Belli and López classify all homothetical surfaces with constant mean curvature in hyperbolic space. In the upper half-space model, these surfaces satisfy z equals phi of x times psi of y. Here phi and psi are smooth functions of one variable. They prove any such surface is necessarily parabolic, meaning either phi or psi is constant. The results cover the minimal case H equals zero, the case H squared not equal to one, and the critical case H squared equals one, extending parabolic surface classification in hyperbolic space.
arxiv-2605-12049: Aaron Spieler, Georg Martius, and Anna Levina ask how to split a fixed parameter budget between unit count, per-unit complexity, and connectivity in recurrent networks. Their ELM Network uses Expressive Leaky Memory neurons mirroring cortical components, allowing independent tuning of all three axes. Performance rises monotonically along each axis alone, but under a fixed budget a clear optimum emerges, with larger budgets favoring more numerous, more complex neurons. Their closed-form information-theoretic model captures the tradeoffs and traces a near-Pareto scaling law.
arxiv-2605-12149: Yi Yuan, Yuanchen Zhao, and Dong E. Liu combine error detection with error cancellation to cut sampling costs. Error cancellation is unbiased but pays overhead, while error-detecting codes drop faults by post-selection yet leave a logical residue. Their scheme maps noise to a weaker channel, then cancels only the residue. Post-selection tangles fault branches, so they build the channel perturbatively to order, shrinking preprocessing from exponential to polynomial. On GHZ preparation with the Iceberg code at 200 qubits, results cut overhead thousands-fold at fidelity near 0.956.
arxiv-2605-12249: Elena Codazzo and nine colleagues test whether the background of binary merger signals hurts continuous gravitational wave searches with the Einstein Telescope. Hundreds of compact binary mergers are already known, and their unresolved superposition will form a background strongest at low frequencies in third-generation detectors. Using realistic simulations of this background with the Frequency-Hough pipeline, they find it acts as extra noise, worst near 7 Hz, where it worsens sensitivity by about 7 to 10 percent.
arxiv-2605-12349: Larroque and Manière ask whether a class that can answer queries makes other database rule classes easy to check. Some rules add domain knowledge to a database, yet even basic reasoning over them may never end. Several rule classes promise useful behaviour, such as a chase algorithm that always stops. The authors show that, inside a class where queries can be decided, membership in chase-stopping classes and in the bounded treewidth set class stays undecidable. That closes a hope for turning abstract classes into concrete tests.
arxiv-2605-12449: Ma and five colleagues lower the barrier to simulation for vision research with LychSim, built on Unreal Engine 5. Modern simulators demand deep graphics and game skills, yet simulation stays vital for closed-loop tuning and tough out-of-distribution tests. LychSim offers a simple Python interface, a procedural pipeline that builds varied, high-quality scenes with rich two- and three-dimensional labels, and native Model Context Protocol support. That last piece turns the simulator into a live playground for reasoning agents.
arxiv-2605-12649: Xia and five colleagues improve dataset distillation with a two-stage setup called DIVER. The goal is a compact proxy data set that is unreadable and non-raw, protecting privacy while enabling efficient learning. Single-stage methods overfit patterns of a prior model, hiding meaning and hurting scores on other models. DIVER uses a ready-made diffusion model for rich meaning return, through meaning passing down, guidance and fusion. High-level meaning moves into latent space, cutting model-own noise and bringing back voice across models.
arxiv-2605-12749: Rodríguez-Nieto and three colleagues study cocommutative Hopf dialgebras through digroups and racks. They prove the rack functor from the adjoint rack bialgebra factorises through its digroup. More precisely, for every dialgebra, the set-like elements in its adjoint rack bialgebra form a rack isomorphic to a conjugation rack. That rack belongs to its digroup. For digroups of that form, with a group acting on the halo, they derive formulas for that rack. Those formulas cover its group, cycle index, fixed polynomial, orbit count and subrack structure.
arxiv-2605-12849: Jia and Xiao investigate commuting maps on inflated algebras, a class of algebraic structures. A map counts as commuting when it always commutes with multiplication in the algebra. They prove every such map takes the form of a scalar multiple plus a central-valued linear map, for algebras over a base field whose characteristic is not 2.
arxiv-2605-13249: Vernon and Bliokh uncover a hidden balance in the laws for elastic waves in uniform solids. The balance yields a saved chirality, a handedness carried by sound like waves in matter. Total chirality tracks the gap between right handed and left handed sideways shakes, while local handedness also involves lengthwise waves. Simple wave patterns show distinct layouts of chirality, spin and false chirality, framing twist as a basic wave trait.
arxiv-2605-13549: F. Hervas-Peters and seventeen colleagues present the first weak lensing catalogue for cosmic-shear cosmology from the Ultraviolet Near Infrared Optical Northern Survey. The team analyses about 3,500 square degrees of northern sky, observed in the r-band by MegaCam on the Canada-France Hawaii Telescope, with median seeing of 0.7 arcseconds. The final catalogue holds 62 million galaxies at an effective density of 4.96 per square arcminute, with shape noise 0.27, opening the first big cosmological analysis by the UNIONS collaboration.
arxiv-2605-13649: The CMS Collaboration hunts for a lone vector-like top quark T that breaks apart into a top quark plus a Higgs boson, leaving two leptons of opposite charge. Their data show no surplus above what background processes alone would give. From that null outcome, they cap the rate for making T times its chance of decaying to tH, at 95 percent confidence. That cap falls from 2.0 picobarns for a 600 GeV T to 0.3 picobarns at 1200 GeV. Its lowest point is 0.1 picobarns at 1000 GeV.
arxiv-2605-13749: Zhouzi Li, Mor Harchol-Balter and Alan Scheller-Wolf study response time tails in the M/G/n multi-server queue under heavy-tailed job sizes. Under heavy-tailed sizes, SRPT-style short-job priority is strongly tail optimal, and any priority to large jobs harms the tail. The authors give the first strongly tail-optimal scheduling rules for the M/G/n queue under heavy-tailed sizes. They show a little sympathy to large jobs is essential to strong tail optimality over the full stability region.
arxiv-2605-13849: Francisco Aguilera Moreno offers Mixed Integer Goal planning for custom meal tuning with user-defined serving sizes. His form uses integer counts for usable serving counts and goal planning gaps for soft nutrient targets, with inverse-target scaling evening multi-nutrient tuning. For meals with 15 or more foods, the integer solution matches the smooth optimum in every test case. Across 810 instances MIGP finds strictly better answers than goal planning with post-hoc rounding in 66 percent of cases, never worse.
arxiv-2605-14049: Wang and Gilpin bridge legal reading and formal logic to make AI legal reasoning more faithful. Language models now help read contracts, draft papers and weigh sources at scale, yet legal work demands rigor current systems lack. The core flaw is not mere hallucination: models draw inferences past what sources support, then dress assumption-heavy conclusions as logically grounded. The proposal pairs model fluency with formal verification checks, aiming for AI legal help that is both able and trustworthy.
arxiv-2605-14849: Seymour, Jenkins, Cote and Such study beliefs and misconceptions around integrated conversational AI. As language-model features sink into workflows, markers of origin and training fade and models look commodified to users. Twenty participants used Copilot features in Microsoft Edge for information retrieval and planning tasks. Participants mixed prior perceptions of language models with internet search habits, and beliefs about answer generation shaped prompting strategies. Citations raised answer trustworthiness without prompting checks, and participants often fact-checked against the same sources the AI used.
arxiv-2605-15249: Stavros Bouras and three others harden AI models deployed in Kubernetes clusters with a Kubeflow MLOps architecture. Cloud running alone offers little model-own security. Their system detects adversarial attacks at inference time and automatically triggers shields that preserve accuracy and reliability. A fast gradient sign attack is applied at run time, and stepped gradient descent hostile training deploys when scores drop. Tests show the defense regains much of the scores lost to attack.
arxiv-2605-15349: Stanislav Kim, Anton Pyrkin, and Oleg Borisov derive a complete quadcopter motion model for dynamic positioning at a specified point. From that model they propose two control algorithms. The first generalizes earlier results to a varying yaw angle, the angle of heading rotation. The second addresses the same positioning task with a simplified regulator-tuning methodology. Together the algorithms cover both the general heading case and a practitioner-friendly tuning route for holding a quadcopter fixed in space.
arxiv-2605-15549: Stefano Riva and fifteen colleagues introduce a common task framework for comparing machine-learning models in nuclear fission and fusion. High-fidelity reactor simulations are costly and model assumptions create gaps with measurements, while the sheer variety of data-driven methods makes fair comparison hard. Their framework curates datasets across nuclear systems, scores methods on twelve established metrics plus sparse-measurement monitoring, and benchmarks standard baselines to expose current limits and raise standards for reproducibility.
arxiv-2605-15649: Pranav Somu, Advay Balakrishnan, Stepan Kravtsov, Aaron McDaniel, and Jason Zutty use frozen language models as trait extractors for neural architecture search. Architectures are fed in as PyTorch class text. No search-specific tuning is needed. The traits pass through a light regression head to form the predictor. Raw code inputs beat other text encodings on two search spaces. On one space, swapping path encodings for code traits cuts the test budget to land within one percent of the best architecture by 34 percent for CIFAR-100 scores.
arxiv-2605-15749: M. Andrés-Carcasona and six colleagues bound primordial black holes from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA data. Using modeling, they set the bounds from 0.6 to 100 solar masses and show sensitivity from 0.0001 to 10,000 solar masses, for monochromatic and log-normal mass functions. Mergers dominate the limits, while the gravitational wave background gives weaker limits. Two data-driven methods make the limits agnostic about the astrophysical population. Allowing primordial holes to explain some catalogued events relaxes solar-mass bounds. The bounds stand independent of assumptions and are stringent in the solar-mass range.
arxiv-2605-15849: Gloria Paoli and Yabo Yang give a symmetry method for the gradient of a bounded-variation function in the anisotropic case. Their work extends a Euclidean result of Amato, Gentile, Nitsch and Trombetti from 2024. The key step splits the regular part of the gradient from its singular part. The main result compares the function with its symmetrized form in L1. As a use, they derive isoperimetric bounds for shape measures tied to twist stiffness.
arxiv-2605-15949: Junji Oaki and three colleagues present a parameter ID plan for CRANE-X7, a low-cost seven-degree-of-freedom arm driven by smart actuators. A 39-factor OpenSYMORO model is identified without CAD inertial data using single-joint and pair excitation, least squares, a conditional semidefinite projection and error refinement. Acceptance rests on a positive-definite audit of the inertia matrix over 221,875 sampled configurations. The reduced model beats the full 65-factor model on held-out tests, and two runs 26 days apart give a 1.25 percent relative spread in held-out error.
arxiv-2605-16149: Ourabah builds large-scale transport rules for quasiequilibrium plasmas, whose makeup departs from Maxwellian form with suprathermal tails. Such plasmas can be read as mixes of Maxwellians, or superstatistics. He works out electric and thermal conductivity, mobility, diffusion, and shear and bulk viscosity. Quasiequilibrium effects raise transport numbers above Maxwellian values across the board, a lift he sizes for the three main classes of such mixes.
