It surveys their roles in immune defense, blood vessel tone, and signaling, and in troubles such as insulin resistance, diabetes, obesity, and chronic inflammation. Promising antioxidant molecules get a hearing as well. The authors stress the review is a perspective, not a full catalogue, in a field publishing thousands of papers a year.
europmc-pmc3471949:
Edin and co-authors counted two kinds of immune cells inside colorectal cancers and linked them to patient outcomes, in a 2012 PLoS ONE study. The cells, macrophages, come in a tumor-fighting form and a tissue-repair form that can help tumors grow. The team stained tumor samples from several hundred patients for one marker of each form, grading how many sat at the tumor's invasive edge.

Both forms rose and fell together, and heavy infiltration of either went with earlier-stage tumors. Patients whose tumors held many of the fighting form lived longer, whatever their tumor's other traits. Edin's group found no survival edge tied to the ratio between the forms. The result supports a helpful role for macrophages in this cancer.
europmc-pmc3491949:
Babies born to mothers who smoked carry chemical marks on their DNA, and Bonnie R. Joubert leads a large team scanning for them in 2012. Using cord blood from 1,062 newborns in the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort, they test methylation at 473,844 sites against cotinine, a smoking marker measured in mothers' blood during pregnancy.

Twenty-six sites in ten genes differ at strict epigenome-wide significance. Findings for AHRR, CYP1A1, and GFI1 repeat in a United States birth cohort. The first two genes sit in a pathway that handles smoke-borne chemicals. The study is the largest of its kind at the time and shows in utero exposures can be read in newborn epigenetic patterns.
europmc-pmc3523549:
Babies grow at the speed the placenta feeds them, and Susanne Lager and Theresa L. Powell review how that feeding is regulated in 2012. Both restricted and excessive fetal growth predict trouble at birth and higher metabolic and heart disease risk later in life.

Transporter proteins ferry amino acids, fatty acids, and glucose across the placenta. Their activity falls in growth restriction and rises in at least some overgrowth, suggesting transport changes help cause abnormal growth rather than merely follow it. The review focuses on the regulatory mechanisms that tune these transporters. Understanding the controls, the authors argue, could yield interventions for pregnancy complications rooted in supply.
europmc-pmc3542149:
Viruses and bacteria share the nose and throat, and Astrid A. T. M. Bosch and five colleagues review how they help and hinder each other in 2013. The upper airway holds a dense mix of harmless residents and would-be pathogens, and carrying them with no symptoms is common.

Residents compete and cooperate all the time. A new virus or germ can upset the balance, letting a quiet resident overgrow and invade. The review lists known pairings of germ with germ and virus with germ, and the ways each is thought to work, from fights over food to provoked immune replies. A simple model ties the web together. Grasping this ecology, the authors argue, is one route to stopping airway disease.
europmc-pmc3549249:
Japan registers its stomach cancer care nationwide, and Atsushi Nashimoto and twelve colleagues present the 2009 annual report of the JGCA registry for patients treated in 2002. From 208 hospitals, records on 13,626 patients were collected, covering operations, pathology, and survival; 13,002 patients who underwent laparotomy form the analyzed set.

Five-year follow-up reaches 83.3 percent, and direct operative death is 0.48 percent. Five-year survival by UICC stage falls from 92.2 percent at stage IA to 14.9 percent at stage IV. Patients over 80 make up 7.8 percent of cases, with survival of 51.6 percent. Outcomes for advanced disease had visibly improved against earlier registry rounds.
europmc-pmc3556649:
Alastair Noyce and colleagues published a meta-analysis in Annals of Neurology in 2012 on early signs and risk factors for Parkinson disease. Many nonmotor features, such as constipation or loss of smell, can appear years before diagnosis. The group combined earlier studies to judge which factors are tied most strongly to a later diagnosis and might suit screening of whole populations.

Family history stood out first: having a close relative with Parkinson disease or tremor at least doubled the odds. Constipation and never having smoked also more than doubled the risk in their pooled results. Anxiety or depression, pesticide exposure, head injury, and farm work raised risk by smaller amounts. Coffee drinking and alcohol were tied to lower risk. The paper gives readers a ranked map of what precedes the disease.
europmc-pmc3561149:
Xiquan Gao and colleagues published a plant immunity study in PLoS Pathogens in 2013 on how Arabidopsis cells answer attack. When a pathogen's effector proteins trip internal sensors called NLR proteins, the plant fires several defenses at once. The response includes cell death at the infection site, a burst of reactive oxygen species, and wide changes in gene activity. The wiring between sensor and responses was poorly mapped.

Screens and biochemistry work singled out six related calcium-dependent protein kinases as the branching point. Two of them, switched on fast, govern the timing of cell death. Four others, held on longer, directly mark a set of WRKY transcription factors that reprogram gene activity and limit pathogen growth. The same kinase group also marks the membrane enzymes that produce the oxygen burst. One protein family thus splits one alarm into separate, timed defense lines.
europmc-pmc3566149:
Saakshi Jalali and colleagues mapped contacts between two classes of noncoding RNA in PLoS ONE in 2013. Long noncoding RNAs are RNA strands that never become proteins yet still steer cell activity, and microRNAs are short strands that silence genes. Hints suggested the two classes talk to each other, but no one had charted those contacts across the whole human transcriptome, the full set of RNA a cell produces.

Using data that capture where Argonaute proteins grip RNA, the group built a genome-scale map of microRNA binding sites on long noncoding RNAs. MicroRNAs target these strands as well as protein-coding ones, forming a fresh layer of regulation. The contact sites cluster toward the middle and tail ends of their targets. One contact was then modeled in zebrafish to check the idea in a living animal. The map gives RNA researchers a new set of links to test.
europmc-pmc3577849:
Louise Kenny and colleagues measured pregnancy risk at older ages in PLoS ONE in 2013, using a large regional birth survey. Mothers in rich countries keep giving birth later in life, and older age has been tied to several poor outcomes. Much older work was small or failed to separate age itself from wealth, body weight, or first-time birth. Their cohort covered all single births in northwest England from 2004 to 2008.

Among 215,344 births, mothers aged forty or more faced clearly higher risk than those in their twenties: stillbirth and caesarean delivery both ran about 1.83 times higher, with preterm birth, very preterm birth, and unusually large babies also raised. Mothers in their thirties sat between the groups. Adjusting for parity, ethnic background, deprivation, and body mass did not remove the pattern. The study gives current, local numbers for counseling older mothers.
europmc-pmc3607849:
Ralph Benedict and colleagues set world standards for a brief thinking test battery in multiple sclerosis in BMC Neurology in 2012. Thinking problems are common in MS, and an expert committee had picked a short battery, BICAMS, covering processing speed and memory. Clinics in many countries wanted it, but translations done carelessly would break comparisons. The paper lays down how each country should validate its version, in five ordered steps.

First, test materials must be remade to fit the local culture and language. Instructions follow, translated in full from the manuals. Then at least sixty-five healthy local volunteers, matched to patients by age, sex, and schooling, set the normal range. A small repeat-testing study checks stability over one to three weeks. Last, patient scores must separate from healthy ones. Early national studies were already running as the standards appeared, aiming at one battery the whole field can trust.
europmc-pmc3620049:
Grietje Krabbe and colleagues filmed the brain's patrol cells failing in Alzheimer-like mice in PLoS ONE in 2013. Microglia cluster around amyloid plaques in Alzheimer disease and look activated, yet whether they are helping or harming stayed contested. Watching cells directly, the team measured two core microglial jobs: steering their arms toward trouble and eating debris. They did this in two mouse models of the disease, using two-photon microscopy and brain slices.

Both jobs ran strongly impaired in diseased mice compared with healthy animals of the same age. The impairment mapped in time and place onto amyloid plaque deposition: where and when plaques spread, function faded. A vaccination-style treatment that lowered amyloid restored the eating capacity of the cells. The results recast the activated look of plaque-side microglia: rather than fighting harder, they are progressively failing, and the failure is reversible if the amyloid load comes down.
europmc-pmc3665549:
Ranking gene changes by harm, then genes by their changes, is the trick of a tool from Carter, Douville, Stenson, Cooper and Karchin in a 2013 BMC Genomics article. Exome reading hands labs thousands of changes per patient. The tool, called VEST in the text, scores each change, then pools scores across a gene to rank genes for disease hunts.

In holdout tests the tool beat two popular rivals on telling harmful from neutral changes. Its gene score then ranked the known causal gene second of over two thousand candidate genes in four cases of Miller syndrome. It did the same in three cases of Freeman-Sheldon syndrome. Scores come with a measure of how far they sit from neutral change scores. The authors offer the tool as a way to cut small case sets into sharp gene leads.
europmc-pmc3668949:
Cancer cells steal power plants from blood vessel cells through tiny tunnels, Pasquier and a large team report in a 2013 Journal of Translational Medicine study. The tunnels, thin bridges between cells, can pass membrane parts, cell fluid and whole organelles. The team watched tunnel formation between support cells and cancer cells in dishes, in floating cell balls and in tumour samples. Wide contact between membranes came first, then the bridges formed.

Cell fluid passed between cancer cells and both kinds of support cell at much the same rate. Power plants, the cell's energy organelles, moved in one favoured direction: from vessel-lining cells into cancer cells. Cancer cells that took in those organelles withstood chemotherapy better. The finding hands blood vessels a role beyond feeding tumours: direct organelle gifts that help cancer resist drugs.
europmc-pmc3691249:
Erho and colleagues built and validated a genomic classifier that predicts which prostate cancers will spread early after surgery. Standard clinical features flag risk only loosely. So the team modelled gene activity in tumour tissue. Their samples came from a large Mayo Clinic case-control series of men treated with radical prostatectomy.

Their twenty-two-marker classifier was trained on expression data from hundreds of patients. Follow-up ran for a median of nearly seventeen years. The classifier predicted early metastasis in a withheld validation set. It beat Gleason score and earlier signatures, and stayed informative alongside clinical factors. High scores also marked earlier death from prostate cancer. The authors propose the test for spotting aggressive disease while it is still confined to the prostate.
europmc-pmc3783449:
H. Andrew Schwartz and a large group of co-authors reported a study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on personality, gender, and age in social media language. They analyzed 700 million words, phrases, and topic instances from the Facebook messages of 75,000 volunteers who also took standard personality tests. Their open-vocabulary method lets the data itself surface the words that distinguish groups.

Striking variations appeared. Some results were face-valid: people living at high elevation talk about mountains. Others matched known research: neurotic people disproportionately use the phrase sick of and the word depressed. New hypotheses emerged too, such as an active life implying emotional stability. Men used the possessive my with wife or girlfriend more than women used it with husband or boyfriend. The authors call it the largest study of its kind.
europmc-pmc3808449:
Calis and colleagues asked in PLoS Computational Biology in 2013 why some peptide fragments shown on MHC class I molecules stir T cells into action while others pass unnoticed. Such fragments are how infected cells advertise their contents to the immune system. They gathered a large data set on the immunogenicity of such peptides across many MHC types.

Two patterns stood out: the middle of the peptide, positions four to six, matters most, and amino acids with large, aromatic side chains raise the odds of a response. Combined into a simple scoring model, these rules predicted immunogenicity in two separate epitope studies. The model also suggested T cells are tuned to spot viral peptides more readily than the body's own.
europmc-pmc3858649:
Aleksandra M. Dudek, Shaun Martin, Abhishek D. Garg, and Patrizia Agostinis review dendritic cells in cancer in Frontiers in Immunology in 2013. Dendritic cells are sentry cells that show foreign marks to the rest of the immune system. How they read dying cancer cells decides whether the body tolerates or attacks the tumor.

The state of the sentry cell is the key switch. Young cells tend to teach tolerance toward cancer. Fully mature cells can fire a strong anti-cancer response when the cancer dies in an alarm-raising way. A middle, semi-mature state can tip either way, toward calm or toward tumor aid. Marker sets, signal mixes, and danger cues from dying cells set the state. The review maps those cues for vaccine design.
europmc-pmc3949149:
Aaron C. Petrey and Carol A. de la Motte review hyaluronan, a sugar polymer that helps govern inflammation, in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Hyaluronan is a major part of the gel between cells, and injured or inflamed tissue builds up and breaks it down quickly. Once treated as mere filler, it is now seen as an active player in inflammation, blood vessel growth, scarring, and cancer.

The review stresses size: long intact chains and short fragments send opposite messages to cells. Through binding partners such as CD44 and Toll-like receptors, hyaluronan steers which inflammatory genes switch on, which cells are recruited, and which signals are released. In some settings it calms inflammation and shields tissue from damage. The authors trace how its turnover shapes both the flare and the resolution of inflammation.
europmc-pmc3953549:
W. Krzysciak, A. Jurczak, D. Koscielniak, B. Bystrowska, and A. Skalniak review how the tooth-decay bacterium Streptococcus mutans builds biofilms, in the European Journal of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases in 2014. Dental caries is the most common disease of the mouth, and this bacterium is a leading cause. Its power comes from living in biofilm, a layered community stuck to the tooth surface, rather than floating free.

The review lists the traits that make the bacterium dangerous in that setting. It glues itself to solid surfaces, survives the acid it and its neighbors produce, which dissolves enamel, and interacts with other mouth microbes to hold its place. The authors walk through biofilm formation step by step and tie each virulence trait to how decay actually develops in a real mouth.
europmc-pmc3961149:
Zhian N. Kamvar, Javier F. Tabima, and Niklaus J. Grünwald introduce poppr, a software package for the R statistics system, in PeerJ in 2014. Many microbe, fungus, and water-mold populations break the rules of standard population genetics: they clone themselves, mix clones with sexual reproduction, or blend lineages. Few analysis tools were built for such data, so studies handled clones in improvised, uneven ways.

Poppr imports data from common formats and lets users define any hierarchy of subpopulations, with clone censoring to correct repeated sampling of the same genetic individual. It adds tools such as Bruvo's distance for repeat markers, batch tests of the index of association, several diversity indices, and graphics including family trees with support values and minimum spanning networks. A manual with worked examples ships with it.
europmc-pmc400249:
Hunter B. Fraser, Aaron E. Hirsh, Guri Giaever, Jochen Kumm, and Michael B. Eisen ask whether random noise in gene activity harms living things, in PLoS Biology in 2004. Cells control how much protein they make, yet the process is jittery. Identical cells can end up with quite different amounts of the same protein.

The team reasoned that two gene classes should suffer most from such noise: genes a yeast cell cannot live without, and genes whose proteins join multi-part teams. Using a tested model of random gene activity, they estimated noise for nearly every gene in baker's yeast. Both classes indeed showed lower noise than most other genes. That pattern fits the idea that noise is a real burden on fitness, and that natural selection has tuned it down where it hurts most. Noise, in short, is not a mere side effect but a trait shaped by evolution.
europmc-pmc4012149:
Robert Lanfear, Brett Calcott, David Kainer, Christoph Mayer, and Alexandros Stamatakis present faster ways to split gene data into model groups, in BMC Evolutionary Biology in 2014. Tree-of-life studies sort DNA sites into groups, called partitions, each with its own model of change. Good grouping sharpens the trees, dates, and rates that follow.

Older tools for picking the best grouping could only handle data sets with fewer than one hundred gene regions. Modern studies often hold thousands. The team built two grouping methods based on clustering like sites together. One favours raw speed on huge sets. The other, a relaxed form, ran nearly as fast and gave far better grouping scores by standard tests. Both ship in the free PartitionFinder program. The authors hope wider use will lift the quality of results drawn from very large gene data sets, which are now the norm in the field.
europmc-pmc4028749:
Syed M. Jamal and Graham J. Belsham review foot-and-mouth disease across past, present, and future, in Veterinary Research in 2013. The disease strikes cloven-hoofed animals such as cattle, pigs, and sheep. It spreads fast and costs dearly when it enters a disease-free country. Where it is settled, it drags down output and blocks trade in animal goods.

Seven types of the virus exist, with many variants, and a vaccine for one type may fail against another. The review covers the virus and its types, then the test kit: virus growth, antibody tests, gene-copying tests, and strip tests for field use. Gene reading now helps trace where an outbreak came from and how strains drift. A joint global pathway for stepwise control in settled regions is set out. Better control where the disease lives, the authors stress, cuts the risk for free regions.
europmc-pmc4053949:
Daniël P. Melters and a large team compare the repeat DNA at centromeres across hundreds of species, in Genome Biology in 2013. Centromeres anchor the machinery that splits chromosomes in cell division. In most plants and animals they sit in vast arrays of repeated DNA, yet the repeat sequences change oddly fast.

Mining genome data from close to three hundred species, the team took each genome's most abundant tandem repeat as its likely centromere repeat, a guess that held where centromeres were already known. Such repeats appeared in nearly every genome. Their unit lengths and letters varied wildly, up to well over a thousand letters per unit. Family trees of the repeats showed almost no shared sequence once species had split more than about fifty million years ago. Still, the repeats evolved in similar ways everywhere.
europmc-pmc4058749:
Mark Barok, Heikki Joensuu, and Jorma Isola reviewed how trastuzumab emtansine, known as T-DM1, works against breast cancer and why it can stop working. Their review appeared in Breast Cancer Research in 2014. T-DM1 joins an antibody to a cell-killing drug, aiming the drug at cancer cells that carry the HER2 marker.

Once the pair binds HER2 and is taken inside the cell, the drug part is freed and blocks cell division. How much drug builds up inside shapes whether the cell dies fast, fails during division, or responds poorly. Trials had shown benefit in advanced disease, including later lines of care. The authors also weigh known and suspected routes of resistance, which remain only partly understood.
europmc-pmc4060849:
Jonathan D. Cherry, John A. Olschowka, and M. Kerry O'Banion reviewed the many activation states of microglia, the brain's resident immune cells. Their review appeared in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2014. Microglia can shift between states that fight threats and states that calm inflammation and support repair.

The authors trace a century of debate over what microglia do, then describe how signals in the brain push them toward distinct states. They review what these states mean in both sudden and long-term brain disease models. Special attention goes to the M2 state, linked with reduced inflammation, as a possible treatment route. They caution that simple good-versus-bad labels no longer fit the evidence.
europmc-pmc4124649:
Quynh N. Dinh, Grant R. Drummond, Christopher G. Sobey, and Sophocles Chrissobolis reviewed how inflammation, oxidative stress, and vessel dysfunction intertwine in high blood pressure. Their review appeared in BioMed Research International in 2014. Hypertension is the commonest cardiovascular risk factor, and in about ninety percent of cases its precise cause is unknown.

Whether inflammation causes hypertension or follows from it is unsettled. Evidence from human and animal studies suggests inflammation can indeed drive blood pressure up. Oxidative stress and failure of the vessel lining are key steps in that cascade, each worsening the other. Ageing, the hormone aldosterone, and an overactive sympathetic nervous system also feed the loop. The authors consider whether anti-inflammatory drugs and statins could serve as pressure treatments.
europmc-pmc4210649:
Hazem M. Kalaji and a team of eleven co-authors wrote a practical guide to chlorophyll fluorescence in Photosynthesis Research in 2014. When leaves catch light, some of it bounces back as fluorescence, and that glow reports how well photosynthesis is running. The method is powerful, but the signals are easy to misread.

Set out as a long question-and-answer list, the guide covers the gear, the routines, and the meaning of each measurement. It explains what different fluorescence techniques can and cannot reveal, how long leaves must sit in darkness before a reading, and how to interpret the rising glow curve after a flash. Physiological background fills in why the procedures work. The authors aim it at users with some practice who still puzzle over results, and as a reference for veterans.
europmc-pmc4222749:
Alan O. Bergland, Dmitri A. Petrov, and four co-authors tracked seasonal gene swings in fruit flies in PLoS Genetics in 2014. In an orchard, summer heat and winter cold press very different demands on a fly population. The team suspected gene variants rise and fall with the seasons, kept in balance by the yearly cycle.

Sampling a North American orchard population across seasons, they found hundreds of DNA variants whose frequencies oscillated in step with the seasons, year after year. The swinging variants tracked weather shifts and matched traits that vary by season. Many appear millions of years old, some older than the split from a sister species. The evidence supports a model where rapid climate swings protect genetic diversity instead of erasing it.
europmc-pmc4231949:
Tae Chul Moon, A. Dean Befus, and Marianna Kulka reviewed how mast cells release their chemicals in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Mast cells sit at body surfaces where the outside world meets tissue. Long known for allergy, they also fight germs and steer immunity, using a store of ready-made and freshly made mediators.

Histamine and its granule mates leave within moments of activation, while lipid mediators, cytokines, and chemokines follow on their own timetable. The trigger decides the mix: an IgE allergy signal and a bacterial sensor signal produce different release patterns. The review gathers what is known about the secretory paths behind that selectivity, and admits the sorting machinery is still poorly mapped. That gap matters for drugs that aim to block only the harmful releases.
europmc-pmc4235049:
Sandeep Kumar Dhanda, Pooja Vir, and Gajendra P. S. Raghava built a predictor for immune-stimulating peptides in Biology Direct in 2013. Interferon gamma, released by helper T cells, is a key weapon against tuberculosis and other infections. Vaccine designers want short protein pieces that both dock onto MHC class II molecules and provoke that release, but testing each candidate in the lab is slow.

Training on 3,705 provoking and 6,728 non-provoking binders, the team found peptide length, residue patterns at set positions, and overall composition all carry signal. Their best model, mixing pattern search with machine learning, sorted peptides with about 82 percent accuracy. A free webserver applies the model, letting researchers screen candidate vaccine pieces before bench work.
europmc-pmc4255749:
Annette Prüss-Ustün and a team of eleven co-authors tallied the 2012 death toll of poor water and sanitation in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2014. Unsafe water, missing toilets, and unwashed hands spread diarrhoea, still a leading killer in poorer countries. Earlier burden estimates were dated, and policy needs fresh numbers by cause.

Using exposure data for 145 countries and the latest risk figures, they attributed 502,000 diarrhoea deaths to inadequate drinking water. They attributed 280,000 more to inadequate sanitation, and about 297,000 to inadequate hand hygiene in 2012. Together the cluster caused an estimated 842,000 diarrhoea deaths, 58 percent of all such deaths, including 361,000 children under five. The authors present the count as a baseline for tracking promised improvements.
europmc-pmc4283449:
Mike W-L Cheung introduces metaSEM, a free R package that runs meta-analysis through structural equation modeling. His paper appeared in Frontiers in Psychology in 2014. Structural equation modeling is a flexible way to test models that link many variables, and framing a meta-analysis in that form extends what pooled studies can answer.

The package handles single outcome, multiple outcome, and three level meta-analyses, and it can pool correlation matrices across studies in two stages. The paper explains the theory briefly, shows how common meta-analytic models translate into this form, and points to worked examples. It is a practical guide for researchers who already use R and want the added reach.
europmc-pmc4302049:
Michael Love, Wolfgang Huber, and Simon Anders published the DESeq2 method in 2014, and it became a standard tool in gene studies. Their subject is RNA-seq, a lab method that counts how active each gene is in a sample. Comparing those counts across samples sounds simple, but small sample sizes and wild swings in the numbers mislead older methods.

DESeq2 steadies the estimates by sharing strength across genes. It shrinks the noisiest fold changes toward safer values and handles samples with very few repeats. The authors call this moderated estimation. Labs studying cancer, infection, and basic cell life now run DESeq2 by default, and the paper is one of the most cited in its field.
europmc-pmc4365749:
Louise Tailford, Emmanuelle Crost, Devon Kavanaugh, and Nathalie Juge reviewed how gut bacteria feed on mucus sugars, in Frontiers in Genetics in 2015. The gut is lined with a mucus layer rich in complex sugars called glycans, built on proteins named mucins. Some bacteria can forage on those sugars, which helps decide which species settle at the gut wall. The review asks what tools those bacteria use, and why their spot next to the immune system matters.

Mucin sugars come in varied, branched forms, capped with extra sugar units that bacteria must trim in sequence. Genome data from mucus degraders is growing fast, but few of their enzymes are well characterized, and studies rarely link enzyme range to real feeding ability. Recent work the review gathers shows how these bacteria adapt to the mucus niche and sway host responses.
europmc-pmc4368749:
Chen Xue and co-authors pooled studies of what raises the risk of combat-related post-traumatic stress disorder, in PLoS ONE in 2015. The disorder follows traumatic events and is a common result of military service, harming daily and social life. The team searched four databases for observational studies of troops and veterans after combat deployment. Thirty-two articles qualified, and the team combined their results with models that allow for variation between studies.

Reported rates of the disorder ranged widely, from about one percent to about 35 percent across studies. Eighteen clear predictors emerged. Risks from before service included prior trauma, prior mental health problems, and many deployments. Risks during service included heavy combat exposure, firing a weapon, and seeing someone wounded or killed. The list gives clinicians and planners concrete flags for early support.
europmc-pmc4379949:
Anupam Singh, Vaibhav Upadhyay, Arun Upadhyay, Surinder Singh, and Amulya Panda reviewed how to recover useful proteins from bacterial clumps, in Microbial Cell Factories in 2015. When Escherichia coli is engineered to make large amounts of a foreign protein, the protein often piles into dense aggregates called inclusion bodies. Pulling active protein out of them is slow work with poor yields. The review covers gentler ways to open the clumps while keeping the protein's natural shape.

Mild methods rest on a key insight: proteins inside inclusion bodies often keep a near-native structure. If the clump is dissolved gently, that shape survives, and later refolding and cleaning steps recover far more active protein. The authors review each step of the process, the factors that sway yield and quality, and a model scheme for high-throughput recovery. Industry stands to gain cheaper protein production.
europmc-pmc4405349:
Charles Duyckaerts and a panel of co-authors argued against splitting a tau pattern off from Alzheimer's disease, in Acta Neuropathologica in 2015. A proposal had named tau tangles confined to memory regions, with little amyloid, as primary age-related tauopathy, or PART, a separate condition. The authors examine whether its mechanism or outlook truly differs from Alzheimer's. They find no property of that tau pattern that predicts limited progression or rules out Alzheimer's development.

The same tau pattern is an invariant feature of Alzheimer's disease itself, they note. Biochemical differences between the two remain unproven. Rather than minting a new disease, they recommend keeping the analytical approach that stages tangles and amyloid phases separately, without inferring disease processes from patterns alone. Naming, in their view, should follow evidence, not precede it.
europmc-pmc4464049:
Anna Renom-Guiteras, Gabriele Meyer, and Petra Thürmann built a European list of risky medicines for older people in the European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology in 2015. Older patients often take many drugs, and some are more likely to harm than help them. A shared list lets countries compare prescribing and helps doctors choose safer options for aging patients.

Starting from a German list and lists from North America and France, thirty experts in geriatric prescribing from seven European countries took part. Some expanded the draft list, many rated each drug in a two-round structured survey, and a final group settled open points. The agreed list names hundreds of substances or drug classes as potentially inappropriate for older people. Some entries apply only at certain doses or durations. The list also suggests dose changes and safer alternatives for practice.
europmc-pmc4474349:
Zhenshan Liu, Mingming Xin, Jinxia Qin, Huiru Peng, Zhongfu Ni, Yingyin Yao, and Qixin Sun profiled gene activity in wheat under heat and drought in BMC Plant Biology in 2015. Bread wheat is a world crop whose yield and quality fall sharply under those stresses, especially together. Wheat also carries three related sub-genomes, so each gene often exists in three homeologous copies that can share the work unevenly.

Seedlings were exposed to drought, heat, or both, for short periods, and their RNA was sequenced over time. Stress-responsive genes overlapped across conditions but also formed complex, condition-specific patterns. Thousands of homeologous copies split their expression, with one copy dominating under a given stress, a division that may help wheat adjust. The data give breeders and molecular biologists a time-resolved map for improving stress tolerance.
europmc-pmc4489249:
Sebastian Salentin, Sven Schreiber, V Joachim Haupt, Melissa Adasme, and Michael Schroeder built PLIP, an automated profiler of protein-ligand interactions, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. How a small molecule grips a protein, contact by contact, is essential knowledge for drug discovery and structural biology. Tools to extract that information existed, but comprehensive ones were not freely available.

PLIP takes a structure from the Protein Data Bank, a protein or ligand name, or a custom complex from docking. It then detects non-covalent contacts atom by atom. Its rule-based algorithm needs no preparation of the structure. It covers seven contact types, from hydrogen bonds and water bridges to halogen bonds and stacking between ring systems. Results come as lists for further computing, publication-ready images, and files for the PyMOL viewer. A command-line mode handles high-throughput profiling, and the code is open source.
europmc-pmc4502549:
Stefano Schiaffino, Alberto Rossi, Vika Smerdu, Leslie Leinwand, and Carlo Reggiani reviewed developmental myosins in Skeletal Muscle in 2015. Myosins are the motor proteins of muscle. Developing muscles use special embryonic and neonatal forms, coded by their own genes, which appear before birth and then vanish as adult fast and slow myosins take over. A light chain shared with the embryonic heart belongs to the same set.

These early myosins persist in a few adult muscles, such as those moving the eye and jaw, and in the sensory fibers of muscle spindles. They return during muscle regeneration, marking repairing fibers in diseased muscle. Mutations in the two heavy chain genes cause distal arthrogryposis syndromes, with congenital joint contractures and facial differences, showing that fetal muscle activity shapes joints and face. What the early myosins do better than adult ones, the authors note, is still only partly understood.
europmc-pmc4526649:
Gitanjali M. Singh leads a ten-author team measuring what the world drinks, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Sugary drinks, fruit juice, and milk all shape health, yet comparable intake figures by country, age, and sex were scarce. The team gathered diet surveys and food supply records to build one consistent global picture for adults in 2010.

They drew on 193 national or regional diet surveys covering over half the world's people, plus United Nations food balance data for 187 countries. A Bayesian model, a method that pools uneven sources while tracking doubt, harmonized the patchwork. The result is a country-by-country account of beverage intake split by age and sex, made to guide nutrition policy and later studies of drink-related disease.
europmc-pmc4581549:
Jaime M. Cyphert, Carol S. Trempus, and Stavros Garantziotis review a sugar whose message depends on its size, in the International Journal of Cell Biology in 2015. Hyaluronan is a simple repeating sugar chain once dismissed as inert filler between cells. No chemical decoration alters it after production, yet it signals strongly, sometimes pushing inflammation and cell movement, sometimes calming both.

The resolution is fragment length. Long chains and short fragments, cut by enzymes or damage, speak differently to cells and produce opposing effects. The review explains how fragments of each size arise, which receptors they engage, and what downstream biology follows. Size-aware thinking, the authors argue, is essential for any drug or biomarker plan involving hyaluronan.
europmc-pmc4587849:
Alexander L. Greninger leads a twelve-author team naming viruses from raw samples with a pocket sequencer, in Genome Medicine in 2015. Hunting an unknown pathogen usually takes targeted tests and days. The team ran unbiased metagenomic sequencing, reading all DNA in a sample, on a MinION nanopore device paired with a new real-time analysis pipeline called MetaPORE.

Four human blood samples carried chikungunya, Ebola, or hepatitis C virus. The heavy infections were flagged within 4 to 10 minutes of sequencing; the lighter hepatitis C case took 40 minutes. Despite a 24% average error per read, the correct strain was identified in all four, and 90% of the chikungunya genome was rebuilt at 97–99% accuracy. Total turnaround ran under six hours.
europmc-pmc4592949:
Joseph D. Mancias and nine colleagues published a 2015 cell biology study on ferritinophagy, the process that breaks down ferritin to release stored iron. Their focus was NCOA4, a protein that carries ferritin to the cell's recycling compartments. How this flow is controlled, and what NCOA4 does in iron-related tasks, was poorly understood. The work appeared in eLife.

Experiments in cells and zebrafish showed that a direct link between NCOA4 and ferritin is needed to deliver ferritin for breakdown. Extra iron lowers NCOA4 levels through a second protein, HERC2, which tags it for removal. NCOA4 also proved essential for red blood cell development. Together, the results explain how cells tie iron release to iron supply.
europmc-pmc4606749:
A 2015 study by Charlotte A. Brighton and colleagues deals with how bile acids trigger release of GLP-1, a gut hormone that helps control blood sugar. Bile acids reach hormone-making L-cells in the gut wall, but which sensor they use, and from which side, was unclear. The work appeared in Endocrinology and used mouse tissue, rat gut preparations, and cell cultures.

One bile acid, TDCA, raised internal signals in L-cells and released more GLP-1 than related bile acids. It worked best from the blood-facing side of the tissue, not the gut-facing side. Mice lacking the bile acid receptor GPBAR1 showed no response at all. The team concludes that bile acids act mainly through GPBAR1 receptors on the outer face of L-cells, a detail that matters for drugs aimed at this pathway.
europmc-pmc4619249:
J. Joshua Smith, together with colleagues, released a 2015 trial protocol on saving the rectum in locally advanced rectal cancer. Standard care mixes chemotherapy, radiation, and removal of the rectum, which impairs quality of life. Some patients' tumours vanish after drug and radiation treatment. The phase II trial tests whether those patients can safely skip surgery. The protocol appeared in BMC Cancer.

Patients receive chemotherapy either before or after chemoradiation, then are re-checked. Those with leftover tumour go to surgery, while complete responders are watched closely instead, with visits every three months for two years. Everyone is followed for at least five years, with three-year disease-free survival as the main measure. The design aims to prove that careful watching can match surgery for selected patients.
europmc-pmc4696349:
Yu Gyoung Tak and Peggy J. Farnham explained how to make sense of genome-wide association studies in Epigenetics and Chromatin in 2015. Such studies scan millions of single-letter DNA differences and link many to diseases. The puzzle is that most linked variants sit in non-coding DNA, which does not build proteins. A variant there cannot change a protein directly, so how does it raise disease risk? The review offers routes from a statistical hit to a working mechanism.

One likely answer is that these variants tune gene activity instead. The authors describe ways to rank candidate variants using maps of gene-control regions, software that predicts effects on expression, and lab tests that find each variant's target genes. By February 2015, thousands of studies had logged over fifteen thousand variant links. The review gives geneticists a practical path for turning that growing list into biology.
europmc-pmc4737249:
Neil Vargesson reviewed the history and mechanisms of thalidomide birth defects in Birth Defects Research in 2015, writing solo. Sold in the late 1950s as a safe sedative and morning-sickness remedy in forty-six countries, thalidomide caused severe malformations in over ten thousand children before its 1961 ban. The drug later found legitimate uses against multiple myeloma and leprosy complications, and damaged children have tragically appeared again in Brazil. How it deforms embryos, though, stayed mysterious for decades.

Recent work, covered here in depth, implicates the protein cereblon, blood-vessel disruption, oxidative stress, and cell death in the forming limb, alongside effects on key growth signals. Vargesson lays out the range of damage, the timeline of the disaster, and what each proposed mechanism explains or fails to explain. Open challenges close the review. It stands as both memorial and progress report for one of medicine's defining catastrophes.
europmc-pmc4743949:
Lasda and Parker ask how cells get rid of circular RNAs. These looped molecules lack the free ends that degradation enzymes attack, so they are unusually stable, with half-lives beyond 48 hours. Working with three cell lines, the pair test whether cells simply export them in extracellular vesicles.

Vesicle preparations from the culture medium do contain established circular RNAs. Better, the circles are enriched in vesicles compared with their linear counterparts inside the producing cells. Export in vesicles thus looks like a clearance route, and possibly a signalling one, since other cells can take vesicles up and receive the circles.
europmc-pmc4767049:
Tamara Kredo and six co-authors map the state of clinical practice guidelines in the International Journal for Quality in Health Care in 2016. Guidelines tell doctors what care fits which case, and thirty years of method research have shifted them from expert opinion toward proof-based advice. The field now brims with terms, tools, and short names that can baffle newcomers.

From a wide document search, the authors set out the standards and systems in plain order: how guidelines are built, reported, fitted to local settings, put into practice, and judged. Building and rollout draw the most work worldwide. Updating, adapting guides made elsewhere, and measuring their impact lag behind. The guide is written for people who order, study, or deliver care, and is built to be refreshed.
europmc-pmc4782049:
Michaela Müller-McNicoll leads ten authors in Genes & Development in 2016 on how finished RNA messages earn their exit from the cell nucleus. The exporter protein NXF1 ferries messages out, but it cannot judge on its own whether a message is fully built. Adaptor proteins must load it on, and which adaptors link the final build steps to export was unclear.

The team shows that SR proteins act as such adaptors. These proteins sit on messages during splicing and end trimming, the last build steps. SR proteins grip both the message and NXF1, ride out with the cargo, and cluster near message ends where the build finishes. The scheme makes export a check on maturity: only messages that passed the final steps carry the full crew needed to leave.
europmc-pmc4810049:
David J. Mellor and Clive J. C. Phillips argue in Animals in 2016 that animal welfare thinking needs an update. The Five Freedoms, set out in the early 1990s, shaped welfare codes worldwide by listing what animals should be free from: hunger, thirst, discomfort, pain, and fear, among them. Two decades of science, the authors say, show the list no longer fits what is known about animal experience.

Some bad feelings can never be removed, only briefly eased, because they are the alarms that keep an animal alive. Others stem from poor housing and can be traded for good experiences when conditions improve. Welfare should thus be judged as a balance: keep negative experiences low and give animals real chances for positive ones. The paper ends with a plain-language picture of welfare as a life worth living, and what that means for minimum standards.
europmc-pmc4835549:
Ivan Sović leads six authors in Nature Communications in 2016 presenting GraphMap, a tool for placing nanopore sequencing reads on a genome. Nanopore machines are cheap and portable and read long DNA stretches, but their raw reads are error-rich, with accuracy far below older machines. Standard placement tools, built for cleaner reads, lose many of them.

GraphMap refines candidate placements step by step and walks a graph structure to stay fast. On test sets it beat short- and long-read rivals, placing over ninety-five percent of bases with ten to eighty percent higher sensitivity. Its placements supported variant calls on a human genome, structural change detection across a wide size range, and naming of germ species and strains from field-style reads. The software is free under an open license.
europmc-pmc4990649:
Nils Gustafsson and five co-authors present SRRF, a method that reaches super-resolution imaging with ordinary dyes and microscopes. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Super-resolution methods usually demand special optics and harsh light that harms living cells. SRRF instead analyzes flicker patterns in normal fluorescence movies, using radial fluctuations in each frame. It ships as a fast plugin for ImageJ, the standard free image tool, accelerated by graphics hardware.

On hard, dim live cell data the method resolved detail finer than a set nanometer bar. On data like that from single molecule methods it nearly matched their resolution. Because it works on widefield, confocal, and TIRF microscopes at far lower light levels, labs can film living cells from minutes to hours. The authors pitch SRRF as super-resolution for the microscopes labs already own.
europmc-pmc5005949:
Debbie A. Lawlor wrote a solo commentary in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2016 on two-sample Mendelian randomization. The method uses gene variants as stand-ins for a risk factor, to test cause rather than mere links. She discusses a study that used public gene-study summary data to test how body fat affects several cancers.

That study linked higher adult body mass to lower breast cancer risk and higher risk of ovarian, lung, and bowel cancers. Lawlor explains why full public summary data make this two-sample design possible and why its use will grow. She also flags weak points: summary data fix the choices made by the first study. Changes for body mass can bias waist-based results toward no effect. Weak gene tools distort the answers. Her piece is a guide to both the promise and the traps of the design.
europmc-pmc5014549:
Joshua R. Wheeler, Tyler Matheny, Saumya Jain, Robert Abrisch, and Roy Parker report in eLife in 2016 on stress granules. These are clumps of RNA and protein that form inside cells when protein building stalls under stress. A granule has two parts: a stable core and a looser shell around it. Which part forms first, and which clears first, was the open question the team set out to answer.

Watching granules over time, they saw cores form early, as untranslated RNA-protein bundles lock together. Those cores then gather into larger granules, likely helped by the shells merging. When stress ends, the order flips: shells melt away first and cores are cleared last. Changes that favor liquid-like separation in test tubes had the opposite effect in living cells, a clue the authors use to argue that stable cores, not liquid drops, start the whole process.
europmc-pmc5018249:
Bryan Briney and a large co-author group report in Cell in 2016 on guiding antibody growth toward HIV protection. A vaccine that raises broadly neutralizing antibodies, able to block many HIV strains, is a top goal. One prized family, VRC01-class, starts from starter B cells that are fairly common in people, and a lab-built primer can wake those starters, but steering them to maturity had not been shown.

The team built booster shots shaped to pull the woken cells step by step toward the mature form. In mice bred to carry the human starter gene, boosting yielded antibodies that blocked near-native HIV strains broadly and native virus weakly. Gene and function checks placed these antibodies partway along the known path to the mature VRC01-class. The work shows that a staged shot series can walk an immune response down a chosen road.
europmc-pmc5020549:
Cecilia A. C. Prinsen and seven co-authors offer a practical guideline in Trials in 2016 on picking measuring tools for core outcome sets. A core outcome set is the agreed minimum list of outcomes every trial in a field should report. Agreeing what to measure is only half the job; trials also need sound tools to measure each outcome, and no shared method existed for choosing them.

The guideline grew out of a literature review and a three-round expert survey run with two research initiatives. Of 481 invited experts, 120 took part, and agreement settled on four steps. Teams should first think through what each outcome means, then find existing tools by a structured search. Then they judge each tool's quality and ease of use, and finally apply shared rules for the pick. The steps give trial builders a common, open way to choose their measures.
europmc-pmc5217749:
Sarah A. Birken and a broad team of colleagues reviewed studies that combined two implementation frameworks in Implementation Science in 2017. More than 60 frameworks exist to guide putting research findings into practice. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, or CFIR, and the Theoretical Domains Framework, or TDF, are both detailed, multi-level tools built from theory, so using both at once seemed possibly redundant.

The search found five protocols and seven finished studies that used the pair together, spanning several countries, health interventions, and study phases. Three studies said the pairing served several purposes at once, and six said it covered several conceptual levels, while four gave no clear reason. The reviewers conclude the pairing can be justified because CFIR aims at a full set of implementation factors, while TDF grew from work on designing interventions.
europmc-pmc5233749:
Marjolein N. Kooijman and colleagues gave the 2017 design and cohort update for the Generation R Study in the European Journal of Epidemiology. Generation R follows children from fetal life into young adulthood in a population-based prospective cohort. Its aim is to find the early environmental and genetic causes behind normal and abnormal growth, development, and health.

In total, 9,778 mothers with delivery dates from April 2002 to January 2006 joined the study, with a 61 percent response at the start and follow-up near 80 percent through age ten. Data come from questionnaires, interviews, physical and ultrasound exams, behavior observation, lung tests, brain and body imaging, and biological samples, with genome-wide and epigenome-wide screens available. Outcomes span behavior, body composition, eyes, hearing, heart, immunity, teeth, breathing, allergy, and skin, in children and their parents.
europmc-pmc5303749:
Sarah Jäkel and Leda Dimou reviewed what killing glial cells has taught neuroscience, in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2017. Glia, microglia, astrocytes, and the oligodendrocyte family, make up between a third and two thirds of the mammalian brain. Yet Virchow and his peers dismissed them as nerve glue, what their Greek-derived name means. A century of work has given them real jobs, but many functions remain unsettled.

The review walks through ablation studies in the adult mouse brain, where modern genetics can delete one glial population at a time and watch the consequences. Microglia, for instance, can be wiped out efficiently, but surviving progenitors rush back to repopulate the emptied territory, and their housekeeping touches ongoing synapse formation. Comparing the depletion experiments cell type by cell type, in health and disease, shows both what each glial class does and how resilient the network is when it loses them.
europmc-pmc5313049:
Adam M. Session led a huge team in reading the genome of the African clawed frog in Nature in 2016. This frog, Xenopus laevis, carries four sets of genes, not the usual two. Its close cousin carries two sets, which gives a clean point of comparison. The team asked how the doubled genome arose and what time did to it.

Marks left by old jumping genes split the genome into two sub-genomes from two parent species. Those parents split apart long ago and joined again to form the four-set frog. More than half of all genes still survive in both copies. The two sub-genomes aged unevenly. One kept more of the old state, while the other lost more genes, moved more parts, and read its genes less. Gene survival tracked gene use and the amount of kept DNA nearby.
europmc-pmc5360849:
Anne Masi, Marilena M. DeMayo, Nicholas Glozier, and Adam J. Guastella gave a broad review of autism in Neuroscience Bulletin in 2017. Since Kanner's first notes in 1943, the name and bounds of the diagnosis have been fought over and reshaped many times. The current view casts autism as a complex, wide-spread condition with many causes, subtypes, and life paths. Diagnosis still rests on watched behavior alone.

Two signs define it: lasting gaps in social talk and shared life, and narrow, repeat patterns of acts and interests. The review walks through the history, rates, and causes of the condition. It then sorts what drives its wide variety: genes, side illnesses, and sex among them. Drug and behavior care with real proof are set out next. Last, the authors look to body markers that could split the condition into true kinds.
europmc-pmc5431549:
Zhou and co-authors test whether transplanting gut microbes can ease fatty liver disease in mice. Their research article appeared in Scientific Reports. The disease is a form of liver inflammation tied to obesity. Few treatments exist for it. Gut microbes are thought to play a key role. The team asked whether a full microbial transplant could reset the gut and calm the liver.

Mice ate a high-fat diet for eight weeks. One group then got fecal transplants for eight more weeks. The treatment fixed the disturbed gut mix. Helpful bacteria, including Lactobacillus, became more common. A useful gut product, butyrate, rose as well. The gut wall sealed more tightly, and toxins leaking into blood fell. Inside the liver, fat buildup dropped. Triglyceride and cholesterol levels fell too. Inflammatory signals eased, and the disease score improved. The authors say the transplant helped by restoring a healthier gut community.
europmc-pmc5469049:
Kreider and co-authors present a position stand in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. The topic is creatine, a popular supplement among athletes. Creatine sits mostly in skeletal muscle and fuels hard effort. Trials link added creatine to better high-intensity performance. The panel updates an earlier society statement on its use.

Supplementation raised muscle creatine stores across many studies, they report. Benefits extend to recovery, injury prevention, and rehab support. Clinical uses span brain diseases, diabetes, ageing, and pregnancy. Doses up to 30 grams a day for five years proved safe. Even modest daily intake may aid health across the lifespan.
europmc-pmc5512649:
Ran and co-authors report a materials study in Nature Communications on solar hydrogen making. Splitting water with sunlight could yield clean fuel at scale. The best helper catalysts rely on platinum, which is rare and costly. The team tested a layered material called Ti3C2 MXene instead. Computer modeling guided the design before lab work began.

Tiny MXene particles were joined with cadmium sulfide, a light absorber. The pair produced hydrogen at a very high rate under visible light, they report. Quantum efficiency reached about 40 percent at one test wavelength. The particles also boosted zinc-based absorbers. MXenes may thus anchor cheap, high-performing solar fuel systems.
europmc-pmc5513949:
Assaha and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Physiology on salt stress in ordinary crop plants. Such plants, called glycophytes, suffer when sodium builds up in their shoots. Sodium crowds out potassium, which cells need for basic chemistry. Keeping the two in balance is the core tolerance trick. Special transporter proteins and channels do that work.

Salt-loving plants use the same machinery, the authors note. The edge lies in gene activity levels and small protein tweaks. Membrane voltage control matters just as much. One antiporter, SOS1, helps hold that voltage steady. Findings may guide breeding for salt-tolerant crops.
europmc-pmc5517149:
Grumati and co-authors report a cell biology study in eLife on how cells recycle their endoplasmic reticulum. This membrane network comes in flat sheets and thin tubules. Worn parts are eaten by selective autophagy, called ER-phagy. Receptors for sheet disposal were already known. The tubule receptor was still missing.

The protein RTN3 fills that role, they report. Its long form clusters together and snaps tubules into fragments. Binding sites on RTN3 grip the autophagy machinery directly. The fragments then travel to lysosomes for breakdown. No other reticulon family member can do this job. Each ER shape now has its own disposal route.
europmc-pmc5520949:
Bhat and co-authors report an immunology study in Cell Death and Disease on interferon gamma and killer T cells. This signal protein is famous for rallying immune defenses. The team asked what it does to the CD8 T cells that release it. Skin grafts in mice served as the living test. Live imaging tracked the cells as they hunted targets.

T cells unable to make interferon failed to reject grafts, they report. The signal sped up T cell movement through tissue. It also sharpened their killing of target skin cells. Blocking the signal slowed the cells and cut their survival. Local supply matters for therapy design, they conclude.
europmc-pmc5539349:
Guo and co-authors present a research article in Cell Research. They introduce single-cell COOL-seq, a method for mouse cells. The method reads several layers of cell control from one cell at once. Those layers include open chromatin, DNA methylation, copy number, and ploidy.

The team applied the method to mouse embryos before implantation. They also tested it on embryonic stem cells. They report fast, broad loss of DNA methylation soon after fertilization. Both parental genomes also opened up, then grew less open after the late zygote stage. The authors trace distinct open and closed gene states across early stages. Readers get a first single-cell, parent-specific map of these early changes.
europmc-pmc5552849:
Griffin, Leaver, and Irving present a meta-analysis in Diabetologia. Their question is whether metformin cuts heart disease risk in type 2 diabetes. The drug is the most prescribed oral glucose-lowering medicine in the world. Past reviews had raised doubts on this point.

The team pooled 13 trials with about 2,079 people on metformin. A like number served in comparison groups. Most outcomes leaned toward metformin, but none reached statistical significance. One large British study supplied most of the data. Event counts were small. The authors say real uncertainty remains. They suggest health records and new trial designs to close the gap. Readers get a frank view of thin evidence behind a first-line drug.
europmc-pmc5582349:
Tiku and co-authors report a longevity finding in Nature Communications. Many pathways can extend animal life, from eating less to weaker insulin signals. Whether they share a common downstream mark was unknown. The team finds that mark inside the cell nucleus.

Long-lived worms, flies, and mice all show small nucleoli. The nucleolus is the cell part that builds ribosomes. A protein called NCL-1 keeps it small and extends life in worms. Lowering another nucleolar protein, fibrillarin, did the same. In normal worms, nucleolus size alone predicted how long each animal would live. Human muscle samples after mild diet limits and exercise also showed small nucleoli. Readers get a visible sign of long life shared across species.
europmc-pmc5593049:
An 1841 review in The British and Foreign Medical Review praises Richard Quain's Anatomy of the Arteries of the Human Body. Quain taught anatomy at University College. Joseph Maclise drew the lithographic plates. The book serves surgeons who operate near large arteries.

Quain built it from years of close observation. He inspected some 930 bodies received for anatomy study. He noted the usual course of each vessel. He also logged every oddity of origin, length, position, and direction. The plates show arteries first alone, then with veins and nerves. A further series sketches the deviations from the standard pattern. The reviewer calls the work excellent in plan and execution. Readers get a period guide to surgical anatomy.
europmc-pmc5625949:
Scutiero and co-authors review oxidative stress in endometriosis for Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Endometriosis plants womb-lining tissue outside the uterus. It brings pelvic pain and infertility to many women. Its cause is still debated.

Oxidative stress means reactive oxygen species outrun the body's defenses. Those molecules inflame tissue and alter cell growth. The review gathers evidence tying that imbalance to the disease. Iron overload in the pelvic cavity feeds the chemistry. Blood from backward menstrual flow brings the iron in. Markers of oxidative damage appear in blood and pelvic fluids. They also appear in the tissue itself. Genes that handle oxidative stress enter the story. Links to infertility and cancer risk are weighed as well. Readers get the full case for a chemical imbalance behind a stubborn disease.
europmc-pmc5653849:
Li and co-authors compare two breast cancer stem cell markers in this research article. The article appeared in Scientific Reports. The markers are the CD44/CD24 pair and ALDH1. Both are widely used in the field. Their expression often disagrees within one subtype. The team compared their functions across cell subtypes.

A high CD44/CD24 ratio marked malignancy. It tied more to cell growth and tumour formation. ALDH1-positive cells migrated more strongly. That marker better flagged metastasis risk. Silencing CD44 or ALDH1 cut both traits. The authors say using both markers together works best. Both signals persisted during spread to distant sites. That persistence supports their use in detection and prognosis.
europmc-pmc5693449:
Smith and co-authors present a review in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. It updates proof on built settings and movement. The team searched databases in June 2015. Studies had to gauge built traits with hard measures. Outcomes covered daily activity and travel choices. Children and adults both qualified for the set. Cost data and equity effects were pulled as well.

Twenty-eight studies met the rules for the review. Walkable streets showed clear gains in activity. Better parks and playgrounds also helped. New routes for walking and biking helped too. Gains may favor richer groups, some proof hints. Bias and weak controls were common flaws. Mixed designs blocked firm claims on cost.
europmc-pmc5696449:
Bellmann and Smuszkiewicz review how antifungal drugs move through the body. Their review appeared in Infection. Invasive fungal infections carry high death rates. Getting drug exposure right is crucial. The authors summarize data for each drug class. They focus on illness effects and tissue reach. Combined therapy gets attention too.

Each class clears the body differently. Some drugs leave through the kidney unchanged. Azole drugs are processed in the liver. They also cause many drug interactions. Echinocandins show fewer interaction problems. Tissue penetration varies by drug. Some reach most tissues well. Others gather in liver and spleen. Combination treatment is standard for cryptococcosis. Its value elsewhere stays disputed.
europmc-pmc5699749:
Wollaston presents a short chemical essay from 1810. It announces a new species of urinary calculus. The stone came from a human bladder. He names its key substance cystic oxide. The essay first corrects slips in his earlier paper. That 1797 paper listed five known kinds of stones. They ran from uric acid to the fusible calculus.

The new kind fits none of those five classes. He first met with such a stone about five years earlier. Its leading properties are described in the essay. The find added a sixth species to the known list. Cystic oxide later became known as cystine. The paper stands as its first description in print.
europmc-pmc5727049:
Turashvili and Brogi review how breast cancer differs from case to case. Tumors vary between patients, and cells vary within a single tumor. The review draws on pathology and molecular studies. It links this spread to test results and to drug response.

The authors cover stage, tumor type, and grade as signs of difference between tumors. They also cover hormone receptors and HER2, which guide targeted drugs. Gene tests can sort patients into low and high risk groups. Within one tumor, mixed cell types can drive drug resistance. The review notes that care rules still make little use of this inner mix.
europmc-pmc5727249:
Sroussi and co-authors review mouth problems caused by radiation for head and neck cancer. Radiation can cause sharp, lasting harm to teeth, gums, and soft tissue. The review covers how each problem shows up and how it tends to progress. It also gives care plans drawn from studies and clinical work.

Problems covered include mouth sores, infections, and changes in saliva. The authors also treat tissue stiffening, loss of feeling, tooth decay, and bone death in the jaw. Many harms need care for life, not just during treatment. The team urges joint care that puts skilled oral health staff on the treatment team from the start.
europmc-pmc5733049:
Dalle, Rossmeislova, and Koppo review how long term low grade inflammation drives muscle loss in old age. That loss, called sarcopenia, cuts strength and raises the risk of falls and frailty. Standard help centers on strength training and extra protein. The review asks what inflammation adds on top of those steps.

The authors trace how inflamed tissue alters muscle protein balance. Signals such as TNF and interleukin 6 speed breakdown and blunt new protein building. Old cells that spread these signals add to the load. Calming inflammation might boost the gains from exercise and diet, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc5736649:
Du and co-authors build a computing system from memristors, devices whose resistance holds a brief memory. The work uses reservoir computing, a scheme for data that change over time. Only the final readout layer needs training in such a scheme. That keeps training cheap and fast.

Their array of dynamic memristors forms the reservoir itself. Ion motion inside each device gives the short term memory the scheme needs. A system with just 88 memristors sorted handwritten digits well. It also solved a second order nonlinear task and forecast its output. The results point to compact hardware for time based tasks.
europmc-pmc5753349:
Leader and co-authors present FlyAtlas 2, a new atlas of gene expression in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. The first FlyAtlas used microarrays, which cannot split one gene's transcripts apart. FlyAtlas 2 rests on RNA-Seq data from the same fly line and diet. It covers adult and larval tissues.

Data now come split by sex for adult body tissues. That allows studies of male and female differences. MicroRNAs and many RNA genes join the coverage. The web interface was reshaped for small mobile screens. Users can view reads beside the genome in the UCSC browser.
europmc-pmc5792849:
Ritchie sets out two forms of chronic heart disease seen at the Glasgow Infirmary. He writes as a senior physician there, from his own case load. The first form begins with blocked flow in the lung vessels and ends with an engorged, stretched right heart. The second starts with structural faults in the aorta or left heart.

Together the two forms made up about a tenth of his medical cases. The first often travels with bronchitis or asthma. The second often follows rheumatism. Ritchie traces each stage, from early signs to the swollen, heavy heart of the last stage.
europmc-pmc5921649:
Dalziel gave lectures on practical points in abdominal surgery in Glasgow. The James Watson Lectures were delivered in March 1913. They appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal in 1914. Dalziel was a surgeon at the Western Infirmary. This part covers deformities met early in life. A thickened pylorus in infants takes first place.

Such infants vomit, waste away, and may die without surgery, he reports. He describes a pyloroplasty that spares the inner lining. Two fragile infants recovered well after the operation, he says. Case histories support his practical advice in detail. Blood loss and sepsis risks were kept low. The lectures record hands-on surgical teaching of the era.
europmc-pmc5939049:
Pan reviews modifications and functional genomics of human transfer RNA. His review appeared in Cell Research. Transfer RNA is the most abundant RNA in a human cell. It is also the most heavily modified, with about 13 changes per molecule. Its classic job is matching amino acids to the genetic code. Modifications shape decoding and many other cell processes.

Levels of tRNA, its modifications, and its charging vary by cell type. How these factors combine to speed translation is still open. The review covers links between tRNA changes and human disease. Mutations in mitochondrial tRNAs and in modification enzymes feature here. Pan closes with prospects for human tRNA biology.
europmc-pmc6017249:
Yang and co-authors review how plant secondary metabolites respond to environmental factors. Their review appeared in Molecules. These compounds defend plants against attack and stress. Humans prize them as medicines, flavours, and food additives. Their build-up depends on genes, development, and surroundings. Light, temperature, and soil water each shift levels. Soil fertility and salinity matter as well. One changed factor alone can alter the whole profile.

The authors compare stressed and unstressed plants factor by factor. A general picture of what drives fluctuation emerges. Growers gain a practical route to consistent quality. The review closes with suggestions for future research.
europmc-pmc6052049:
Klopfenstein and co-authors present GOATOOLS, a Python library for gene ontology work. Their article appeared in Scientific Reports. Gene ontology terms describe what gene products do and where they act. Enrichment tests show which terms cluster in a gene list. Results can run to hundreds of terms in one flat list.

The library keeps pace with daily ontology updates. It runs enrichment tests for over- and under-represented terms. A grouping method then sorts results for clearer reading. The team tested it on simulated data and a real RNA-seq study. It matched or beat two rival tools, DAVID and GOstats. The code is free on GitHub. Readers get a pipeline-ready tool for gene list analysis.
europmc-pmc6113849:
Rocha and co-authors wrote a review in Clinics on why tumors stop responding to cisplatin, a widely used cancer drug. Cisplatin attacks the DNA of tumor cells. The damage can kill the cells if it is not fixed. Yet many tumors resist the drug from the start or learn to resist it.

The review explains how cells repair the harm cisplatin causes. It also covers how cells can live with damage they cannot fix. Those repair skills help tumors survive treatment. Recent clinic data link repair status to patient response. The authors note that blocking repair could make the drug work better.
europmc-pmc6178349:
Meira and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on a hippocampal circuit for social memory in mice. Remembering other individuals needs the dorsal CA2 region of the hippocampus. A subset of ventral CA1 neurons is also involved. Whether the two form one chain or parallel paths was unclear.

Using drugs and light to silence cells briefly and reversibly, the team tested each phase of memory. Dorsal CA2 activity proved vital for forming, storing, and recalling social memories. Tracing showed CA2 sends strong excitatory input to the exact ventral CA1 zone that holds social memory neurons. The study draws the circuit as a single chain, active at every stage.
europmc-pmc6213249:
Janeiro and co-authors review a gut-linked molecule called TMAO. Gut microbes make TMAO from choline, betaine, and carnitine. Blood levels depend on diet, gut flora, and liver action. The review appeared in Nutrients. It asks if TMAO is a marker or a drug target.

High blood TMAO links to higher heart event risk. A link to nerve disorders has also been proposed. The authors review food sources and metabolic pathways. They screen studies on heart and brain disease. They discuss the role of inflammation in those links. They also cover ways to cut TMAO levels. Options include antibiotics and new targeted molecules. The authors say TMAO's true role is still unclear.
europmc-pmc6244749:
Chambers and co-authors review fats made by gut microbes and their effects on health. Their review appeared in Current Nutrition Reports. The fats are short-chain fatty acids. Gut microbes make them when they ferment dietary fibre. These small fats act in the gut and in organs beyond it. The review asks how they link to weight, blood sugar, and heart disease.

Evidence links the fats to better gut wall function and blood sugar control. They also affect immune balance, hunger signals, and fat storage. Such effects may explain part of the benefit of high fibre diets. Heart risk markers may improve through both direct and indirect paths. The authors see these fats as a promising route to protect health against energy rich diets. More human trials are still needed.
europmc-pmc6274649:
Zhou and co-authors found a new path by which iron helps kill melanoma cells. Their study appeared in Cell Research. Iron raises reactive oxygen species, which can drive several death forms. Whether it could drive pyroptosis, a fiery cell death, was unknown. Melanoma cells carry high levels of a key pore protein for that death. That trait made them a good test case.

Iron boosted oxygen signals started by a stress drug. A mitochondrial protein called Tom20 sensed those signals and clumped together. It then drew in Bax, which freed signals that switched on a cutting enzyme. That enzyme split the pore protein, and the cells died by pyroptosis. Adding iron at patient level doses boosted standard drugs in mouse tumours. Growth and spread both slowed, with no clear harm to normal organs.
europmc-pmc6307949:
Sharp and co-authors track a hormone receptor variant in prostate cancer tissue. Their study appeared in the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The variant is called AR-V7. Blood tests had linked it to poor response to hormone therapy. Little was known about its presence in tumor tissue. The team built a new antibody to stain for it.

They tested 358 primary tumors and 293 metastatic samples. AR-V7 appeared in under 1 percent of primary tumors. After hormone deprivation therapy, 75 percent showed it. Levels rose further after modern hormone drugs. Patients without AR-V7 responded better and lived longer. The results argue for drugs that block this variant.
europmc-pmc6324349:
Goniewicz and co-authors compare toxicant exposure in e-cigarette users and smokers. Their cohort study appeared in JAMA Network Open. Burning cigarettes expose users to thousands of chemicals. E-cigarettes heat liquid instead of burning tobacco. The team studied 5,105 adults in a population sample. Body samples were tested for chemical biomarkers.

People who only vaped had higher marker levels than never users. That held for nicotine, nitrosamines, and some metals. Volatile organic compounds were also higher than in never users. But levels sat well below those of cigarette smokers. Dual users of both products matched smokers more closely. The authors say vaping cuts exposure versus smoking. It does not remove exposure to known tobacco toxicants.
europmc-pmc6379049:
Wang and co-authors present a resource research article in Molecular Systems Biology. They built a paired atlas of protein and RNA levels across 29 healthy human tissues. The atlas covers 18,072 transcripts and 13,640 proteins, including 37 proteins with no prior protein-level proof.

Hundreds of proteins stayed undetectable even where their RNA was abundant, above all in testis. Few proteins were truly tissue-specific, and protein levels varied less across tissues than RNA levels did. Only 238 of 9,848 genetic variants could be confirmed at the protein level. The authors offer the atlas for studying gene control and for checking biomarker specificity.
europmc-pmc6432749:
Nilsen and Bernhardsson map how implementation science frameworks describe context, the setting factors that decide whether a proven practice actually takes hold in health care. Dozens of theories and checklists claim to capture these determinants, yet they disagree on basic terms. The scoping review asks how the frameworks were built and what they count as context.

Searches of MEDLINE and EMBASE plus textbooks yielded 17 distinct frameworks. Only six named context directly, and just four defined it outright; the rest implied it through category lists. Twelve context dimensions emerged, with organizational support, money, social support, and leadership most common. The inconsistency itself is the warning for researchers choosing a framework.
europmc-pmc6441149:
McAndrews and Kalluri review how cancer cells build and release exosomes, the nanovesicles that carry messages between tumor cells and to distant organs. Traffic in these vesicles shapes tumor growth and spread, so throttling their release is an appealing treatment idea. The machinery of release is only partly mapped.

Formation runs through multivesicular bodies, with routes depending on ceramide or on ESCRT sorting complexes, and sometimes on neither. Rab proteins then guide the bodies to the surface, with effects that differ by cell type. Autophagy can raise or lower release depending on context.
