The work tied to a plea to waive claims under the pension law. The firm paid the agency back for the study cost. The agency asked if it could keep the cash.

GAO held that it could not. The sum was not a gift the agency could take. No law lets the agency charge for this work and keep the fee. Cash got for the government must go to the Treasury. The firm must be told the sum goes there, not to agency funds.
gao-gaoreports-b-400049:
Barnesville Development Corporation lost its protest. GAO decided B-400049 on June 30, 2008. The General Services Administration sought office space in Melbourne, Florida. The space would house a Social Security office. The call set a floor shape rule for the space. The floor could be no more than twice as long as wide. The firm's block broke that shape rule on its face.

GAO denied the protest. The toss of the bid was fair on the call's terms. A layout clause did not waive the shape rule. The two clauses can be read to stand side by side. Terms that can both stand must both be heeded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-249:
Capital Financing, GAO-05-249 of April 8, 2005, weighs a new way to pay for big federal builds. A capital fund, as drawn, would spread a build's cost through yearly budgets. That spread could smooth the spikes that big builds cause. It would keep the rule that full cost is pledged up front. Two test cases, at Agriculture and Interior, ground the study.

GAO shows how such funds would run in real life. It weighs their gains and their snags. It names simpler paths to the same gains, per the title. It closes with points to weigh before any fund is built, drawn from budget experts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-349:
Military Personnel, GAO-05-349 of April 26, 2005, is the mate study on loans that prey on troops. A harsh loan hides its sting in fees, traps, or lies. Such debt can sink a troop's credit and career, and sap a unit's will. The Pentagon holds tools to fight back. Off-limits lists can bar a bad shop from a base. Classes can warn troops off bad deals.

GAO asks how many troops on duty hold such loans. It asks if the tools are used in full, by the Pentagon and by troops. They are not, the title finds. Dormant tools leave the prey path open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1049:
Chesapeake Bay gateways and their grants are audited in GAO-06-1049, a report from September 14, 2006. A 1998 law built a linked network of parks, ports, and museums where the public can reach the bay. The Park Service backs the sites with grants. In 2005, Congress raised doubts about its management. GAO tested how sites are picked, what grants fund, and what fixes are under way.

Headings state the findings. The criteria for picking gateways are not always transparent. They may not be applied in a consistent way. Most grants reviewed funded interpretation of the bay and access to it. Thirty-nine gateways drew multiple grants for those aims. The Park Service has not yet judged whether the grants meet program goals. It has taken steps to manage grants better, GAO found. Oversight and accountability weaknesses remain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-149:
Disability claims processing and the offices that handle it are studied in GAO-06-149, dated December 9, 2005. The Veterans Benefits Administration runs compensation and pension claims through a field office network. Senate leaders asked GAO to review efforts to reshape that network. Years of backlogs and uneven service drive the push for change. GAO catalogued the realignment steps taken so far. It then asked whether deeper changes could lift performance further.

The report weighs how work is spread across offices. Some offices carry loads that fit their staff poorly. Moving claims to offices with spare capacity or special skill could speed decisions. GAO tested that logic against the record of past realignments. Any new structure must guard quality as well as speed. The study gives Congress options for a system that veterans judge by how fast and how fairly it answers them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-349:
A Marine vehicle meant to swim to shore and fight on land was in trouble. GAO's May 1, 2006 report, GAO-06-349, reviews the Expeditionary Fighting Vehicle. The vehicle would replace the current amphibious assault craft. It was the Corps' top ground system priority. It took 25.5 percent of the Corps' buying budget for fiscal years 2006 through 2011.

GAO tracked cost, schedule, and performance in design work. It also weighed the causes of the strain and the risks ahead. The title states the core result plainly. The program met hard problems in design demonstration. It faced more risk as it neared production. Readers get a clear early warning on a major weapon buy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-449:
Small, quick satellites were meant to give field commanders space help sooner. Dated March 14, 2006, GAO-06-449 reviews tactical space work at the Defense Department. Commanders had reported shortfalls in space capability despite heavy investment. The department began building TacSats, small satellites made within tight time and cost limits. It also sought small, low-cost launch vehicles for them.

GAO checked results to date for both efforts. It named the challenges they face. It asked whether lessons could inform major space buys. GAO said the department needs a department-wide strategy. Readers get early results on a new approach to space.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-49:
Drone aircraft work best when services can share data, controls, and lessons. In GAO-06-49 (December 13, 2005), GAO reviews unmanned aircraft systems. Such a system joins an aircraft, payloads, and ground controls. Demand from U.S. forces is high and rising. The Defense Department is investing more and often fields systems still in development. Past GAO work warned of interoperability problems that could hurt joint operations.

GAO reviewed how these systems performed in recent joint operations. It judged the soundness of the department's approach to grading joint performance. More effective promotion of interoperability is needed, GAO said. Better performance checks are also needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-649:
Federal foster care and adoption funds are reviewed in GAO-06-649, a GAO report dated June 15, 2006. The programs help states care for children who cannot stay safely at home and support adoptions. Federal spending was estimated to rise from about $6 billion in fiscal year 2003 to $8 billion in fiscal year 2008. Lawmakers worried about how much of that growth came from state administrative costs.

GAO found that spending on administrative costs had grown, but weak data limited analysis of what drove it. State spending shifted with staffing, caseloads, and claiming practices, and the effect on services was unclear. GAO said oversight by the Department of Health and Human Services lacked a strategic, risk-based focus. Stronger oversight would safeguard funds and support states more evenly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-149:
Train wrecks have killed fewer people since 1980, but the accident rate stopped falling a decade ago. GAO examined rail safety oversight in GAO-07-149, issued January 26, 2007. The Federal Railroad Administration writes safety rules and inspects railroads. A wreck in Graniteville, South Carolina, killed 9 people and injured 292. GAO asked how the agency targets its work and judges its own impact.

The agency was aiming its oversight at the top risks, GAO found. Its action plan targets the two main causes of wrecks: human error and bad track. Inspectors now use data models to pick sites likely to have problems. New rules and track inspection vehicles were also in motion. But most steps were not fully in place yet. Their effect on safety would take years to show. GAO said the agency still lacked measures of what its inspections achieve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-49:
New drug output has stalled even as research budgets climb, and GAO-07-49, dated November 17, 2006, asks why. Before a drug reaches market, the Food and Drug Administration must approve a new drug application packed with test data. Hopes ran high that science gains would yield more breakthrough drugs. Yet new molecular entities, drugs with never-marketed ingredients, had gone flat.

GAO studied every one of the 1,264 applications filed from 1993 through 2004. It weighed spending trends against filing and approval counts. It then asked experts what slows the pipeline. They named science hurdles, business calls, patent fights, and rule burdens. Their fix ideas range from better early science to clearer review paths. The report gives Congress a fact base for a debate that mixes health, profit, and risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-549:
Winning the peace after the war is a skill the Pentagon is still building, and GAO-07-549, dated May 31, 2007, grades the effort. Stability and rebuilding missions since the Cold War often run 5 to 8 years. They can cost more lives and money than the combat phase. A 2005 presidential directive told the Defense and State departments to weave stability work into war plans.

GAO reviewed plans at three combatant commands and read the policy stack. The department had a stated approach but thin follow-through. It had not pinned down which skills its forces need for such missions. Measures to judge success were also vague. Joint planning with civilian agencies lagged the directive's call. Lessons from Bosnia, Kosovo, Afghanistan, and Iraq were applied unevenly. GAO urged clear skill lists and firm measures, so the next mission starts from knowledge, not improvisation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-349:
Army Corps of Engineers land records are examined in GAO report GAO-08-349, issued May 9, 2008. The Corps, the fourth largest federal landholder, logs its civil works land in the Real Estate Management Information System (REMIS). GAO tested whether REMIS gave sound data on land disposals from fiscal years 1996 through 2006.

GAO found the disposal data unreliable, as were the records of land held as of September 30, 2006. In two of four districts checked, the same person entered disposal data and checked it, a basic control failure. The system's design also let users pull inconsistent results for the same query. GAO recommended tighter controls, a redesign of the disposal module, clearer guidance, and user training. The Department of Defense agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-49:
With its report GAO-08-49, dated November 16, 2007, GAO turns to Women's Business Centers. The centers train and counsel women who run businesses, with a focus on those facing social and economic disadvantage. In fiscal year 2007, the Small Business Administration funded 99 centers.

Funding for the centers long carried a hard stop: after 10 years, a center was meant to stand on its own. In May 2007, Congress allowed renewable 3-year awards for graduated centers and current ones. Oversight lags, GAO found, since district staff who watch the centers carry many other duties and may lack the right skills. Poor communication left some centers unsure of program rules. GAO also gives guidance to cut overlap with two sister programs, the Small Business Development Center and SCORE programs. The agency gave no comments on the draft.
gdr-constitution-1949:
The German Democratic Republic adopted its first constitution in October 1949, founding East Germany out of the Soviet occupation zone. The text was approved days before the state itself was proclaimed, as Germany split into two rival republics. Its drafters modeled parts of it on the Weimar charter, in the hope of claiming all-German legitimacy.

On paper, the charter promises a democratic republic with free elections, basic rights, and a parliament of the people. In fact, the Socialist Unity Party, backed by Soviet power, ruled without real opposition from the start. The founding law of the workers' and peasants' state thus wore a democratic form over a Leninist reality. A new constitution in 1968 dropped the pretense and named the party's leading role outright. The 1949 text closed the founding act of socialism's forty-year German experiment.
geneva-convention-1-1949:
The first of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 protects wounded and sick soldiers in armies on land. Nations redrafted the rules in Geneva after the Second World War, building on a line of agreements going back to 1864. The aim was to make sure that a soldier out of the fight through wounds or sickness is never treated as fair game.

The articles require armies to collect and care for the wounded of both sides, without favor. Medical staff, ambulances, and hospitals are protected, and the red cross emblem marks that protection. Attacking the wounded or those who care for them is forbidden. Nearly every nation on earth has accepted the 1949 conventions.
geneva-convention-2-1949:
The second Geneva Convention of 1949 carries the protection of the wounded to warfare at sea. It adapts the older Hague rules and the land convention to sailors, marines, and others fighting on the water. Two world wars had shown how exposed the wounded and shipwrecked were when ships went down far from help.

Under its articles, the wounded, sick, and shipwrecked at sea must be rescued and cared for by whichever side finds them. Hospital ships are protected from attack and capture, and their crews must be respected. The convention also covers coastal rescue craft and medical aircraft over the sea. Together with its three sister conventions, it forms the core of modern war law.
geneva-convention-3-1949:
Prisoners of war are the subject of the third Geneva Convention of 1949. Written after a war in which prisoners had been starved and murdered in great numbers, it sets firm limits on captors. The text builds on earlier prisoner rules from 1929 that had too often been ignored.

Captured fighters must be treated with respect, given enough food and shelter, and shielded from insults and public display. They may send and receive mail, and the Red Cross may visit their camps. Torture and medical experiments are banned outright. When the fighting ends, prisoners must be sent home without delay, a standard still cited in every modern conflict.
geneva-convention-4-1949:
Civilians in wartime gained their own full shield in the fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. Earlier war law had guarded soldiers and prisoners, while civilians in occupied lands were left with thin protection. The deportations and mass killings of the Second World War made the gap impossible to ignore.

The articles ban murder, torture, hostage-taking, and collective punishment against civilians under an army's control. Forced deportation from occupied land is forbidden, and children, the sick, and the wounded get special care. Occupying powers must keep food and medical supplies flowing to the people under their rule. The convention remains the main legal guard for civilians caught in modern wars.
german-basic-law-1949:
West Germany adopted its Basic Law in May 1949, written by a Parliamentary Council at Bonn. The drafters avoided the word constitution, since the country was divided and the law was meant to be temporary. Its lessons came straight from the Nazi years: never again a republic too weak to defend itself, never again a state above human dignity.

The text opens by declaring human dignity beyond all touch, the clause every other article serves. Power is split between the federation and the states, and the charter arms democracy against its foes, banning parties that seek to destroy it. A powerful constitutional court guards the whole design. The charter of the Federal Republic's economic and moral recovery still governs united Germany today, its temporary name now a badge of permanence.
haddock-somnolism-psycheism-1849:
Joseph Haddock lectured on mesmeric clairvoyance in Somnolism and Psycheism, first printed in 1849. His titles name the states he studies: somnolism, the mesmeric sleep, and psycheism, its mental wonders. Haddock treats clairvoyance as a subject for physiology and philosophy alike. An appendix adds mesmeric and psychical experiments of his circle.

Haddock worked in Bolton, far from London's learned societies. His book gives the movement a provincial English voice of real weight. His case reports rest on sittings with entranced subjects from his own circle. The lectures argue that the soul's powers show themselves in trance. Readers meet mesmerism as small town practice and print. The first edition holds his case entire.
hahnemann-organon-1849:
Samuel Hahnemann was a German doctor who broke with the harsh cures of his day. His Organon of Medicine lays out the scheme he called homeopathy. Charles Dudgeon's English dress of 1849 brought the work to British readers. The book is the root text of the whole school.

Like cures like, Hahnemann holds: a drug that makes a sign in health can cure that sign in the sick. He bids the doctor use the least dose that can still act. Rules for case work and drug tests fill the text. Homeopaths still treat the book as law.
hartley-observations-on-man-vol1-1749:
David Hartley, an English physician, published the first volume of Observations on Man in 1749. The title promises a study of man's frame, his duty, and his hopes. Hartley aimed at nothing less than a full science of the mind built from two simple tools: vibrations in the nerves and the association of ideas.

Volume 1 lays out the theory that all thought grows from linked sensations. Simple impressions join into complex ideas, feelings, and habits through repeated pairing. The scheme made the mind look like a machine of habit, which thrilled some readers and alarmed others. James Mill and later psychologists built on Hartley's foundation, and the book stands as the founding work of association psychology.
hartley-observations-on-man-vol2-1749:
The second volume of Hartley's Observations on Man appeared in 1749 with the first, completing his great system. Hartley was a physician who wanted one theory to cover body, mind, and faith. Volume 1 had set out his psychology of association; the second half puts that psychology to work.

Volume 2 applies the laws of association to religion and morals. Duty, hope, prayer, and the expectation of a life to come are all explained through the linking of ideas and feelings. Hartley, a devout man, meant the system to strengthen faith, not to dissolve it. The result is psychology in the service of religion, unusual for its age. Together the two volumes founded the associationist school that shaped British thought about the mind for a century.
heart-sutra-muller-sbe49:
A few hundred words hold the core of Mahayana Buddhism in the Heart Sutra. The Heart Sutra, in the English rendering of Friedrich Max Müller from 1894, gives that core text in full. Müller's version stood in the Sacred Books of the East, the great Victorian shelf of world faiths.

The sutra says form is emptiness and emptiness is form, and sweeps away each prop the mind would clutch. Monks and lay folk chant it daily from Tibet to Japan. Its end is a mantra that promises passage to the far shore of waking. No Buddhist text so short carries so much weight.
herodian-history-hart-1749:
Herodian lived through the wild years he writes about. His History, finished around 238 CE, tells the Roman Empire from the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 to the rise of Gordian III. J. Hart turned it into English in 1749, and he added an appendix that carries the story on to Constantine.

Eight books hold Commodus on the throne, the year of five emperors, the Severan house, and the chaos of the third century. Herodian writes as a minor official who saw courts at close range. His tale is vivid, moral, and often sharp. For these years he is one of the few full sources that survive.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
Volume 7 of In the Fire of the Forge, by Georg Ebers, lets the Ortlieb sisters leave the Town Hall with glad news. Ebers wraps Els and Eva in white head cloths that hide their faces, then lets them watch old Herr Vorchtel cross the square on the arm of the young burgomaster. A city clerk shares a piece of gossip meant to please them both in this volume.

Chapter X reports that Ursula Vorchtel is engaged to the talented young merchant walking with her father. The match will help the old man and his younger son run their large business. Even in deep mourning, Ursula looks out at the world again like a happy girl. Better still, the reproach that spoiled so many hours for the sisters now stands removed. Private relief and a neighbor's engagement close the hearing day on a rare bright note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-mari-ben-e:
Abba Mari ben Eligdor, also called Senior Astruc de Noves, was a noted Talmudist, thinker, and student of physics and the stars. He flourished in the fourteenth century in Salonica, and by 1335 he was already very old. He wrote on the Pentateuch, on Job, on parts of the Talmud, and on science and logic. Only bits of his work survive, and those in manuscript.

His work on Job is a study of why the good suffer, not a plain verse-by-verse reading. In it, Job's four friends stand for four views of evil. One denies evil is real, one looks to reward in the life to come, and one pleads man's ignorance of God's will. The entry counts Abba Mari a loyal student of Maimonides. His book of Refutations against Joseph Caspi has since been lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aberdeen-scotla: Aberdeen is the chief city of northern Scotland and the capital of Aberdeenshire. Jews, the entry says, have only lately settled in the city. Its one synagogue, at 34 Marischal street, was founded in 1893. Six years later the whole Jewish population came to seventeen families. Of those families, no fewer than twenty-three persons held seats in the synagogue. That small set of facts, drawn from a Jewish year-book of 1899, is the whole of this short city notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abolafio-juan-f: Juan Fernandez Abolafio was a Marano of Seville in the fifteenth century. He worked hard to keep the Inquisition out of Seville in 1480. That effort cost him his life at the stake. He was a learned man who served for years as alcalde de justicia, a criminal judge. He also farmed the royal taxes. The entry rests on two Spanish histories of the Jews in Spain, and gives no birth date for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acre-called-als:
Acre is a city and port of Phenicia. It sits on a point of land at the foot of Mount Carmel. In 1901 it held about 9,800 people, a few of them Jews. Egyptian texts name it about 1500 B.C. as A-ka. Asher claimed the town but could not take it. Sennacherib took Akkú in 701 B.C. and gave it to the king of Sidon.

As a port on a coast with few harbors, Acre held great weight in war. It served as a base in the Maccabean wars. Jonathan the Maccabee was killed there by treachery. Rome made it a colony under Claudius. The Arabs took it in 668. In Crusader days it rose to its peak. It was a seat of the Latin kingdom and of the Knights of St. John, who called it St. Jean d'Acre. Later notes mark its stand against Bonaparte in 1799.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-sar-ha-bira:
Aha Sar ha-Birah, called "Castellan," was a Palestinian amora of the third generation, in the fourth century. He was a contemporary of Tanhum b. Hiyya of Kefar Acco. No ruling or doctrine of his own is recorded in the Talmud. Instead, he reported several Halakot and precedents for others.

His standing seems to have let him help less fortunate fellow Jews. Once, with Tanhum's aid, he ransomed Jewish captives brought to Tiberias. He is also said to have laid Halakot before the sages at Usha twice. Usha, a former seat of the Sanhedrin, still drew learned Jews in his day. The entry notes, though, that the reporter in those cases may have been a tanna of the same name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akron-ohio-1049:
Akron, Ohio, is the capital of Summit county, forty miles from Cleveland. Jews first settled there in 1850. The Akron Hebrew Congregation, a Reform body, was organized on April 2, 1865. It was incorporated on September 16, 1866, and bought its burial-ground the same day. Its present synagogue was acquired in April 1885 and dedicated that August.

The entry lists the congregation's rabbis and the town's Jewish societies. They include a benevolent Schwesterbund from 1865 and a literary Montefiore Society from 1883. An Orthodox congregation bought a lot for its own synagogue in 1900. Of about 50,000 people in Akron, 225 families were Jewish. Their trades ran from merchant and lawyer to cigarmaker, foundryman, and bookkeeper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-of-mi:
Alexander of Miletus is known as Polyhistor, for the sheer number of his writings. He flourished between 105 and 40 B.C. His subjects ran from geography and history to grammar and philosophy. His book "Upon the Jews" survives only in fragments. Eusebius and Clement of Alexandria preserved them. The work was a string of excerpts from Jewish, Samaritan, and heathen writers on early Jewish history.

The entry calls him a compiler with no taste or judgment. Yet his scrapbook has real value. Whole authors are known to later ages only through his extracts. Among them are the epic poet Philo and the tragedian Ezekiel. Eupolemus, Demetrius, Artapanus, and Aristeas stand in the same debt. Even the anti-Jewish rhetorician Molon survives in his pages. Josephus and Eusebius both drew on the work. Alexander did make plain errors: he wrote that a woman named Moso gave the Jews their Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkan-alphonse-:
Alphonse Alkan, called Alkan the elder, was a French printer and writer. He was born in Paris in 1809. He died at Neuilly-sur-Seine in 1889. He began as a working printer. He then wrote for trade journals on printing. Later he served as secretary to the Count de Clarac. Clarac kept the Museum of Antiquities at the Louvre.

His books deal with the craft and past of printing. One book treats women who set type in 1794. One gives lives of portrait engravers in France. One tells the past of the Paris book trade. Shorter works take up book foes and book labels. The entry lists his chief books with their years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amado-joshua-ju: Joshua Judah Amado was a Talmudist of Spanish stock. His family had settled at Salonica. He worked early in the nineteenth century. He wrote a book called the Tents of Judah. It came out at Salonica in 1820. The book holds two kinds of matter. One part gives sermons on the Pentateuch. The other part gives legal talks on Maimonides. A short tract and a set of diet laws are added.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anacletus-ii-pi:
Anacletus II was an antipope who held Rome for eight years. His true name was Pietro Pierleoni. He stood against Innocent II from 1130 to 1138. His line traced back to a Jewish forebear. That fact drew slurs on him all his life. Voltaire in jest called him the Jewish Pope.

His forebear Baruch grew rich as a lender in Rome. On taking the Christian faith he took the name Benedict. His house rose high at the papal court. Anacletus was picked as pope by one Rome faction. Most of Europe backed his rival in the schism. Rome stood by him to the last, the entry notes. Base tales of theft and worse were spread by his foes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anna-1549: Anna was a daughter of Rabbi Eleazar of Worms. She lived at Erfurt. The entry, only a few lines long, records that Crusaders killed her there as a martyr on December 6, in 1213 or 1214. Her mother, Dolce, and her sister, Bellette, met the same fate. It gives no account of her life beyond her family and her death, and it cites Kayserling's work on Jewish women for the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apollonius-of-t:
Apollonius of Tyana was a Pythagorean philosopher and worker of wonders, born about the year 3 B.C. Some sources, the entry notes, give him a death at only thirty-eight years of age. In Arabic writing his name appears as Balinas or Belenus, a form often mistaken for Pliny.

Arabs called him the Author of Talismans and credited him with a work on the sway of spirit powers over the world of sense. A warning at the end of one translation calls the whole book worthless, copied only to guard readers against strange gods. The entry traces copies of the work in later Jewish libraries and catalogs, and weighs which magical writings truly bear his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arendt-otto-174:
Otto Arendt was a German economist, author, and member of the Prussian Diet, born in Berlin on October 10, 1854. He took his doctorate at Berlin University and entered a literary career with the ultraconservative side of Prussia. He led the cause of bimetalism and protective tariffs, and of policies that kept Prussia's quasi-feudal remains.

So firm was his loyalty, the entry says, that he left his religion, took Christianity, and at times used anti-Semitic phrases. He edited the Deutsche Wochenblatt and wrote many books, from a work on treaty double currency in 1878 to one on the fall of silver in 1899. His handbook of currency policy ran through seventeen editions. His wife Olga taught elocution and wrote tales for the stage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkelon-1949:
Ashkelon, a city on the southern coast of Palestine, appears in Egyptian texts as Askaruni among the cities rising against Rameses II and Meneptah. In the Amarna letters its prince Yitia is shown obedient to Egypt. The city never seems to have rested in Israelite hands, though Samson pressed it hard. Judges chapter 1 says Judah took Ashkelon, but the Greek version of that verse says the opposite.

Assyria handled the city often. Tiglath-pileser subdued it and, about 732 B.C., set Rukibti on its throne in place of Mitinti. Sennacherib in 701 B.C. seized its king Sidka as a rebel and restored Sharruludari, Rukibti's son. The city's realm then held Joppa and other towns. Herodotus tells how the Scythians plundered its temple on their march.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asti-2049:
Asti is a town in the province of Alessandria, Italy, on the left bank of the Tanaro. Its population is given as 32,000. In the Middle Ages it was a trade center and the capital of a strong republic in northern Italy. Its relative freedom drew Jews there. Many French Jews expelled in 1322 by Charles IV. took refuge in Asti.

Those settlers brought a French prayer rite, kept in Asti to the entry's own day. It is called the Rite Afm, from the first letters of Asti, Fassano, and Monclavo, the towns that use it. The eighteenth of Iyyar is a special feast day in Asti. Hymns by Joseph Conzio are sung then. The entry also names Jewish scholars born in Asti across four centuries, from Isaac Santon d'Hugeli to David Mordecai Terracina.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-austerlitz-2149:
Austerlitz is a town in Moravia, Austria. Its Jewish congregation is among the oldest in the province, by some accounts from the start of the twelfth century. Records point to a tribute paid by its Jews to King Wenzel in 1288. The payment later passed to the counts of Kaunitz. The tribute for 1757 even included pepper, ginger, and other spices.

Jewish merchants of Austerlitz traded across the Mediterranean ports in goods of the Orient. Their main trade at home was starch and lime. From that trade, Jewish records call the town 'Ir Laban, the White City. Ties with Christian neighbors stayed friendly, even in Hussite times. About 445 Jews lived there in thirty-four houses. When Maria Theresa capped the Jewish families of Moravia at 5,100, Austerlitz was allowed 72 families. The entry also notes its societies for the sick and its schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ba-al-shem-plur:
Ba'al Shem was a title for men said to work miracles through the name of God. Belief in the power of the sacred Name is very old. The title itself, the entry says, arose among German-Polish Jews as they met the practical Cabala of Luria's school. Elijah of Chelm, about 1500, is the first man known to bear it.

What began as a rare honor for a saint turned, in two centuries, into a trade. The later Ba'ale Shem mixed quack doctor, healer, and cabalist in one person. They wrote amulets, gave folk medicines, and cast out spirits. That trade brought them into sharp rivalry with trained physicians. The entry prints a prayer one Ba'al Shem wrote for himself and his fellows. It asks for peace between them and the doctors, and for respect in the doctors' eyes. A list of known Ba'ale Shem follows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bage-la-ville-2: Bagé-la Ville is a village in the department of Ain, France. The entry about it is only two sentences long. It says the village was inhabited by Jews in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. It adds one dated detail: in 1331 those Jews were divided into elder and younger. No names, no events, and no account of the community's end are given. The only support offered is a set of references to a printed inventory of departmental archives for the Côte d'Or.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-banquets-hebrew:
Banquets, in Hebrew "mishteh" and in Talmudic use "se'udah," are festive meals for times of joy, at home, in the community, or in worship. They marked welcomes and partings between friends as well. The entry holds that they grew out of sacrificial feasts. It quotes W. Robertson Smith: no sacrifice was complete without guests, and shares went freely to rich and poor.

In Bible times the religious side ruled. Feasts kept the harvest, sealed covenants, and crowned weddings, thanksgivings, and sheep-shearings. A child's weaning called for a feast, and birthday feasts appear for non-Jewish kings. Eating a heathen sacrifice was barred, since sharing the meal meant covenanting with its god. The entry follows the custom on through later Jewish practice, with its rules and blessings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barrios-daniel-:
Daniel Levi (Miguel) de Barrios, Spanish poet and historian, was born in 1625 at Montilla, Spain, and died in February, 1701, at Amsterdam. His father, a Marano, fled the Inquisition to Portugal and then to Algeria. Miguel went to Italy, stayed at Nice and Leghorn, and there declared himself publicly a Jew. He married Deborah Vaez. On July 20, 1660, he sailed with 152 coreligionists for the West Indies. His young wife died soon after they reached Tobago, and he returned to Europe.

At Brussels he entered Spanish military service and rose to captain. There he wrote his best poetry, including "Flor de Apolo" (1663), with romances, 62 sonnets, and three comedies. He was the most fruitful poet among the Spanish-Portuguese Jews of his time. Hardly a year passed without a new publication. He composed his own epitaph on the death of his second wife, Abigail, whom he had married in 1662 and who died in 1686.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basurto-diego-e: Diego Enriquez Basurto was a Marano poet of the seventeenth century, born in Spain. Like his father Antonio Enriquez Gomez, he lived for years at Rouen and at last settled in Holland. A fellow poet left a blunt sketch of his looks, from his broad nose and spectacles to his cane. Basurto wrote a poem on the triumph of virtue and the patience of Job, printed at Rouen in 1646 and inscribed to the mother of Louis the Fourteenth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-rachel-274: Rachel Beer was an English journalist, a daughter of Sassoon D. Sassoon. She was schooled in private and spent two years training in a hospital. Since October of 1893 she has owned, managed, and edited the Sunday Times in London. She belongs to two institutes for journalists, one of them for women in that trade. She has also composed and published piano and other instrumental music. Her husband, Frederick Arthur Beer, edited the Observer newspaper in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-r-2949: Benjamin, a tanna of the second century, appears in debate with Eleazar ben Shammu'a on points of law. He also stands near Symmachus in the sources, and in one place he reports a ruling in the name of Akiba. His name shows up in several variant forms, among them Minyamin and Penimon. One teaching of his holds that no prayer counts unless it is offered in the public house of worship. Another warns of the evil spirits that fill the world, unseen by human eyes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berenice-3049: Berenice, daughter of Costobar and Salome, was a sister of Herod the First. Her marriage to her cousin Aristobulus proved unhappy. He taunted her with low birth, proud of his own Maccabean descent. She complained to her mother, and ill feeling deepened. When Aristobulus was killed in 6 B.C., many believed she had a share in his death. She later married twice more, last to Archelaus, and went with him to Rome. There she won the favor of Augustus and the friendship of Antonia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-napht: Naphtali Herz Bernstein was a Russian author of the early nineteenth century. He worked in business. He spent his free hours on Biblical study. His only published work appeared after his death. It was "Eder Ḥakamim," or Mantle of the Wise. The book defends the Talmud against McCaul's attack. Bernstein wrote it in London. It was printed at Odessa in 1868. He dedicated it to Chief Rabbi Solomon Herschel. The entry notes one weakness. The book defends broad principles only. It never answers McCaul point by point.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bhorupkar-samue:
Samuel Bapuji Bhorupkar was a Beni-Israel soldier. He was born near Bombay about 1790. He joined the Fourth Bombay Regiment in 1811. The entry traces his service year by year. He fought in Katyawar, Guzerat, and Malwa. He was present at the capture of many forts across those regions. His Malwa campaign pursued Holkar in 1817-18.

His promotions came in steady steps. He became jemidar in 1828 and subedar in 1833. In 1839 he rose to subedar-major. In 1841 he entered the Order of British India. That honor carried the title bahadur. He retired from service in February 1847.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boccaccio-giova:
Boccaccio in Jewish literature is treated through one small translated book. Seven tales from the Decameron of Boccaccio (1313-75) were put into Judaeo-German by Joseph of Maarsen. The volume came out in Amsterdam in 1710.

The 36-folio book was called Schöne Artliche Geschichten. Its tales include Beritola, Landolf, and the Sultan of Babylon's daughter. The source may have been a Dutch version from 1644. In his preface the translator explains his plain middle style. He avoided Hebrew words, holding it wrong to mix the holy tongue with a strange one. On the title page he also promised further parts beyond the first one. A rhymed note there praised the merits of the little book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonsenyor-isaac: Isaac Bonsenyor gets the shortest record in this run of entries. He was a son or grandson of Judah Bonsenyor, and the entry is unsure which. He lived in Barcelona. In 1391 he became a Christian. On conversion he took the name Ferrario Gracia de Gualbis. The entry states only those facts. It gives no birth date, no trade, no works, and no account of his later life after that change of faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-braudes-reuben-:
Reuben Asher Braudes was a Hebrew novelist and journalist born at Wilna in 1851. He died in Vienna on Oct. 18, 1902. Talmudical schooling came first, then the influence of the Maskilim.

Braudes wrote for Ha-Lebanon from 1868 on topics of the day. His first novel ran in a Vienna monthly in 1874. Later novels treated the repentant sinner and the clash of religion and life. The Two Extremes of 1885 pictured Orthodox and Reformed camps in bright colors. After the riots of 1882 he joined the Zionist movement. He published papers in Bucharest and later in Cracow, the second lasting nine months for lack of funds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brown-william-3:
William Brown was a Scottish clergyman born in 1766 and long the minister of Eskdalemuir. He served there for forty-three years and died in 1835. His fame in this encyclopedia rests on one large work about the Jews. It appeared in London in 1820, with a second edition at Edinburgh in 1826.

Antiquities of the Jews ran to two volumes and included a ground plan of the Temple. Brown compiled it from Latin, French, and English sources, drawing much from Lightfoot. For the second edition he added Surenhusius' Latin Mishnah and treatises by Maimonides and Abravanel. The entry notes his Hebrew was limited. It judges the work of more interest to bibliographers than to students.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-camondo-3949:
Camondo was a famed family of Jewish financiers and givers, of Spanish Portuguese origin. After centuries at Venice, the family settled in Constantinople in the nineteenth century. Its giant figure is Count Abraham Camondo, born there in 1785. He inherited a fortune in 1832 and grew it to an estimated 125,000,000 francs.

Abraham banked for the Ottoman government before the Ottoman Bank existed. He won the decree that let foreigners own real estate in Turkey, then built many houses at Pera. For Jews he set up a central consistory at Constantinople and founded a school in 1858 in its poorest suburb. Fanatical rabbis excommunicated him over that school, yet it trained most Jewish officials in Ottoman service. He died at Paris in 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catechisms-4149:
Catechisms are manuals for religious instruction. Judaism took both the name and the form from the Christian Church in modern times, as teaching grew more systematic. In the early Church, catechism prepared converts for admission. It listed sins to shun, duties to practice, and parts of the creed.

Old Judaism felt no need for such a book. Cases of converts were rare, and regular study covered the whole Torah, Bible and Talmud alike. No plan existed for teaching the creed as a system to the young. The first sign of change was Abraham Jagel's Leḳaḥ Ṭob, printed at Venice in 1587. Jagel modeled his work on the smaller catechism of the Catholic Peter Canisius. Luther's catechism of 1529, built on the Decalogue, had set the wider movement going.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cholera-asiatic:
Cholera Asiatica is defined as a catching disease marked by violent vomiting and purging, steady in parts of India and spreading in waves across the world. The entry puts deaths at about 50 per cent of those attacked. It dates the first European outbreak to 1817 in Lower Bengal and lists six later returns, ending with 1892-96.

Most of the article tests one claim: that Jews suffered less in most epidemics. Figures from Algiers, Budapest, Hamburg, Berlin, and Nicolayev compare Jewish and non-Jewish death rates. The entry gathers these reports carefully, city by city. Readers get an early, data-driven look at disease, place, and community health.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coen-moses-vita: Moses Vita Coen was a banker at Ferrara, Italy, in the eighteenth century. He did business often with Pope Clement XIII and with Clement XIV after him. On Feb. 22, 1764, Clement XIII asked him to supply the papal government with corn. The order included 4,000 sacks of Indian wheat. With Clement XIV he grew closer still, becoming a trusted friend and adviser. In the famine of 1772-73 he supplied 5,000 more sacks of Indian wheat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cordova-isaac-h: Isaac Hezekiah b. Jacob de Cordova was a publisher of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. He was a son of Jacob b. Moses Raphael de Cordova. After a stay in Brazil, he settled in Amsterdam. Like his brother Abraham, he became a printer there. In 1688 he published the Spanish sermons of Joshua de Silva. Between 1706 and 1709 he issued other works in Spanish and Hebrew. In 1709 he moved to Hamburg. The brief entry gives his family, trade, and main dates, but little more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremieux-moses-: Moses ben Solomon Crémieux, or Crémieu, was a scholar born at Carpentras, France, in 1766. He died on May 4, 1837. He was a nephew and son-in-law of Mordecai Crémieux. In 1790 he moved to Aix, in Provence. There he set up a Hebrew printing office. From 1829 to 1835 he issued a corrected prayer book for four French communities, with his own commentary. He also published notes on Ibn Ezra's Bible commentaries in 1833-36. The entry rates the prayer book as the finer work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dagon-hebrew-48:
Dagon was a Philistine god, named in Judges, First Samuel, and First Maccabees. Town names like Beth-dagon show how wide his worship ran. A Phenician royal inscription also speaks of towns of Dagon. His name most likely derives from the Hebrew word for fish. Pictures of him join a man's body with a fish's form. A Louvre relief is noted in the entry. Berosus's Odakon, rising from the Persian Gulf, may be the same god.

The article weighs whether Dagon matches the Assyrian god Dakan-Dagan. Some scholars deny any link; the entry finds one quite possible. Fish-man figures from Assyria and Babylonia are set beside the Samuel account. In that account the fallen idol keeps a man's head and hands. The parallels, the entry holds, support the match rather than break it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-jacob-jul:
Jacob Julius David was an Austrian journalist and author born at Weisskirchen, Moravia, on February 6, 1859. His father died of cholera when the boy was seven. After gymnasium schooling in three towns, he entered the University of Vienna in 1878 to study philology. Poverty slowed his studies, and he passed his doctorate examinations only in 1890.

David then gave himself wholly to writing. He published poems, stories, essays, and novels, and a four-act drama, "Hagar's Sohn," performed at Vienna's Landestheater on January 20, 1891. The entry praises his rich imagination and fine realistic style. He also edited and wrote theater criticism for Viennese papers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deism-5049:
Deism is a system of belief that accepts God as the cause of all things but rejects revelation and God's rule over events. It trusts natural law alone. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the word came to mean natural religion, and a deist was a freethinker.

England and France were its strongholds, and the long entry follows its writers in order. Lord Herbert, called the father of English deism, set out five religious truths held by reason alone. Hobbes, Locke, Toland, and Collins follow. Locke argued that the moral part of Moses' law matches natural law. Toland held that revelation informs but never proves. The article continues through later English and French deists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-doczy-dux-ludwi:
Ludwig Dóczy, born Dux, was a Hungarian poet born at Sopron on Nov. 30, 1845. He studied law at Vienna while writing for the Presse. His pieces backed the Ausgleich with Austria and won notice. In 1868 he became a clerk in the prime minister's office.

Dóczy followed Count Andrássy to the Foreign Office at Vienna and rose to Hofrath. He was made a baron in 1899 and retired in 1902. His fame rests on plays and translations, not state work. His comedy Csók, The Kiss, won the Hungarian Academy prize in 1871. He also turned Goethe's Faust into Hungarian and wrote libretti for Goldmark and Strauss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dubosary-5349: Dubosary was a village in the government of Kherson, Russia. In 1897 it held 13,276 people, about 5,000 of them Jews. Many of those Jews grow tobacco, and many others work in wine-making and fruit-growing. Dried fruits and tobacco are the chief goods of trade. The entry counts 940 artisans and 186 day-laborers. The village has the usual charities, a hospital, and a dispensary. Its schools include a Talmud Torah with 130 pupils and a private school with 580 Jewish pupils.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eggs-5449:
Eggs, in the Bible, belong to birds and to vipers. The ostrich leaves hers in warm sand to hatch by the sun's heat. A humane law forbids taking the mother bird with the eggs. Isaiah uses gathered eggs as a picture of helpless nations.

The rabbis read an egg's shape to tell clean birds from unclean ones. Clean eggs are pointed at one end and blunt at the other. They also knew the shell's strength and the chick's growth. A roasted egg stands on the Seder table for the festival offering. Eggs open the Seder meal, joining joy with a touch of mourning. Folk belief even tied a double yolk to childbearing luck.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-of-modi:
Eleazar of Modi'im was a scholar of the first and second centuries. He was a pupil of Johanan ben Zakkai. Gamaliel the Second often bowed to his readings of Scripture. The Moda'i's views are still a must, Gamaliel would admit. Eleazar was famed above all as a haggadist. One turns on the manna in the desert. He who makes the day makes its food, he taught. A man with food for today who frets for tomorrow lacks faith.

His end came in Bethar during the revolt of Bar Kokba. The entry retells the tale of his death at length. Each day of the siege he fasted and prayed for the town. A Samaritan spy slipped in and faked a whispered talk with him. Bar Kokba raged at the old man's plea that he had heard nothing. Eleazar fell dead from the blow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-ben-ezek: Elijah ben Ezekiel was rabbi of Byelgorai in Poland. He lived in the eighteenth century. His father Ezekiel was rabbi of Ostrovtsi in Galicia. He was a friend of Hayyim Rapoport, rabbi of Lemberg. The entry lists three books and a set of responsa. One gathers his rulings in the order of the law code. One gives fresh notes on Talmud tracts. The third is a kind of index to one part of the code. All three are named in his own preface.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-encyclopedia-57:
Encyclopedia is the name for a book of all knowledge. Such a work holds facts on all topics, or all of one. Its matter stands in a set order, most often by letter. The East knew such books in old times, the entry says. Greek and Syriac churchmen built theirs on talks of creation. Muslim writers raised a large crop of such works in time. One of the first dates to the years 975 to 997.

The first Hebrew work of the kind came about 1150. Abraham bar Hiyya of Barcelona wrote that math compendium. It treated counting, measure, optics, the stars, and music. Only bits of that work are still in hand today. A century later Gershon ben Solomon wrote a wider one. His Gate of Heaven falls into three parts by topic. Earth science, star lore, and theology fill those parts. A like work from Toledo in 1247 is also named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eschatology-fro:
Eschatology is the doctrine of the last things, and this long entry traces it through Jewish sources. Its chief concern, the entry says, is the final fate of the Jewish nation and the world. The fate of single persons comes second. Bible history, law, and prophecy all lean toward a coming victory of God's truth and justice.

The prophets shaped the Day of the Lord into a day of judgment. For Amos and Isaiah it brought ruin on Israel as well as on other nations. Later hope pictured a remnant saved and enemy powers destroyed. Rabbinic and apocryphal passages add a renewed earth, long life, healed bodies, and peace. The Messiah, in that picture, teaches the nations and repeats the wonders of Moses on a larger scale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezekias-5949: Ezekias was a high priest named by Josephus, and the entry doubts he ever lived. Josephus says Ezekias joined Ptolemy's party going to Egypt after the battle of Gaza in 320 B.C. He was then sixty-six years old, a skilled speaker and a man of affairs. He is said to have explained to Hekataeus how peoples differed in homes and laws. The doubt comes from Josephus himself: elsewhere his priestly line runs from Jaddua to Onias I to Simeon I, leaving no room for Ezekias.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-federation-of-a:
The Federation of American Zionists was a Zionist body formed in 1897 as a federation of societies of greater New York. It grew by drawing in societies beyond New York. A New York convention on July 4, 1898 made it a national body under the new name. The state of New York chartered it in 1902. It began with twenty-four societies and about 1,000 members.

By the Boston convention of May 1901, the count stood at 152 societies and 8,000 members. From New York it issued a monthly magazine, The Maccabean, founded in October 1902, plus pamphlets by Gottheil, Bentwich, and others. Richard Gottheil presided from the start. A western subfederation, the Knights of Zion, sat at Chicago.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischer-marcus-: Marcus Maier Fischer was an Austrian Hebraist born at Vienna in 1783. He died at Prague on May 22, 1853. He was a son of Moses Fischer, rabbi of the Vienna Jewish community. In Hebrew he wrote a full history of the Jews under Mahdi and Imam Idris, kings of Mauretania. It was printed at Prague in 1818. He also translated a Czech chronicle of the Jews of Prague in Hussite times into German. Both that manuscript and his translation have since been lost, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-freud-sigmund-6:
Sigmund Freud was an Austrian physician born on May 6, 1856, at Freiberg in Moravia. He was educated at the University of Vienna and took his medical degree there in 1881. In 1885 the university admitted him as a junior lecturer. In 1885-86 he heard the lectures of Charcot at Paris. Coming back to Vienna, he made diseases of the nerves his specialty.

In 1903 the university gave him the honorary title of professor. His medical works treat the fine structure of tissue and the anatomy of the brain. They also treat nervous diseases. Named works cover cocaine, printed in 1884, and loss of speech, printed in 1891. With Breuer he printed studies on hysteria in 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gabishon-abraha: Abraham ben Jacob Gabishon, an Algerian physician and scholar from a Granada family, died at Tlemcen in 1605. He set up as a doctor at Algiers in 1574 and built a large practice. He wrote a comment on Proverbs called Omer ha-Shikhah. In it he quotes Meiri and Levi ben Gershon most often. Well read in Arabic letters, he uses Arabic proverbs to clear up the biblical text. Poems by him, his son, and his grandson close the book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ghayyat-solomon: Solomon ben Judah Ghayyat, a Hebrew poet of the twelfth century, may have been a grandson of Isaac Ghayyat of Lucena. He stood on close terms with Judah ha-Levi. Ha-Levi gave him one of the great poems of his Diwan. That poem answers one by Ghayyat and shows the high regard Ha-Levi held for his friend verse. Only two poems by Ghayyat survive, both of them religious in kind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldfogle-henry: Henry Mayer Goldfogle was an American lawyer and politician. He was born in New York city on May 23, 1856. He entered the bar in 1877. In 1888 he won a seat as municipal court judge. Voters returned him unopposed in 1893. He left the bench in 1900 to practice law again. In 1901 his ninth district sent him to the Fifty-seventh Congress. It reelected him to the Fifty-eighth in 1903. The entry notes his 1902 steps in Congress. They aimed at easing limits on American Jews traveling in Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gradis-6849:
Gradis is the name of a great Bordeaux merchant family. It came first from Spain and rose in the eighteenth century. David Gradis founded the house in 1696. Its trade reached England, Holland, Canada, and the French West Indies. The firm sent alcohol, linen, meal, and wine to the colonies. It took sugar and indigo in return.

David's son Abraham raised the house still higher. He shipped war supplies to Canada at the firm's own cost. The state repaid him only in part. In 1748 he founded the Society of Canada. During famine he sent seventeen shiploads of food to the colonies, the abbé Grégoire noted. Martinique granted him full civil rights in 1779. Later money troubles after France's wars close the family's story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gunzburg-gabrie: Gabriel Jacob Günzburg was a Lithuanian financier and philanthropist. He was born at Wilna about 1793. He died at Simferopol, Crimea, on May 2, 1853. After his marriage at Vitebsk he settled at Kamenetz-Podolsk. His business spread across many places, and he lived a while at St. Petersburg. His giving served four towns: Wilna, Vitebsk, Kamenetz-Podolsk, and Simferopol. In Simferopol he built a hospital. At the finance minister's urging, Nicholas I named him honorary and hereditary citizen on Oct. 22, 1848.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hai-ben-david-7: Hai ben David was a dayyan, and later gaon in Pumbedita from 890 to 897. He is named in Isaac ibn Ghayyat's "Halakot" over a curious Bagdad custom: the reciting of the 'Abodah on the morning of the Day of Atonement. Even Hai could not end that custom. He likely wrote in Hebrew. Karaite sources of doubtful worth credit him with a book against the Karaites, written to defend the Rabbinite calendar. The entry gives no birth date or other works for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hammon-7149: Hammon is a name with three senses in this entry. First, it is a place in Asher's territory, named at Joshua xix, 28 between Rehob and Kanah. Ruins called Ummel-'Amud are thought to mark its site. Second, it is a city of Naphtali given to the Levites, to the sons of Gershom. Third, it is the name of a deity, El-Ḥammon, found in two Phoenician inscriptions from those same ruins. One inscription is dated 221 B.C., under Ptolemy III. The Bible place-names may tie to the god.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harby-7249:
Harby is the name of an American family based in the southern United States. Solomon Harby first settled at Charleston, South Carolina. His son Isaac, born in 1788, became a journalist, playwright, and school founder. Isaac edited several Charleston papers and wrote plays such as "Alberti."

The entry gives short lives for many family members. Isaac helped found the Reform Society of Israelites in 1825, an early Reform move in America. His brother Levi Myers Harby served in the United States navy and later for the Confederacy. Other relatives worked as teachers, doctors, and writers. Leah Cohen Harby wrote on history and led civic groups.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyun-abraham-: Abraham ben Nissim Hayyun was a Portuguese scholar of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. He was the father of Don Joseph Hayyun, who became rabbi of Lisbon. One work of his is named. "Amarot Tehorot" is a book on ethics and right conduct. It was printed at Constantinople in 1516. The entry is only a few lines long. It gives no town where he lived and no dates for his birth or death. Three modern sources are cited for the little that is known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hement-felix-75:
Felix Hement, born at Avignon on Jan. 22, 1827, was a French educator. He taught school all his life and rose to primary inspector for the Seine department. He retired in 1886 with an honorary top title in public instruction. During the war of 1870 he did special work for the defense of a Paris fort.

Hement lectured across France to spread popular schooling. His many books bring science to common readers. Titles cover early man, instinct, the origin of living things, and falling stars. One book was crowned by the French Academy. He held the Legion of Honor. He died on Oct. 5, 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hess-moses-mori:
Moses Moritz Hess, born at Bonn on June 21, 1812, was a Jewish socialist and nationalist. Mostly self-taught, he edited a paper and moved from liberal views toward social democracy with Marx and Engels. The Damascus affair renewed his interest in Jewish matters.

Hess left politics after 1848 for natural science, then returned to Jewish national thought. His chief work, printed at Leipsic in 1862, argued Jews would stay strangers in Europe. It held Jewish nationality could not be uprooted. Its answer was settling Palestine, with French help hoped for. The book met a cold welcome then, the entry says. It later became a basic work of Zionism. Hess died in Paris on April 6, 1875.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirschberg-juli:
Julius Hirschberg, born at Potsdam on Sept. 18, 1843, was a German eye doctor. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1867 and joined Graefe's eye clinic that year. In 1869 he began practice and founded a private eye hospital. Berlin admitted him to its medical faculty in 1870.

Hirschberg rose to assistant professor in 1879 and honorary professor in 1900. He traveled widely to visit eye hospitals on three continents. In 1877 he founded a journal for practical eye medicine. His writings neared 200 by 1895. Books cover eye statistics, eye care guides, eye surgery with magnets, and the history of eye medicine in old times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-honig-sidonie-7: Sidonie Honig, born at Vienna in 1871, was an Austrian actress and a prize winner at the Vienna Conservatorium. She debuted in 1889 at the Carlsruhe court theater. Her first role was Jane Eyre in a play drawn from that novel, the entry says. In 1890 she went to a Vienna people's theater. Two years later she joined the Hamburg city theater. Beside Jane Eyre, her most successful roles are listed as Desdemona, Rutland, and Philippine Welser. Two stage reference works are the entry's listed sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hurwitz-judah-b:
Judah ben Mordecai ha-Levi Hurwitz was a Russian physician and author born at Wilna in the first half of the eighteenth century. He died at Grodno on November 12, 1797. He took his medical degree at Padua, traveled widely in Europe, and served as physician to the Wilna Jewish community.

Later posts took him to Ponedeli, Zhagory, Mitau, and Grodno. His books lean to morals and belief. One treats moral philosophy and won approval from Mendelssohn. Another holds 360 ethical sentences. Others cover the soul's immortality and the quarrels of cabalists, Talmudists, and philosophers. He also wrote Hebrew poems and verse translations of German fables, kept in manuscript at Mitau.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-identity-proof-:
Proof of identity in Jewish law is treated here across crime, lost goods, and missing husbands. In criminal cases witnesses had to be sure of the accused, the victim, and the victim's nation. If a suspect melted into a crowd, there could be no trial. Their word alone was believed, with no added proofs.

A loser claiming a found object had to give telling signs, such as size, weight, count, or place. A scholar famed for truth got his goods back on his bare word. For a wife seeking freedom, the rules cut both ways. Word of a husband's death was taken lightly, but a corpse had to be known by strong marks, such as a missing limb or a known face, within three days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-incantation-139:
Incantation names the spoken words meant to command gods and demons, harm foes or guard against harm. Hebrew's root word for magic seems to mean "to murmur" or "to mutter," so the magician was one who muttered formulas, though the Bible preserves no example of one. Rabbinic literature, by contrast, keeps a large number, most labeled heathen and forbidden and a few recommended.

Thirty-two Hebrew and Aramaic formulas are counted here. One cure for too much wine rubbed oil and salt on palm and knee with a spoken wish. One for fever used a new jug turned seven times around the head at a river. The shrinking word SHABRIRI was spoken against the demon of blindness. Later, practical Cabala and folk custom kept such formulas alive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-8149: Isaac, the envoy of 797, joined the embassy Charlemagne sent to Harun al-Rashid, calif at Bagdad, probably as interpreter for the noblemen Sigismund and Landfried. Both noblemen died on the way back. Isaac alone brought home the calif's answer and presents, among them a magnificent elephant. The emperor sent the notary Erchenbald to Liguria to arrange the elephant's transport. Isaac reached Vendres in Oct., 801, wintered at Verceil because the Alps were snowed in, and was received at Aix-la-Chapelle in the summer of 802.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-itze-isaac-of-c: Itze Isaac of Chernigov was a Russian scholar of the twelfth century, often consulted by his contemporaries on Bible questions. He is probably the Isaac of Russia found in English records of 1181. His note on the word "yabam," backed by a likeness in the Russian language, is quoted in the lexicon "Sefer ha-Shoham." Zunz, and Harkavy after him, saw a point of weight in that note: it shows that Russian Jews of his day spoke the country's own tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-obadi: Jacob ben Obadiah Sforno was an Italian scholar who lived at Venice in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. He is named as the author of "Iggeret ha-Te'amim," a work on the Hebrew accents, printed at Venice in 1600. Steinschneider, though, believed that work is one and the same as the "Iggeret ha-Te'amim" of Aaron Abraham ben Baruch. The entry is only a few lines long, and it records nothing else about Sforno's life or writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeduthun-8549: Jeduthun names one of the three great orders of Temple singers charged with the music of the Temple from David's day into later times. Chronicles places Jeduthun beside Heman before the Ark and names him father of a class of doorkeepers. With Asaph and Heman he heads the music service, and one passage calls him the king's seer. The entry notes that the name Ethan seems to stand in his place in some lists, and that three psalms carry his name in their titles, perhaps as a music direction.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-quarterl: Jewish Quarterly Review is a journal of Jewish science founded in London in October 1888. Israel Abrahams and C. G. Montefiore edited it. Most of its pages hold learned pieces on Jewish writing and history, though current topics, above all church questions, also appear. Many of Schechter's finds from the Cairo store room, with pieces of an old wisdom book, first saw print in its pages, often in photo copy. Named writers include Bacher, Kaufmann, Neubauer, Steinschneider, and Zangwill, whose poems also ran there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-jaco:
Joseph ben Jacob ibn Zaddik was a Spanish rabbi, poet, and thinker who died at Cordova in 1149. A Talmudist of high standing, he became a judge at Cordova in 1138 and held the post with Maimon, the father of Maimonides, until his death. His religious poems stand in Sephardic and African prayer books.

His fame rests on a short Arabic treatise, rendered into Hebrew as Olam Katan, the Microcosmus. Its core thought compares the outer world with man, the small world. In four parts he treats how the soul forms ideas, matter and form, the makeup of the world, and the being and unity of God. He argues that the world was created because it is finite. The entry calls him no deep innovator, but a man fully at home in Arab learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judenstattigkei: Judenstaettigkeit is an old technical term for the legal standing of a Jewish community, the same idea as Judenschutz, or Jewish protection. It seems to have been used only at Frankfort-on-the-Main and Worms. The first Frankfort edition was printed by the guilds in 1613 as a tool of political agitation. Laws under that name were renewed by emperors in 1617, 1661, and 1705. A new one came from Prince Dalberg in 1807. It was wiped out in 1811, when the Jews gained full rights as citizens.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalisch-bertha-: Bertha Kalisch was an Austrian actress born at Lemberg. She first acted there in 1893. Her first part was a small role in "Mignon," sung in Polish. Her success won her a place at the Jewish theater in the same city. She went on to act in Budapest and Bucharest. At Bucharest a theater director hired her for Rumanian plays. In 1895 she moved to New York city. There she acted in Yiddish plays at the Thalia Theater. Her greatest success came in plays by Jacob Gordin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-karmi-4049:
Karmi is a family name, the same as the Bible's "Carmi." The entry links it to the French town of Crémieu. Many Jews lived there in the Middle Ages. Early in the seventeenth century the name was changed to Crémieux. The article then gives short lives of Karmis across France and Italy.

Among them stands David ben Joseph Karmi, who preached at Carpentras in 1621 and 1622. Elijah Karmi gathered the prayers of four French communities into one book. Joseph Jedidiah Karmi printed his own prayer book at Venice in 1626. Mordecai Karmi, who died at Aix in 1825, ranks among the most learned rabbis of France. His son Moses served as rabbi at Aix as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kavala-or-caval: Kavala, also spelled Cavala, is a settlement in Macedonia. It stands on the Ægean Sea, across from the island of Thasos. It lies nine miles southwest of Old Kavala, the ancient Neapolis. The town held 4,000 people, about one fourth of them Jews. Those Jews came first from Salonica and Serres. The community dates from 1860. It ran a school for forty boys and a synagogue built in 1883. Most of its Jews worked at making tobacco goods, in summer only.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kish-9349: Kish was the father of Saul, the first king of Israel. He was a wealthy and powerful Benjamite. Scripture calls him the son of Ner and the grandson of Abiel. One passage places his home at Gibeah. Another puts the family tomb at Zelah, where Saul and Jonathan were buried. The entry notes that the text here is no doubt corrupt. The one incident told of Kish is that he sent Saul out in search of some of his lost asses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kompert-leopold:
Leopold Kompert, an Austrian author born at Münchengrätz in Bohemia on May 15, 1822, died at Vienna on Nov. 23, 1886. He studied at Prague and Vienna and worked as a tutor before joining the Vienna Creditanstalt in 1857. Council and congregational posts kept him busy with schooling and with care for orphans.

Fame came from his ghetto stories, which won him the label of the Auerbach of the ghetto. They picture Bohemian Jewish life, custom, and manners in close detail. Many show families torn between the narrow ghetto and open farm life under modern pressure. The entry lists story collections from 1848 to 1883 and notes a complete edition in eight volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lasker-eduard-9:
Eduard Lasker, a German politician born at Jarotschin in Posen on Oct. 14, 1829, died in New York on Jan. 5, 1884. As a student he joined the Vienna rising of 1848. Law exams led to a Berlin judgeship in 1858 and the bar in 1870. From 1865 he sat in Prussian and German parliaments.

National Liberal leadership made Lasker first Bismarck's partner, then a sharp critic. He backed the chancellor until a revenue turn in 1879, then split away in 1880. Two speeches in early 1873 helped break a stock promotion swindle. Worn out, he left politics in 1883 and died on an American health trip.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lengfeld-felix-: Felix Lengfeld, an American chemist, was born at San Francisco on Feb. 18, 1863. He studied at the San Francisco College of Pharmacy, the University of California, and Johns Hopkins. He also studied at Zurich, Liége, Munich, and Paris. He taught chemistry at the South Dakota School of Mines and at the University of California. From 1892 to 1901 he taught at the University of Chicago. He wrote a laboratory manual on inorganic preparations and many papers for science journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-mendel-ca:
Mendel Levin, also called Lefin and Satanower, was a Polish scholar and author. He was born in Satanow, Podolia, about 1741 and died in Mikolayev in 1819. He was trained as a Talmudist. Reading Delmedigo's "Elim" opened the world of science to him, and he left for Berlin.

In Berlin Levin joined the circle round Moses Mendelssohn and stayed several years. Back east, he shaped early Haskalah figures in Galicia. Prince Adam Czartoryski hired him to teach his children. His books include a popular medicine from the French, an ethics work after Franklin printed in 1809, and sea travels after Campe. Mendelssohn approved his "Moda la-Binah" of 1789.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-libraries-9949:
Libraries, in the Jewish sense, are the subject of this long entry. Very little is known, it begins, about how Jews gathered and kept books in early times. The Bible says nothing clear on the point. Royal archives at Jerusalem may be guessed from the titles recorder and scribe, but the guess is not proof.

For Talmudic times and the Middle Ages the record is also thin. Scrolls were kept in covers of leather or metal. They stood in cases of wood, leather, glass, bone, or metal. Such cases match the Roman bookcase form. The entry points to early pictures of the Ark on glass, from the third century, in that same form. Sometimes scrolls stood in a cupboard on a base, with a cover.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loans-elijah-be:
Elijah ben Moses Loans was a German rabbi and cabalist born at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1555, and he died at Worms in July, 1636. He came from the family of Rashi. He studied at Frankfort and at Cracow, where he prepared a work by Moses Isserles for print.

Loans served as rabbi at Fulda, then at Hanau, Friedberg in 1620, and Worms in 1630. He was a keen student of cabala and was called Ba'al Shem. Legends grew around him. He wrote commentaries on Canticles, Ecclesiastes, and the Zohar, and edited legal works printed at Basel in 1599 and 1600.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstein-baru:
Baruch Solomon Löwenstein, a Russian mathematician born at Wolodarka in the second quarter of the nineteenth century, is the subject of a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The article, by Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer, records a scholar who worked where Jewish learning met mathematics and astronomy.

Löwenstein wrote “Bikkure ha-Limmudiyyot,” a work explaining mathematical passages in the writings of Abraham ibn Ezra, Moses Maimonides, and Joseph Delmedigo. He also annotated and published a second edition of “Shebile di-Reḳia,” a book on the rules of the calendar with the elements of geometry, trigonometry, and astronomy, issued at Warsaw in 1863. The entry preserves the name and books of a little-known figure who explained older Jewish texts through mathematics, and it gives readers a compact record of that work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandans-10349:
Mandaeans, an eastern religious sect of lower Babylonia, are described in a long Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The sect mixes Christian, Jewish, and heathen doctrines and customs. Its members live around Wasit and Basra, speaking Arabic and Persian. Their sacred books use an Aramaic dialect close to the Babylonian Talmud's.

The article untangles their names and books. Mandaean comes from Manda, the word of life, a central figure in their system. To outsiders they call themselves Sabians, and their learned men Nasoraeans. Europeans long misnamed them Christians of Saint John, for their reverence for John and their frequent baptisms. Their chief book, the Treasure, dates from between 650 and 900. Part serves the living and part the burial of priests. The system it teaches is a form of ancient Gnosticism. Jewish influence shows plainly inside it. The entry remains a rich early survey of a small, secretive faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-berthe-104:
Berthe Marx, a French pianist, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 from Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn. Born at Paris on July 28, 1859, she started piano at four with her father, a cellist in the Conservatoire and Grand Opera orchestras. At the Conservatoire she studied with Henri Herz and won first prize at fifteen.

Her career turned on a meeting in Brussels with the violinist Sarasate, who engaged her as soloist and accompanist. She toured with him through Europe and America, reaching Mexico and California, and played in about 600 concerts in all. The entry also credits her with several Spanish rhapsodies of her own and with piano arrangements of Sarasate's Spanish dances.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-zioni-z:
Menahem Zioni of Speyer was a cabalist of the middle of the fifteenth century. He takes his name from his work, the "Ziyyuni." That work is a cabalistic commentary on the Pentateuch. Joseph Jacobs and A. Biram treat it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The book builds on Rashi and Nahmanides. It builds on the older cabalistic literature of the geonic age too. It opens with acrostic poems. With Maimonides quoted at length, it argues for the doctrine of creation. Short poems bridge the weekly portions.

The book had a violent birth in print. Vincentio Conti issued it at Cremona in 1559, in rabbinic type. Marauding Spanish soldiers burned that edition the same year. It was reprinted there in 1560. Quoted often in the "Yalkut Re'ubeni," it became a standard cabalistic gloss. The entry ends with a separation. It parts its author from a twelfth-century hymn-writer of a similar name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-annie-nee:
Annie Nathan Meyer, born in New York City on February 19, 1867, was an American writer profiled by Cyrus Adler and M. H. Harris in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She published early in The Critic, Harper's Bazar, Lippincott's, and The Bookman. Her best-known short story was Vorbei, and some of her tales drew on Jewish life.

She married Dr. Alfred Meyer in 1887 and went on to write the novel Robert Annys, Poor Priest in 1901 and to edit Woman's Work, a standard book of 1898. Her public work mattered as much as her books: she chaired a literature committee at the Chicago World's Fair congress. Most of all, her energy helped found Barnard College, gathering its promoters and raising its first-year funds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minerbi-hirsche:
Hirschel de Minerbi, Count of Oscarre, was an Italian diplomat from a wealthy and illustrious Jewish family of Triest, born on April 25, 1838. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione sketch him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took a law degree at Padua in 1864 and entered the Italian government service three years later.

His postings carried him to Paris, Bern, Constantinople, London, and Brussels, and back to London, where he stayed until he left the service. The entry's most telling detail comes at the end: before retiring to private life, Minerbi set aside 80,000 lire as the seed of an institute for the widows and orphans of diplomats. It is a short entry for a long career of quiet postings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monogamy-10949:
Monogamy in Judaism was custom outrunning law, Joseph Jacobs and Israel Abrahams argue in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Law tolerated polygamy without enacting it; the people, from the return from Babylon onward, made one wife the ideal and the practice. Scripture itself leans that way from its first page, the creation of one man and one woman.

Even the patriarchs' plural marriages are told, the writers note, with apology, as infringements needing excuse. The Wisdom books assume monogamy entire: Proverbs' perfect wife of chapter thirty-one has no rival in her house, and Ben Sira and Tobit confirm the picture. A social-history entry arguing that practice reformed the law long before any statute did.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-11049:
Moses, the lawgiver who led Israel out of Egypt, is the subject of one of the Jewish Encyclopedia's central articles. Six scholars share the byline, among them Wilhelm Bacher, Kaufmann Kohler, and Crawford Howell Toy. The article tells his life from the Bible: hidden by his mother Jochebed, set adrift on the Nile, and found by Pharaoh's daughter.

It follows his flight to Midian after he killed an Egyptian, and his call at the burning bush. Then come the ten plagues, the crossing of the sea, and the giving of the Law at Sinai. The article ends with the wilderness years, the fighting east of the Jordan, and Moses' farewell address and death on Mount Nebo. It is a full period retelling of the Exodus story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-simha:
