The finding links a salt-sensing switch to intestinal disease. A leaky barrier is a hallmark of gut inflammation. SPAK may be one of its controllers.
plos-pone-0005149:
Blood vessels must stay sealed and alive. Cells lining them, endothelial cells, maintain that seal. Signals from neighboring pericytes help stabilize vessels. Tony Walshe and colleagues tested one signal's necessity in PLOS ONE in 2009. The signal is TGF-beta. Their earlier work showed it stabilizing vessels in dishes.

TGF-beta proved required for the adult microvasculature. Without it, the vascular barrier fails. Endothelial survival and vessel homeostasis fail too. Tiny vessels suffer first and worst. The finding names a master keeper of the vasculature. Leaky vessels appear in many diseases, from sepsis to diabetes. Knowing what holds the seal suggests how to repair it. The study moves a dish observation into living tissue.
plos-pone-0005249:
When cells divide, chromosomes are usually pulled apart by spindle fibers gripped at kinetochores. Egg cells build their spindles differently from ordinary dividing cells, though. Deng and colleagues reported a surprise in mouse eggs in PLOS ONE in 2009.

During the second meiotic division, chromosomes moved toward the poles even without kinetochore control. A backup route for moving chromosomes exists in these cells. The finding revises a textbook rule of cell division and may help explain errors that lead to abnormal egg cells. Egg cells must split their genes with great care, since one small slip can end a pregnancy or leave a child with the wrong gene count.
plos-pone-0005349:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects about a third of the world's people. Active disease involves fast-growing bacteria, while latent infection involves slow or non-growing ones. Beste and colleagues mapped the genes needed for each growth mode in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The genetic requirements for fast and slow growth differ, as separate gene sets keep each state alive. Drugs that kill fast growers may miss the latent reservoir entirely. Knowing the slow-growth gene list gives drug hunters targets against the hidden form of TB. Most TB drugs were found by their kill of fast-growing germs in a dish. So the slow set has long been a blind spot that this gene list at last brings into view.
plos-pone-0005449:
Daniel Williams and Peter Novick studied cell shipping in yeast in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Yeast cells grow and divide by moving materials to the right place at the right time. Proteins called SNAREs make membranes fuse, which is how those materials get delivered.

The team studied what happens when one SNARE gene, SEC9, is held back. Watching the effects showed how this one part links membrane fusion to the wider health of the cell. The work adds detail to the basic rules that all cells, not just yeast, use to move cargo inside themselves.
plos-pone-0005549:
Beth Tamburini and co-authors studied a blood vessel cancer in dogs for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Hemangiosarcoma is a fast-moving cancer of blood vessel cells in dogs. Earlier work found set chromosome changes in tumours from golden retrievers that were rarer in other breeds.

The team compared gene activity in tumours across breeds. The patterns of activity tied closely to breed, even for tumours that arise without a known inherited cause. Breed background shaping tumour behaviour matters for dog care and may hint at similar effects in people. Dog cancers arise naturally and share features with human cancers, so breed lessons may run both ways.
plos-pone-0005649:
Irene Granlund, Michael Hall, and Thomas Kieselbach studied proteins in a hidden plant compartment in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Photosynthesis runs in membranes inside leaf cells, and the space inside those membranes holds well over a hundred proteins. That lumen space is thin and hard to study.

The team measured how light changes protein levels there in a model plant. They also found that the genes for those proteins are regulated in a uniform way. Light reaching even this hidden space in a coordinated fashion helps leaves adjust to the day. The lumen was long a blank space in diagrams, and a full parts list changes how photosynthesis is taught.
plos-pone-0005749:
J. A. Scott Kelso and co-authors linked a person to a virtual partner in 2009 to study how new shared behaviors arise. The setup pairs a human's hand movements with a computer partner that reacts in real time. It borrows its logic from a device used to probe single nerve cells.

Subjects and the virtual partner had to coordinate, and fresh patterns of joint motion emerged. The team uses those patterns to test theories of coordination dynamics. A machine partner can be tuned precisely, which a human partner cannot. That control lets researchers probe the rules of social timing itself.
plos-pone-0005849:
Jackie Cheung and co-authors analyzed in 2009 a two-part signaling system that controls toxin output in a food-poisoning bacterium. Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene and food poisoning with a battery of toxins. The VirSR system, a sensor plus a responder, acts as the master switch.

The team worked out how the responder VirR passes the signal to its target genes. Knowing the relay's wiring shows where it might be jammed. Blocking toxin production, rather than killing the bacterium, is a gentler anti-virulence strategy. The functional details here guide that idea for a common and dangerous germ.
plos-pone-0005949:
Inherited changes in one gene form the most common known genetic cause of Parkinson's disease. The gene is LRRK2, and Xiaodong Ding and Matthew Goldberg studied how the cell controls its protein in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper asks what keeps LRRK2 levels steady, since the protein's exact day job is still unclear.

An enzyme called CHIP, which tags worn proteins for disposal, turns out to govern how stable LRRK2 is. A disposal route of this kind gives drug hunters a new handle on a key Parkinson's protein. If LRRK2 levels can be trimmed safely, that approach could one day sit beside drugs that only block the protein's action.
plos-pone-0006049:
Tbx1 is a gene best known for its link to DiGeorge syndrome, a birth condition affecting the heart and face. Gabriella Fulcoli, Tuong Huynh, Peter Scambler and colleagues found the gene doing unexpected work in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper shows Tbx1 binding Smad1, a signal carrier in the BMP pathway that patterns the growing body.

The surprise is the manner: Tbx1 damps the BMP-Smad1 signal without acting as a transcription factor, its usual trade. A gene with a second, quieter job helps explain why its loss causes such a wide pattern of defects. The result also adds a new kind of control to a pathway that guides bone, heart and much more.
plos-pone-0006149:
Hantaviruses were long thought to belong to rodents alone, until shrews broke the story. Hae Ji Kang, Shannon Bennett, Laarni Sumibcay and colleagues added a mole to the plot in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper reports a genetically divergent hantavirus harbored by the European common mole, and reads what it reveals about the family's evolution.

A virus far from the known branches, in a host outside the rodent order, pushes the family's roots deeper and wider. Each new host redraws the map of where hantaviruses hide, which matters since some cause severe human disease. The mole virus is a clue that the family's true host range is still being discovered.
plos-pone-0006249:
Spores of Clostridium perfringens survive cooking that kills most bacteria, then cause food poisoning. Jihong Li and colleagues studied a small spore protein called Ssp4 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Type A strains carrying a toxin gene make spores with exceptional resistance to heat and nitrites.

Earlier work tied much of that toughness to Ssp4. The team further characterised the protein's properties and when it is produced. Knowing what armours spores helps food makers design safer processing. It also explains why some strains survive where others perish. Food makers need such facts to set safe cooking and storage rules.
plos-pone-0006349:
Cattle deploy small RNA regulators when viruses attack, and cataloguing them shows the defence in action. Evgeny Glazov and colleagues surveyed bovine micro RNAs and similar small RNAs expressed upon viral infection, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Several classes of small regulatory RNAs had been discovered in recent years.

The study extends the repertoire of characterised small RNAs in mammals. Which regulators appear during infection reveals immune strategy at the molecular level. Livestock health has direct economic stakes in such knowledge. The catalogue also serves comparison with human antiviral responses.
plos-pone-0006449:
Frank ter Veld and co-authors improved newborn screening tests in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Screening now flags babies who may lack one of two fat-burning enzymes, MCAD or VLCAD. The screen uses a method called tandem mass spectrometry on blood markers. It has raised the number of babies found with fatty acid oxidation disorders, so confirming the result quickly matters.

The authors present a new tandem mass spectrometry method for rapid confirmation. A fast, sure second test separates true cases from false alarms. That protects babies who need care from being missed. It also spares healthy babies from needless worry and treatment. The method strengthens a screening program used on newborns.
plos-pone-0006549:
Sung-Cherl Jung and Dax Hoffman studied how nerve cells tune their own firing in PLOS ONE in 2009. When links between nerve cells grow strong for good, the cells also grow more apt to fire. This is called intrinsic plasticity. The team worked on cells in the hippocampus, a brain area key for memory. They focused on a kind of potassium channel in the cell body.

Their title says these channels are turned down in two phases, which lets the cell fire more with ease. Less braking by the channel is the core of the change. The work shows in fine detail how a cell's own tuning helps it learn. Such tuning works hand in hand with changes at the links between cells.
plos-pone-0006649:
Nicolas Marsollier, Nadim Kassis, Karima Mezghenna, and colleagues studied brain-liver cross-talk in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Deregulation of hypothalamic fatty acid sensing leads to hepatic insulin resistance. That may partly contribute to further impairment of glucose homeostasis. The team investigated deregulation of hepatic insulin sensitivity induced by central lipid infusion in rats.

Their title reports the effect is mediated by nitric oxide signaling. Fat sensed in the brain changes how the liver handles insulin. The brain-liver axis is a promising target in diabetes. Their work traces one messenger in that conversation.
plos-pone-0006749:
Michael Czisch and co-authors studied how the sleeping brain reacts to odd sounds in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sleep needs reduced responsiveness to outside stimuli. Yet sleepers still process signals that could mean danger. The brain must filter without fully waking. The team used an acoustic oddball task during non-REM sleep.

Unusual sounds were mixed among repeated standard sounds. They recorded brain activity with EEG and fMRI together. Combining both methods shows timing and location of responses. The results reveal how the sleeping brain keeps watch. That watchfulness explains why a baby's cry wakes a parent while traffic does not.
plos-pone-0006849:
Hua Zhang and his team read the small RNAs of a child's blood cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. Small RNAs called microRNAs steer much of what cells do. In cancers, they can brake growth or feed it. The cancer here is acute lymphoblastic leukemia. It is the most seen cancer of childhood. A full list of its small RNAs could bring fresh leads.

Deep gene reads logged small RNAs through the whole genome. Brand-new microRNAs turned up in the reads. Each new one is a fresh lead on how this cancer grows. The list is a store for later lab work. In time, it may yield marks for diagnosis or aims for drugs.
plos-pone-0006949:
Laura Heath, Alan Fox, Jan McClure, and colleagues compared HIV in lung and blood in PLOS ONE in 2009. HIV-1 is often found in the lungs of infected people. The virus likely helps drive lung infections that strike these patients. The lung has its own environment, rich in alveolar macrophages and local immune responses.

The team asked whether lung viruses form a separate genetic compartment. Their evidence pointed to only limited separation from blood viruses. That finding shapes how doctors think about drug resistance and viral reservoirs. If lung and blood viruses mix freely, blood tests tell more about the lung than expected.
plos-pone-0007049:
Debojyoti Dhar, Musturi Venkataramana, Anand Ponnuswamy, and colleagues studied protein production control in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was interferon regulatory factor 2, or IRF2. Earlier work showed its RNA can start translation from inside, not just the usual start point. A protein called PTB was suspected to help with that internal start.

The team confirmed PTB's role in driving this route. Internal initiation lets cells keep making key proteins under stress. IRF2 helps balance gene expression in hard conditions. The mechanism is one way cells protect vital output when normal translation falters.
plos-pone-0007149:
Ricardo Dinis-Oliveira, Paula Guedes de Pinho, Liliana Santos, and colleagues reviewed fatal herbicide poisonings in PLOS ONE in 2009. Paraquat is a weed killer that kills people who swallow it, often in self-poisoning. Doctors try gut decontamination to block absorption. They also use anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing treatments to slow its toxic path.

The team analyzed postmortem evidence from human cases. Those analyses showed the therapies work poorly in practice. An honest verdict matters more than hope here. It pushes research toward new approaches instead of repeating treatments that autopsies show failing.
plos-pone-0007249:
Nicholas J. Hudson, Antonio Reverter, YongHong Wang, and colleagues mapped gene regulation in cow muscle in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Decoding causal transcriptional regulation remains hard, even with modern tools. The problem grows in less studied organisms, and when only gene expression data are available to researchers.

Muscle has only a small set of well characterized regulators. The authors integrate co-expression networks, groups of genes that rise and fall together. They infer the transcriptional landscape of bovine skeletal muscle from those patterns. Livestock scientists can use the map to study meat production and muscle biology.
plos-pone-0007349:
R. Prasobh and Narayanan Manoj cataloged signaling proteins in a marine animal in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Heterotrimeric G proteins and their regulators are key partners in GPCR signaling. GPCR receptors form a highly versatile system for sensing signals outside cells, from hormones to light and odors.

The versatility comes from coupling many receptors to varied G proteins. The authors compile the repertoire of both protein families in Ciona intestinalis, a sea squirt. This animal is a close invertebrate relative of vertebrates. Their catalog supports evolutionary comparisons of signaling systems.
plos-pone-0007449:
Stephen Gilmore and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on telling dangerous skin spots from harmless ones. Early diagnosis of melanoma is critical for survival. Doctors now rely on examining lesions by eye, but interest in automated help is growing. The team tested a mathematical measure called lacunarity, which describes how patchy or gappy a pattern looks.

Applied to images of moles and melanomas, the measure separated the two groups. Malignant lesions showed a different patchiness signature than benign naevi. An automated score of this kind could support clinicians screening large numbers of skin spots. It would not replace medical judgment, but it could flag lesions that deserve a closer look. The study offers a promising route toward computer-assisted skin checks.
plos-pone-0007549:
Sodiomon Sirima and colleagues published a clinical trial report in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a malaria vaccine candidate called MSP3. MSP3 is a protein on the surface of the malaria parasite's blood stage. An earlier trial in European adults showed the vaccine raised antibodies that kill parasites in the lab. The new trial moved to the group that needs protection most: children aged twelve to twenty-four months in Burkina Faso.

The trial checked safety and immune response in those young children. A vaccine meant for toddlers in malaria regions must clear this bar before wider testing. Favorable results move the candidate one step closer to the field. Malaria kills mainly small children, so a vaccine proven gentle and active in them is the real goal. The study is one careful rung on that ladder.
plos-pone-0007649:
Konstantinos Lefkimmiatis and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 introducing a tool for one of the cell's most universal messengers. Cyclic AMP, or cAMP, relays signals inside nearly every cell. To learn what a signal does, researchers need to raise it, lower it, and buffer it on demand. The team built a molecular buffer they named the cAMP sponge. It soaks up the messenger inside living cells.

By sponging up cAMP, researchers can damp the signal in a controlled way. That reveals which cell behaviors truly depend on the messenger's level. Tools that tune a signal are as valuable as tools that measure it. The cAMP sponge gives cell biologists a new hand on a universal pathway. Studies of hormones, heart cells, and neurons all use such control. The paper is a methods contribution with wide reach.
plos-pone-0007749:
Kwame Shanaube and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It measures the yearly risk of TB infection in Zambia and South Africa. Both countries carry heavy burdens of TB and HIV. The yearly risk figure is a key sign of how fast TB spreads in a community.

Surveys use the tuberculin skin test to estimate how many people are infected. Several methods can turn those test results into a risk figure. The authors compare what the methods imply in high-burden settings. Choosing the right method matters, since health programs plan around this number.
plos-pone-0007849:
John Waitumbi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It checks whether a malaria vaccine changes which parasite strains infect trial volunteers. The vaccine candidate, RTS,S, is built in yeast from part of a parasite surface protein. It is joined to a hepatitis B protein, and mixed with strong boosters called adjuvants.

The team compared parasite genotypes in adults given two vaccine formulas. They used the AS02A and AS01B adjuvant versions. If a vaccine blocks only strains matching its design, other strains may fill the gap. Tracking that shift early helps vaccine makers judge strain-specific protection.
plos-pone-0007949:
Eunsun Lee and colleagues studied a protein that can hold back cancer spread, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, Nm23-H1, also does plain housekeeping work in cells and can switch genes on. Much about how the cell steers its many jobs stayed unclear.

The team found the steering comes from the cell's redox system, the set of reactions that add or remove oxygen-based tags. As that balance shifts, the protein's jobs shift with it. The link ties the protein's fight against tumor spread to the cell's inner chemistry, a tie drug makers may be able to use.
plos-pone-0008049:
Chengyun Li and colleagues put mixed planting to a large field test in PLOS ONE in 2009. Farmers have long grown several crops in one field, in rows or in turns, claiming bigger harvests and less disease. Hard proof at real farm scale was thin.

Field trials across wide areas showed the mixes did yield more than single crops grown alone. Diversity in the field paid in grain, not just in theory. At a time of tight land and food demand, the result backs a cheap, low-tech way to grow more on the same ground.
plos-pone-0008149:
Agnieszka Klosowska-Wardega and colleagues lowered the fluid pressure inside mouse tumors with a paired drug attack in PLOS ONE in 2009. Solid tumors build leaky vessels and trap fluid, so pressure inside runs high. High pressure keeps chemotherapy from soaking in, a plain physical bar to cure.

Blocking two vessel growth signals at once, PDGF and VEGF, dropped that pressure in mouse carcinomas. With the pressure down, drugs should reach more of the tumor. The pairing offers a way to open the door before the real medicine knocks. Timing the pairing well will be the next test.
plos-pone-0008249:
Gisela Pöll and colleagues studied ribosome building in yeast in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Ribosomes are the cell's protein-making machines. The large subunit contains three ribosomal RNAs and about forty-six proteins. Assembly is dynamic and involves more than one hundred fifty helper proteins. The team depleted yeast cells of large subunit proteins to see what happens.

They tracked how ribosomal RNA matures when those proteins are missing. Each missing protein stalls the process in revealing ways. Mapping those stalls shows the order of assembly steps. The work is basic research on how every cell builds its core machinery.
plos-pone-0008349:
David N. Ruskin, Masahito Kawamura, and Susan A. Masino fed rats a special diet in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The ketogenic diet is high in fat and low in carbohydrate. It forces cells to burn ketones rather than glucose. Clinically, the diet has proven effective for pediatric epilepsy and type II diabetes. Its wider effects were under study.

Rats on the diet showed reduced pain and inflammation. Both juvenile and adult animals benefited in their tests. A diet that eases pain without drugs would be valuable. The findings support more research on ketogenic therapy.
plos-pone-0008449:
Stuart Edelstein and co-authors write on signal systems in cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cells sense signals when molecules bind to receptors on their surface. Often the binding is cooperative, so one binding helps the next. In the body, signal levels are often close to the level that half fills the receptors. At such levels, using up the signal matters.

The authors show that ligand depletion changes the range of signals a cell can sense. It also changes how sharp the response is. Their model helps explain real cell behavior. Lab tests that ignore depletion may give a false picture.
plos-pone-0008549:
Daniel Fernandez-Ayala and co-authors profile gene expression in a fly model in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A point mutation in the fly gene technical knockout causes mitochondrial disease. That gene encodes a mitochondrial ribosomal protein called S12. Mutant flies show respiratory chain deficiency and developmental delay. They also show neurological abnormalities similar to human mitochondrial patients. The team measure gene expression across the whole genome in these flies.

Their profile shows which genes rise or fall when mitochondria fail. Coordinated changes reveal how cells compensate for lost energy. Some changes may themselves drive symptoms such as neurological problems. The fly model helps dissect human mitochondrial disease mechanisms.
plos-pone-0008649:
KyeongJin Kim and co-authors study a hepatitis B protein and insulin in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis B virus X protein is a viral regulator made in infected liver cells. Diabetes and insulin resistance are more common in hepatitis B patients. The authors' abstract centers on hepatic insulin signaling, the liver's response to insulin. Two molecules feature in that signaling: IRS1, a relay protein, and SOCS3, a suppressor of signaling. The team test how the X protein affects both.

They find the X protein impairs hepatic insulin signaling. It does so through degradation of IRS1 and induction of SOCS3. Both hits weaken the insulin message in liver cells. That mechanism links chronic hepatitis B to diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0008749:
Eric Grossman, David Lee, Jing Tao, and colleagues asked whether steady blood sugar helps insulin cells regrow. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin-making beta cells sit in the pancreas. A toxin called streptozotocin kills many of them, modeling diabetes. Some beta cells regrow afterward. Conditions favoring that regrowth could matter for patients.

Diabetic mice received insulin treatment to hold sugar near normal. Their beta cells regenerated better than in untreated mice. Good sugar control itself seems to create a friendlier setting for regrowth. The finding supports tight control as more than damage prevention.
plos-pone-0008849:
Siddharth Pathi, Christine Kowalczewski, Ramya Tadipatri, and colleagues built a mineralized 3-D model of tumors spreading to bone. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Advanced breast cancer often spreads into bone, causing pain and fractures. Bone mineral, called hydroxyapatite, may itself encourage that spread. Flat dish cultures cannot capture a mineral setting. A three-dimensional mineral culture was needed.

Cancer cells grew within the mineralized scaffold in bone-like conditions. The model lets researchers watch tumor-bone interactions directly. Drug tests in realistic settings beat tests on plastic. The system should speed the search for treatments against bone metastasis.
plos-pone-0008949:
Danny Bitton and colleagues built a pipeline to hunt for unknown human proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Protein studies usually match lab readings against lists of already known proteins. Anything not on the list stays invisible, even if the genome truly encodes it. The team instead searched readings against the whole human genome, translated in the computer.

Their pipeline filtered the flood of matches down to credible new coding regions. Several stretches of DNA, not listed as genes, showed real protein evidence. Each find adds a piece to the map of what human DNA actually makes. A fuller protein map sharpens both basic biology and disease gene hunts.
plos-pone-0009049:
Rachel Jenkins and co-authors counted how doctor migration drains psychiatrists from poorer countries, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health workers have long left poorer countries to work in rich ones. Donor countries lose staff their health systems badly need. Psychiatry, already short-staffed, was the paper's focus.

The team used international data to trace where psychiatrists trained and where they practise. Poor countries train doctors who then serve wealthy health systems. The imbalance leaves mental health care thinnest where burdens are growing. The census gives policymakers numbers for a debate often run on anecdotes.
plos-pone-0009149:
Larissa Estes and co-authors asked women in an HIV programme how a talking computer interview felt, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Audio computer-assisted self-interviewing, or ACASI, asks sensitive questions by recorded voice. Answers given in private come out more honest than face-to-face replies. Few studies had asked the participants about the experience itself.

The women were taking part in an HIV-positive prevention programme. Interviews explored privacy, ease of use, and trust in the machine. Their views can make future surveys both kinder and more accurate. Good data on health and risk behaviour starts with tools people accept.
plos-pone-0009249:
Xu Dong and co-authors published this inflammation modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inflammation is a complex response that shifts over time and defies simple formulas. A single-variable model cannot capture its tangled feedback. The authors turned to agent-based modeling, where many simple actors interact in a simulation.

Their model follows human blood leukocytes exposed to endotoxin, a bacterial trigger of inflammation. Each cell in the simulation follows local rules, and the overall response emerges. Such models can reproduce the nonlinear surges real blood shows. They offer a test bed for ideas about sepsis and other runaway inflammatory states.
plos-pone-0009349:
Otfried Kistner and co-authors published this flu vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A new swine-origin H1N1 flu spread fast and became the century's first influenza pandemic. Vaccines were rushed from labs toward mass campaigns. The team's candidate used whole virus rather than split pieces of it.

In mice, the whole virus vaccine proved highly immunogenic, stirring strong immune responses. It protected animals given the vaccine directly. It also protected through passive transfer, where antibodies from vaccinated animals shielded others. Strong results in both modes supported moving this vaccine design toward people.
plos-pone-0009449:
Rauf Latif, Krzysztof Michalek, and Syed Morshed studied the receptor for thyroid stimulating hormone in PLOS ONE in 2010. That hormone tells the thyroid gland to grow and to release its own hormones. It acts through this receptor on thyroid cells. The receptor is a large protein that can join with copies of itself to form groups.

They found that one building block, a tyrosine, helps keep those groups stable. Small changes there can alter how the receptor is built after it is made. Knowing how the groups form helps explain faults behind thyroid disease. It may also guide drugs that aim at this receptor.
plos-pone-0009549:
Chungen Pan and co-authors read the genome of the 2009 pandemic flu virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus, a swine origin H1N1, caused the first flu pandemic of the century. What let it pass so well from person to person was unclear. The team analyzed the pattern of its genome and how its mutations trended over time.

Certain genomic marks set the pandemic strain apart from seasonal strains. Tracking how those marks change helps trace the virus's adaptation to people. Such clues could flag dangerous strains earlier in future outbreaks. The work turns sequence data into an early warning tool.
plos-pone-0009649:
Rachel Schwartz and Rachel Mueller issued a warning to evolution researchers in PLOS ONE in 2010. Molecular clocks estimate species split times from DNA change rates. Those rates are often said to vary between lineages. The team simulated DNA data that evolved at a perfectly steady rate. They then ran standard tests for rate variation on that clock like data.

The tests wrongly reported variation that was not there. In other words, the method can invent the pattern it seeks. That is a sobering result for a widely used tool. It calls for caution and better tests before claims about uneven clocks are believed.
plos-pone-0009749:
Hector Hernandez-Vargas and co-authors published a cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study maps DNA methylation, a chemical tag on genes, in liver cancer, a fast and late-found disease. The team compared tags in 30 tumors with tags in the tissue around them.

One tag pattern marked liver cancer apart from nearby tissue and from other tumor types, whatever the cause. A second set of tags tracked tumor growth and risk factors such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and alcohol use. A third set was strongly tied to how long patients lived after treatment.
plos-pone-0009849:
Cells must copy their centrioles once, and only once, before dividing. Annekatrin Krause and Ingrid Hoffmann found a trigger for that copying step. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Centrioles are small barrels that help organize cell division.

The trigger runs through polo-like kinase 2, an enzyme that tags other proteins. It phosphorylates NPM, also called B23, on serine 4, adding a phosphate group at one spot. That single tag sets centriole duplication in motion. Precise control keeps cells from copying their division machinery too often. Errors here can leave cells with too many or too few centrioles.
plos-pone-0009949:
Arrow worms are glassy predators that drift in every ocean, yet their species are hard to tell apart. Robert Jennings, Ann Bucklin, and Annelies Pierrot-Bults used DNA barcodes to sort them. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Barcoding reads a short standard gene to identify a species. Samples came from three oceans, giving a wide view of genetic diversity. Arrow worms form the phylum Chaetognatha, an enigmatic group whose evolution is still debated. Genetic data reveal hidden species and redraw the phylum's story. Arrow worms snatch small prey with hooks by the mouth.
plos-pone-0010049:
The authors were Jason Schmidberger, Mark Bate, Cyril Reboul, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper presented software called MrGrid. Solving a protein structure by crystallography can demand heavy computing. Hard cases run faster on high-performance machines, but those machines are not easy for many labs to use.

MrGrid is a portable pipeline for molecular replacement, a common crystallography method. That method uses a known related structure to help solve a new one. A portable, grid-based tool lets more researchers bring big computing power to difficult structures. The authors describe the design for use across different computer systems.
plos-pone-0010149:
The authors were Xiaolin Luo, Qiurong Ding, Min Wang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study altered a signaling pathway in mouse airways. TGF-beta signaling helps keep airway lining tissue stable. It also plays a role in cancers arising from such lining tissue. Asthma research on it had focused mostly on immune cells.

By disrupting the pathway with a blocker protein called Smad7, the team eased allergic asthma. The same change, though, aggravated lung cancer development in the mice. That trade-off warns that asthma treatments touching this pathway need careful cancer watching.
plos-pone-0010249:
The authors were Christian Willberg, Keith Garrison, R. Brad Jones, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study followed immune responses in early HIV infection. One gene variant, HLA-B35-Px, is tied to rapid HIV progression. A close variant, HLA-B35-Py, lacks that bad record, and the contrast between them has long puzzled HIV researchers.

The team tracked killer T cell responses restricted by these variants over time. Rapidly progressing patients recognized vestigial epitopes, leftover viral targets of little use. That misdirected response may help explain why this variant offers such poor protection.
plos-pone-0010349:
Shubha Gopal, Daniela Berg, Nicole Hagen and others studied how Listeria bacteria eat sugars, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Listeria monocytogenes can cause severe food-borne illness. In soil, water, and the gut, these bacteria meet complex sugars such as maltose and maltodextrin. Using such foods takes special intake machinery. The team set out to find and test that machinery.

They showed the bacteria rely on a switchable transport system to pull these sugars inside. The system belongs to a large family of molecular pumps. It stays off when glucose, a simpler sugar, is present. That order of use is common in bacteria: eat the easy food first. Knowing the intake route may help predict where Listeria thrives.
plos-pone-0010449:
Johan Lundberg, Stefan Jonsson and Staffan Holmin developed a new way to exit blood vessels from inside, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reaching organs through vessels avoids big surgical cuts. Some organs, though, sit in spots surgery reaches poorly. The team proposed punching out through the vessel wall itself, under control, to reach tissue beyond. They built the tools and tested the method stepwise.

Testing moved from a simulator to rats, then rabbits, with full clinical-style integration. Each stage checked that the exit could be made and sealed safely. A working transvascular route could open treatments for hard-to-reach tumors or organs. It is an engineering-heavy study, unusual among biology papers. The goal is simple: turn blood vessels into doorways, not just roads.
plos-pone-0010549:
Jessica Jordão and colleagues used focused ultrasound to deliver antibodies into mouse brains and shrink Alzheimer's plaques in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antibody treatment for Alzheimer's relies on antibodies that clear toxic amyloid from the brain. Most injected antibody never crosses the blood-brain barrier. Earlier work injected it directly into the brain, which is impractical for patients. Guided ultrasound can open the barrier briefly at chosen spots.

With ultrasound targeting, blood-borne antibodies reached the brain and plaque load fell. The mice carried a strong Alzheimer's model mutation. Non-invasive delivery is the breakthrough this approach promises. Safety of repeated barrier opening remains the key question. Still, the study shows a path around a famous obstacle.
plos-pone-0010649:
Kim Appler and colleagues tracked West Nile virus in mice long after the first illness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most RNA virus infections clear within weeks. Reports in people hinted that West Nile virus, carried by mosquitoes, might not always leave.

The team searched the brain, spinal cord, and other organs over a long follow-up. Viral material persisted in the central nervous system and in some outside tissues. Lingering virus could help explain lasting symptoms some patients report after recovery. The mouse work gives doctors a model for studying those long tails of infection.
plos-pone-0010749:
Sheila McKenna and Peter Etnoyer surveyed stony corals on Saba Bank, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bank's reefs face damage from shipping, above all from anchors of tankers serving nearby oil terminals. Drawing zones that protect the richest reefs requires a map of what lives where.

The rapid survey recorded coral species and reef condition across the bank. Some areas held far richer and healthier coral growth than others. Those hotspots now stand out on the map. A baseline survey taken before zoning lets officials judge later whether the zones actually protect the corals they were drawn around.
plos-pone-0010849:
Robert Castellino, Benjamin Barwick, Matthew Schniederjan and co-authors published this mouse cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Medulloblastoma is a brain tumor of childhood, and two growth pathways, called PI-3 kinase and sonic hedgehog, are both known to feed it. The team crossed mice prone to these tumors through the hedgehog route with mice lacking one copy of Pten, a gene that normally restrains the other pathway.

Losing even one copy of Pten doubled the share of mice showing tumor symptoms and cut survival. Tumors in these mice showed stronger PI-3 kinase signaling and more blood vessel growth, while hedgehog-linked genes fell quieter. Castellino and colleagues show the two pathways do not simply add up; weakening one brake reshapes the whole tumor. That insight may help doctors match medulloblastoma treatments to a tumor's gene profile.
plos-pone-0010949:
Daniele Dell'Orco, Martin Lundqvist, Cecilia Oslakovic and co-authors published this nanoparticle study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The moment a nanoparticle enters blood, proteins coat it, forming a corona that decides what the body actually sees. That coat is not fixed: proteins arrive and leave until a stable mix settles, and predicting the mix matters for medical uses of nanoparticles.

The authors built a simple dynamic model that forecasts the corona's makeup over time from each protein's binding strength, capacity, and exchange rates. They applied it to human plasma proteins meeting polymer nanoparticles of a defined size, adding new measurements for one blood fat carrier. Dell'Orco and colleagues give designers a way to anticipate a particle's biological identity before animal testing, a step toward safer nanomedicines.
plos-pone-0011049:
Henning Zimmermann, Sebastian Seidler, Jacob Nattermann and co-authors published this liver study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Liver scarring, fibrosis, is driven by macrophages that arrive as blood monocytes after injury. Mouse work blamed the classical monocyte type, but humans also carry a non-classical type marked by CD16, and the authors suspected that overlooked population does the damage in people.

They analyzed blood monocyte subsets from more than two hundred patients with chronic liver disease and nearly as many healthy controls. The non-classical monocytes were elevated in patients and showed inflammatory and scar-promoting behavior relevant to disease progression. Zimmermann and colleagues shift the human story away from the mouse template. If this subset drives human fibrosis, it becomes a measurable marker and a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0011149:
Nakajima, Nishikawa, Iguchi and colleagues studied a reef coral in PLOS ONE in 2010. This coral releases spawn into the sea, so its young drift on currents. At the northern edge of its range, the team measured how genes flow between groups and how varied those groups are.

Their data map how connected these edge groups are to each other. Connection allows new genes to rescue a fading group, while isolation raises risk. Edge groups may also hold traits suited to cooler water. Protecting their links matters as seas warm and ranges shift, making this a guide for reef conservation.
plos-pone-0011249:
Howard and Merrifield mapped water dependent nature in California for PLOS ONE in 2010. Many wetlands, springs and riverside woods survive on groundwater rather than rain alone. The authors charted where such groundwater dependent ecosystems occur across the state.

Their map links hidden aquifers to visible wildlife habitat. When wells draw aquifers down, those habitats can dry out even far from the pumping site. Water rules that ignore this link can harm nature by accident. The map gives managers a starting point to protect both water supplies and the wild places that share them.
plos-pone-0011349:
Ann-Karin Olsen and colleagues examined in 2010 whether chemicals in the environment can leave marks in sperm that pass to the next generation. Damage to sperm DNA is linked to poor sperm quality and lost pregnancies, and some diseases in children begin as new mutations from the father. Earlier work by the group showed that rodent testis cells repair bulky DNA damage poorly.

The team tracked chemical tags stuck to DNA in mouse sperm and the rise of fresh mutations as sperm were being made. Their results connect exposure of the male germ line to changes that arise during sperm formation itself. That link matters for fathers as well as mothers. Safety testing that only watches the exposed animal may miss harm that surfaces in its offspring, so the paper argues for watching sperm directly.
plos-pone-0011449:
Jiaxing Zhang and co-authors used brain imaging in 2010 to watch how the brain changes as people adjust to high altitude. Moving to thin air starves the brain of oxygen, and newcomers suffer headaches and poor sleep before adapting over weeks. Whether the brain's very structure remodels during that adaptation, beyond short-term chemical shifts, was not well charted.

Scans taken as lowlanders acclimatized showed measurable structural changes in the brain over the adjustment period. The brain thus physically rebuilds part of itself under oxygen stress, not merely coping minute by minute. Documenting that remodeling helps explain altitude sickness and why some people adapt slowly. It also reveals a broader capacity of the adult brain to reshape its structure when the environment demands it, a hopeful sign for rehabilitation science.
plos-pone-0011549:
Kinga Gawlik and co-authors dissected in 2010 which parts of a muscle glue protein can substitute for a missing relative. Laminins glue muscle fibers to their surroundings, and loss of the alpha2 chain causes a severe congenital muscular dystrophy. A related chain, alpha1, can partly rescue the defect in mice, and the team tested which of its globular domains, its bead-like end sections, do the rescuing.

Different domains carried distinct roles in the rescue, with some sections essential and others dispensable. A domain-by-domain map tells protein engineers exactly which pieces a replacement therapy must include. That precision matters for designing shortened substitute proteins small enough to deliver as gene therapy. Children with this dystrophy have few options, so a parts list for a working patch is real progress toward a treatment.
plos-pone-0011649:
Sanne van Kampen and colleagues reported the view from national tuberculosis programmes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. New TB tests are approved at global level faster than countries can put them to work. The Stop TB Partnership needed first-hand information on how far national programmes had got with new diagnostic recommendations.

The authors gathered the programmes' own perspective on adopting new tools. Their account flags practical hurdles, from supply and training to funding, that slow adoption. Closing the gap between a recommended test and a test in routine use is essential if better diagnostics are to save lives.
plos-pone-0011749:
Patric Delhanty and co-authors studied an overlooked form of the hunger hormone ghrelin, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Unacylated ghrelin appears to improve insulin sensitivity and blood sugar control. How it acts is not fully understood, because no receptor for this form has been discovered.

Working in mice lacking the known ghrelin receptor, the team showed the unacylated form rapidly changes gene expression for fat making and insulin signalling in active tissues. Effects without the known receptor imply a second signalling route. Finding it could open new approaches to diabetes and weight control.
plos-pone-0011849:
Munyaradzi Dimairo and colleagues followed patients in Harare, Zimbabwe, for twelve months in a study published in 2010. The patients were suspected of having tuberculosis, but the standard sputum smear test came back negative. Such smear-negative cases have grown common where HIV is widespread, and they are hard for clinics to judge.

The cohort was tracked to measure how many of these suspects were later diagnosed with tuberculosis, and how long that took. Knowing the risk and the timing helps clinics decide how long to keep watching people whose first test misses the disease. In places with limited labs, that timing can decide who gets treatment early and who falls through the cracks.
plos-pone-0011949:
Nathanael McCurley and Ira Mellman compared in 2010 how different human dendritic cells digest what they capture. Dendritic cells present pieces of invaders to the immune system, and careful, limited digestion is their trademark: too much breakdown destroys the evidence. Mouse work had suggested their lysosomes carry unusually few cutting enzymes.

Measuring lysosomal proteolysis across human dendritic cell populations, the team found that cells derived from monocytes digest considerably more than the others. Human populations thus differ from each other, and from the mouse picture. Those differences matter for vaccine design, since the cell type chosen to carry a vaccine shapes how its cargo gets presented.
plos-pone-0012049:
Peter Skorupski and Lars Chittka charted in 2010, with care, the full range of light that the eyes of a bumblebee can catch. The bee kind they used has become a workhorse for tests of how bees see color, and for maze and choice tests that lean on bees telling one hue from the next. Oddly, the base data were not on hand: no one had set down how each of the bee's three eye cell types replies across the whole range of light.

Their tests now give those reply curves in full, from the far red end down into the deep violet rays that we cannot see at all. Choice tests in the lab are only as sound as these curves. With them, a lab can say at last what a bee sees when it picks a bloom, not what a human would guess it sees.
plos-pone-0012149:
Jialei Xie, Igor Vilchez, and Mariana Mateos studied a fruit fly, its tenant bacteria, and a parasitic wasp in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many insects carry bacteria passed down from mother to offspring. Some of these tenants are optional extras, neither clearly helpful nor required, which raises the question of how they persist in wild populations at all.

The fly's Spiroplasma bacteria turned out to protect their host when a parasitic wasp attacked. Wasps lay eggs inside fly larvae, and the bacteria improve the fly's odds of surviving that attack. A defense service like this explains why the bacteria spread: hosts that carry them leave more offspring where wasps hunt.
plos-pone-0012249:
Aniruddha Sengupta, Ulrike Lichti, Bradley Carlson, and co-authors studied selenium-related proteins in skin using mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Selenium in the diet protects skin against sun damage and cancer, and too little of it weakens the skin's antioxidant defenses; people lacking it can show skin and hair problems. The proteins that carry selenium do the actual work, yet their role in skin development was murky.

Removing those proteins in mice disturbed the skin cells' proper function and the skin's development itself. That proves the proteins are not optional extras but core equipment for skin. It also gives a biological basis for the skin troubles seen in selenium deficiency and in some inherited conditions.
plos-pone-0012349:
Ariel Pani, Holly Hobart, Colleen Morris and co-workers scanned the genomes of people with intellectual disability in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Learning disability affects a few in every hundred people, and known syndromes explain only part of the cases. The team focused on patients sent for testing with signs that hinted at Williams syndrome, a known genetic condition.

Using SNP chips that read many genome spots at once, they found rearrangements — missing, extra, or moved chunks of DNA — in several patients. Some changes matched known syndromes, while others were new. Each find gives a family a firmer answer and shows why broad genome scans help when single-gene tests come up empty.
plos-pone-0012449:
Ann Vanreusel, Annelies De Groote, Sabine Gollner and colleagues reviewed tiny worms living at deep-sea chemical sites, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Where methane seeps and hot vents leak chemicals, bacteria feed dense animal communities without sunlight. Free-living nematodes, the most abundant animals there, were the review's focus.

The authors ask whether the same nematode traits and species recur across such sites worldwide and what drives the patterns. Their synthesis shows both shared strategies and strong local differences. As mining companies eye deep-sea minerals, baseline knowledge of these fragile communities is the only way to judge what would be lost.
plos-pone-0012549:
Kelly Andrews, Greg Williams and Phillip Levin tracked sixgill sharks through seasons and life stages, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. How an animal moves decides where it feeds, mates, and meets threats, so movement data underpin conservation. Sixgill sharks are large, deep-living, and poorly known, yet they visit shallow bays where tagging is possible.

The team found movement patterns that shift with the seasons and as the sharks mature. Young and adult sharks use their habitat differently across the year. Such detail lets managers time protections, like seasonal closures, to when and where each life stage is most exposed.
plos-pone-0012649:
Kular, Gogliotti and Opal deleted a gene called Cpd-1 in mice and looked for effects on the brain. The gene's protein belongs to an old family involved in gene control, cell traffic and cell death. It shows up strongly in the developing nervous system, hinting at a brain role.

Their 2010 knockout mice showed only a mild nerve-related pattern, not the severe harm one might expect. A subtle result still teaches a lot, since it suggests backup systems cover for the missing gene. Such studies map which genes the brain truly cannot do without.
plos-pone-0012749:
Piekarski, Place and Zucker tested which hormone forms drive male sexual behaviour in Syrian hamsters. Testosterone runs this behaviour, yet its two main breakdown products each failed to do the job alone, even at high doses. Their 2010 study tried giving dihydrotestosterone and testosterone together.

The pair together restored full behaviour where each part alone fell short. Hormones often work as teams, and this case gives a clean example. The result refines how scientists read hormone replacement studies in other animals, including people.  Hamsters are a long-standing model for hormone and behaviour work.
plos-pone-0012849:
Mulrennan, Tempone, Ling and co-authors tested two standard tools against pneumonia from the 2009 pandemic flu. Early reports showed many pandemic H1N1 patients developed a viral pneumonia directly from the flu. Doctors needed a severity score they could trust and a reliable way to confirm the infection.

Their 2010 study found the CURB-65 severity score unreliable for this pneumonia, and nose-throat sampling likewise unreliable for diagnosis. Naming weak tools in a crisis is as useful as finding strong ones. Their results pushed clinicians toward better tests during that pandemic.
plos-pone-0319549:
Shruthi Venkataraman and colleagues used a national survey of over thirty-seven thousand American medical students. They asked how gender bias during training shapes a young doctor's growth. Students rated how often they were denied chances, insulted, or marked down because of gender. They also rated whether their school had raised them as people and as future doctors.

Women reported far more bias than men. About a third of women faced it, in single events or again and again. For men the share was about a tenth. Students of both sexes who faced repeat bias were much less likely to feel their school had fostered them. The cost showed in both personal and professional growth.
plos-pone-0329049:
Mary Elizabeth Snow and colleagues gathered lived accounts of forced psychiatric care under British Columbias Mental Health Act in Canada. Forced admissions have risen for fifteen years there. Focus groups heard twenty three people who had been held and treated against their will, led by facilitators with the same lived experience. Staff interviews added provider views.

Seven themes emerged. Voluntary options were scarce before crisis hit. Poverty, housing strain, and other social pressures deepened crises. Proof that forced care helps stayed thin in participants eyes, while harms touched patients and staff alike. Peer support stood out as a bright spot. Reform should grow voluntary, community care upstream, the authors argue, so force becomes rarer.
plos-pone-0333649:
Jose Manuel Burgos-Bragado and his team set out a plan for a trial in bowel cancer care. The trial tests work-out help sent by screen, with no live calls. Folk set for bowel surgery oft face a hard road back. Fit work pre and post surgery helps, but trips to a gym can block it. The screen route is meant to clear that block.

Fifty-six folk will be split in two groups by lot. One gets the screen plan: two weeks of work pre surgery, then four weeks post. The rest get the old book of tips. Walk tests lead the checks, with strength, sleep, mood, and life scores in tow. This is a plan, not a set of results.
plos-pone-0336549:
Bahari Yusuf and a team in northern Uganda followed newborns with birth asphyxia in 2026, watching their blood salts. Babies deprived of oxygen around birth often develop off-balance sodium, potassium, or calcium, which can worsen brain injury.

Term babies admitted to Lira hospital had blood tests on arrival and again over two weeks if they stayed. The team recorded mother and birth details, then modelled what predicts imbalance and how babies fared early. Such local figures help small hospitals, where lab tests are scarce, decide which asphyxiated babies need the closest chemical monitoring.
plos-pone-0336749:
Marco Alderighi and co-authors built an artificial intelligence system to predict tourist traffic in Italy's Aosta Valley. Their 2026 paper draws on more than forty-one million vehicle passages recorded at fourteen road sensors, combined with weather data and calendar information. The goal was forecasts that stay accurate when seasons change or sudden events disrupt travel.

The system blends four different prediction methods and constantly reweights them according to recent performance, season, and weather. In tests it beat every single method on its own, cutting average errors by roughly a quarter and holding up well through seasonal swings and extreme weather. Valley managers could use such forecasts to plan staffing, ease congestion, and size tourism facilities.
plos-pone-0339549:
Janet Kobusinge Lubega and colleagues tracked a warning sign in HIV care: virus levels too low to count as failure, yet high enough to hint that treatment may be slipping. Their 2026 PLOS One paper covers Ugandan children and teenagers from 2014 to 2023, using close to a million routine viral load tests.

The share of tests in this low range climbed from about one in ten to about one in six over the decade. The rise appeared in boys and girls alike and was steepest among infants. The authors say watching this signal closely could help clinics act before full treatment failure sets in.
plos-pone-0339949:
Md Khobair Hossain led a team of eight authors on this 2026 interview study inside a clean cookstove trial in Bangladesh. Families in the trial received liquefied gas stoves, and researchers interviewed mothers, husbands, and mothers-in-law about how childcare and housework shifted. The original trial targeted smoke exposure, not family routines.

Gas cooking cut cooking time and workload, freeing mothers to feed, play with, and watch their infants more closely and to juggle tasks with less strain. Hossain calls these spillover gains real but in need of measurement in future quantitative studies.
plos-pone-0340749:
Jonathan Mokhtar and colleagues reviewed nearly six hundred confirmed skin melanoma cases from a specialist lab in the United Arab Emirates from 2017 to 2025. The sunny, multi ethnic Emirates had little published melanoma data. Records covered ancestry, body site, subtype, depth, and invasion signs, with models hunting predictors of thick, dangerous tumours.

People of European ancestry made up nearly three quarters of cases. The spreading surface subtype led, and just under half of tumours were thin. Men grew thicker tumours than women and favoured the trunk, while women favoured legs. A nodular subtype overwhelmingly predicted thick tumours. Sun safety campaigns should target fair skinned residents and men most.
plos-pone-0342949: Chandroth and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on guarding smart home gadgets from hackers. Their system blends a deep neural network with a memory-based model to spot intrusions on consumer device networks. A search method named ACO tunes the system. As homes fill with connected devices, guards that catch attacks early without slowing gadgets down are in demand.
plos-pone-0343349:
Lwanga Nanziri and colleagues examine in 2026 whether phone based money improves life for women and young people in Mozambique. They used a large household survey from a fragile, post conflict country hit by climate shocks. Careful statistical methods tried to separate the effect of the service from who chooses to use it.

Active use, not simply holding an account, drove the gains. Households relied less on growing their own food, smoothed spending, and put more into schooling and health, often through money sent by others. Women gained more say over money. The authors caution that one key assumption behind their method cannot be fully tested.
plos-pone-0344449:
Abdullah Al Rakib and co-authors surveyed people in Bangladesh to ask why antibiotics so often fail against the germs they once killed. Their study links survey answers from more than two hundred and fifty respondents using a statistical model. The model tests how money pressure, weak testing, and mistaken beliefs about medicine connect with overuse of the drugs.

Money incentives, uncertain diagnoses, thin health services, and local beliefs all pushed people toward using antibiotics too freely. The authors argue that fixing the problem takes more than new drugs. They call for better testing tools, rules that curb needless prescribing, and public campaigns that correct common misunderstandings about when antibiotics actually help.
plos-pone-0344649:
Bennett H. Price and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on whether boat noise hushes the spawning choruses of red drum, a prized estuary fish in Saint Andrew Bay, Florida. Male red drum drum together at dusk in spawning season, and those choruses may guide reproduction. Underwater recorders listened across two seasons while the team modeled chorus loudness against vessel noise and weather.

In the first year, louder boat noise went with measurably quieter choruses, and earlier noise predicted reduced calling too, a pattern repeating in year two. At times the chorus dipped below its level just before a boat passed, suggesting fish quieted or left. During peak spawning months, vessel noise appeared in nearly a third of recordings, and on some dates in every single one. Chronic traffic noise, they warn, could be interfering with a behavior these fish need to reproduce.
plos-pone-0345449:
Sujesh Sudarsan, Jonas Van Caeneghem, Ramesh Vinayagam, and Raja Selvaraj turned almond peel waste into a sunlight-powered cleaner for dye-polluted water. Using peel extract as the only helper chemical, they grew flower-shaped zinc oxide particles at low temperature. The 2026 study characterised the material thoroughly, confirming pure crystals built from radiating rods, with a porous texture and a plant-derived coating.

Under natural sunlight the particles destroyed up to about eighty-two percent of a stubborn red dye in four and a half hours, driven mainly by superoxide radicals. After four reuse cycles they kept most of their power. The authors present the route as cheap valorisation of an agricultural residue.
plos-pone-0345549:
Bo Li, Wei Zhou, and Haijun Li built a hybrid AI model for medical scans. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The model outlines organs so doctors can plan treatment. One model family reads fine detail but sees little of the whole scan. Another sees the whole scan but costs heavy computing power.

The new design runs both paths side by side. A fusion step weighs fine detail against broad shape at several scales. On two public scan sets, the model matched expert outlines closely. One set held many organs. The other held the aorta and its branches. Tools like this could cut the long hand-drawing work in hospitals.
plos-pone-0345749:
Aya Atomi and colleagues present a 2026 PLOS ONE study of an exercise program done entirely lying on one's back. The program links steady control of the trunk with smooth, coordinated leg movements. The researchers tested it on healthy young adults because keeping the head, chest, and pelvis lined up is central to standing balance.

In one trial, seventeen men did the program ten minutes a day for two weeks, and a second study followed twenty-two adults with motion tracking during a side-step test. Standing balance, side-step movement, and seated trunk bending improved, while strength and power tests did not change. The authors suggest the safe, low-load routine could aid fall prevention and early rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0346949:
Fengjiao Han, Haiyang Guo, and Yang Zheng study air pollution's effect on people already carrying tangled heart, kidney, and metabolic risk. Their 2026 prospective cohort follows such patients at early disease stages. Five common pollutants were tracked: three sizes of airborne particles, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone. Heart disease outcomes were modelled against exposure, singly and as mixtures. Several statistical engines cross-checked the mixture results.

Single pollutants told a consistent story. Each step up in particle or nitrogen dioxide exposure raised heart disease risk by roughly a third to a half. Ozone alone showed no clear link. Mixture analyses weighed the pollutants together, apportioning blame among them. Lag checks guarded against reverse causation. These patients sit at a dangerous crossroads where hearts, kidneys, and metabolism all strain. Showing that the air they breathe pushes them toward heart disease strengthens the case for protecting this group first when pollution spikes.
plos-pone-0347349:
Frederick Daenen and colleagues interviewed people around Belgium's earliest-stage cancer drug trials: sixteen patients, five family caregivers, and dozens of doctors, nurses, and specialists. Patients in these trials have advanced cancer and slim prospects, yet palliative care, which focuses on comfort and quality of life, is rarely built into the trials. The 2026 study asked why.

Patients mostly prized the trial as a last chance that gave hope and routine. Comfort care, though, arrived late and reactively, if at all. Many confused palliative care with giving up, and trial teams and outside doctors barely communicated. Participants suggested making comfort conversations a normal, flexible part of trial care from the start.
plos-pone-0347549:
Jina Kim and co-workers read the full genome of a newly found freshwater bacterium from Korea and test what it can do. The microbe belongs to a versatile family known for useful chemistry. Their 2026 study assembles its single chromosome completely, proves it is a distinct species, and screens both its genes and its living behavior for valuable traits.

The strain fought other microbes, made compounds that grab iron, and broke down sugars with a wide enzyme kit. It also carried an unusual cluster for using urea and showed early signs tied to anti-obesity and antiviral effects. Lab-grown tests must still confirm much of this promise. Even so, the strain joins the shelf of microbes biotech firms may draw on.
plos-pone-0347649:
Kevin Siebels and his team mapped COVID-19 in the streets of Toronto. They split the spread into three waves, from late 2020 to late 2021. For each wave they asked which traits of a place drove case counts. The traits ran from pay and school years to home size and first tongue. Shots were weighed too.

The drivers changed from wave to wave. Rules on crowds, shop stops, and work from home hit groups in unlike ways. Low pay and low school years kept the worst risk in all waves. The team backs watch systems that track social facts with case counts.
plos-pone-0347749:
Rebecca G Evey and colleagues read the life stories of seven Rice's whales, the rarest baleen whales on Earth, written in their own baleen. Fewer than fifty adults of this Gulf of Mexico species remain. Baleen, the filtering curtain in the mouth, grows steadily and traps hormones as it grows, so drilling along a plate yields a timeline of stress and reproduction hormones spanning years.

Every assay worked on the species for the first time. Two whales thought to have starved showed all four measured hormones surging in their final growth, a pattern seen in other whales after long illness or injury. A female with a known recent pregnancy carried a long stretch of raised pregnancy hormone, proving the method can spot pregnancies. Male yearly cycles, by contrast, left no clear trace.
plos-pone-0347949:
Mariam Komeili, Jessi Robinson, and Hannah Akrigg set out in 2026 a plan for mapping Canadian writing on fair and safe speech language care. Their protocol covers work with Indigenous peoples and with other groups that face unfair treatment. Earlier reviews, they note, often mixed this field with other rehab fields or covered only one age group.

The planned search will cover both journal and grey sources across the whole lifespan. A scale running from basic awareness to full safety will guide how findings are sorted. The aim is a clear map of current practice claims and gaps, to guide teaching and future study.
plos-pone-0348349:
Emrah Altun, Fulya Gezer, and Hana Alqifari extend a classic income distribution model, the generalized gamma. Their version can deliver the standard inequality measures economists rely on: the Gini coefficient and the Theil, Atkinson, and Pietra indexes. Real income data often arrive grouped into brackets, so they estimate the model's parameters with a distance method suited to grouped data and check it in simulations.

They apply the machinery to United States income data from three different years, showing how inequality readings move. To make the method usable, they built a free web tool that computes the measures and draws the graphs for any practitioner. Good inequality numbers underpin tax and welfare debates, so lowering the technical barrier matters.
plos-pone-0348949:
Einat Sandbank and co-workers survey fish and tiny drifting animals across the Polar Front in the Barents Sea, where cold and warmer waters meet. Fronts often gather life, but the Arctic changes fast with the seasons. Their 2026 study pairs continuous sound and water recordings with net samples in spring, summer, and winter.

The front's grip on life proved strongest in spring. Fish and their tiny prey often peaked at opposite ends of the survey lines, and in spring the prey gained a refuge from grazing fish. Melting and forming sea ice also shaped where species gathered. Water temperature was the best single predictor of biomass, so a front famous for richness does not stay rich all year.
plos-pone-0349249:
Sajjan Kumar, Pankaj Kumar, and co-authors tackled a balancing act faced by solar power plants tied to the electricity grid. Plants usually chase maximum power, but the grid also needs spare capacity held back to absorb sudden swings. Their 2026 study proposes a controller that watches both sunlight and grid conditions, then decides how much reserve to keep moment by moment.

The controller blends flexible tracking with maximum-power tracking so the plant can switch smoothly between holding reserve and producing fully. Tests in both simulation and real hardware showed it reacting to live frequency changes while keeping output clean. Electrical distortion fell by more than half against one standard approach. The authors argue such dynamic control helps solar farms support, rather than strain, grid stability.
plos-pone-0349749:
Yuhui Gong and colleagues combined single cell and bulk gene data from glioma, an invasive brain tumour, to build a three gene outlook signature. Survival models with shrinkage selection landed on three genes tied to malignant behaviour. The score was checked in two large patient cohorts from the United States and China and explored for drug response and immune cell links.

The signature sorted patients by outlook in both cohorts. One gene, studied in depth, tracked with more suppressive immune cells and killer T cells alike in tumours, and its partners sit largely on immune and tumour cells. A compact gene score could sharpen prognosis talk and point to new drug targets in a cancer short on both.
plos-pone-0349949:
Annie O’Brien and co-authors re-examined a school social and emotional learning trial in 2026 through a multiverse lens. The question was whether pupils who actually take part benefit, an answer that depends heavily on how taking part is defined.

The original cluster trial covered sixty-two schools and more than two thousand children. The team pre-registered ten plausible model versions, varying five definitions of compliance and two cut-offs. Relational outcomes like bullying and peer support were then read across all versions. Showing every reasonable answer, rather than one chosen analysis, exposes how fragile or firm the intervention's claims really are.
plos-pone-0350049:
HPV testing usually needs a clinic pelvic sample. Many women avoid that exam. Self-sampling could widen screening dramatically. Nigus Telele and colleagues compared two self-collected options. One was a vaginal swab. The other was first-morning urine. Participants were girls and women aged fifteen to twenty-five.

About seven hundred fifty participants joined across three countries. They lived in Bangladesh, Nepal, and Pakistan. Each woman provided both sample types. One laboratory method tested every sample. Shared protocols kept the steps identical. The team measured detection rates and type-by-type agreement. The work feeds a wider project on HPV burden in poorer countries.
plos-pone-0350149:
Maad S Ytemi and A El-Shabasy led a field guide to five plant species in Saudi Arabia. The plants belong to a dry-land group called Commicarpus. They grow mostly in the west and southwest of the country. The species look much alike, so naming them takes care. The team compared stems, leaves, blooms, and fruits. They also sliced plant parts for study under the microscope.

Leaf and stem traits split the species well. The stalk that holds each leaf proved most useful of all. Pollen grains also differed in size, shape, and surface marks. Three species bear very large grains. The team built two keys for naming the plants. One key uses traits seen by eye. The other uses stalk anatomy.
plos-pone-0350549:
Valeria Caragli and co-authors compared doctors with ChatGPT on treatment choices for sudden hearing loss in 2026. The condition, a rapid loss of hearing without clear cause, demands quick decisions, often including steroids, and artificial intelligence advice is untested there.

Records of eighty-six patients were stripped of names and given to the model through staged prompts mimicking team discussion. Its suggestions were then scored against the treating doctors' actual choices. Agreement measures showed where the model matched human judgment and where it strayed. The study treats the tool as a junior colleague to be audited, not an authority.
plos-pone-0350749:
Borbála Német and colleagues validated a Hungarian version of the Skindex-Mini, a three-question tool that gauges how much a skin disease burdens daily life. Dermatologists need fast measures, and this one had only been tested in English and Spanish. Five hundred seventy-eight patients with a range of skin conditions filled it in alongside longer, established questionnaires on life quality, emotion control, and stigma.

The three questions hung together as one scale, sorted patients sharply, and behaved the same across different patient groups. Scores lined up moderately with stigma and distress, and stayed properly separate from general well-being. With reliability and validity in order, Hungarian clinics gain a one-minute screen for skin-related suffering, quick enough for busy visits and useful for flagging who needs a longer conversation about coping.
plos-pone-0351149:
Lu Xing and Xueqi Wu surveyed just under five hundred student preschool teachers in China during internships in spring 2024. Many early childhood graduates hesitate to enter the field, which threatens workforce supply. The survey asked whether feeling matched with a kindergartens values and needs linked with internship satisfaction, and whether confidence and felt skill carried that link.

Fit linked positively with satisfaction, confidence, and felt competence. Confidence and competence each carried part of the fit to satisfaction link, and a chain ran from fit through confidence to competence to satisfaction. Universities and kindergartens should match values early and build skills step by step, the authors argue, to keep interns in the profession.
plos-pone-0351249:
Zilu Shang, Yu Li, Yun Zhang, and Yajuan Gong trace one chain of events behind pain after surgery. Their rat study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Pain following an operation is a very common complaint. The team used a standard model. A small cut is made in a rat's paw. Then they followed an inflammatory signal called TNF-alpha. It travels into the cluster of nerve cells serving the paw.

The signal switches on a controller protein. That protein raises production of a sodium channel. The channel makes pain fibres easier to trigger. Blocking this chain appeals to drug hunters. A medicine could quiet the exact channel surgery leaves overactive. It would not need to dull the whole nervous system.
plos-pone-0351549:
Rating how good a photo looks, without a clean original to compare it with, is the problem Yanru Jia and Longsheng Wei take on in this 2026 PLOS One paper. Phone cameras and sharing apps need such automatic scores, but blur, noise, and compression each damage pictures in different ways.

Their method first trains a vision network that adjusts itself, then arranges sample images in a graph linking damage type, damage level, and picture content. On four public test collections the scores lined up with human judgments better than older hand-built and deep learning methods. Tests removing one part at a time showed each piece added accuracy.
plos-pone-0351649:
Shymaa Damfo and six colleagues combine case records with virus genomics to profile dengue fever in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Dengue has circulated in the country's west since the nineteen nineties, spread by mosquitoes and swollen by pilgrimage traffic, yet its local molecular picture was missing. The team reviewed confirmed cases from the first ten months of 2024 — citizens, residents, and religious visitors alike — and sequenced the genome of the commonest virus type.

Family trees built from the sequence place the Jeddah virus among its regional relatives and catalogue its mutations. Knowing exactly which strain circulates, and how it is changing, is groundwork for any future vaccine or antiviral aimed at this population.
plos-pone-0351749:
Heavy bleeding after childbirth kills mothers worldwide, and quick, skilled action saves lives. María Jose Montiel Bravo and co-authors present a plan, published in PLOS One in 2026, for reviewing whether virtual and augmented reality training helps health workers learn to manage this emergency.

As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. It sets out which databases will be searched, which study designs count, and how bias will be judged with standard checklists. Two reviewers will screen studies on their own, with a third settling disagreements. The finished review aims to show whether immersive practice truly improves learning.
plos-pone-0351849:
Biao Wang and six colleagues build a prognostic model for glioblastoma around a new chemical tag on proteins. Their 2026 study concerns lactylation, a modification driven by lactate. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive brain tumour, with grim survival. The team merged single-cell and bulk gene data from public cohorts. Nine major cell types appeared in the tumours. One macrophage group scored highest for lactate metabolism genes. Machine learning then distilled the signal into a risk model.

Three key genes anchor the model, including one called CD93. High and low risk groups differed in immune cell infiltration and predicted drug sensitivity. The team validated CD93's behaviour in laboratory cells. Such a model could help doctors sort patients by likely course. It also spotlights lactylation as biology worth drugging. For a cancer where prognosis guides hard choices about aggressive treatment, even modest prediction gains matter to patients and families.
plos-pone-0351949:
Thong Duc Hong and colleagues used engine simulation software to find the best ignition timing for a diesel engine burning diesel-methanol blends. Methanol mixes change how the charge burns, so the spark of combustion must shift with blend, load, and burn speed. Their single-cylinder model, checked against real engine data within a few percent, swept blends up to half methanol across three loads.

For each condition they located the timing that maximized power and the timing that minimized fuel use per unit of work, then fit formulas tying those optima to the inputs. Burn duration ruled the answer, blend came second, and load mattered least, and the relationships were simple straight lines.
