Engine calibrators get usable equations rather than a lookup table, ready for controllers that must retime an engine as its fuel changes.
plos-pone-0352149:
Rahil Mirabi Moghaddam and four colleagues feed honey bees a special diet. It mixes helpful bacteria with the fibre that feeds them. The question was whether diet can armour bees against heat and cold. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Newly emerged workers ate the supplement for three weeks. Conditions stayed comfortable during that time. Then the bees faced cold, cool, ideal, or hot settings. Survival and antioxidant enzymes were tracked.

Bees on the highest dose survived thermal stress best. They beat lightly dosed and unsupplemented bees clearly. In unsupplemented bees, stress drove antioxidant enzymes sharply up. That is a sign of strain. Supplemented bees stayed calmer, in step with the dose. Their gut microbes were richer too. For beekeepers facing erratic weather, feed may be a cheap defence.
plos-pone-0352249:
Jean-Luc Jung and colleagues carry out in 2026 the first water DNA survey of marine vertebrates in the city waters of Abu Dhabi. The Arabian Gulf is shallow, very hot in summer, and salty, putting sea life near its limits while city activity adds pressure. Water samples from a marina, a new development, a seagrass bed, and a protected mangrove were screened for DNA traces.

More than eighty kinds were detected, mostly bony fish, plus birds, rays or sharks, and one marine mammal. Kind counts were alike across sites, but family tree diversity lagged at the new development and matched richness best at the mangrove. The method supports long term watching.
plos-pone-0352349:
Adrián Díaz-Faes, Pablo D'Este, and Anne Ter Wal study how scientists use their contacts while doing research. Their 2026 paper draws on detailed data from biomedical researchers. Two habits are contrasted. Some scientists hedge, asking several people about the same need. Others compartmentalise, turning to one specialist per need. Networks rich in diversity and gaps were already known to help. This study asks how people actually work those networks.

Hedging paid off. Scientists who consulted multiple contacts for the same resource more often produced high-impact work. The advantage held beyond the benefits of a diverse or sparse network. Under uncertainty, a second opinion is not indecision. It is insurance against one contact's blind spots, delays, or failure. The findings speak to research managers too. Cultures that normalise wide consultation may quietly raise the impact of the science they host.
plos-pone-0352449:
Melina Eitzel and three colleagues use volunteer observations to test whether California's marine parks change human behaviour. Their 2026 study draws on MPA Watch, a programme where trained surveyors record coastal activities. Twelve groups agreed the protocol across the state. From 2012 to 2020, nearly nineteen hundred surveyors logged over thirty-one thousand surveys. They counted more than a million actions at one hundred four sites, inside parks and outside them.

Fishing-type actions told the key story. Consumptive uses ran significantly lower inside the strictest parks than outside. Non-consumptive recreation, like beachgoing and tidepooling, showed no difference. The models corrected for weather, tides, timing, and beach features, and for the biases volunteers bring. Protection, in other words, is not just lines on a map. Ordinary people, watching systematically for eight years, documented that the rules change what visitors actually do.
plos-pone-0352649:
Rodrigues and colleagues showed how an HIV protein weakens the cell's virus alarm system in a 2026 study. The alarm pathway switches on antiviral genes when interferon signals danger. The viral protein, present early in infection and found in patients' blood, was tested in a T-cell line that makes it steadily.

Cells making the viral protein lost a key alarm messenger, which the protein sent for destruction by the cell's recycling machinery. With that messenger gone, interferon could not fully switch on its defenses. The finding helps explain why interferon treatment works poorly against this virus. Blocking the viral protein's trick could restore a natural defense line.
plos-pone-0353349:
Hongliang Sun and three colleagues optimise a factory wireless network. Part of it talks through light. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Ceiling lamps carry the light signals. A radio link backs them up. Several devices share one channel by power layering. Data travel in short packets to keep delay low. The design targets industrial machines. Such machines cannot wait, and cannot fail.

The team derived each user's odds of successful delivery. They defined the service capacity of each channel. Then they built an algorithm. It tunes packet length and power together. The aim is maximum capacity under strict reliability limits. In simulations the hybrid beat light-only schemes. It also beat simpler sharing schemes, especially with short packets.
plos-pone-0353849:
Ravikumar Chinthaginjala and co-authors present in 2026 a layered learning system for predicting how long people live in countries worldwide. Training used tens of thousands of country year records and many health indicators from the World Health Organization. The design stacks several models, adds an explanation method, and adjusts its own error ranges so stated confidence matches real coverage.

On held back test data the system predicted life expectancy within about a year on average, and its confidence bands hit their target closely. Most of the explanatory weight came from population and structural factors rather than single diseases. Planners could use such forecasts to guide health spending with clearer uncertainty.
plos-pone-0353949:
Tamar Zurashvili and five colleagues convene patients and providers in Georgia. Their task was to pick a support tool. It should help people with HIV decide whether to share their status. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Telling family, partners, or employers can bring support. It can also bring stigma. No decision aid existed for the Georgian setting. A structured consensus method worked through nine options. The group met in separate sessions, then a joint one.

Providers favoured digital tools for their reach. Patients favoured face-to-face sessions. They stressed trust and peer involvement. The joint session settled on a blend of both. Local content on law, treatment, and support will be added. Adaptation and pilot testing come next.
plos-pone-0354049:
Qiuyuan Peng, Minglin Wu, and Qiang Feng published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their subject is the sport industry in China between 2018 and 2024. The authors track how work and money shifted toward services inside that industry, and how much value each part of it produced.

Working as a longitudinal accounting analysis, the study follows the same industry accounts across seven years so changes can be compared over time. It looks at where jobs and spending moved as service activities grew, and at how strongly different segments added value. Readers in sport management and economic policy get a year-by-year picture of an industry reorganizing itself around services rather than goods.
plos-pone-0354149:
Yoon and colleagues, in a 2026 study, build a small device that measures radiation dose inside the rectum during prostate cancer treatment. Modern treatment gives radiation in fewer, larger doses, guided by MRI scans, so checking the real dose delivered near the rectum matters for safety. Their device pairs a radiation-sensitive plastic layer with a marker that shows up on MRI, held by an applicator made in five sizes.

One rubber-like material won as the clearest MRI marker. The sensing layer darkens in proportion to dose, its reading settles by two hours after treatment, and its uncertainty was small at clinical doses. In two patients, measured doses ran somewhat higher than the planning computer predicted, by a few percent on average. The authors blame placement wobble in zones where dose changes fast. They present the device as a workable in-body check for MRI-guided treatment.
plos-pone-0354249:
Mohammed Kanani and Ronald Kwon build in 2026 fully automatic tools for measuring body size and shape in adult zebrafish from three dimensional scans. Zebrafish are a major model for bone, muscle, and growth research, but measuring lean volume, body slimness, swim bladder parts, and standard length by hand is slow and varies between observers. Their methods combine built in functions of free image software.

Automatic measures matched hand and partly automatic measures well, while greatly raising speed and removing observer differences. The tools are released as ready macros for a popular image program. Labs can now gather body measures from many fish with far less labour.
plos-pone-0354749:
Kleber Resende Silva and colleagues dissected a small Amazonian plant that lives only on the ironstone outcrops of Carajás, Brazil, to learn how its body survives sun-blasted, drought-prone rock. Their 2026 anatomical study compared wild plants of this threatened species against greenhouse-grown specimens, tracking stems, leaves, and cell structure across wet and dry seasons.

Wild plants were armored: stiff, secondarily thickened stems, thick leaf blades, and mucilage cells riding the veins, none of which the pampered greenhouse plants developed. Dry season leaves lignified their bundles to hold even dying leaves up, and the species barely tolerated cultivation at all. Conservation, the authors conclude, means protecting the outcrops themselves, since the plant's adaptations are inseparable from its harsh home.
plos-pone-0355549:
Hannes Junker and Clara T Schoeder benchmarked the artificial intelligence tools now used to invent new peptide drugs for G protein-coupled receptors, the cell-surface switches targeted by a large share of medicines. Their 2026 two-part study first asked three structure predictors to reproduce ninety-one known receptor and peptide pairings, then asked three generative tools to design fresh peptides from scratch.

The sobering result: predictors often reported high confidence for peptides placed in the wrong position, and some outputs showed signs of memorizing known examples rather than inventing. Generators explored shapes well but wrote weak amino acid sequences, partly fixable with a separate sequence tool. The benchmark gives drug designers a realistic map of where these pipelines can and cannot yet be trusted.
plos-pone-0355649:
Yanjun Liu, Zanfu Ma, and Hao Zhan propose in 2026 a new way to read efficiency scores used to compare units such as cities or firms. Standard scores mix two things: how much a unit makes and how its inputs and outputs are valued by weights the method itself picks. Their work pulls those two strands apart.

Using a peer appraisal table, they build one index for amount related gaps and another for value related gaps. Tests on data from Chinese cities show how changing the assumed technology reshapes both parts. The point is insight into why scores differ, not a fresh ranking method.
plos-pone-0355749:
Yi Yang and colleagues worked alongside caregivers in China who raise autistic children, designing an education programme shaped by the caregivers themselves. Such programmes help families, yet little was known about what Chinese caregivers actually want from them. Their 2026 study ran two focus groups with fourteen caregivers, then showed the group draft videos for comment.

Analysis produced three themes about content and two about delivery. Caregivers asked for practical, everyday guidance and for formats that fit busy family life. The authors' central point is procedural: programme makers should keep asking intended users for input at every stage, not just at the start. The resulting design process itself is offered as a model for community-engaged work.
plos-pone-0355849:
Yang Geng, Jaap van Dieën, and Sjoerd Bruijn compared in 2026 how people keep their balance while standing and while walking. At first glance the two tasks look like versions of one skill, yet their study argues the body stabilizes them through different mechanisms. Standing balance leans on correcting sway in place, while walking balance is woven into the pattern of steps themselves.

Beneath those different tools, the authors find a shared aim at the level of the whole task: keeping the body upright and moving safely. The distinction matters for fall prevention and rehabilitation, since training that improves standing still may not transfer to walking. Their analysis gives therapists a cleaner picture of what to train for each.
plos-pone-0356149:
Hao Dun, Maura Sticco-Ivins, Gianni Bonnici, Hannah Beatty, and Benjamin Kopecky wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It presents a surgical technique for transplanting the aorta in mice. Their method uses a single aortotomy, one opening cut in the aorta, in an end-to-side connection.

Mouse aortic transplants are a standard model for studying vessel disease and rejection, but the surgery is delicate and slow. A simpler technique can make experiments more consistent between surgeons and labs. Cardiovascular researchers who run transplant models in mice are the readers who would adopt or test this shortcut.
plos-pone-0356249:
David J. Varricchio and Heath R. Caldwell published a 2026 paleontology paper in PLOS ONE describing the pelvis and hindlimbs of a troodontid dinosaur from the late Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Montana. Troodontids, small feathered relatives of birds, are usually known from scraps, so a growth series from embryo to adult is rare. The Flagg Butte material gives an almost full picture of this stretch of the skeleton for the animal they assign, following recent proposals, to Troodon formosus.

Bone shape stayed remarkably consistent across growth: most adult landmarks appear in the young, the real changes being robustness, fusion, and surface texture at predictable stages. Many foot bones showed pathology, a recurring oddity in troodontid samples the authors document rather than hide. Because growth changes so little anatomy, immature specimens elsewhere can be judged taxonomically with more confidence, strengthening study of large North American troodontids.
plos-pone-0356549:
Sydney F. Hope and coauthors published a 2026 animal cognition study in PLOS ONE testing whether Asian elephants can control an impulse, a basic executive skill. Sixteen elephants at Thailand's National Elephant Institute learned to reach around an opaque box to take food from a side opening. Then came a transparent box with tempting front holes, where success meant ignoring visible food straight ahead and reaching around, as before.

The elephants detoured around the see-through box about as well as the opaque one. That may show strong self-control, or the see-through cues may simply have been too weak to tempt them, and the authors hold both readings open. When the box flipped so the learned direction was wrong, hesitation jumped, proof a real habit had to be overridden, and performance recovered quickly across trials. Elephants now join the comparative map of how inhibition evolves.
plos-pone-0357049:
Mariam Adam Al-Hassan, Jodie Bigalky, and Solina Richter set out a protocol, published in 2026. It will map what helps or hinders pregnant women with dangerous blood pressure disorders. The focus is getting care in poorer countries. These disorders are leading killers of mothers and babies. Delays in seeking help are often the difference between a managed case and an emergency.

The team follows established scoping review methods. It has completed searching and screening the literature. It is now extracting findings on barriers and facilitators. These range from cost and distance to beliefs and clinic failures. No results are reported yet. The finished map is meant to show governments and clinics where the path to care breaks down. Fixes can then target the real obstacles.
plos-pone-0358049:
Yi He published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on spotting deepfakes, manipulated images and videos that fool viewers, without needing labeled fakes for training. Most detectors learn from collections of marked forgeries and still miss subtle edits. He's framework, SDDA, trains itself instead, comparing each image in two domains at once: its ordinary appearance and its frequency pattern, which records fine repeating detail.

Two encoders extract features from both views and an alignment step forces them to agree, while four custom measures flag inconsistencies in the learned features. A contrastive objective sharpens the separation between normal and odd patterns, and the author reports the system stayed robust under compression and lighting changes that often defeat detectors. In the reported experiments it beat leading baselines, especially on manipulation types it had never seen. The design aims at an interpretable detector that does not depend on huge labeled fake collections.
plos-pone-0358349:
Bahetibieke Tuohetaerbaike and colleagues charted in 2026 the course of tuberculosis across China and its Central Asian neighbors, looking back to 1990 and forward to 2050. Tuberculosis remains one of the world's great infectious killers, and this region carries a heavy and uneven share of it. The team analyzed trends in the disease burden across more than three decades of data.

They also weigh the drivers behind the trends and project where the burden is heading by mid century under current patterns. Projections like these let health ministries see whether control programs are on pace and where drug resistant disease threatens progress. The regional view matters because tuberculosis crosses the borders that the region's people cross daily.
plos-pone-0358449:
Monika Talarowska-Dublicka, Aleksandra Gapińska, and Maria Finogenow studied the roots of loneliness in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They linked primal emotional systems, the deep drives wired into the brain long before language, to the modern sense of loneliness. Between the two sit early maladaptive schemas, lasting patterns formed in childhood.

The team's model traces how deep emotional wiring can harden into adult isolation through those schemas. That chain suggests where therapy might intervene: not only on lonely behavior, but on the schemas carrying the effect. Loneliness is now treated as a health risk in its own right. Work that maps its inner route gives counselors more than sympathy to offer; it gives them points of leverage.
plos-pone-0358549:
Shengxiang Ma and Wei Jiang published a safety study on subway operations in PLOS ONE in 2026. Subway crashes and failures rarely have a single cause; one fault can trigger the next in a chain. The authors set out to find which risk factors sit at the center of those chains.

Ma and Jiang combined real accident data with network analysis, treating each factor as a node linked to others. The factors with the most and strongest links are the ones worth fixing first, since they feed many kinds of failure. For transit operators, that ranking turns a long list of worries into a short list of priorities for training, checks, and design changes.
plos-pone-0358749:
Lin Qin and four colleagues test a waste based recipe for taming swelling soils, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Expansive soils swell and shrink with the weather, cracking roads and foundations, and the standard cements used to stabilize them are costly and dirty. Their binder, called LSP, mixes lime and sodium silicate into phosphogypsum, an industrial byproduct. Lab samples were then punished with repeated drying and wetting cycles to simulate seasons of abuse.

The treated soil packed denser, needed less water, and swelled far less, with the free swelling measure dropping from well over half to under a third. But the weather cycles bit back: strength fell by about a quarter after fifteen rounds, and water passed through more easily as micro cracks spread. Microscopy credited the improvement mainly to phosphogypsum grains physically filling pores. The study maps both the promise and the expiry date of a greener stabilizer.
plos-pone-0358849:
Rajitra Nawawonganun and two colleagues uncover a paradox for clean air campaigners in Thailand, in PLOS ONE in 2026. They surveyed five hundred fifty-seven parents of primary school children in Khon Kaen, a traffic heavy city in the northeast, during the hot, polluted season of 2025. The question was what drives psychological distress about traffic pollution: the exposure itself, or knowing about it.

Distress was widespread, with about sixty-two percent of parents moderately to highly distressed. The strongest single correlate was awareness itself, in a graded pattern. The more parents knew about air pollution, the more distressed they were. The most aware group carried over four times the odds of the least aware. Using an air quality app also tracked with distress. The authors name the dilemma plainly: education campaigns that raise awareness may raise anxiety too, unless paired with ways to act.
plos-pone-0359349:
Talema Moged Reda leads a team of eight in a 2026 PLOS ONE study mapping damaged land in Ethiopia's Southern Main Ethiopian Rift. Erosion and soil decline there threaten farming, water, and local livelihoods, and hot, salty ground adds stress that is poorly documented. The authors set out to chart where the land is most vulnerable so that limited protection efforts can be aimed well.

They combined satellite imagery from Landsat and Sentinel-2 with rainfall records, elevation data, soil information, and field checks, processed through mapping software and machine learning. Separate layers for erosion, land cover, vegetation health, drought, surface heat, and salt were merged into a single vulnerability map. The result gives planners a picture of which parts of the rift need attention first and where the pressures overlap.
plos-pone-0359549: Nguyen and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on why students say they cheat with AI help. The students were undergraduates reporting their own views. The team weighed five drivers: unclear ethics, what the tools make easy, gaps in school rules, study pressure, and comparing oneself with peers. Knowing which drivers matter most can help universities write clearer rules and fairer tasks.
plos-pone-0360249:
Alexa Keeling and Vijay Daniels published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its subject is the neurological examination, the hands-on set of tests doctors use to check the nervous system. The authors study medical residents, doctors in training, and how confident they feel performing this exam.

Alongside confidence, the study looks at exam avoidance, the habit of skipping parts of the exam or the whole thing. Residents who avoid the neuro exam may miss signs of stroke and other urgent problems. Medical educators can use evidence about confidence and avoidance to fix training where it leaves young doctors unsure.
pmc-10336149:
Zhang, Xiao, Mao, and co-authors review how swelling and immune activity in the brain may help drive diseases that kill nerve cells. Their review covers Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, ALS, and Huntington's disease. Work in these fields once treated brain swelling as a late side effect of damage.

The authors argue the evidence now points the other way as well. Immune activity in the brain can help push the disease forward, not just follow it. That shift matters because it opens new treatment ideas. If swelling helps cause the damage, calming the right immune signals early could slow loss of memory and movement.
pmc-10655349:
Ni Xiaofeng and six co-authors study the gut microbes of patients with bowel cancer after drug treatment. The treatment often lowers white blood cell counts, a side effect that can turn risky. The team took stool samples from fifty-five patients and fifty-six healthy people. Patients split into groups with low or normal white cell counts, and the team compared their gut mixes.

Gut variety was lower in patients than in healthy people. Fifteen kinds of bacteria set the groups apart. A machine learning model using three kinds of gut bacteria best flagged which patients had low counts. The paper links gut makeup to this treatment side effect.
pmc-10656449:
Emilie Khattignavong and co-authors build, in a 2023 paper, an easy computational way to measure how disordered collagen networks are in disease. Collagen is the body's main structural fiber, and its nanoscale weave shifts in connective tissue disorders. Reading that weave by eye from microscope images is slow and subjective. Their method pairs atomic force microscope images with a Fourier transform, a standard tool that turns patterns into orientation data.

The team tested the approach on skin from mice bred to mimic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Diseased fibers showed murkier edges, altered banding, and less orderly alignment than healthy ones. The transform measured the disorganization and the fibers' direction spread directly, turning pictures into numbers a clinic could use. The authors propose the pipeline as a step toward automated diagnosis of this family of disorders, and a sharper tool for basic collagen research.
pmc-10657349:
Alon Stern and co-authors present a way to read metabolism separately inside a cell's two main workspaces, in a 2023 paper. Cells run chemistry in the cytosol and inside mitochondria, and watching each space on its own has long been a barrier. Studying isolated organelles distorts the picture. Their method works on whole, intact cells fed with traced isotopes.

A computer step splits the isotope patterns into the part belonging to each space, then ties them to flows and amounts with models of metabolism and energy. The split cut uncertainty in flows tenfold and in amounts a thousandfold against older modeling. Across cultured cell lines, one shuttle pathway between the spaces varied widely. The authors expect the tool to serve disease research and bioengineering.
pmc-10670249:
Rachel Boyd and eight colleagues published a 2023 study of ring chromosomes in blood cancers. A ring chromosome forms when a chromosome's ends fuse into a circle. Rings appear in under 10 percent of patients with hematological malignancies and are linked to poor prognosis, but only small patient groups had been characterized.

The team analyzed chromosomes from more than 13,000 patients at Johns Hopkins Hospital and found 98 with ring chromosomes. Of these, 90 had myeloid cancers and 8 had lymphoid cancers. Targeted DNA sequencing showed the rings are associated with mutations in TP53, a key tumor suppressor gene, and with characteristic patterns of copy number change. The large cohort sharpens the picture of this rare abnormality.
pmc-10671449:
Sheiphali Gandhi and five colleagues review the environmental and workplace causes of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This lung disease scars the lungs and grows steadily worse; it mostly strikes older men. The disease is called idiopathic, yet age is its strongest risk factor, and many exposures raise risk further. They include metal dust, wood dust, air pollution, smoking, and diet.

The same factors can trigger acute flare-ups that carry poor outlooks. Recent work stresses inhalation injuries among World Trade Center first responders and military personnel. The review explains how exposures likely interact with genetic susceptibility to start and drive the disease. The authors picked exposures by overall disease burden rather than trying to list them all.
pmc-10674249:
Eight researchers led by Elena Formisano ran a trial of a very low-carb, protein-sparing fast in adults with obesity. Half got the liquid formula through a nose tube that feeds the stomach all day. The other half took the same diet by mouth. Forty-four patients were followed for one hundred fifty days.

Weight and waist size fell much the same in both groups. The tube group kept more lean tissue and muscle, and carried less fat, by the end. Their insulin levels were also much lower. The authors say tube feeding of this diet improves body makeup and blood sugar control more than the same diet by mouth.
pmc-10675649:
Laura Jiaxuan Li and co-authors reviewed zeolites in dentistry in a 2023 paper. Zeolites are porous crystal minerals that swap ions readily and stay stable under heat and chemicals. A kin class built with metal links shares the porous frame. Both are gentle on body tissue, which makes them fit for mouth care.

The review covers the main dental forms, such as silver, zinc, calcium, and strontium zeolites, and two kin frames. Uses span fillings, coatings, and germ-fighting adds for dental goods. Their pores can hold and shed helpful ions right where a tooth needs them. The authors chart where proof is strong and where trials are still due.
pmc-10688149:
Fulang Wu and colleagues catalogued an oxygen-burst gene family in grasses in 2023. These genes make reactive oxygen species. They help plants handle microbe encounters. Most past work covered broadleaf plants. Grass family knowledge stayed thin before. Seven grass species were analysed together.

More than one hundred genes were found. Evolution links were mapped across species. Maize work then tested fungal partnership roles. Friendly root fungi need these genes. Arbuscule structures develop properly with them. Early partnership steps mattered less here. Fine development control was the key role. Crop symbiosis research gains useful leads.
pmc-10689849:
Xiang and co-authors study how the Sun's outer layer rotates in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. They use daily measures of sunlight at several wavelength bands, plus four kinds of small magnetic features on the Sun. Their aim is to see which features drive changes in the spin of the corona over time.

Using wave-based tools and correlation tests, they find the drivers change with the solar cycle. At solar maximum, one kind of small magnetic element dominates the pattern. In quiet times, two kinds share control, and one grows stronger as activity falls. The authors say this helps explain why past studies disagreed, and why the corona spins faster than the surface below it.
pmc-10690949:
Soundarya Rajapitamahuni, Eun Sun Lyou, Bo Ram Kang, and Tae Kwon Lee wrote a study in twenty twenty-three on Staphylococcus aureus, a common bacterium behind ills from skin boils to sepsis. When iron is scarce, such bacteria send out siderophores, small molecules that grab iron for them. The team asked how life alongside other microbes changes this output.

First they tuned the growth medium, and a glycerol alanine salts medium gave the steadiest output of varied siderophores. Output peaked at neutral pH and at low iron. They then grew the bacterium with other strains and tracked how its output changed. Growth with Pseudomonas aeruginosa wiped the output out, while other partners cut it to one or two kinds. These shifts pushed the bacterium into distinct forms, a sign that microbes act unlike when alone and when in company.
pmc-10693549:
Anna Diez-Villanueva and co-authors hunt for inherited epigenetic marks in family trios in this 2023 paper. Much of the heritability of common disease is still unexplained by gene variants. DNA methylation, a chemical mark on DNA, might pass traits across generations directly. The team read methylation across the whole genome in four healthy families.

Each family held two parents and one child. About 1.5 million sites varied between parents in a pattern fit for inheritance checks. Of those, only 3,488 sites showed no link to any nearby gene variant. Those sites are candidates for true epigenetic inheritance. They sat across the genome, often near promoters, and tended to be fully marked or fully unmarked. The study gives a starting map for follow up work.
pmc-10695049:
Alexandre de Assis Bueno and co-authors map how ethics is taught in Brazilian public nursing programs, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Program plans for over one hundred active degrees were read in document form. Beyond a set ethics course, ethical themes ran across many subjects.

Care contexts, pharmacology, surgical nursing, and care planning all carried ethics threads. So did topics from palliative care to diversity and mental health. Management and epidemiology joined the list as well. The authors name the core challenge: weaving ethics into every act of caring, teaching, and managing, rather than parking it in one course.
pmc-10696049:
Toka Hassan, Eman Kandeel, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It turns waste from vegetable oil making into eco-friendly cutting fluids for metalworking, replacing toxic petroleum oils with something renewable and safer.

The team recovered oil from spent bleaching earth, a factory waste, and built a family of emulsifiers on it. Some were charged, some not, some doubled as rust blockers and microbe killers. Mixed emulsifier recipes were blended into cutting fluid formulas at various loadings. Certain mixtures formed stable emulsions where single emulsifiers failed. Two formulas stood out in the reported tests. Spectroscopic checks confirmed the molecules' structures along the way. The authors present the fluids as proof that an industrial waste stream can feed a second industry cleanly, cutting both disposal and drilling into new resources.
pmc-10696749:
Justin Baker and a large team of colleagues set out a plan for a clinical trial on group therapy to prevent suicide among military service members. Their protocol paper, published in twenty twenty-three, notes that suicide harms both health and readiness, and that a shortage of clinicians limits care. The trial compares two group formats given in person at a United States naval medical center. One is a brief cognitive behavioral therapy adapted for groups. The other teaches skills drawn from dialectical behavior therapy.

Participants are active-duty members with recent suicidal thoughts or behavior. They answer electronic questionnaires before treatment, after each session, and at follow-ups months later. The main question is whether the brief therapy is no worse than the skills group at reducing suicidal thinking. The paper describes the design only; results will come when the trial is complete.
pmc-10701749:
Chenglong Cao and co-authors report a rare cause of face pain in a case paper from two thousand twenty-three. Trigeminal neuralgia brings severe pain to one side of the face. In this patient, two problems pressed on the nerve at once: a bony growth near the skull base and a loop of blood vessel.

The patient was a man aged forty-six with three years of severe pain on the right side of his face. Scans showed both the growth and the vessel loop. Surgeons removed the growth and freed the nerve from the vessel in one combined operation. He left the hospital without complications and free of pain. The authors urge doctors to consider this rare double cause.
pmc-10708549:
Vera-Loor and three co-authors tested in twenty twenty-three two green chem routes to turn paper pulp into a finer grade that melts for cloth and films. Mills want such a swap on site with mild chemicals. One route used a peroxide wash at a few base levels.

Peroxide alone did not strip a pulp part, hemicellulose, in full to lift melt skill. A two-step route, with a salt first and peroxide next, did far better. That route cut the stray part and raised the pure share of the pulp. The team weighs shine, thick flow, and use paths for the end pulp.
pmc-10709349:
Liver transplants can be harmed when blood flow returns and iron-driven cell death sweeps the organ. Changbiao Li and co-authors study a protein called Gp78 in that injury in a 2023 paper, using mice bred with the gene removed or boosted in liver cells.

Patients and mice both showed lower Gp78 after flow returned, and lower levels tracked with worse damage. Mice lacking the protein in liver cells suffered less injury and inflammation. Mice with extra protein fared worse. Gene, protein, and chemical scans showed the protein reshapes fat handling so that burn-prone lipids pile up, feeding the iron-driven death through a partner enzyme. Blocking that death route or the partner erased the harm.
pmc-10709549:
Faysal Al-Ghoula, Khushbu Patel, Sam Falde, and four colleagues test whether radiomics tools agree across users in this two thousand twenty-three study. CT lung screening saves lives, but tools that score nodules from scan texture depend on someone first outlining the nodule, a source of variability. Three observers of different training levels, a medical student, a resident, and a radiology fellow, segmented ninety-five malignant nodules from two institutions. Each ran two validated tools, BRODERS and CANARY.

Agreement was strong. Correlation coefficients reached zero point seven seven for nodule volume and zero point nine eight and zero point nine seven for the BRODERS cancer probability and CANARY aggression score. Overlap of the segmentations scored about zero point eight at both centers. The authors conclude both tools are robust to who performs the segmentation, a precondition for using radiomics scores in real screening programs where expert time is scarce.
pmc-10711849:
Lijie Wang and co-authors set out, in 2023, a protocol for gathering what breast cancer patients say about hormone therapy side effects and the help they want. Such symptoms can bring pain, anxiety, and fear of the cancer returning. Poor support lowers drug adherence, which raises relapse and death risk, so patient needs must be mapped first.

Seven databases plus grey literature were searched for qualitative and mixed-method studies, with no date limit. This follow-up focused on those positive for plasma p-tau217, a marker of Alzheimer's pathology. In that subgroup the team examined thinking scores, daily living scores, and immune response to the vaccine. The authors say biomarker-selected subgroups may show a vaccine's effect more clearly than the full mixed trial population.
pmc-11585549:
Parkinson's disease harms movement and thinking, yet its roots inside the brain remain unclear. A large team of researchers built a detailed atlas of the disease in 2024 by reading the gene activity of single cell nuclei. They drew on 100 donated brains, cases and healthy controls spanning the full range of disease severity, and covered five brain regions.

Alongside the cell data, they gathered whole-genome data for the same donors. Careful checks kept the data clean, and the finished atlas is posted openly on a public research platform. The authors offer it as a shared tool for finding the molecular roots of Parkinson's and speeding new treatments.
pmc-11585949:
Daisuke Sugiura and colleagues build a low-cost microcontroller system for measuring how crops use water. Their 2024 article addresses the need for higher-throughput ways to find varieties with better water-use efficiency.

The system combines pot weighing, automated water supply, and real-time monitoring over Wi-Fi. It was validated on rice, soybean, and maize under salt, waterlogging, and drought stress. Salt-tolerant rice kept using more water and growing better under salinity than sensitive rice. Waterlogged soybean used less water and grew less. Long experiments revealed efficiency differences between rice varieties and root-shoot changes in drought-stressed maize.
pmc-11590849:
Stephen Oakley, Samantha Stott, Kerri Gill, and Lyanne Weston test whether built-in body stiffness links rheumatoid arthritis severity to its excess heart disease. Their study came out in 2024. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune joint disease, and patients die early from cardiovascular disease more often than others.

The team measured joint flexibility, artery stiffness, and skin stretch in fifty-eight patients and fifty-seven controls. Joint stiffness tracked with both artery and skin stiffness in the same person. Patients whose joint damage advanced fastest had stiffer joints and arteries, and stiffer skin early in the disease. Since the disease does not attack skin, the authors argue that stiffness is a constitutional trait present from birth. That trait may drive both worse arthritis and worse heart outcomes. Prospective studies are needed to test causality.
pmc-11591149:
A team including Zhuo Yang studies how a giant clam guards its cells against harm from oxygen. The clam lives with tiny algae that make food from light, and that close tie needs a fine balance of cell chemistry. The researchers found a gene switch, TsNfe2l, that turns on defense genes. One gene it controls makes carnosine, a shield against cell harm.

When the switch could not bind to DNA, the shield gene fell quiet and fat damage in the gill rose. The work names a key chain that keeps the clam's cell balance steady.
pmc-11591949:
Stelios Psarras reviews, in twenty twenty-four, how two cell types in the heart shape repair and scarring. The heart heals poorly after injury, and that failure can lead to heart failure. Fibroblasts are cells that build the tissue scaffold. When overactive, they lay down too much collagen, stiffening the heart. That scarring process is called fibrosis. Macrophages are immune cells that can help or harm fibroblasts, depending on their state and subtype.

Psarras argues the pair should be read as a dipole, two poles that shape each other. The influence runs both ways, not just from immune cells to scaffold cells. That two-way talk offers points where treatment might steer repair toward healing and away from scarring.
pmc-11600549:
Jiapeng Xu and co-authors published this review in 2024. It updates what is known about flu viruses resisting neuraminidase inhibitor drugs, the class that includes common antivirals. The team gathered worldwide reports of resistant strains and cataloged the gene changes behind them. One change, H274Y, peaked back in 2008 and hit public health hard in places like Japan and the United States.

Resistance arises three ways: changes at the drug's target site, structural blocking, and shifts in protein stability. Global resistance rates for the main flu types sit near one percent and have held steady. Still, stray resistant strains keep appearing. Some pick up extra changes that restore their spread. The authors urge continued watching, careful drug use, and better vaccine coverage, plus fresh antiviral strategies.
pmc-11600949:
Kaige Ma and co-authors test a sedative drug in Alzheimer's model mice in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The disease involves amyloid buildup, brain inflammation, and nerve cell loss. The drug is known to calm inflammation and protect nerves, but its effect in this disease was unclear.

Mice given amyloid in the brain showed poorer memory and more anxiety-like behavior. Treatment with the drug eased both problems and raised the number of surviving neurons in a key memory area. It also lowered a signaling molecule called CXCL2 and other inflammation markers. Forcing that molecule up, or blocking the drug, removed the benefit. The authors suggest the drug may hold promise for this disease.
pmc-11604949:
Hanzhi Du and colleagues linked heart tracing patterns to lymphoma survival in two thousand twenty-four. This aggressive lymphoma raises heart rhythm risks. Certain wave patterns on heart tracings predict rhythm trouble. Their meaning for lymphoma survival was unknown. Newly diagnosed patients were reviewed retrospectively. Follow-up lasted well over a year typically.

Over a third of patients showed abnormal wave patterns. That group included more men proportionally. Kidney markers also ran higher in that group. Death rates were clearly higher with abnormalities. Two specific wave measures predicted death independently. Other factors for abnormal patterns were modeled too. A simple heart tracing may refine prognosis cheaply.
pmc-11605049:
A team of co-authors presents a study from two thousand twenty-four on prostate cancer in Sudanese men. The team asked whether diagnosis patterns differ among the country's three major ethnolinguistic groups. Such data are scarce for Sudan and can guide where screening and care are most needed.

Five hundred thirty-two men with biopsy-confirmed cancer took part at six centers. Most, about eighty-four percent, were diagnosed at an advanced stage. The cancer's grade did not differ clearly between groups. One group showed higher levels of a blood marker and younger ages at diagnosis, while another group was mostly over sixty. Matched analysis found one invasion pattern more common in that older group.
pmc-11605549:
Hidenobu Yoshitake and co-authors report, in a conference abstract, a lymphoma that lives inside blood vessels and its rare move into the brain. Their report appeared in 2024. This cancer normally grows only within small vessels and never invades the wall. The team followed cases where brain lymphoma appeared during or after treatment of the vessel form. They stained the tumors for two glue proteins that this cancer characteristically loses.

In ordinary brain lymphoma, both proteins showed strongly around vessels and tumor cells but vanished where cells spread diffusely into brain tissue. The comparison aims to explain how the vessel-bound cancer crosses into the brain. The authors say the adhesion pattern may mark the crossing cases.
pmc-11605749:
A common diabetes drug probably triggered one man's psoriasis, report Simal Qureshi, Sarah Finch, and Michelle Pratt in a 2024 case study. The patient, aged 76, developed the scaly skin disease after starting dapagliflozin, a drug with no classic link to the condition.

Three clues point at the drug: the sudden start, skin samples showing features that fit a drug reaction, and full clearing once the drug stopped. The authors note that drug driven psoriasis has no firm test and can mimic the ordinary kind, from small plaques to whole body redness. They urge doctors to ask about new medicines when skin erupts.
pmc-11605849:
How creative young adults believe they are shapes what they attempt and how they express themselves. Ananya Gupta, Swati Pathak, and Neeraj Panwar explore what sits behind that self-view. They survey 200 young adults, with an average age of about 21, on personality traits, feelings about emotions, and creative self-concept.

A stronger creative self-view went with being open, careful, outgoing, and agreeable. It also went with certain stances toward sadness and fear. When the authors tested which factors predict the self-view, openness explained the largest share, about 27 percent. Neuroticism and attitude toward sadness added small shares of about 2 percent each. The authors suggest that teachers and counselors who know these links can better support creative growth. Personality and emotional attitudes, they argue, are worth attention in programs that build creative confidence.
pmc-11606049:
Kai Liu and colleagues catalogue a cell-wall gene family across the grapevine genome. Their study from twenty twenty-four then tests one gene against salt stress. These LRX genes shape plant growth and stress resistance. Grapevine lacked a full family inventory until now.

Fourteen family members were found and grouped into four branches. Duplication events explained much of the family's expansion. Tissue patterns suggested roles in growth and stress alike. Salt treatment switched several family genes on. One gene, VvLRX7, was characterised in depth functionally. Cell wall proteins mediate how plants sense their surroundings. Breeders gain candidate genes for salt-tolerant vines.
pmc-11607449:
Yang Luo and a large international team compared genomes of tuberculosis patients with genomes of the bacteria infecting them, hunting for interacting pairs. Infection outcomes depend on both sides, yet most genetic studies look at only one. The cohort came from Lima, Peru, and paired samples numbered well over a thousand. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team reports one strong pairing: a variant in a human gene involved in cell membrane rafts tracked with a subgroup of a major bacterial lineage. Tests in infected immune cells supported a real link.

Cells carrying one form of the variant showed stronger interferon responses, while the paired strains carried a mutation changing their chemical balance. In a later cohort gathered during the pandemic, the strain had grown much more common but no longer tracked with the human variant. The authors stress that host, pathogen, and environment jointly shape tuberculosis.
pmc-11608449:
Diarrhea still kills widely in poorer countries, and dirty surroundings may drive more of it than germs alone. Eudora Nwanaforo and four co-authors reviewed the evidence linking pollutant exposure to diarrhea risk in a 2024 systematic review. From nearly 500 papers, eleven met their quality bar, covering pesticides, heavy metals, smoke-related chemicals, microplastics, and preservatives.

Several exposures tracked with more diarrhea: a banned pesticide sprayed before birth, arsenic, cadmium, and microplastics among them. The chemicals may stir gut motion, upset gut microbes, and weaken immune defenses. The authors note big gaps in where studies were done and call for wider, better research on the link.
pmc-11608549:
Xiying He and nine colleagues investigate how a Chinese herbal fever medicine for children reshapes the gut during fever. They compared the granules with ibuprofen in young febrile rats, tracking temperature longer than in earlier work, then sequenced gut microbes and profiled metabolites in colon contents.

The herbal treatment kept fever down longer than ibuprofen. It also nudged the disturbed gut flora back toward normal, boosting two short-chain fatty acid producing species and raising butyric acid levels and its receptor. Anti-inflammatory metabolites rose while fever-linked metabolites and inflammatory signals in the colon fell to normal. The authors attribute part of the medicine's effect to restoring gut microbial balance.
pmc-11608649:
Okano, Nakayama, and Nishizawa test when to drink citrate for clearing lactate after exercise in twenty twenty-four. Citrate drinks are popular and may speed lactate removal from blood. Whether intake before or after exercise works better was unknown. Forty-one healthy male students were assigned to four conditions.

Groups took citric acid before or after exercise, water after, or nothing. All cycled for five minutes on an ergometer. Lactate was measured before exercise and up to thirty minutes after. Overall lactate values and removal rates did not differ significantly among groups. Removal kept rising with citric acid intake regardless of timing. The authors conclude timing mattered little in this small trial.
pmc-11610549:
Na Liu, Lei Wang, Lin Luan, and Huaqing Wang test whether a pneumonia vaccine lowers hospital stays for older adults in China. Their 2024 study covers the 23-valent vaccine against pneumococcal disease. The patients lived in Suzhou City, and the cases were new pneumonia caught outside hospital.

The team compared pneumonia patients with patients who had other chest infections. The pneumonia group had a lower rate of recent vaccination than the control group. After adjusting for other factors, vaccinated adults over sixty had a notably lower risk of hospital care for pneumonia. The effect held for severe cases as well. The findings support wider vaccine use in older adults, a group for whom strong local evidence had been thin.
pmc-11612149:
Louis and a team including Pétré match single asthma symptoms to body traits in five hundred five treated adults in twenty twenty-four. Each of five symptoms was scored for strength on a five point scale. Lung tests and inflammation markers were modeled against them. The symptoms did not move as one block.

Cough tied to smoking, low lung score, and high eosinophils. Breathlessness tied to female sex, high body weight, and low lung score. Wheeze and chest tightness each had their own mix of age, sex, and lung traits. Mucus linked mainly to smoking. The split backs symptom tailored care, they argue.
pmc-11615549:
Shu Jing and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper setting out a trial to raise HPV vaccination among young girls in central and western China. The virus can cause cervical cancer, and vaccinating girls aged nine to fourteen prevents it. Free programs exist in some cities, yet cost, supply, and parent hesitancy keep rates low elsewhere.

The planned trial uses a phone mini-program that teaches parents and girls about the vaccine. Its design follows a model that joins information, motivation, and practical skills. Families are assigned by chance to the program or usual care, across several centers. The protocol paper lays out the plan before results exist, so the test of the idea stays honest.
pmc-11616749:
Yihao Chen and co-authors nominate a transport protein as a biomarker for a rare adrenal cancer in a 2024 study. Adrenocortical carcinoma strikes children and adults alike, with a grim outlook and high death rates. Standard chemotherapy helps inconsistently and brings heavy side effects, so better markers are badly needed.

Profiling tumors across several omics layers, the team found karyopherin subunit alpha 2, a protein that ferries cargo into the cell nucleus, standing out. Its levels track prognosis and may predict who responds to immunotherapy. A marker that does both jobs could steer patients to the right trial early. The study gives this rare cancer a rare gift: a testable lead with clinical uses attached.
pmc-11618349:
Grouping data into clusters is easy; explaining afterward why the groups make sense is the hard part, especially for odd shapes in many dimensions. Tao Zeng and co-authors propose describing each cluster with a handful of boxes in a 2025 paper. Boxes start small to cover a cluster, then merge step by step along a family tree until their shape hugs the cluster well.

A tightening pass then shrinks the boxes for precision. The tree structure finds the right number of boxes on its own and reveals how they relate. Tests against older explanation methods showed tighter, more accurate descriptions, which the authors offer for pattern work where people must defend the grouping.
pmc-11621249:
Lefan Zhuang and co-authors report a rare case of a stem cell product clotting after collection, in a case report from 2024. Stem cell products are gathered by a filtering process that needs blood thinners to keep the lines and the product fluid. Clots during later freezing are known, but clots in a fresh product had not been reported.

The product came from a matched unrelated donor. On arrival, thin white threads of clot floated in the bag. Staff split the product into syringes under sterile care to isolate the clot. Within an hour, the small clots merged into a pink, jelly-like cylinder ringed by serum. The authors suggest adding a blood thinner to the product before such isolation in future cases.
pmc-11621349:
Xiao-Jiao Cui and colleagues test whether simple blood ratios can predict outcomes in severe pneumonia, in a 2024 study. Severe community-acquired pneumonia fills hospitals and kills many patients. Ratios between white cell types and platelets are cheap to get from a routine blood count. The team checked five such ratios against what happened to patients.

The study covered 554 patients treated for the disease. Two ratios, built from neutrophils and basophils against lymphocytes, tracked with death in hospital and shorter survival. A third ratio, built from eosinophils, pointed the other way, toward longer stays but better survival. Several ratios also tracked with admission to intensive care. None stood as a fully independent predictor of death, though. The authors see the ratios as helpful signals to combine with other clinical signs.
pmc-11625749:
Sangavi and five colleagues test a brown seaweed extract against the main tooth decay germ in twenty twenty-four. The germ builds sticky films that shrug off antibiotics. The extract fought the film without killing the germ itself. At top dose it cut film growth by over nine tenths.

Sub killing doses slashed sticking, acid making, and sugar glue output. Surface grip and loose DNA fell as well. Gene checks showed the film and glue genes turned down. Human cheek cells stayed unharmed in safety tests. Three fatty acids in the extract carried much of the punch, the team found.
pmc-11626449:
Andrea Silverj and a large team of co-authors trace West Nile virus lineage one in Italy, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. The mosquito-borne virus sickens people, horses, and birds. Italy saw 330 brain cases and thirty-seven deaths in the twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-two season.

The team built a bank of all public virus genomes plus thirty-one new Italian ones. Their tree suggests the lineage first entered Italy from North Africa around nineteen eighty-five. Two distinct strains now circulate in the country. Fresh mutations mark the Italian strains, and the authors urge joint watch across Europe and Africa.
pmc-11630049:
Dongdong Luo leads a team on a ring RNA in glioma brain tumors. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with circATP8B4 and its partners. Ring RNAs are often off track in human glioma.

The ring is high in glioma, but its role was unclear. Lab tests showed cutting it slowed tumor cell growth and spread. It also made cells more prone to radiation harm. The ring soaks up a small RNA that would curb a key protein. Mouse tumor tests backed the lab finds in live animals. The chain may offer new cure goals.
pmc-11631049:
Frédéric Thomas and co-authors answer a comment on their cancer evolution paper in a 2024 journal exchange. Their earlier article argued that tumors progress not only by single-cell fitness but by selection for what the tumor as a whole can do. A reader, Dr. Mesut Tez, praised the view and linked it to older ideas about black-box epidemiology and self-organizing systems. The authors reply with thanks and expansion.

They stress the collective adaptability of cancer cell groups, which they frame as group phenotypic composition. Tumors, on this view, act like quick problem-solvers in hostile tissue. The exchange shows a theory being sharpened in public by friendly fire. Such replies help readers see where a new idea agrees with its ancestors.
pmc-11631549:
A patient with a swollen pancreas formed an abscess deep in its tail, too far from the stomach wall for the usual drain route through the stomach. Ping Yue and co-authors report how they reached it anyway in a 2024 case report. The man, sixty-five, had heart stents placed a month before, which raised the stakes of any operation.

A scope passed into the pancreatic duct, but wires and tools kept jamming at tight narrowings in the duct. A cutting tool borrowed from cyst work, driven by electric current, burned the narrowing open. A drain tube then drew off a large volume of pus, and the abscess vanished within days. A stent followed, and the man recovered without incident. The authors offer the borrowed tool as a rescue when standard gear cannot pass.
pmc-11631749:
Yong Li and three co-authors assess how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped early breast cancer care in the United States. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Lockdowns and strained hospitals delayed screening and surgery across many cancers.

Using a national cancer registry, the team compared over one hundred forty-two thousand patients from twenty twenty with the two prior years. Diagnoses and surgeries both fell in twenty twenty. The stage mix shifted later, with fewer stage zero to one cases. Breast-conserving surgery and radiation shares dropped, while chemotherapy rose. Treatment delays, oddly, shortened. Survival for the twenty twenty group ran worse than for twenty eighteen patients. The authors document a lasting scar on early cancer care.
pmc-11631949:
Mateus de Castro, Mayana Zatz, and a team of co-authors hunt for why some exposed people never caught COVID-19. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, follows six women who lived with infected partners. The partners were sick and tested positive, some more than once. Yet the women stayed free of symptoms or infection.

Blood immune cells from the couples were prodded in the lab. One gene, switched on by interferon, stood out in the protected women alone. That gene, IFIT3, helps cells fight viruses. Its rise appeared only in the exposed but uninfected group. The team proposes it as a shield factor worth deeper study.
pmc-11632249:
Germaine Loo and Chi Keong Ching wrote an editorial in two thousand twenty-four on Japan's national registry for catheter ablation. Ablation treats faulty heart rhythms by scarring the tissue that causes them. Registries in several countries now track how the procedure is used and how safe and effective it is in real practice.

Rhythm disorders are rising with aging populations and better detection, and ablation volumes with them. Japan's registry grew from about forty thousand ablation cases in two thousand eighteen to over sixty-eight thousand in two thousand twenty-two. With ninety thousand cases in total, it is among the largest such registries reported.
pmc-11632949:
Xu and co-authors marry copper cobalt oxide sheets with peptide fibers for tumor heat therapy. Peptide fibers self-build and are kind to body tissue. The hybrid pairs those fibers with bimetallic nanosheets. Light-to-heat conversion hit 31.57 percent for the hybrid. That rate suits heat-based tumor cell killing.

The fibers cut the sheets' harm to normal cells. Heat killed over 95 percent of one lung cancer line. A second line lost over 90 percent of cells. A ranked score put total performance at 0.741. The authors say the peptide design guides future hybrids.
pmc-11635249:
Xi and six co-authors studied a gene called PSMD11 in lung adenocarcinoma in twenty twenty-four. The gene helps run the proteasome, the cell's machine for shredding tagged proteins. It has been linked to cancer growth, but its value in this lung cancer type was unclear.

Using data analysis across many datasets, they found the gene far more active in tumor tissue than in normal lung. High activity tracked with DNA copying pathways and certain immune cell patterns. It correlated positively with some helper and regulatory T cells, and negatively with B cells and killer T cells. Links also appeared with genes tied to copper-driven cell death. Cell co-culture tests probed immune escape. The authors propose the gene as a possible drug target and marker.
pmc-11638049:
Yang Luo and four co-authors present a 2024 meta-analysis on how two workout styles feel to people with excess weight. High-intensity interval training alternates hard bursts with rest, while moderate continuous training keeps a steady pace. Both help health, but which one people enjoy more was disputed. The team pooled sixteen studies with 537 participants, using standard scales for enjoyment and feelings during exercise.

Programs ran from one to sixteen weeks, with adults up to age seventy. The pooled result found interval training gave higher enjoyment than steady training. Felt responses during exercise were similar between the two. The authors conclude both styles leave people feeling positive, which matters because enjoyment keeps people exercising. Interval training's slight enjoyment edge, in shorter total time, may suit busy schedules. They still note wide variation across the studies pooled.
pmc-11638349: A set of answer keys from twenty twenty-four gives the right answers to short quiz sets tied to past journal articles. Each set has five questions, and the answers are listed as plain letter codes. The linked articles cover topics such as wrist scans, care for sick children, brain scans, and skin care during treatment. Health workers use these sets to claim learning credit for their own records.
pmc-11638949:
Xinyang Lv and colleagues published a 2024 biotechnology study on making a human milk sugar. The sugar supports infant immune health. Formula makers increasingly add it to products. The team engineered E. coli bacteria to produce it. Earlier routes were too inefficient.

Genes that break down a key building block were deleted. New genes for building the sugar were inserted. Enzyme levels were balanced in modules. A helper chemical supply was recycled more efficiently. Transport proteins were screened to export the product. Output rose substantially. Fermentation could supply this ingredient at industrial scale.
pmc-11640349:
Hiroharu Natsume, Shogo Okamoto, and Derek V Byrne present a two thousand twenty-four study predicting moment-by-moment liking of strawberries from changing sensations. Food tasters can record which sensation dominates over time. A parallel method tracks liking itself, but running both is costly.

A reservoir neural network learned to forecast liking curves from sensation curves. Strawberry data from an earlier study trained the models. Forecasts were often highly accurate. Two sensitivity measures ranked which sensations steer liking most. Sweetness led for strawberries. The method could let developers infer preference shifts from cheaper sensation testing alone.
pmc-11640549:
Lucia Biagini and co-authors test, in a 2024 poultry study, giving probiotics to chicks before they hatch. Live microbes delivered in the egg can meet the embryo early, and pairing them with the standard Marek's disease vaccine would simplify hatchery work.

One hundred five fertile eggs received the vaccine alone, or the vaccine carrying a multi-strain probiotic at two doses. Chicks were then raised for thirty-five days while growth, gut shape, and parasite shedding were tracked. A gut parasite, Eimeria, was monitored weekly in droppings, and intestinal tissue was checked for lesions at slaughter. The design weighs early probiotics against growth and gut health.
pmc-11640649:
Circular RNAs are rings of genetic material with no loose ends, which makes them hard for cells to break down. A 2024 review by Xiaocai Yin, Hongjun Li, and Yan Zhou surveys what these rings do during virus infection and how they might serve in treatment.

Both host cells and viruses produce the rings, and they can help or hinder a virus depending on the case. The review covers their roles across coronaviruses, herpesviruses, HIV, and others, their part in the host's antiviral defense, and their promise as markers that could flag an infection. The authors argue the rings form an overlooked layer of control in infected cells.
pmc-11641649:
Damián Pereira-Payo and co-authors study poverty and health in 2024 among middle-aged and older adults in the United States. Low income is known to track with worse health, but the team wanted the full pattern in one national data set. They used a decade of the national health survey program, covering over ten thousand adults.

Adults below the poverty line were more likely to be inactive, eat poorly, and have a history of heavy drinking. They also had higher rates of high blood pressure, diabetes, liver and kidney disease, arthritis, stroke, and heart attacks. The more of these diseases piled up in one person, the stronger the income link grew. The authors flag this group as needing targeted policy help.
pmc-11642349:
Aiko Ishizaki-Terauchi and colleagues published a clinical study in twenty twenty-four about small screws used to anchor teeth during orthodontic treatment. They looked back at records for Japanese patients who had screws placed in the upper jaw. All of the operators were right-handed and had several years of experience. The team compared screws placed by hand with screws placed using a motor, and they compared the right side of the mouth with the left side.

Hand-placed screws held less often on the left side than on the right side. Motor-placed screws held about equally well on both sides. Overall success did not differ much between the two methods. The authors link the left-side problem to the working position of a right-handed clinician, and they note that operator experience also mattered.
pmc-11642449:
Mariah Balmaceno-Criss and co-authors review how to spot a worsening neck spinal cord disease, in work from two thousand twenty-four. Wear and tear in the neck can slowly press the cord, causing nerve harm that grows with age in the population. Early, exact diagnosis matters because late finds can leave lasting damage.

Signs are often faint and vague, such as poor sleep, more falls, and trouble driving. That vagueness leads to missed or wrong calls. The review gathers history clues, exam findings, and look-alike diseases from recent papers. Surgery to free the cord is advised in most cases to halt decline.
pmc-11642949:
Sven Schwabe and colleagues published a 2024 protocol for a study of suicide assistance in Germany. Helping a person end their life is a multi-step process, from first talks about end-of-life options to care for grieving family. Who takes part varies by country and by local rules.

In 2020, Germany's top court lifted the ban on organized assistance, but the field stayed unregulated. No solid data show how such help is given in practice. The planned study will ask patients, families, and practitioners about their experience. It aims to map each stage of real cases. Clear facts could guide future rules and safer practice.
pmc-11644049:
Yang Peng and colleagues study how a rare riverside plant handles cadmium in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Cadmium is a toxic metal spread by industry and cities. It can stunt or kill plants. The plant here, Myricaria laxiflora, is rare and endangered. It grows along the upper Yangtze River, where cadmium pollution varies by site. How the metal stresses this plant was unknown.

The team raised seedlings and exposed them to cadmium. They measured growth, body chemistry, and the activity of thousands of genes. The combined data show how the plant senses and answers the poison. Such insight can guide efforts to protect wild stands of the species. It may also reveal tolerance tricks useful for cleaning polluted soils.
pmc-11644849:
Xuantuo Huang and co-authors build, in a 2024 paper, a virtual training ground for sighted helpers who guide blind people from afar. In remote-sighted assistance, a helper watches live video and sends coded vibration commands, but video delay and imperfect execution make guiding hard to learn on real people.

Their platform, built in the Unreal Engine, simulates a visually impaired person following instructions in a realistic space. Helpers practice the vibration command set safely until it becomes fluent. Trained agents then guided people along the same route about thirty-two percent faster, with over half fewer bumps into surroundings, than untrained novices. The simulator offers cheap, repeatable practice.
pmc-11644949:
Wang, Wu, Wang, and Xia present a study from twenty twenty-four on a wider way to make pictures with light. Ghost imaging builds a picture from light patterns, not from a direct view of the object. It resists noise well, but its view range has stayed narrow. The team adds a second light path so the system can gather facts from a wider area. They feed both paths into a smart network that rebuilds the target picture.

The network also has a focus step that shifts weight to the most useful signals. Tests in simulation show the method works and rebuilds pictures well. The authors say the wider range makes ghost imaging more useful in real settings. It offers a fresh path for later imaging tools.
pmc-11645449:
Perrine Burdeyron and co-authors tried repairing pig kidneys before transplant using tiny parcels shed by urine stem cells in a 2024 proof-of-concept study. A donor kidney suffers when blood flow stops and restarts, a harm called ischemia-reperfusion injury. Cell therapy might condition the organ during storage, but living cells bring risks.

Extracellular vesicles, the membrane parcels cells use to send signals, could deliver the benefit without the cells. The team perfused pig kidneys with vesicles from urine progenitor cells and checked the grafts. Conditioning an organ on the pump would fit real transplant workflow. A positive signal here justifies testing whether vesicles cut early graft failure in people.
pmc-11645649:
Mary Maldarelli and her team study air made foul by wild fires in Canada and the load of heart and lung ills in the east of the United States. Their 2024 case-just study uses files from a sick bay net in Maryland.

Meets on high foul air days in June twenty twenty-three were set next to matched days in two past Junes. On those days, fine bits in the air went past state norms. Finds took in stays, walk-in care, and rush room meets for heart and lung states. Checks were set right for side traits with known tests and math checks. Strong wild fires near homes come more and more, yet health acts of far smoke dose stay in doubt. The folk in the study were wide in life state and in group traits, which made the finds count for more folk.
pmc-11647349:
Han and co-authors lay out a plan to review trials that pair chemotherapy with immunotherapy for stomach cancer, in this 2024 paper. The pairing has become a new standard of care, yet reviews so far cover only parts of the field. A full account of benefits and harms is still needed.

The protocol follows standard reporting rules for review plans. The team will search three major databases and screen studies in two rounds by two authors. Only randomized trials in English that compare the pairing against chemotherapy alone will count, in both surgical and first-line settings. The finished review aims to guide care and future research.
pmc-11648149:
Rodrigo Carrillo-Larco and Ian Hambleton describe the daily work of a cohorts consortium that pools health data across Latin America and the Caribbean. Pooled cohort data let small lands make region level risk gauges. The article came out in twenty twenty-four.

A steering group of regional experts set the project up. Members who agree to share person level data help set goals and coauthor papers. A systematic search found data holders, and a manual logs all steps. By the study year, the pool held dozens of units from over a dozen lands, with a vast total sample. Past outputs include region risk gauges for heart and metabolism traits.
pmc-11648249:
Heyue Jin and a team of co-authors map gene and protein shifts in placentas of small babies, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Babies small for their age face stillbirth risk and lasting harm, often from a weak placenta. The team paired gene readouts with protein measures in placental tissue.

Two linked modules of genes and proteins split small-baby placentas from healthy ones. Core driver molecules were traced to their upstream switches. A separate group of samples confirmed those drivers. The work names fresh targets that may drive the placenta's failure to feed the baby well.
pmc-11648549:
Zheng, Pei, and Huang map research trends on dexmedetomidine in perioperative medicine. The drug calms, eases pain, and cuts stress in surgical patients. It also shows anti-inflammatory and anxiolytic effects in that setting. The team pulled 1,652 papers from the Web of Science Core Collection. That set held 1,497 articles and 155 reviews. Output rose sharply after 2013 in this field.

China led output, with the United States second. One journal, BMC Anesthesiology, printed the most papers on the topic. Anesthesiology led on citations per paper and co-citation rank. Ji Fuhai was the most prolific author in the set. Hot topics were older patients and post-surgery confusion.
pmc-11648749:
Saeid Joveini and co-authors compare two plant compounds against chronic inflammation in rats in this 2024 study. Both compounds come from plants of the carrot family. Inflammation signals named in the title are the readouts of interest. Sixty male rats were split into ten groups. Once lasting inflammation was confirmed, treated groups got one compound by mouth for nine days. Tissue samples were examined after the course ended.

Body weight changes were tracked as a health sign. One compound at a set dose raised weight gain clearly. Blood levels of the two signal proteins showed distinct patterns per compound. The pair are not interchangeable, the results suggest. Such differences matter for picking a lead compound for arthritis research. The study is an animal experiment, not a human trial. Doses and effects are fully tabled in the article.
pmc-11650149:
Yen-Ting Lin and Yu-San Han survey glass eels in Yilan, Taiwan, in a 2024 study. Glass eels are the young stage of freshwater eels, and Yilan is the first place in East Asia where they arrive on ocean currents. Knowing which species arrive matters for ecology and fisheries.

The team netted eels in a river estuary twice a month for over thirteen years. Shape checks and a gene test identified seven species. Three species made up most catches, a few were rare, and two were new records for Taiwan. The count of eel species known there rises from five to seven.
pmc-11650349:
Seo, Jung, and Song discuss in twenty twenty-four a bladder-sparing option for a hard-to-treat form of bladder cancer. The cancer sits in the bladder lining and no longer responds to the standard bladder drug treatment. The usual next step is to remove the bladder, a major operation many patients decline or cannot face.

The authors review a trial plan that pairs focused radiation with a drug that makes radiation work harder. Patients keep their bladder while doctors check how many are clear of cancer at six months. They also weigh how long the effect lasts and how safe the mix is. The piece weighs this path against newer bladder drugs and body-wide treatments.
pmc-11652049:
Yang and four co-authors tested image fusion for judging lung tumor ablation during the procedure itself in twenty twenty-four. Microwave ablation destroys early lung tumors with heat in patients who cannot tolerate surgery. During treatment, the tumor and the burned zone can look alike on CT scans, hiding whether the tumor is fully covered.

In twenty-nine patients with thirty-two lesions, a radiologist fused before-and-after CT images, a process taking about ten minutes with a ninety-seven percent success rate. Two physicians then judged the tumor's position relative to the ablation zone. On plain scans they were right only about eight to thirteen percent of the time. On fused images they reached about eighty-seven percent, and they agreed strongly. Judgments from fused images matched six-month follow-up perfectly. The authors call fusion a valuable intraoperative check.
pmc-11652549:
Yazan Alwadi and six co-authors measure heat's toll on Kuwaiti hearts in a 2024 paper. Kuwait is heating fast under climate change. Heart disease already leads its mortality statistics. Hospital records from 2010 to 2019 anchor the analysis.

Over two hundred sixty thousand heart admissions were recorded in that decade. About twenty thousand of them were attributed to heat. Risk climbed as temperatures passed forty one degrees. Statistical models adjusted for humidity and season. Future climates from global models extended the trend to 2099. Both moderate and extreme scenarios raised the projected burden. The authors warn health systems to plan for hotter decades. Their numbers give Kuwait a baseline for adaptation policy.
pmc-11654349:
Xuelian Liu and six co-authors find, in a 2024 study, two genes that steer sepal and petal development in the lotus. The lotus is a prized aquatic plant grown for ornament, food, and medicine.
