Its blooms range from few petals to a thousand, which makes it a fine case for how flowers form. The genes are lotus counterparts of a well-known flower gene called APETALA2.

Both genes were most active in buds and petals, and their proteins sat mainly in the nucleus, as gene switches should. When the genes were switched on in a model plant, its blooms grew extra sepals and petals. Each gene also repaired the flawed blooms of a mutant that lacks its own AP2. Tests show the lotus proteins team with other flower organ proteins. The team say the pair shape the outer rings of the lotus bloom, a lead for breeders.
pmc-11655549:
Samantha Hartke and five co-authors introduce GARD-LENS, a high-resolution climate dataset built to separate forced change from the climate's own wobble, in this 2024 data paper. The set sharpens three big global model ensembles down to daily rain and temperature maps. Coverage spans the continental United States at twelve-kilometer grid size, Alaska at four, and Hawaii at one.

Two hundred ensemble members across one hundred fifty years give users deep statistics on trends and extremes. Because each parent model starts many runs from slightly different states, the dataset is the first of its kind to show natural variability at street-level detail. The authors aim it at scientists and planners who must budget for uncertainty in adaptation work.
pmc-11656549:
Hatefi, Biglari, and Babakhani check if ankle bend range and stiffness predict landing balance. Both traits have been tied to non-contact injury risk. Twenty male amateur athletes joined the tests. Ankle bend was gauged with a weight-bearing lunge test. Balance was scored on one-leg landings with two index tools.

No clear link joined ankle bend, stiffness, and landing scores. A mid-level tie between bend range and stiffness did not reach significance. Bend range and time to steady stance also showed a weak tie. The authors say stiffness alone does not set landing balance. Sex, age, and task type may change the picture.
pmc-11658149:
Jonas Manschel and co-authors published this metasynthesis in 2024. Osteopathy, a hands-on manual therapy, is regulated very differently across Europe. Switzerland legally recognizes the profession, while Germany and Austria do not. The COCO project set out to learn how osteopaths themselves see their work in the three German-speaking countries. After a systematic search, the team synthesized thirty interview-based studies.

Practitioners described their core resources as manual treatment, a whole-person approach, and unhurried sessions. Teachers and prominent figures strongly shaped their outlook. The deepest challenge was identity: many struggled to define what osteopathy even is. Training paths and qualifications varied widely, the largest difference between the countries. Internal disagreements over standards added friction. On the bright side, osteopaths reported satisfying work and strong public demand. The authors say the field's future depends on settling its identity and training questions.
pmc-11658349:
Bin Xia and nineteen co-authors ask whether healthy eating patterns lower the risk of inflammatory bowel disease. Proof on diet and the two main forms of the disease, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, has been thin. The team followed nearly two hundred thousand adults in a British cohort who were free of the disease at the start. Four healthy diet scores were read from their food records.

Over the follow-up, 260 people developed Crohn's disease and 601 developed ulcerative colitis. Two diet scores, for a Mediterranean-style diet and a general healthy index, went with lower Crohn's risk but not colitis risk. Low body inflammation carried part of the benefit. The paper ties everyday eating to one form of the disease.
pmc-11658949:
Ni Shi and nine colleagues link pro-inflammatory and high-insulin dietary patterns to specific gut microbiome profiles, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Two empirical diet scores capture how strongly eating patterns drive inflammation and insulin response. Whether the colon's microbes mediate their disease effects was poorly understood. The analysis used over sixteen hundred adults in a British twin cohort.

Microbiome profiles were built from dozens of bacterial genera for each diet score. Higher profile scores tracked with higher insulin and insulin resistance. Six genera were shared between the two dietary patterns, some positive and some inverse. Predicted microbial pathways involved fatty acid building, sugar acid breakdown, and mevalonate metabolism. Those pathways also associated with the dietary scores themselves. The authors suggest diet may shape chronic disease risk partly through gut microbes.
pmc-11662949:
Yangning Zhou, Yan Wang, and Limin Xu pick out risk factors for postoperative cognitive dysfunction. That state can come after vessel treatment, done as an emergency for stroke, with general anaesthesia. Their 2024 study builds a model to forecast it, from signs in patients.

Three hundred thirty-three patients with acute ischaemic stroke took part. About a third of them got cognitive dysfunction. Regression analysis picked two markers of inflammation and three signs of brain injury. They were used for a nomogram model used as a set. The measures picked took in a score for how severe the stroke was, a peptide tied to the heart, and a protein tied to brain injury. Checks of the model took in calibration and curves for how much use it is in clinics. Results also hinted at links through anaesthesia depth, cognitive impairment, and inflammatory response in these patients.
pmc-11663549:
Maric sums up recent work in twenty twenty-five on how plants remember cold stress. Plants that survive a mild cold spell can build a kind of memory at the gene level. That memory helps them cope better when cold strikes again, unlike plants that meet cold for the first time.

She explains two kinds of memory genes. Some stay switched at a new level after stress ends. Others return to normal, then react more strongly the next time. A study on young cucumber plants traced changes during the rest phase after cold. It found more work on making proteins and less on folding them. Marks on the gene packaging help hold these states in place.
pmc-11664049:
Onur Mutlu, Bengi Türk, and Furkan Asan report a rare seizure case in pregnancy in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Absence status epilepticus is a long stretch of blank, unresponsive episodes driven by seizure activity. It can appear for the first time in adults with no prior epilepsy.

Their patient was a woman aged twenty-two, pregnant, with no history of seizures. She arrived with reduced speech and a puzzled state. A brain wave test showed continuous, whole-brain spike-wave patterns at a steady rhythm. She improved after a sedative and a seizure drug. The authors say this is the first reported case of this condition starting during pregnancy.
pmc-11664249:
Majd Almech and co-authors survey medical students in Saudi Arabia on herbal medicine in a 2024 study. Herbal remedies are woven into the country's health culture, and its Vision 2030 plan promotes alternative practices with a stress on safety through education and research. Future doctors will meet patients who use these remedies daily, so what students know and believe about them matters.

The team surveyed students at three medical colleges over six months in 2024. They scored knowledge and perceptions and tested how the two vary with background traits. The title poses the paper's pointed question: should medical schools act now? Gaps in student knowledge, if found, would argue for teaching that covers benefits, risks, and drug interactions before these students prescribe.
pmc-11665549:
Jinoll, Workalemahu, and Adugna assessed mixed land-use planning in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in twenty twenty-four, asking what blending homes, shops, and leisure spaces does to a fast-growing city. Mixed planning promises shorter trips and livelier streets, but its full effects in the capital were unmeasured.

The team surveyed three hundred eighty-four households, forty planning specialists, and fourteen key informants in two sub-cities, drawing on data from twenty oh two to twenty seventeen. Effects on travel and access to services varied sharply from place to place. Planners and residents praised gains in economic life and social mixing, yet flagged real strains as well. The authors conclude there is no single recipe: each district's mix must fit its own conditions. Their recommendations aim at planning that supports growth without surrendering fairness or green space.
pmc-11666549:
Jose DeAndres and co-authors, editors of a research collection on the topic, survey the state of neuraxial therapeutics for pain. The term covers drugs delivered into the spaces around the spinal cord, rather than swallowed or injected into a vein. The approach is widely used for pain and other spinal disorders, and thousands of papers on it appeared in just the past five years.

Writing as a perspective, the authors explain why interest runs so high and lay out the major themes in how the spine encodes pain signals. They discuss how spinal delivery can place medicine close to its target while sparing the rest of the body. The piece serves as an invitation and a map for the research collection they edit. It points toward open questions about dosing, safety, and new drug forms.
pmc-11672649:
Yusuke Ota and co-authors examine hospital wastewater to see which drug-resistance genes are active there, not just present. Their study appeared in 2024. Hospital drains gather resistant bacteria, yet gene surveys based on DNA alone cannot tell which genes are switched on. The team combined gene reading of both DNA and RNA from the water. They also tested the water for antibiotic traces.

They found several common antibiotics in the sample, which can push bacteria to switch resistance genes on. Genes for resistance to many drugs were the most common. Gene copies carried on plasmids, small DNA rings that jump between bacteria, showed high activity for their amount. The authors say watching active genes gives a truer picture of the risk hospital wastewater poses.
pmc-11672849:
Khury and five co-authors revisit antibiotic cement spacers for diabetic foot bone infection with long follow-up, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Diabetic osteomyelitis prevalence rises despite better living standards globally. Fifty-five patients with grade two B wounds receive debridement plus cement spacer fixation. Median follow-up approaches two and a half years.

Over half achieve primary eradication without further intervention. Another share succeeds after a secondary procedure. Most reoperations occur within a month of the primary procedure. Age, sex, and gentamicin-only cement correlate with reoperation risk. Staphylococcus infection correlates inversely with reoperation in this cohort. Most cured patients never need cement removal at all.
pmc-11673249:
Marina Danalache and co-authors compared how two stem cell types respond mechanically to culture conditions, in a 2024 study. Cell behavior bends under physical forces, and growing conditions may reshape the cells meant for therapy. The team grew jaw periosteal cells and lab-induced stem cells under normal and low oxygen, with and without bone-forming cues, on two coatings.

Force microscopy measured each cell's stiffness and the stiffness of the mineral deposits the cells laid down. The induced cells stayed softer yet formed harder deposits in several settings. The two cell types answered the same conditions in opposite ways, a caution for standardizing cell products.
pmc-11673549:
Polina Klauzen, Liubov Basovich, Daria Shishkova, and colleagues review the role of macrophages in heart valve hardening in this two thousand twenty-four paper. In calcific aortic valve disease, immune cells, macrophages above all, help drive the valve's hardening. Macrophages inside narrowed valves show strong swelling activity, tilted toward pro-swelling types. Those cells release cytokines, chemokines, and microRNA that act straight on resident valve cells and push them toward hardening.

The review gathers proof that patient macrophages carry stronger pro-swelling traits. Soluble signals passed between cells shape them, but so do other forces. Notch signaling by direct cell contact also plays a part. Factors acting on parent cells as they mature matter too. The authors set out the data on these passed and contact-based signals. Their aim is a clearer picture of how immune cells steer valve disease and point to drug targets.
pmc-11673749:
Paulo Cezar de Freitas Mathias and a large research team published a rat study in two thousand twenty-four on how a mother's poor diet shapes her pups' metabolism. Mothers fed little protein while nursing can leave lasting marks on offspring. The team focused on stress hormones and sugar control in male offspring.

Rat mothers got a low-protein or normal diet for the first two weeks of nursing. At ninety days old, the male pups faced fasting or doses of a stress-hormone-like drug. Pups of low-protein mothers barely reacted to long fasting or to the drug given into the brain. Given the drug body-wide, both groups had blood sugar swings, but the low-protein pups reacted more strongly. The findings tie early diet to lifelong sugar handling.
pmc-11673849:
Yuqiao Dai leads a team on shape control of soft robots. Their work from twenty twenty-four uses neural networks for shape reading. Soft robots bend in a smooth line, unlike stiff arm robots.

To know their shape is hard, which blocks fine control. The team pulls outlines from camera views to get shape traits. A neural net learns how motor inputs map to shape output. A sim world then tests shape guesses and shape control. Results show the method can guess and copy soft shapes well. It offers a path to better soft robot control.
pmc-11675349:
Hua Zhang and five co-authors line up stem cells on a gel using magnetism, coaxing them toward bone, in a 2024 paper. Many tissues are anisotropic, built in aligned patterns that give them direction-specific strength. Copying that alignment in soft wet gels is hard. The team let magnetic iron oxide particles self-assemble on a polyethylene glycol gel under a steady magnet. The particles formed ordered ridges a few hundred nanometers high and about ten micrometers wide.

Layer-by-layer building varied the ridge density and height, and tilting the field stacked patterns into three dimensions. Bone marrow stem cells grown on the patterns aligned and leaned into bone formation. Aligned scaffolds like these could guide regrowth of tendon, muscle, and bone along their natural grain.
pmc-11675749:
Monika Jokubaite and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, whether water-based gels can unlock the skin benefits of caffeic acid. This plant compound fights oxidation and germs, which makes it attractive for skin care, but it needs a good carrier to reach the skin in useful amounts.

The team built gels from two common polymers and their mix, at varied strengths, and measured how fast the acid escaped each gel. Thicker gels released it more slowly, letting the team tune delivery. The finished gels killed a common skin bacterium and a yeast in tests. The work supports gels as practical carriers for plant compounds in creams and treatments.
pmc-11676749:
Manal Khowdiary and a large team analyze the chemistry of a salt-tough desert shrub and test its extract against disease models. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The shrub, Nitraria retusa, survives drought and salty ground and has a history in folk remedies.

Chemical scans found three plant acids as the main contents. In lab tests the extract fought free radicals slightly better than vitamin C at matched doses. It slowed several cancer cell lines while largely sparing a normal cell line, with a colon cancer line the most sensitive. It also blocked two enzymes that break down starch and sugar, a sign of possible diabetes use. The authors present the shrub as a source of natural compounds worth deeper study for therapy.
pmc-11676849:
Ryo Uchimido and co-authors describe a 2024 study of how body chemistry shifts over time in severe COVID-19. A skewed metabolism is a known part of the disease, but its path across the weeks of severe illness was unclear. The team tracked blood samples from patients on breathing machines in one intensive care unit.

They grouped samples into three spans: the first days, the next two weeks, and the month mark. Hundreds of small molecules were read at each span. Early on, non-survivors showed raised fuel burning across sugar, protein, and fat paths. Later, fat and hormone paths split the groups in fresh ways. Some paths stayed skewed at all spans. The authors say timing shapes what care could target.
pmc-11677249:
Pitiwat Lueangwitchajaroen and colleagues teach a computer to name human actions in video using only ordinary color frames, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Action recognition feeds fields from health care to self-driving cars. Richer sensors help, but depth cameras and motion rigs are rare outside labs, so the team squeezed more from plain video.

From color frames alone, pre-trained tools pulled out two extra streams: skeleton poses and optical flow, the pattern of motion. Their method fuses the three streams at three depths of the network, early, middle, and late, rather than only at the end. Using a large public video set and an EfficientNet model, the fusion reached ninety-one point five percent accuracy, beating single-stream and single-view rivals. The authors say the cheap trick rivals far costlier setups.
pmc-11677349:
Luca Landini and co-authors followed four patients with late-stage age-related macular degeneration who received a tiny implantable telescope in one eye, in a case series published in 2024. The device, placed through a smaller cut than its forerunner, magnifies central images for people whose central vision is largely gone. The team tracked electrical responses of the retina as well as reading vision.

Six months after surgery, all four patients had gained in both distance and near vision scores. The retina's response density rose in every eye, most strongly at the center of gaze and fading outward in rings. Response strength also rose overall, with one dip in one patient's center. The authors call the early results promising while stressing the series is only four cases.
pmc-11677649:
Mokgadi Makgobole and colleagues squeeze collagen from fish scales with a buffer borrowed from protein labs, and optimize the recipe statistically, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Fish processing waste is a sustainable collagen source if extraction cooperates. A Taguchi design varied acid strength, soaking time, and buffer volume to find the sweet spot with few experiments.

The optimum used half-molar acetic acid, a hundred milliliters, two hours of soaking, and ten milliliters of Tris-Glycine buffer. Temperature and buffer concentration proved the influential knobs. The product checked out as genuine type I collagen: infrared spectra showed the classic amide bands, and gel separation matched collagen's weight pattern. The amino acid mix was rich in glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline, the fibrous signature. Yield purity reached about seventeen milligrams per gram. The authors present the method as efficient and waste-cutting, pending scale-up validation.
pmc-11677849:
Lee and five co-authors study caffeine and gut aging in a worm model, in work from twenty twenty-four. Intestinal aging brings declining protein control as proteasome activity falls. That decline is a hallmark of age related disease.

Prior work showed caffeine improved gut integrity in aged Caenorhabditis elegans worms by reducing a yolk protein called vitellogenin. The new study traced the regulatory mechanism. Caffeine raised two proteasome related genes, pas-1 and pas-3. Higher proteasome action lowered the yolk protein load. The worm work names a pathway by which a common dietary compound may protect the aging gut.
pmc-11678149:
Anthony Salib and co-authors checked whether CT scans of the heart arteries stay readable in patients with high body weight. Doctors often avoid this scan, called CTCA, in obese patients for fear the images will be too poor to judge. The team reviewed scans from 703 consecutive patients sent for suspected artery disease, grouping them by body mass index and grading image quality.

Nearly 94 percent of studies were fully readable. Among the few poor studies, nine in ten of the wide, near-heart artery segments could still be judged, and only seven patients had unreadable main segments. The authors conclude the scan remains a sound test for the segments that matter most to prognosis, whatever a patient's weight.
pmc-11678349:
Mária Mörtl and co-authors test how bioplastic carrier bags break down at a full-size compost plant in a 2024 study. The bags were made of starch, additives, and a plastic called PBAT. Many past tests were small lab trials, so the team ran a large trial that matches real plant practice.

The trial mixed tons of manure and wood with tons of bags over twelve weeks. Heat in the piles peaked at seventy degrees and stayed high for weeks. By the last week, ninety-five percent of the bags had fallen apart. Tests with seeds showed mixed effects on sprouting, so the residue needs care. Lab checks traced how the bag material changed in form and makeup. The authors say the work can help sharpen compost rules.
pmc-11679649:
Jiadai Xue and co-authors published a 2024 study on polishing the metal molds used to shape X-ray telescope mirrors. The mirrors curve in complex ways, so a polishing tool must press evenly as the curve changes, or the surface ends up wavy. The team built a model that predicts how a soft, flexible tool removes material on such curved molds, tying pressure to contact size and angle.

The model draws on flat-surface polishing data and adjusts it for the mold's changing curve. The team also corrected the tool's effect in real time across several polishing rounds. Tests showed clear gains in surface shape, smoothness, and mirror performance. The work supports the fine optics needed for X-ray astronomy.
pmc-11680149:
A team of virologists compares epidemic and vaccine strains of orf virus in a paper from 2024. The catalog adds a ninth author absent from the head byline, so team framing is used here. Orf sickens livestock and sometimes people, and live vaccines guard herds. The epidemic and vaccine genomes proved ninety-nine point eight percent identical. Still, small changes clustered in telling places. The vaccine strain lost a stretch of non-coding DNA near the genome end.

Three point mutations changed proteins, and one frameshift broke another gene. Such terminal genes often tune virulence rather than growth. The authors argue these edits likely explain the vaccine's mildness. Matching vaccines to field strains could improve protection.
pmc-11681849:
Clement Delage leads a team with a case of Alport syndrome in a family. Their report from twenty twenty-four uses full gene code reads. Alport syndrome harms the kidneys, hearing, and eyes over time in those affected.

Three kin in one family had the dominant form of the disease. Full reads found a new large change in a collagen gene. That change had not been seen as a cause before. The case shows full reads can work as a first test. Large gene changes are a key cause of such diseases.
pmc-11682549:
Raziyeh Barzegar-Bafrouei and four co-authors measure how often Salmonella bacteria contaminate traditional dairy products and raw milk in one Iranian province, and how drug-resistant those germs are. Their study came out in 2024. Salmonella food poisoning is among the most common foodborne infections worldwide.

From three hundred fifty samples, about one in fifteen carried the bacterium, confirmed by a genetic marker test. Contamination did not cluster in particular products or sources. Resistance was highest against an older antibiotic, while three stronger drugs still worked against over nine in ten isolates. The authors warn that both contamination and multi-drug resistance are rising in traditional dairy production there. Their findings argue for tighter hygiene in small-scale dairy supply.
pmc-11682749:
Young teeth that die before their roots finish growing are hard to save, since the root stays thin and open at the tip. Mohamed Abdelsalam and co-authors tested ways to regrow tissue inside such teeth in a 2024 animal study. They compared a plain blood clot with the same clot plus one of two soft gels used as a frame for new growth.

Sixteen young dog teeth were cleaned, treated, and checked under a lens three months later. All treated roots grew more tissue and showed less swelling near the tip than roots left alone. The gel made from a natural body sugar did not calm cell counts as well as hoped. Even so, the basic cleaning and clot method helped on its own, which keeps the simpler route in play for young patients.
pmc-11683649:
Ajay Khopade and Nitin Chitranshi published a materials study in 2024. They built tiny drug-carrying particles with layered cores. The core pairs an antibiotic, tobramycin sulfate, with a fatty acid. Together they form thin repeating layers at nanoscale size. A common dispersing agent helped form separate particles. The team tuned mixing to control particle size. They named the core-shell particles lamellosomes.

Tests showed the layered core survived strong mixing. Particles carried a mild negative surface charge. They stayed separate in salty water at tested levels. Acid changes could clump or break them apart. The core could also hold a second drug, dexamethasone. That drug was released much more slowly. Such carriers could suit controlled drug delivery.
pmc-11685149:
Sandra Evans and co-authors argue in a 2024 policy brief that better data should drive national vaccine decisions. Vaccination across the whole lifespan, not just childhood, brings broad value that spans generations. Showing that value takes stronger data systems, teamwork across fields, and shared methods.

New tools such as machine learning and language processing can sharpen analysis and live tracking of disease and uptake. The brief backs a grading process for evidence, strengthened with real-world data from daily practice. Mixing many study types helps capture how behavior and local settings change results. Decision makers get a plan for evidence that keeps pace with fast outbreaks and uneven local needs.
pmc-11689649:
Matt Yousefzadeh gives an overview, from twenty twenty-four, of how aging changes the immune system. As people age, the immune system works less well. That loss makes it harder to fight germs. It also plays a role in many long-term illnesses of old age. A second process is steady, low-level swelling in the body even when no germ is present.

Yousefzadeh notes that much is still not known. Scientists do not yet fully grasp how immune aging talks to the rest of the body. The talk points to new work at basic, applied, and treatment levels. Readers get a plain map of two core ideas and the open questions.
pmc-11690349:
Jacqueline Mogle and co-authors ask why people fail to finish intended daily activities in a 2024 diary study. Completing chores, exercise, or work tasks draws on planning and other thinking skills. Yet when people explain a missed task, they may cite time, health, or forgetfulness rather than cognition.

More than two hundred adults kept evening diaries for a week. On about half of days, at least one of eight intended activities went unfinished. Not enough time was the most common reason. Older adults reported unfinished activities more often than younger adults, and also blamed lack of time more.
pmc-11690649:
Anna-Christina Kainradl writes, in twenty twenty-four, on the care stories of older migrants. Her paper is a theory and ethics piece, not a data study. She notes that race, sex, class, nation, and age can combine to block fair care. Most accounts of these lives come from staff or family, not from the older people themselves.

Kainradl uses a lens that looks at how those forces overlap. She applies it to stories told by older migrants and by care staff. She asks what the lens adds to the study of aging. She also weighs postcolonial views, which stress the lasting weight of empire, as a further tool.
pmc-11691049:
Chiung-Jung Wen and co-authors track what pushes older patients into or out of frailty in a 2024 prospective study. Frailty, the state of low reserve that makes a fall or illness dangerous, is not one-way: people worsen, hold steady, or improve. Little work had pinned down the factors behind those moves. The team recruited patients from a geriatric outpatient clinic at a medical center.

Frailty was scored at the start and again one year later with a modified standard checklist, next to background, health, and geriatric measures. Of one hundred forty participants, nearly half worsened over the year, a small share improved, and the rest held steady. After adjustment for other traits, the analysis names the factors tied to change. Knowing them lets clinics aim support at the patients most likely to slide.
pmc-11691249:
Theresa Allison, Alexander Smith, Jennie Gubner, and Kenneth Covinsky published a 2024 study of home dementia care, drawn from two ethnographic projects on music and daily life. The team coded interviews and field notes from 83 people: 38 living with dementia, 34 family care partners, and 11 professionals. Contact ranged from one phone interview to eight home visits over two years.

Families described a recurring mismatch: the help on offer did not fit the care actually needed. The gap bit hardest in the walking-around stages of dementia and when the care partner also had several illnesses. Spirituality stood out as a strong motive to keep caring. Solid social support and money were named as critical. The authors call for support designs that fit real home situations.
pmc-11692049:
M K Kirsten Chui and co-authors present a 2024 study testing whether boosting a key cellular fuel calms the inflammation behind delirium in mice. Delirium, an acute confusional state often triggered by illness, has no effective drug treatment. It travels with inflammation and metabolic trouble. The fuel in question, NAD+, supports energy production and moderates immune activity.

The team gave mice a direct precursor of NAD+ alongside a bacterial toxin that induces sickness resembling delirium. Blood profiling followed. The supplement did not rescue the sickness behaviour or the metabolic disturbance, the authors report, but it did modulate the wider inflammatory response. The mixed result still maps where this lever acts and where it does not.
pmc-11692649:
Cristina de Rosa and Yu-Ping Chang published a study in 2024 on a mobile app teaching mindfulness-based stress reduction to older adults in underserved communities. Mindfulness practices involve calm breathing and focused attention. The community in the study was primarily African American and faced barriers to mental health care during the COVID-19 pandemic and afterward.

Seventeen adults took part in an eight-week intervention delivered through the app, then shared their experiences in interviews. Most participants were women aged around sixty-six. Four themes emerged. The app made participants open to the practice and broke down barriers to care. It helped them notice themselves and the world around them more clearly. They could draw on the practice whenever they chose, in calm times and in difficult ones. It also helped them build routines that kept them calm. The researchers found the app feasible and well liked.
pmc-11692849:
Joseph Shen and four co-authors measure how losing several senses at once relates to depression in older adults. Their study came out in 2024. Hearing, vision, smell, and touch each fade with age, and each loss alone has been tied to low mood.

The study covered just over eight hundred participants in their seventies to nineties with objective tests of all four senses. Most had at least one loss, and a small share had all four. Each additional sensory loss came with about a ten percent higher depression symptom score, after full adjustment. The effect stacked up sense by sense rather than appearing only at the extreme. The authors urge clinicians to treat combined sensory loss as a mental health risk worth acting on.
pmc-11693049:
Barbekka Hurtt and a team of co-authors explore running as part of healthy aging over fifty years, in two thousand twenty-four. Running is easy to start and has a low barrier for any age. Social and population shifts over that span may have changed what running means to older adults.

The team gathered surveys and interviews through social media, running groups, and marathon events. Older runners linked the sport to stronger bones, heart, and mood. All said their mood worsened when they took time off. Interviewees praised older athletes, yet most disliked the phrase about playing like an old person. Many wanted better local chances for older runners.
pmc-11708949:
Sibel Kara and co-authors compare lung cancer in patients whose lungs are scarred by fibrosis, in a 2024 study from several centers. Lung cancer is a known companion of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, the unexplained scarring form, but less is known about cancer in other scarring types. The team reviewed records from 2010 to 2022.

The study covers 251 patients, 164 with the idiopathic form and 87 with other forms. Most were older men with a history of smoking. Scan patterns differed: a honeycomb look marked the idiopathic group, while haze and air trapping marked the other. The most common cancer type was squamous cell carcinoma, then adenocarcinoma. Survival was short in both groups, with a median of about two years, and five-year death rates above 60 percent.
pmc-11709549:
Aina Comas-Alberti and co-authors study gene activity in blood from people with the inherited form of Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 paper. This rare form runs in families and stems from faults in one of three genes. It makes up only a small share of all cases. Most gene studies focus on the common late-onset form and on brain tissue, not blood.

Earlier work by the group found nine genes whose activity differed in both brain tissue and lab-grown cells from patients. Here they test those genes, plus three genes tied to the disease, in whole blood. The goal is to find blood signs that track the disease and hint at how it harms the brain. Easy blood markers could aid early trials and diagnosis in these families.
pmc-11710049:
Marta Olah reviews a 2025 conference abstract on microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, and Alzheimer's disease. Two findings reshaped the field in the past decade. Many risk genes for the disease act mainly in microglia, and the cells come in far more varied states than once thought. Whether those two facts connect has stayed unclear.

Olah's team measured disease-linked proteins within single microglia subsets from aged and diseased human brains. The pattern of proteins differed by subset, which means the cell's state shapes what a risk gene does. The talk argues that future gene studies and drugs must reckon with this variety.
pmc-11710549:
Lucineia Danielski and co-authors describe a 2025 rat study of vitamin D and a memory drug after loss of female hormones. Low hormone levels after the change of life may raise dementia risk. Vitamin D has shown guard effects in the brain, so the team tested doses in rats.

Female rats had their ovaries removed and were then given vitamin D, the drug, or both for three weeks. Brain areas tied to memory and planning were checked for swelling signals. One month after surgery, two harm signals rose, and the higher vitamin D dose brought them back down. After eight months, one signal still rose and the same dose helped. The authors see a dose linked guard effect.
pmc-11712249:
Roos J Jutten and co-authors ask whether a standard computer test battery tracks decline in Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. The battery, the NIH Toolbox, was built to give research studies one shared, brief test set. The team used data from 178 adults in the ARMADA study across nine United States centers.

Participants fell into three groups: healthy, symptom-free with brain amyloid, and early disease with amyloid. The early disease group scored lower at the start on most thinking tasks. Over two years they also fell faster on speed and working memory tasks. The battery showed no gap for the symptom-free amyloid group. The authors say the tests suit early symptomatic disease better than silent disease.
pmc-11712349:
Aldana Lizarraga and co-authors study brain network links in the earliest stage of Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 report. They used data from 328 adults with normal thinking in the ALFA cohort, average age near sixty-one. Spinal fluid tests showed amyloid and tau status, and resting brain scans measured how regions sync their activity.

About thirty-eight percent had positive amyloid markers in their fluid. Low amyloid ratios went with stronger sync between visual areas and the default-mode network, a set of regions active at rest. High tau shifted links in other region pairs. The amyloid-linked sync pattern predicted later decline in memory and planning over about three years of follow-up. The authors say early network change may warn of decline before symptoms.
pmc-11712449:
Samantha Shah and co-authors report a dementia screening toolkit built into the electronic health record in this 2025 paper. Alzheimer's disease touches at least one in ten people over sixty-five, yet their hospital's records showed four percent of such patients carried the diagnosis. The gap fell hardest on Black and Hispanic patients.

The tool takes under five minutes: three questions about changes in language, memory, and personality for the patient and a family informant, then a memory test if needed. A Spanish version was shaped for the Hispanic community. Patients answer through the record system before visits, and results flow into the doctor's note with advice. In fourteen months at a diverse Los Angeles clinic, over a thousand patients were screened. Thirty-one received a dementia diagnosis and eighty-one were sent to neurology. The authors present the build as a model for fairer screening.
pmc-11712749:
Andrew Mao, Sebastian Flassbeck, Elisa Marchetto, Henry Rusinek, and Jakob Assländer test a brain scan method, published in 2025, that might track amyloid without tracers. The method is called quantitative magnetization transfer MRI. It senses large molecules in tissue, and amyloid is one of them. Earlier work suggested it could separate patients from healthy people. The team asked whether it works before symptoms start.

Fourteen people with no thinking problems took the special scan, which took twelve minutes. Standard scans mapped each brain, and past tracer scans gave amyloid levels. Two measures from the new scan fell as amyloid rose, most clearly in the temporal lobe. One of those links is new, since most methods fix that value. The size of the large-molecule pool did not change. The authors call the method promising but say a larger group must confirm it.
pmc-11712849:
Ying Xia and colleagues published a long-term study in 2025 on early Alzheimer disease, using data from a large Australian aging study. Hundreds of older adults without dementia had brain scans, memory tests, and amyloid imaging over many years. The team tracked shrinkage in a small brain region that supports memory and attention.

Adults with amyloid buildup lost volume faster in that region and in the hippocampus, and their scores fell faster too. Shrinkage helped explain how amyloid buildup connects to falling scores, with different regions mattering more for memory than for attention. The findings point to early brain change as a key link in the disease.
pmc-11712949:
Lloyd Tran, Zung Vu Tran, and Fern Vu present a 2025 paper linking two drug candidates, one for Alzheimer's disease and one for obesity. The first drug is said to protect nerve cells and support new cell growth and memory. The second is a close cousin that acts on three hormone signals tied to weight and blood sugar.

The paper reports a trial of the first drug in 112 people with mild to moderate disease, where scores improved more than with placebo over twenty-four weeks. It also reports a short mouse study of the second drug, with marked weight loss. The authors use both results to argue the two conditions share drug pathways.
pmc-11713049:
Swastik G Pattanashetty and co-authors describe a 2025 lab study that tests an old drug, terazosin, as a possible treatment for Alzheimer's disease. The drug is already approved for other uses, so its safety in people is well known. The team tested it in rats bred to develop the disease over time.

The drug works in two ways: it blocks one receptor and boosts an enzyme that helps cells make energy. Treated rats did better than untreated rats on tests of place learning and memory at nine and eleven months of age. The results support more study of the drug as a way to protect the brain.
pmc-11713249:
Slutsky-Ganesh and co-authors study how a year of exercise affects brain volume in adults at high risk for Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 paper. A gene variant raises risk and speeds shrinkage of the hippocampus, a memory hub. Exercise can grow that area in older adults, but midlife effects were unclear.

Forty-four inactive adults with a family history of the disease joined the trial subset. About half carried the risk gene. One group trained for a year while the other kept usual care. Scans at the start, middle, and end measured the memory hub. The authors test whether training helps, and whether the gene changes the benefit.
pmc-11714649:
Andrew Christopher Miguel and co-authors present a 2025 estimate of how much dementia goes unseen in Brazil. The number of cases there is set to triple by mid-century. Yet no national count of missed cases existed. The team worked from drug records in the public health system for one year. They combined those records with published shares for disease stage and drug use. That let them infer how many diagnosed cases there must be in total.

More than four in five people with dementia over age sixty appear to be undiagnosed. The share was highest in the north of the country and lowest in the southeast. Missed cases were more common in men than in women. They were also most common in the youngest old group, those aged sixty to sixty-four. The authors call the gap one of the highest in the world and urge faster action.
pmc-11714849:
Kensaku Kasuga and co-authors test blood markers for Alzheimer's disease in Japan in this 2025 study. New antibody drugs require biomarker proof of disease, but brain scans and spinal fluid tests are costly, scarce, or invasive. Blood tests promise cheap, repeatable screening.

The team studied two hundred seventeen patients who had spinal fluid testing, over half with an Alzheimer's clinical picture. A blood form of tau sorted disease from non-disease with high accuracy and tracked the key spinal marker well. Another blood marker separated Alzheimer's from a related vessel inflammation that mimics a drug side effect. The authors expect blood screening to guide who should get antibody therapy.
pmc-11715049:
Sofia Toniolo and co-authors test, in 2025, whether an online thinking test plus blood markers can spot Alzheimer's disease and mild subjective decline. Blood markers can flag the disease early, but tracking subtle thinking changes at scale needs remote tools. Their portal hosts validated tasks in memory, attention, and mental flexibility, plus two new visual memory tasks.

One hundred fourteen people took part: patients with the disease, people with subjective complaints, and healthy controls. The online test separated the complaint group from controls with fair accuracy, and all took standard in-person testing too. Blood measures of four markers were collected. The authors argue remote testing could support screening and follow-up at scale.
pmc-11715649:
Seth Robey, Ka Lai Yee, and Julie A Stone build a mathematical model that lines up many Alzheimer's biomarkers on one shared disease clock. The clock starts when amyloid, the first hallmark protein, turns positive. The markers do not move in step, so a shared clock helps trials pick the right patients. Their 2025 model was trained on records from ADNI, a large shared database in the United States.

Training used 831 adults who were amyloid positive, with scan and test scores over time. The model placed scans for both hallmark proteins and three cognitive test scores on the shared clock. It recovered the order of disease stages with no outside guide. When fed only baseline data for 76 new adults, it matched their real course two to seven years later. The authors see it as a tool for trial selection and personal forecasts.
pmc-11716949:
Naresh Damuka and co-authors present a 2025 study imaging the skeleton inside neurons as Alzheimer's disease unfolds. Microtubules are the rails that move cargo in brain cells, and tau protein normally steadies them. When tau falls away, the rails destabilize early in the disease, before plaques and tangles fully form.

A PET tracer built for microtubules let the team watch that change in living mouse brains over time. Two mouse models were followed, one for amyloid pathology and one for tau. Standard scans image the plaques and tangles themselves; this one aims at the earlier rail failure that links them. The longitudinal design tracks whether the signal grows with disease stage. An early marker could open treatment windows that current scans miss.
pmc-11717349:
Kanwar Parhar and co-authors pilot a peer coaching program for heart surgery patients, in a study from 2024. After heart surgery, rehab exercise cuts risk and aids survival. Yet only about a quarter of patients take part. The program paired new patients with a coach who had been through the same kind of surgery.

Ten patients joined and got four hour-long video sessions with the coach. Seven finished the program, and all of them went on to rehab. They averaged about nineteen rehab sessions each. Mood scores did not shift by a clear margin. Still, patients rated the coaching high for easing worry and for nudging them into rehab. The authors say the pilot shows promise but needs a bigger trial. A larger study with a control group could confirm the gains.
pmc-11727549:
Bondar and co-authors run in 2024 a pilot study of gender gaps in depression among patients with ischemic heart disease in Romania. Heart disease weighs on mental health, with unlike responses by gender. They recruited 183 adults with artery disease and depression at one hospital psychiatry unit from 2021 to 2024.

A self built questionnaire, paired with standard scales, profiled demographic, clinical, and social traits. Women showed higher emotional distress and more severe depression than men in the results. Women also reported greater social isolation and a stronger wish named in the head. Reliability of the new tool was checked by standard scores. The pilot maps where gender tailored support may help.
pmc-11728249:
Patricia Bermudez-Gomez and co-authors optimize in 2024 how mushroom stems can be turned into functional flour. Stems are a major waste product of mushroom farms. Two common species are studied, one whose stems stick to peat.

For the peat-stuck stems, abrasive peeling cleaned best, with low germ counts and good work rate. For drying, a dehydrator beat oven and freeze-dryer on color and energy use. Drying at fifty degrees for a day kept plant compounds as well as slower, cooler drying. The final process balances quality, cost, and speed for flour making.
pmc-11728449:
A rice-grown kefir product trimmed fat gain in mice fed a rich diet, and the gut seems to carry the tale. Takuto Kurakawa and eight co-authors dosed the mice in 2024 and watched weight, liver fat, and sugar handling. All three leaned the right way, sugar by a modest step. Droppings showed the gut crowd shift as the gains came.

Two germ clans tied to fatness thinned out, while two tied to leanness grew. A fat-burning acid in the droppings rose with the shift. Gene-path guesses from the germ mix pointed to sugar handling as the worked lever. The team read the product as a postbiotic, a germ-made good that works without live germs, and call for the chain to be traced link by link.
pmc-11728749:
Wenxia Bu and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four review of how polystyrene nanoplastics harm cells. Tiny plastic particles from pollution collect in living tissue. Their small size lets them enter cells and disturb basic machinery.

The review gathers evidence on oxidative stress, power plant damage, and DNA injury. Inflammation and faulty self-cleaning also appear. Several distinct death programs can be triggered, from quiet cell suicide to fiery inflammatory death. Particle size, surface treatment, other pollutants, and protein coatings all change the harm. The authors urge more mechanism research and stronger rules.
pmc-11728849:
Erik Turner and co-authors asked whether the temperature a mosquito actually lives at, indoors or out, changes how fast Zika and chikungunya grow inside it, in this 2024 study. Weather stations miss that difference, yet Aedes aegypti mosquitoes prefer homes. Using temperature records from Neiva, Colombia, the team ran both viruses through mosquitoes under indoor and outdoor profiles.

Mosquito survival barely moved. Infection rates shifted only slightly, though virus amounts in the body differed at several time points. Modeling told a stronger story for chikungunya: indoor warmth produced a much taller, earlier outbreak peak than outdoor conditions. For Zika, both settings gave high spread odds but few cases. The authors urge finer temperature data in risk models.
pmc-11774649:
Omar Larentis and co-authors report, in a paper whose head is dated 2024, a joint study of three mummies kept at a cliffside sanctuary in Italy. The hermits' bodies date from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries and were revered locally, yet science knew little about them. Moving the bodies was impossible, so the team brought portable X-ray gear to the site.

Mobile digital X-rays let experts from many fields read cloth, past repairs, insect traces, bone traits, and disease signs in place. The approach trades the depth of a full body scanner for access where none exists. New facts about the hermits' lives and deaths emerged, bringing these figures into the scientific record for the first time.
pmc-11784049:
Anan Chaokaur and six colleagues published a goat feeding study in two thousand twenty-four on purple Napier grass silage. The purple pigment, anthocyanin, is a strong antioxidant. It may protect dairy animals from cell stress and lift production.

Nine milking crossbred goats were fed corn silage, plain Napier grass silage, or the purple version. Intake and digestion were tracked, and milk and blood were tested for makeup and antioxidant power. Goats on corn silage ate the most feed and fibre. Protein intake was similar across the three diets. The study sets up a comparison of whether the pigment-rich silage brings blood or milk benefits beyond the plain grass.
pmc-11803449:
Samantha González-Téllez and Meritxell Riquelme (2024) identified a helper protein that ships a wall-building enzyme out of the fungal cell's packaging center. Chitin gives fungal walls their strength, and enzymes called chitin synthases make it. In baker's yeast, a chaperone escorts one such enzyme from the endoplasmic reticulum onward. The mold Neurospora crassa carries two versions of that escort. Earlier work tied the first version to one synthase. This study tested the second, named CSE-8.

Deleting the gene for CSE-8 kept the class I synthase CHS-3 from reaching its work sites. The glowing tagged enzyme vanished from the growing tip and cross-walls. Sexual development also faltered in the mutant, and removing both escorts cut chitin content and slowed growth. Stress tests supported the picture of CSE-8 as a reticulum worker. The authors map a division of labor between the two escorts in filamentous fungi.
pmc-11808149:
Peng and eight co-authors study Chinese peony flowers as a new food ingredient, in work dated twenty twenty-four. The root of peony is a known Chinese herb. Its flowers are a major waste by product that may hold value.

Samples from four cultivars were profiled with a high resolution mass method in a three level strategy. One hundred fifty compounds were identified, more than fifty of them new reports for this species. Targeted measures split flower parts clearly. Cell tests and four chemical assays checked anti swelling and antioxidant power. Turning herb waste into a food ingredient could add income and cut waste.
pmc-11835849:
Catherine Wilkinson wrote this reflective paper, published in 2024 though the catalog lists 2025, on designing research with and for people who live with chronic pain. Wilkinson writes as a researcher who also lives with two painful long term conditions. Study designs often bend for participants' pain, with breaks for flare ups and quiet spells. The researcher's own pain is rarely planned for.

The paper draws lessons from that double view. It asks how methods can serve the bodies of both sides of the study at once. It also reflects on the bond between researcher and participant when pain is shared ground. The aim is research ties that are both kinder and more productive.
pmc-11842349:
Rongjing Xu and co-authors explore what older adults in Shanghai know about mental health in a study published in 2024. Mental health literacy means knowing how to spot mental illness, hold sound views about it, and act to stay well. China's older population is growing fast, and gaps in this knowledge can delay care.

Twenty older adults from four city communities sat for deep interviews. Three themes came out of the talks. Knowledge of mental health and illness was thin. Views on keeping the mind healthy and preventing illness leaned negative, with stigma in the mix. Daily habits to guard mental health were patchy. The authors call for joint effort by people, families, and society to teach, to fight stigma, and to support healthy habits. They tie the work to a national healthy aging plan.
pmc-11881649:
Caleb Nault reviewed a 2024 book by Andrea Jamison on decentering whiteness in library collections. The book offers a framework for more inclusive collection management. It appears amid book bans and protests aimed at works by or about marginalized groups.

Jamison draws on long work in school libraries and teaching. The book gives practical steps to review collection policies for bias. Nault places it within wider efforts on diversity and fair hiring in libraries. He presents it as a useful guide for staff who want collections that serve all readers more fairly.
pmc-11883249:
Tuba Demirci Yildirim and co-authors weigh how well young patients move from paediatric to adult rheumatology care. Their 2024 study looks back on past cases. It covers moves of care in Turkey from 2013 to 2023.

Of more than twenty-five hundred patients who were sent on, about eight percent moved with success. That was set by their keeping up visits each year to the adult clinic. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and familial Mediterranean fever were the diseases seen in most cases. The median time for the move was four months. Close to half moved early. Use of biologic drugs was linked to an early move. Higher education, and one diagnosis, were linked to a late move. Care changed for about half the patients after the move. The study sets those changes out.
pmc-12008349:
Houyem Khiari and co-authors present a 2024 report from the Northern Tunisia Cancer Registry. Cancer is a leading cause of illness and death in Tunisia. The registry tallied estimated new cases for 2023 and projected rates out to 2040, giving planners a view of the coming burden.

Standardized incidence reached about 166 per 100,000 men and 141 per 100,000 women, counting skin cancers. In men, lung, colorectal, bladder, prostate, and stomach cancers led the list. In women, breast cancer led by a wide margin, followed by colorectal, uterine, thyroid, and lung cancers. The registry gathers cases actively from public and private care. Projections used an age-period-cohort model. The numbers guide screening and treatment planning.
pmc-12384249:
An and Yang study what drives fall prevention acts by long-term care nurses in Korea. Falls harm many older hospital patients each year. The survey held 136 nurses from four large care hospitals. Data were gathered in August 2021. Belief scales and safety culture scores were the predictors.

Safety culture views and age each predicted prevention acts. Perceived seriousness and action drive also added weight. Perceived barriers cut acts, with a negative weight. The full model explained 44.5 percent of the spread. The authors urge culture work plus belief-based training for nurses.
pmc-12539549:
Alicja Nowak and Małgorzata Ogurkowska review how physical activity shapes bone health in a 2024 paper. Bone adapts to the loads placed on it, most where stress is greatest. The response differs between spongy and dense bone tissue.

Both mechanical forces and body-wide signals steer bone metabolism during exercise. Hormones, muscle factors, and immune signals all play a part. Bone-building cells burn much glucose, so nutrition matters when activity raises energy demand. Training effects vary with age and sex. The authors stress picking the right dose of intensity, duration, and frequency for each person.
pmc-12661849:
Kajganic and five co-authors test a stimulation pattern for paralyzed leg muscles during cycling therapy, in work from twenty twenty-five. Functional electrical stimulation cycling moves paralyzed legs by stimulating the quadriceps. Muscle fatigue limits session length and power.

Spatially distributed sequential stimulation spreads the pulses across muscle sites in sequence. It had shown greater fatigue reduction and power in static contractions than conventional stimulation. The study applied it during motor assisted cycling, a more realistic therapy task. Better endurance in cycling sessions could raise the training dose that spinal cord injury patients can tolerate.
pmc-12662949:
Florence Leduc and co-authors review work that pairs tree-ring records with satellite data to watch forests, in a review from two thousand twenty-five. Rings track wood growth year by year, while satellite greenness tracks leaf activity and canopy cover. The two views differ in scale and can enrich each other.

Seventy-eight studies were sorted into three themes: links to climate, long-term growth trends, and responses to shocks. Ring and greenness records often moved together within single years. Over long spans they often split apart. Rings showed deeper, longer drops after shocks than greenness did. Scale mismatch remains a core hurdle.
pmc-12663549:
Tufa and co-authors test in 2025 how well drugs work in the lab against a parasite from patients in northwest Ethiopia. The parasite causes visceral leishmaniasis, and HIV co infection makes care hard, with relapse a common problem. Samples came from a treatment center in Gondar during 2020.

They tested 30 parasite isolates from first episodes and relapses, in patients with and without HIV. Three standard drugs were checked at one parasite stage, and ten isolates were retested at a second stage. Mean doses needed to halt growth are reported for each drug. Such profiles help judge whether drug resistance plays a part in relapse.
pmc-12664149:
Mehtap Gürler Balta and co-authors compare two nerve block methods for pain relief after breast removal surgery, in a randomized trial from 2025. Good pain control after surgery shapes how well patients recover. Both blocks numb the chest wall, but their effect on overall recovery quality was unproven.

Sixty-eight women having the surgery were split at random between the two blocks. Recovery quality was scored with a standard forty-item survey at one and two days after surgery. Pain scores, opioid use, and time to first pain request were also tracked. The two groups scored almost the same on recovery quality. The first pain request came after a long delay in both groups. The authors treat the blocks as near equals for this surgery.
pmc-12664249:
Mohammad Hassan Emamian and a large team track the safety of the Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine in young people in this two thousand twenty-five study from Iran. The vaccine had proved safe in adults and children, but data for teens stayed thin. The study followed children and teens aged five to eighteen in eight cities. Families joined after the first dose. Staff phoned them daily for a week after each dose.

The callers logged sore arms, fever, and other reactions. They also watched for breakthrough infections and serious events over a longer span. This style of study, called cohort event monitoring, catches side effects as they happen. The findings add real-world safety data for a vaccine given to millions of young people. Parents and health officials can use it to weigh risks.
pmc-12693549:
Martin Eckert, Thomas Ostermann, Jan Peter Ehlers, and Gregor Hohenberg test an open-world virtual reality program for people with dementia. Their 2025 pilot study builds on talking therapy that stimulates thinking, a drug-free aid for dementia care. Open virtual worlds that users can explore freely have been little studied for this group.

Three men with dementia took one seated session, moving an avatar with arm and head motions. All finished with no adverse events, and the average session ran close to half an hour. Surveys showed acceptance and a positive view of ease of use. Mood changed only a little, but reports told of deep immersion and memories being stirred. The small pilot supports larger tests of safety and benefit.
pmc-12694149:
Salty soils already spoil about a fifth of irrigated farmland, and the share is set to grow. Sajida and co-authors review in this 2025 paper two helpers that shield crops from salt: helpful root bacteria and tiny particles of silicon, plus the newer idea of using both together.

Each helper on its own steadies plant ions, builds protective compounds, and switches on stress genes. Together they may do more, but trials at field scale are still scarce, and questions remain about particle stability and microbe compatibility. The review maps the mechanisms and case studies, and it marks where proof is still missing.
pmc-12695949:
Yaqi Wu and five co-authors reveal the three dimensional structure of the machine that herpes simplex virus uses to copy its DNA, in this 2025 study. The machine, a three part primosome, unwinds the viral DNA and lays down starter pieces for copying. It is a prized drug target, but how it works had stayed murky.

Using electron microscopy, the team froze the machine holding a strand of DNA and read its shape at fine detail. The picture shows an open groove where DNA sits and tight contacts among all three parts. Follow-up tests mapped the active sites and the joints between parts. The authors propose the machine unwinds DNA through a two way rotation, switching between unwinding and starter making. The design is shared across the herpes family, which may aid broad antiviral design.
pmc-12700149:
Steinmann and six co-authors test if first grade takes shift by school race in this twenty twenty-five study. Young heal hands of far roots oft score low in ward grade rounds. First takes may stick or shift as act grades change in a meet.

Inside, medics watched tapes of school acts that rose or fell cross time. First takes at one mark showed no race gap in the grades. Rise acts won high end grades for far-root youth from young medics. Grade shifts tween first and end takes ran large for that band. Both rise and fall tapes drew those large shifts in the runs.
pmc-12700549:
Yue Li and co-authors find, in a 2025 mouse study, that a swollen spleen cell type actively feeds leukemia growth by rewiring the cancer cells' fat use. As the marrow fails in this blood cancer, the spleen takes over blood making. A marked class of young red blood cells ballooned in the spleens of sick mice.

Those cells poured out a signal protein that latched onto the cancer cells and switched on a growth pathway. The cancer cells then shifted their fat balance, hoarding whole fats over broken ones. Adding back the broken fats, or cutting a key gene, restored balance and blunted the tumor boost. The crosstalk names new drug targets.
pmc-12701049:
Chih-Chieh Hsu and co-authors uncover in 2025 how a mouth bacterium survives in the bloodstream during heart valve infection. Streptococcus gordonii can cause infective endocarditis. It carries a type VII secretion system that exports a protein called EsxA, whose role was unclear.

Deleting the export machinery stopped the protein's release; restoring it brought release back. In rats, bacteria lacking the protein survived poorly in blood and built smaller growths on heart valves. The secreted protein also made neutrophils cast out their DNA nets, and pure protein alone triggered the nets dose by dose. The authors conclude the nets, meant as traps, instead help the bacterium persist and grow.
pmc-12701849:
Hartleif and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on using a scope test to rule out a blocked bile duct disease in jaundiced newborns. The disease scars and closes the bile ducts, and early surgery gives the child's own liver its best chance. No blood or scan test can rule it out for sure, so open surgery has been the default proof. The team tested whether a camera passed into the bile duct could do the job.

Sixty infants at one German hospital were scheduled for the scope test at a median age of fifty days. The test worked in all but two. In twenty-three babies the ducts could not be shown, which pointed to the disease. In thirty-five the ducts looked normal and the disease was ruled out. The test caught every true case with no major side effects.
pmc-12705749:
Dexiang Li and five co-authors compare how an invasive water plant and a native water plant shift their root and leaf traits when nitrogen is added. Trait links across organs show how plants invade and adapt. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

A space for time design varied invasion degree and nitrogen dose. Added nitrogen grew both species, but the invader gained more mass and pushed the native out at mid and high invasion levels. Invasion, nitrogen, and their interplay moved most traits in both species, yet their root and leaf replies split sharply. Trait to mass links ran stronger in the invader.
pmc-12706049:
Butrint Aliu and seven co-authors report a 2025 study of a sugar-coated polymer built to clear harmful antibodies from the blood. The target is a nerve disease in which the immune system makes IgM antibodies against a sugar mark on nerve insulation. Those antibodies strip the insulation and cause numbness and weak balance. The polymer, called PPSGG, copies the sugar mark so the antibodies bind to it instead.

Tests show the long, strongly charged polymer is picked up by scavenger cells in the liver and spleen. It binds the harmful antibodies one-to-one or one-to-two, without forming clumps. The paired loads are then eaten and broken down by those cells, in mice and in human cells in the lab. No liver harm was seen, and the team calls it a path to the first targeted care for the disease.
pmc-12706749:
Carissa Lange and colleagues published a school environment study in 2025. They measured air and noise pollution in Accra schools. Children spend much of their day at school. Little data existed for African school settings before. Ninety schoolyards across Greater Accra were monitored. Measurements ran for a full week at each site. Fine particles, black carbon, and sound were recorded. Yard surfaces, greenery, and roads were documented. Over one thousand children answered noise surveys too.

Particle levels exceeded health guidelines by large margins. Pollution varied strongly between schools in the city. Nearby roads and yard features helped explain differences. Private and public schools faced different exposure patterns. Noise annoyed many children during school hours. Cleaner, quieter schoolyards could support learning and health.
pmc-12707149:
Dongqiang Song, Xueyi Feng, Yingting Zhou, Yu Cai, and Tongchun Xue present a 2025 study on a combined treatment for liver cancer that cannot be cut out. The method threads a catheter into the tumor's blood supply and blocks it with drug-loaded beads plus an oily contrast agent called lipiodol.

The study enrolled 120 patients treated between December 2017 and August 2020. Median survival reached about thirty-one months, and three quarters of patients had their disease controlled for a time. About a fifth saw strong tumor shrinkage. Tumor size and later conversion therapy were the two factors that independently shaped survival. Side effects were mostly the expected post-procedure syndrome, liver tests wobbled briefly, and no severe grade four events occurred.
pmc-12708649:
Simin Nie and three co-authors compute how doping changes superconductors in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Superconductors carry current with no loss below a transition temperature. Recent high-pressure hydrides revived the hunt for higher temperatures. The team used first-principles calculations on five pure elements: molybdenum, niobium, lead, aluminum, and zirconium. They added or removed electrons to mimic doping.

Both kinds of doping strengthened the link between electrons and lattice vibrations. That link sets the transition temperature, so it rose in each case. Softer vibrations and certain key phonons drove the gain. Each element showed a best doping level for the highest temperature. The study gives materials hunters a cheap screen before lab work.
pmc-12708749:
Pamela Alebna and four co-authors published a 2025 review of treating obesity in heart failure, where heavier patients oddly survive longer, the so-called obesity paradox. Once heart failure sets in, higher body mass seems protective in observational data. The review weighs fitness and lean mass as the deeper drivers behind that pattern, and examines new incretin-based weight-loss drugs.

These drugs cut weight and help some heart failure types, but their role in reduced-function hearts is unsettled. Big weight loss may also burn lean mass, a danger for frail patients. The authors urge judging treatment by fitness, walk capacity, and quality of life, not weight alone. They call for fresh studies matching modern drugs to the right patients.
pmc-12716549:
Frank Peinemann and co-authors present a 2025 review of two drug strategies for advanced melanoma with a BRAF gene change. One strategy pairs two immune drugs that free the body's own attack. The other pairs two targeted drugs that hit the tumor's growth path. Both are used as first care, and head-to-head proof is thin. The team pooled the trial proof on survival and harm.

The search found just two trials with 305 patients in all. Both trials used chance-based splits and full-group analysis. The reviewers graded how sure the pooled proof is and weighed bias in each trial. Sparse proof is itself a finding for such a costly choice. The review gives doctors a clear view of what is known and what is not.
pmc-12717449:
Butler and six colleagues map where a soft tick that can carry African swine fever lives in the United States in twenty twenty-five. The fever is a deadly pig disease not yet in the country. Wild hogs plus this tick could let it take root if it arrives. The team gathered tick records from papers and field work, mostly in Texas.

Six weather and land traits best predicted where the tick can live. The map runs from southern California to Texas, with a lone zone in Florida. Most of Texas looks highly fit for the tick. Host species were richest in Florida and central Texas, which the team flags for close watch. Ticks in warthog burrows raise the stakes.
pmc-12721049:
Blood cultures take days and miss hard-to-grow germs, so Qichuan Fu and co-authors look for fingerprints in the fragments of DNA that pathogens shed into blood. Their 2025 study sequenced plasma from about one hundred patients with bacterial, viral, or parasitic bloodstream infections. Pathogen fragments ran shorter than human ones, and each kingdom had its own length signature.

Bacterial pieces averaged shortest, viral pieces a bit longer, and one virus that hides in a protein shell mimicked human lengths. Parasite pieces spread too widely to read by length. The authors see fragment patterns as a fast companion to culture, pending bigger validation.
pmc-12722049:
How a country treats its animals begins with what its people believe animals feel. Azadeh Jalali-Motahari and co-authors run the first broad survey of those beliefs in Iran in a 2025 study of three hundred twenty-five respondents.

The validated questionnaire covered farmed, companion, and wild animals. Most respondents rated animal welfare important and wanted practices improved. Support for protective laws was broad, despite uneven familiarity with different species. Over nine in ten agreed chickens feel pain, and four in five credited them with emotions, though scores varied by animal. Cultural, religious, and legal threads run through the answers. The authors offer the results as groundwork for Iranian welfare policy.
pmc-12723849:
Saeid Mirzaei and co-authors compared four drug treatment settings in Iran in a 2025 study. Drug use disorder is a lasting public health load in Iran, and several care types run side by side there. They range from daily methadone care and drop-in centers to live-in groups and forced care under a court rule.

The team followed clients in 15 routine centers in Kerman Province from May 2023 to May 2024. Of 493 who enrolled, 470 finished the follow-up span. Each setting was judged on its own change over the year. The side-by-side view may help Iran steer funds to the care forms that hold gains.
pmc-12727049:
Laura Giglio and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-five study of brain predictors for whether aphasia therapy gains spread to everyday discourse. Naming practice helps word-finding, but conversation is the real prize. Brain integrity before treatment might forecast that transfer.

Eighty-eight people with chronic post-stroke aphasia received semantic or sound-based therapy. Lesion and white-matter maps were related to discourse measures before and after treatment, and months later. Baseline talking productivity tied to dorsal-stream language pathways. The design separates predictors of starting ability from predictors of generalization, guiding realistic therapy planning.
pmc-12731449:
Swati Mamidanna and fifteen colleagues review the rise, fall, and partial revival of preventive brain radiation in small cell lung cancer. This aggressive cancer seeds the brain often. Irradiating the cranium after successful initial treatment once clearly extended survival, above all in limited-stage disease.

Newer trials with routine MRI surveillance found no survival benefit in extensive-stage disease. That makes watchful scanning, with salvage treatment if needed, a real alternative. Memory damage remains the chief cost, though hippocampus-sparing methods and protective drugs soften it. The arrival of immunotherapy scrambles the calculus further. The review maps where preventive irradiation still earns its place and where scans have taken its place.
pmc-12731549:
Hooman Soleymani Majd and a large surgical team describe a technique for a dangerous pregnancy condition in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In severe placenta accreta, the placenta grows too deeply into the womb wall. Delivery can then cause catastrophic bleeding. Many centers use radiology balloons to cut blood flow, but that service is costly and not always at hand. The team's method instead ties off pelvic arteries step by step under direct sight.

The technique forms part of their approach to caesarean hysterectomy for these cases. The paper sets out the surgical steps in detail. It also compares short- and long-term outcomes against the radiology route. Direct ligation, they argue, is safe and workable where radiology support is scarce. Obstetric surgeons facing this emergency are the readers.
pmc-12732649: Fernandez-Ferreiro and Giralddez-Fernandez introduce a special issue on dry eye at the molecular scale. Dry eye disease is a common disorder of the eye surface with many causes. It shows as tear film instability, eye discomfort, swelling, and blurred vision that comes and goes. The issue gathers work on the molecular roots of the illness and on new ways to understand and treat it.
pmc-12733549:
Some patients with atrial fibrillation keep a fast, irregular heartbeat despite drugs. One last resort treatment burns the heart's electrical relay node. A pacing defibrillator device is then implanted to keep both sides of the heart in step. Bagdat Akhyt and co-authors followed one hundred one such patients for five years at one center. Thirteen cardiovascular deaths occurred in that time. The team used machine learning methods to find which measures best predicted death.

Five measures carried the signal. They were how strongly the main pumping chamber squeezes, walking distance in six minutes, pressure in the lung artery, a relaxation measure, and the leakage of one heart valve. A model built on them classified outcomes with high accuracy. The authors are careful to call the analysis exploratory. They present the factors as candidates for personal risk checks and for designing future studies, not as settled rules.
pmc-12734149:
Çakan Demirel and a large team check in twenty twenty-five whether blood scores for inflammation and nutrition predict survival in advanced voice-box cancer. Such scores help forecast outcomes in many cancers, but their value in this cancer was untested. The team reviewed close to one hundred and fifty patients treated over a decade and computed six combined scores from routine blood tests.

Median survival was about four and a half years. High scores on most measures tied to shorter overall and progression-free survival. One combined score stood out as an independent predictor alongside stage and response to chemotherapy, while surgery helped survival. The authors urge routine use of these cheap scores to sort patients by risk.
pmc-12738749:
Andrea Vitores-Calero, Vanessa Paredes-Gallardo, and eight co-authors checked if a vibrating mouth device heats the mouth, in work from twenty twenty-five. The device, AcceleDent, is sold to speed tooth movement with clear aligners. Backers say it stirs cells and bone. Heat was the key test here: if the device warms tissue, that might help explain its effects, or raise safety flags.

Twenty-two adults in aligner care wore the device on and off on two days. A heat camera read gum and tooth surfaces after each use. No gap in heat showed up between the on and off days, at rest or after use. The team calls the device safe on heat grounds.
pmc-12740749:
Rolf Weimer and co-authors report five year results on immune effects after kidney transplantation across blood groups in a 2025 prospective pilot study.
