Such transplants carry higher risk of severe infection and antibody mediated rejection. A drug called rituximab is used at induction, and its long term immune effects needed tracking.

Eighty five recipients were followed, including living donor groups with compatible and incompatible blood groups and a deceased donor group. Incompatible recipients had double the severe infections in two years. Their B cell subsets stayed deeply reduced, B cell responses were impaired, and T cell counts were lower at six months.
pmc-12743849:
Visnes and co-authors use a national registry to count two knee injuries found during ACL repair surgery in Norway. Meniscus repair during ACL surgery has grown more common. Two injury types draw special concern: root tears of the outer meniscus and ramp lesions. Past counts came from small, selected patient groups. Registry data from 2018 to 2023 covered isolated ACL repairs across the country.

The team compared traits of patients with and without these injuries. They also recorded how surgeons chose to treat each injury. Weight, age, sex, and activity data fed the comparison. The study gives a population-wide view of how often these injuries appear. It also shows current practice for handling them.
pmc-12744949:
Usama Abdelgwad leads a team that compares two pain blocks for hernia repair. Their study from twenty twenty-five is set at Dubai Hospital. Keyhole hernia repair often brings early pain from the belly wall.

One group got a sheath block before the cut was made. The other got local numbing drug in the wound after. Drug needs in and after surgery were compared by group. The block aims at nerve ends in the belly sheath. Sound guidance is used to place the block dose. Past compare proof for adults was thin.
pmc-12746749:
Xiao-Meng Huang and co-authors weigh a care model that joins treatment with prevention for older adults in a 2025 paper. The model serves people with long-term illness, mainly high blood pressure and diabetes. The team looks at costs and fairness, not just health gains. Their work feeds into a national plan for a healthier China.

The study covers 10,236 adults over sixty from nine areas in three provinces. Cost data were modeled in two stages, and staff also ran case studies and interviews. The team built measures for savings, efficiency, and fairness between city and country areas. Gaps for poorer regions and weaker groups are named plainly. The results can help leaders spread the model without deepening unfairness.
pmc-12748249:
Javier Goena and eleven co-authors mine fifteen years of social media posts about psychotherapy in two languages, in a two thousand twenty-five digital psychiatry paper. Public talk about therapy reveals cultural framings that clinics rarely see.

About one hundred three thousand posts on X from two thousand eight to two thousand twenty-two, three quarters English, covered four therapies. Cognitive behavioral therapy dominated mentions. English posts leaned toward professional promotion with fear the prevailing emotion. Spanish posts shared personal experience instead: joy led for acceptance therapy and narrative therapy, while anger, tied to misunderstanding, marked psychodynamic therapy posts. Volume surged after two thousand twenty. The authors urge culturally adapted mental health communication.
pmc-12748949:
Keying Su and six co-authors build a heat-responsive catalyst for formic acid fuel cells in a study from 2025. Single-atom catalysts are highly active but hard to switch off. Their design places single rhodium atoms on palladium sheets coated with a polymer that opens or closes with temperature, like a gate for the reaction.

Below the gate's switching point, near thirty-five degrees, the catalyst oxidized formic acid with high activity and strong resistance to poisoning. Above it, activity fell sharply. In a working fuel cell, power stayed high below the switch point and dropped above it, giving a built-in heat guard for the cell.
pmc-12749049:
Salma Hatem and three co-authors study printed dental crowns in this two thousand twenty-five lab study. Dentists now print crowns from hybrid ceramic material, but the best curing steps are not yet clear. The team asked how curing time and aging affect how well such crowns resist breaking. They designed one standard lower premolar crown shape on a computer. Then they printed eighty copies of it.

The crowns were split by curing time, ten or twenty minutes under UV light. Groups also went through heat-and-cold cycles that mimic aging in the mouth. The team then broke the crowns and studied the crack patterns. Their findings help labs pick curing and aging steps that yield stronger crowns. The work is lab work only, not a trial in patients.
pmc-12750149:
Rebecca Merchant and a large team of colleagues report the full gene sequences of three viruses that infect soil bacteria, found in Socorro, New Mexico. Such viruses, called phages, were grown on two host germs taken from soil samples. Two phages came from one host species, and the third from another.

Gene content placed the first two in a known phage cluster, and the third in a different one. All three share the long-tailed shape typical of their kind. Short genome reports like this one build the catalog that lets scientists sort phage diversity and trace how these viruses relate.
pmc-12750449:
Greg Courville and co-authors describe an open-source robot system that splits and reseeds cell cultures in 96-well plates. Plate cell culture is slow hand work, prone to drift between people and days. Their Automated Cell Culture Splitter is built round an Opentrons OT-2 liquid handling robot. A camera-based counter sits on the deck and counts cells.

Because the system sees cell density well by well, it can correct for uneven growth across a source plate. It then seeds each new well with a set number of cells. In tests it cut hands-on time by 61%. Seeding was tight, with well-to-well variation under 11%, and the cells fared as well as with manual care. All code and designs are free under open licenses. A lab that can buy one robot gains round-the-clock, repeatable cell culture.
pmc-12751249:
Edosa Amente Gutema and co-authors review in 2025 how funding cuts affect supplies for maternal and newborn health in low- and middle-income countries. Aid cuts strain already weak health systems and raise death and suffering. The review maps the challenges that shrinking funds create for basic supplies.

Searches of four databases yielded close to a thousand records, and fifteen articles passed full review. Weak domestic funding and supply chains made the cuts bite harder. Pregnant women and newborns face gaps in care when stocks run out. The authors present the findings in text, tables, and figures to guide response.
pmc-12751449:
Sonia Johnson and a large team published a feasibility study in two thousand twenty-five on preventing forced psychiatric readmissions. Compulsory admissions in England are rising and often traumatic. Joint crisis planning is the most promising counter, yet hard to deliver well.

The FINCH team, including service users and carers, adapted a Swiss approach into personal crisis plans with a year of follow-up support. Eighty people leaving compulsory admission joined a pilot randomised trial across three areas. Recruitment hit its target on time, and forty participants came from groups over-represented in detention. The study tested whether a full trial can recruit and retain people. Findings guide a larger definitive trial.
pmc-12751549:
Rosemarie Gideonse and colleagues publish the protocol for a Dutch trial of Beat the Kick, a motivation program for adults with mild intellectual disabilities who use substances in harmful ways. People with mild intellectual disabilities face raised risk of substance-use problems. Yet standard addiction treatment assumes thinking capacities they may not have. Beat the Kick is an adapted pre-treatment program built on motivation.

The open-label multicenter trial will take in one hundred thirty-eight adults from six disability care groups. Those who qualify have mild or borderline intellectual functioning with adaptive limits. They have long hazardous alcohol or drug use below dependence-treatment thresholds. A Zelen design assigns before consent, comparing the program with care as usual. The primary question is whether it raises self-driven motivation to enter substance-use treatment.
pmc-12752249:
Luise Holberg Lindgren and co-authors set out a trial plan for nurse-led self-care training in new inflammatory arthritis, in a protocol from two thousand twenty-five. New patients face body, mind, and social strain despite better drugs. One hundred thirty adults from three Danish hospitals will join by lot.

Half get the training plus usual care, and half get usual care alone. Training means three solo nurse sessions plus two optional group sessions over a year. Skill gain at one year is the main yardstick, with a two-year extension check. Fixed analysis rules and gap handling are set in advance. Readers get a full blueprint, with results still to come.
pmc-12752349:
Nicholas Awodele Awolola and co-authors tracked appendix disease over 16 years in a 2025 hospital study in Nigeria. The appendix can host a range of ills, with sudden inflammation the most common. Cases are rising in Nigeria, and wrong calls lead to healthy organs being cut out, so exact diagnosis and routine tissue checks matter.

The team reviewed every appendix cut out at their teaching hospital across the span. They charted how the mix of findings shifted over time and whether past claims about the pattern still hold. Such a long view helps surgeons judge when to act. It also shows where diagnosis can be sharpened to cut needless surgery.
pmc-12753049:
Naoyuki Okamoto and co-authors test why people claim skill for wins but blame luck for losses when pay is unsure. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. A hand-move task let pay hinge on skill in some rounds and on chance in others. That split let the team watch how each result was judged.

Players gave wins to their own skill and losses to chance, and that slant shaped their next choices. Model work split the slant into two parts: a warped view of own skill and a rose view in skill rounds. Warped self-view drove acts but not trust. Blame sent outwards, not self-view, fed excess trust. The authors stress tight task design plus models to pull such slants apart.
pmc-12753649:
Shuo Yuan, Lingling Cai, and Man Su pool trials of natural antioxidants for ulcerative colitis in a 2025 analysis. The authors conclude that natural antioxidants strengthened the body's defenses and eased disease activity in these trials. They present the work as a basis for choosing add-on therapies, pending stronger trials.
pmc-12754049:
Po-Hung Lin and co-authors report, in a 2025 trial, results for prostate removal done with a single-port robot through one small cut. Every operation in the trial finished with the single-port system, with no switch to multi-port or open surgery. Patients reported less pain and left hospital sooner than typical reports suggest. Most needed no drain tube. Cancer control and continence recovery were much the same for both routes, and most men regained continence within three months. The authors call the approach feasible and effective.
pmc-12756149:
Yating Zhang and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on how moxibustion, a traditional heat therapy, changes brain activity in vascular dementia. The illness follows blood vessel damage in the brain. The team had already seen the therapy lift test scores and wanted to watch the brain changes behind the gains.

Fifty-five patients were treated at three head and back points every other day, and fifty healthy adults served as a comparison group. After treatment, standard thinking scores rose clearly. Resting brain scans showed activity shifts in the memory hub and linked regions, and the wiring between areas changed too. The scans hint at how the therapy may act.
pmc-12763949:
Carmen Cabezaolias and co-authors measured what happens to the opposing arm muscle when its partner is treated with focused vibration. After five minutes of vibration, triceps activity fell and stayed reduced for up to twenty minutes, while a rest-only session changed nothing. Surface sensors proved sensitive enough to catch the effect. The authors say vibration of one muscle can quietly damp its antagonist, a finding that could guide rehabilitation dosing.
pmc-12764149:
Pankaj Aggarwal and co-authors report a bullet left in place inside a patient's heart, in work from 2025. A man aged thirty-seven was shot in the right chest, and the bullet lodged in the wall between the heart's lower chambers. Removal is the usual call, given risks of fluid crush, rhythm flaws, travel of the bullet, or infection.

Scans showed the bullet sat still, with no fluid around the heart and sound heart action. A joint team chose watchful care: a chest drain, broad germ drugs, and close checks. A year of follow-ups found no shift, travel, or infection. The authors back case-by-case calls for stable patients.
pmc-12766849:
Jiying Ling, Annie Kao, and Xining Yang ask whether living far from healthy food blunted a mindful eating program for rural families. Their study appeared in 2025. The data come from 154 low-income parent-child pairs at twenty-six Head Start centers. Parents reported habits, feeding attitudes, and food insecurity; children's growth and body fat were measured directly. Home food access was estimated by mapping zip codes to food outlets.

The children averaged about four years old; many parents were single, unemployed, or earning under twenty thousand dollars a year. The team tested whether food access changed the program's effects on eating and body measures. The authors say interventions cannot be judged apart from the food landscape families actually shop in.
pmc-12767049:
Eiman Wazwaz and co-authors tested a lower dose of a transplant drug in a 2025 study. Thymoglobulin wipes out immune cells to protect a new kidney, but dosing varies by center with no firm standard. The study compared 196 low-risk patients treated before and after the change, from 2020 to 2024. The reduced dose met the bar for noninferiority: the combined outcome of rejection, graft loss, or death was actually lower, at three percent versus eleven. Low blood counts and viral infections were also less common. The authors endorse the smaller dose as safer for this group.
pmc-12772549:
Laura Ojanpera and co-authors compare, in twenty twenty-five, spacer devices that help small children inhale asthma medicine. A spacer is a chamber between an inhaler and the child's mouth. It holds the spray so the child can breathe it in slowly. Disposable paper spacers may suit some clinic uses, but data were scarce. They used three child breathing patterns, calm and blocked. One reusable chamber gave the highest fine dose that can reach the lungs. Blocked breathing raised throat deposits for all spacers. Reusable chambers beat disposable ones overall. Of the disposable pair, the valved one did better.
pmc-12775249:
Xinyi Zhao, Quan Zhang, Vivian Lou, and Siqing Tao sort older Chinese adults by their mix of caregiving loads, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Many juggle care for parents, a spouse, and grandchildren at once. Data followed 11,775 people aged fifty and up across seven years.

Four patterns emerged, from part-time care for all to full-time spouse care. Spouse caregivers, part- or full-time, showed more depressive symptoms years later. Full-time parent-plus-grandchild carers fared no worse than the light group. The authors urge services shaped to each pattern, not one plan for all.
pmc-12780449:
Jieqi Peng and co-authors (2025) followed patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to see how eosinophil levels predict flare-ups. Blood levels told the same story at smaller strength. Lung function decline, however, did not differ between groups. The authors conclude that a single measurement undersells the risk: persistence itself is the warning sign. They suggest repeated eosinophil checks should guide how closely COPD patients are watched.
pmc-12788349:
Vourna, Falara, Ktena, Hristoforou, and Papadopoulos review a magnetic sensor method for testing materials in twenty twenty-five. The method listens to tiny magnetic noise from steel and other magnetic materials. That noise reflects grain structure, stress, and other internal traits. It allows testing without damaging the part.

The review covers theory, sensor design, signal processing, and industry uses. New sensors are smaller and can work in harsh settings. Modern methods, including deep learning, extract more information from the raw signals. Uses include factory quality control, railway checks, and health monitoring of structures. Reported accuracy is good for stress and hardness measures. The authors list open needs, such as common standards and more robust learning methods.
pmc-12801649:
Hyun Ji Park and four co-authors study quality of life in pregnancy in a 2025 paper. They ask how a woman's body weight before pregnancy shapes her well being during pregnancy, and what sits in between. The team surveyed two hundred forty pregnant women in Korea with self report forms.

Their path model fit the data well and explained over half the variation in quality of life. Weight before pregnancy had no direct link to quality of life. Instead, its effect ran through sleep problems, depressive symptoms, and how women rated their own health. Sleep mattered mainly through its effect on mood and health perception. The findings point to mood and sleep care as routes to better pregnancy well being.
pmc-12801949:
Anna Rogachevskaya and eight co-authors published a study in 2025 on a little-known gene, C1orf50, and its links to cancer behavior. The gene makes a small, ancient protein whose job is unclear. Screening public tumor data across many cancers, the team focused on ovarian cancer, where the gene's story looked strongest.

Copies of the gene were gained or amplified most often in ovarian tumors, and more copies meant more gene activity. High activity tracked with more mutations, weaker DNA repair, faster cell-cycle programs, and an immune mix tilted toward suppression. In ovarian samples the gene's activity rose step by step with clinical stage and traveled with changes in the famous BRCA repair genes. Whether the gene drives these patterns or merely reports them remains open.
pmc-12804849:
Ravindra Singh and co-authors published this farm study in 2025 on cumin in dry Rajasthan, India. Sandy soils and fierce evaporation starve border-watered fields. The team tested drip lines that feed water and fertilizer together, over three years. Ten setups mixed three drip rates with three fertilizer doses, against a flooded control.

The top drip rate with a full fertilizer dose won on growth, seed yield, and profit, and lifted the spice's prized oil content. Leaner drip rates saved far more water and used each drop best. All drip setups cut seasonal water use by a fifth to over half against flooding. Year weather swayed which setup paid most. The authors back drip feeding as the sound path for spice farms in arid lands.
pmc-12812549:
Zixuan Yuan, Yutong Pan, Haodong Yuan, and Aihua Gong review a promising target for cancer immunotherapy, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. The target is a receptor on T cells that, when switched on by its partner molecule, helps those cells multiply, survive, and attack tumors. It also damps the cells that normally hold immunity back.

Pairing the drugs with other treatments raised response rates but also raised severe side effects. The authors call for sharper drugs that act mainly inside tumors, to balance gain and safety.
pmc-12812649:
Xiaotao Cao, Jiaxing Xu, Mingyang Li, and Li Zheng compare clinical research nurse roles across countries. Their review deals with developed and developing nations. Trial quality leans on these nurses as core team members.

Role views, duty splits, and promotion paths are compared. China serves as the example developing country case. Blocks to nurse career growth there are analyzed. Role perception gaps stand among the contrasts. The aim is a reference for building the profession. Better training and management modes are the goals. High quality trial growth is the wider aim.
pmc-12817649:
Rohana Abdul Ghani, Firdaus Mukhtar, Barakatun Nisak Mohd Yusof, and Zubaidah Nor Hanipah published a survey study in 2025 on how Malaysian health professionals see obesity. pmc-12844049:

pmc-12849149:

pmc-12849249:

pmc-12849349:

pmc-12849549:

pmc-12849749:

pmc-12852749:

pmc-12858849:

pmc-12859949:

pmc-12866349:

pmc-13185949:
Muhamad Ali Shakhatreh and co-authors study a strep germ carried by pregnant women in Jordan, in a paper from 2026. The germ, Streptococcus agalactiae, is a major cause of severe infection in newborns. Knowing how often mothers carry it, and how drug-resistant it is, guides prevention.

The isolates resisted an older antibiotic, tetracycline, in most cases, and a second drug in a third of cases. All were still killed by several frontline drugs, including ampicillin. Every isolate could form biofilms, the slimy layers that shield germs. Gene tests screened for harm and resistance genes.
pmc-13192349:
Christoph Bueschl leads a 2026 software paper presenting AnnoMe, a tool for classifying mass spectrometry spectra in natural product discovery. Finding new compounds of a familiar chemical class requires sorting thousands of spectra into relevant and other, a task usually done by experts or by models trained on huge databases. AnnoMe lets users train their own classifier instead.

Users supply reference spectra labeled relevant or other, and the Python package combines them with structure-informed embeddings, numeric fingerprints of spectra, to train custom models judged by majority vote. A demonstration hunted prenylated flavonoids, plant compounds with an added carbon chain, for follow-up study. Code, documentation, and datasets are freely posted online, the authors note.
pmc-13194149:
Ali Uzair, Anees Ur Rehman, Zikria Saleem, and Masaad Almutairi mapped management-level actions against antimicrobial resistance worldwide in 2026. Global plans stress system-wide responses, yet the part played by administration and governance inside stewardship programmes has been little studied. Their scoping review covered all World Health Organization regions to fill that gap.

Interventions were sorted into six groups, running from rules on rational use and dispensing through accountability schemes to technology-based training and infection prevention. Governance-driven actions, the authors conclude, play a crucial role in making stewardship work. Policy-ready lessons are offered for strengthening the management side of stewardship in different health systems.
pmc-13194549:
Simon Moubarak and five co-authors use data-driven grouping to split a kidney vessel disease into three distinct types. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The disease, thrombotic microangiopathy, injures small vessels and can spring from many causes, which blurs treatment choices.

The team reviewed two hundred and eighty-three patients with biopsy-proven kidney disease from twenty ten to twenty twenty, using sixty-four clinical and tissue measures. Clustering found three groups. The first leaned to women and immune-linked causes, with rich immune deposits in tissue. The second held the oldest patients, often drug-linked, with marked vessel lining damage. A third group rounded out the split. Knowing the type could point doctors toward the true cause and the right care sooner.
pmc-13195049:
Awadh M Ali leads a 2026 analytical chemistry study developing greener quality control tests for avapritinib, a targeted drug for certain stomach and gut tumors. Routine drug checking lacked convenient methods for this medicine. The authors built two high-throughput tests based on charge-transfer complexation, a reaction where the drug pairs with a colored partner compound.

Run in ninety-six well plates with tiny volumes, the colored reactions were measured by light absorption. Both methods proved linear, precise, and accurate across useful ranges, and computer modeling explained why one partner bound the drug more strongly. Ten assessment tools rated the methods highly green and practical, processing about five hundred samples an hour with minimal solvent.
pmc-13197249:
Zewei Yang and Zixia Huang trace gene families in a 2026 study of mammal genomes. Noncoding RNAs regulate genes without making proteins, but how their family sizes changed across mammals was unmapped. The team predicted copy counts for five hundred eighty-eight conserved families across sixty mammal genomes.

Family sizes varied mostly by lineage, not by genome size or assembly quality. An early burst of growth in the ancestor of placental mammals was driven by two RNA families tied to splicing and chemical tagging. Many microRNA families, by contrast, grew in single lineages. Highly variable families often overlapped with jumping DNA elements and used distinct copying styles, from tight clusters to scattered spreads. The survey lays a base for studying RNA duplication.
pmc-13197649:
Suttitas Tongkamsai and colleagues tested drug resistance in a poultry gut parasite in Thailand in 2026. Coccidiosis, caused by Eimeria parasites, cuts chicken growth and farm output. Drugs in feed control it, but rotating drug programs have bred resistance, so the team checked three common drugs.

They gathered parasites from Thai broiler farms and infected test chicks under set doses. Four scoring methods rated drug performance, covering lesions, egg output in droppings, and weight gain. Two drugs cut lesions and egg output versus no treatment, but only partly. Results pointed to weakened drug response in the field strains. Knowing which drugs still work can guide farm prevention plans.
pmc-13198049:
Maria Zink and colleagues interviewed nurse leaders in Germany on pandemic workplace changes in 2026. COVID-19 forced fast reorganization in hospitals and long-term care homes. Nurse leaders drove much of that change, so the team asked which changes they judged a success and why.

Fifty-three leaders across management levels in Saxony took part, with added organizational data. Leaders rated thirty-six of fifty-one changes as successful. Wins clustered in infection control, staff scheduling, and teamwork. Good collaboration, leader backing, and staff drive aided success. Barriers included staff shortages, weak infrastructure, and mental strain. Staff acceptance tracked closely with rated success. The lessons may help build tougher care systems.
pmc-13198549:
Fabian Dellefant and colleagues present a 2026 method to read past fire temperatures from charcoal. Charcoal's inner structure changes with the heat that formed it. A laser method called Raman spectroscopy can read that structure, but past work was slow and prone to analyst bias.

Their calibration uses a pine wood reference set and a band ratio to estimate charring temperature. Set rules also flag crystal clustering and weathering by air exposure. A free web tool, CHARM, automates the full pipeline from cleaning to temperature output. Tests on ancient pottery gave sound readings with no sample damage. Volcanic charcoals also yielded readable ranges despite weathering. The tool suits both field areas.
pmc-13202049:
Hearing loss is a leading modifiable risk factor for dementia, and a 2026 study protocol by Lisa M Shulman lays out a three-year comparison of two hearing treatments. The protocol describes the ARCH study, which follows older adults using cochlear implants or hearing aids at an academic medical center.

The study will enroll 210 older adults in six subgroups defined by hearing level, device use, and cognitive status. Its main outcome is change in real-time, patient-reported listening experience gathered through ecological momentary assessment in daily life. Laboratory hearing and thinking tests, plus measures of loneliness, mood, and quality of life, support the comparison through completion in 2029.
pmc-13202249:
Marianne Månsson and her three co-authors, publishing in 2026, dig into a puzzle inside Europe's big prostate screening trial. Overall, screening cut prostate cancer deaths by about 20 percent over sixteen years. But the two centers they compare diverged wildly: Sweden's cut reached 37 percent, Finland's just 9. The teams started with very different sizes, about 65,000 Finnish men against 10,700 Swedish.

The screening recipes differed too. Swedes were invited every two years with a lower biopsy threshold; Finns every four with a higher one. Screening raised cancer detection in both, 44 percent in Sweden and 21 percent in Finland. The key surprise sat in Finland's control group, whose death rates ran unexpectedly low from the start. The authors blame widespread informal testing blurring the trial's contrast, a warning for screening research everywhere.
pmc-13205649:
Newer tobacco products are popular with teenagers, and a 2026 analysis led by Jinyoung Kim links them to asthma diagnoses in South Korea. Drawing on the national Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey from 2022 to 2024, the study compares asthma prevalence across patterns of cigarette, e-cigarette, and heated tobacco use.

The dataset held more than one hundred fifty-nine thousand students in grades seven through twelve. Asthma was uncommon overall, yet odds were higher for every user group than for non-users after adjustment in the authors' models. Teenagers using both e-cigarettes and heated products showed the highest odds, and the authors stress the design cannot prove these products cause asthma.
pmc-13205949:
Xingdong Yang and co-authors build a fast test for a deadly food toxin in a 2026 study. Bongkrekic acid comes from a bacterium that spoils fermented rice and wheat foods, snow fungus, and black fungus. It attacks breathing at the cell level and has caused fatal outbreaks. A quick on-site screen could stop poisoned food before it is eaten.

The team raised a monoclonal antibody that binds the toxin tightly and built a glowing enzyme test around it. In the competitive format, toxin in the sample dims the glow in proportion to its amount. The test reads down to a few picograms per milliliter, works across a wide range, and runs many samples at once. They target two risky foods named in the title: tremella fungus and rice noodles.
pmc-13206449:
Brain scans must correct for head size, and a 2026 study led by Aliza Brzezinski-Rittner asks which correction method distorts sex differences least. Working with UK Biobank imaging, the authors compare four ways of adjusting for total intracranial volume when estimating how male and female brains differ.

They built a reference standard by matching men and women on age and head size, removing the confound directly. Against that benchmark, simply adding head size as a covariate in the model performed best across brain measures and brain regions. Common smoothing of the imaging data could itself bias the estimates, a caution the authors raise for the field.
pmc-13207549:
Drugs that block one of the brain's cannabis-style switches, while staying out of the brain itself, are hoped to help several diseases without mental side effects. Patryk Remiszewski and co-authors check what such a blocker does to blood pressure in a 2026 short report. Their rats had a hormone-and-salt form of high blood pressure, and the team tested the body's own cannabis-style signals on top.

The blocker alone did not move blood pressure. It did blunt both the rise and the fall caused by a stable copy of one body signal. A drug that raises the body's own signal lowered pressure, and the blocker erased that drop in the high-pressure rats while boosting it in normal ones. The authors warn that heart effects of this drug class swing with the model used.
pmc-13207849:
An old blue dye might guard aging brains through surgery, and a 2026 review authored by Yu Wu builds the case for methylene blue. The article pulls together early and clinical evidence on perioperative neurocognitive disorders, which strike a large share of elderly patients after surgery and raise later dementia risk.

Proposed mechanisms converge on mitochondria: the dye can shuttle electrons, switch on antioxidant defenses, calm brain-cell inflammation, block tau clumping, and protect the blood-brain barrier. Small randomized trials report that one dose by vein during surgery cut delirium after surgery sharply in older patients having major non-cardiac surgery. The authors call for large trials at many centers to confirm dosing and benefit.
pmc-13207949:
Two decades of pancreatitis research are mapped in a 2026 bibliometric analysis authored by Chenlu Huang. The study retrieves basic research on acute pancreatitis causes and therapies published between 2003 and 2025 from the Web of Science, then visualizes authorship, institutions, journals, and keywords with standard mapping tools.

Six hundred thirty-two publications formed the dataset for the analysis. China produced the most papers while the United States carried the greatest citation impact in the field. Enduring themes included oxidative stress, a master inflammatory switch, and premature enzyme activation, while gut microbes, autophagy, and two forms of cell death emerged as recent hotspots for therapy ideas.
pmc-13208549:
Lihua Chen and seven co-authors present a 2026 study predicting the bursting pressure of pipelines with two neighboring corrosion pits. Real corrosion comes in clusters, and nearby pits tug on each other's stress field, changing how the pipe fails. Standard assessment codes simplify the pair into one defect, which can overshoot or undershoot the true danger.

Using a common pipeline steel, the team built computer models of twin uniform pits in two layouts: side by side along the pipe, and around it. They varied pit spacing, depth, and length to see which combinations weaken the pipe most. The results feed a failure pressure prediction that respects the interaction.
pmc-13210249:
Júlia dos Santos Fonseca and co-authors published a 2026 review of how worm-fighting fungi are formulated so they survive to do their work in the field. Such fungi are an environmentally friendly way to cut gut worms in farm animals and root worms in crops. A formulation must keep the fungal spores alive through manufacture, storage, and delivery. That is the hard part.

In animal care, a predatory fungus consumes the young of the worm after it passes through the gut and germinates in dung. Egg-killing fungi strike the eggs and hard cysts. The two kinds complement each other, so formulations that combine them could hit hard. The review names the commercial products on sale, and the obstacles to farm adoption: dose, route of delivery, and habit. In crops, solid formulations dominate one market, because dry stock lasts. Liquid and oil formulations serve particular tasks.
pmc-13210749:
Jian Shen, Hanye Liu, Zhilin Chen, and co-authors present a vision system that traces the outlines of gravel pieces on a conveyor belt in this 2026 paper. Rock plants need particle counts and sizes, read from depth maps of the moving load. Factory depth data is messy, with weak breaks, holes, and speckle.

Their framework pairs a compact transformer encoder with depth-based cues: the raw depth, its slope strength, and a second response that marks edges. A light local branch and a gated fusion step sharpen the trace, and a final pass restores full resolution. On their main dataset the scores neared the top of the scale. A test set shot under changed conditions scored nearly as well with no retraining. Repeated scans of fixed objects agreed to within a third of a pixel. The system runs at about forty-nine frames per second, fast enough for live belts.
pmc-13211149:
Shuai Li and co-authors automate the search for stable gene therapy virus formulas. Adeno-associated virus products need recipes that keep them potent in storage. New capsid types multiply the recipe space past what hand work can cover. Their platform mixes ninety-six formulas in forty minutes flat.

One plate of virus compounding takes twenty minutes more. Acidity, buffers, and virus strength are set with tight control. A proof run screened 128 recipes for the AAV1 type. Winners held high strength through frozen, chilled, and room storage. The system saves scarce virus while widening the search a great deal.
pmc-13212849:
Hongrong Zhang and four co-authors are named in a 2026 retraction notice from Discover Oncology covering their 2025 paper on a gene called BRCA1 in gastric cancer. An institutional review at a Chinese medical university triggered the withdrawal.

The review found the first author had sent in the article without a co-author's consent. It also found false details for that co-author, and a list of authors that did not match who did the work. Zhang acknowledged misrepresenting authorship. The editor-in-chief therefore lost confidence in the article's reliability. All authors agree with the retraction, which closes a case about credit and consent rather than data fabrication.
pmc-13213049:
Jacob Sampson leads a large team mapping in 2026 how genetic differences tune gene activity in the human retina. They paired whole-genome sequencing with gene activity readings from two retinal tissues taken from 201 donated eyes.

Millions of small genetic variants influenced nearby genes, far more in the light-sensing layer than in its supporting layer, though many effects were shared. The team also flagged over a thousand people whose gene activity sat far outside the usual range. Rare variants plausibly explained more than a quarter of those outlier cases. The catalogue should help interpret genetic findings in both common and rare eye diseases.
pmc-13215049:
Hanze Du and a large team chart in 2026 how a simple insulin-resistance index, built from fasting glucose and triglycerides, varies by age and sex across China. Reference ranges matter, because a value that is ordinary at one age may signal risk at another.

Data from a national health survey covered 4,621 adults aged twenty to eighty. Men ran higher on body mass, fats, glucose, and the index itself, with male values peaking around age forty. Women's lower range overtook men's near age fifty, and after sixty their upper range sat higher. The crossover pattern gives clinicians age-aware cut-offs for judging sugar and fat metabolism in Chinese adults.
pmc-13215549:
Josphat Kosgei and colleagues report a 2026 analysis of hepatitis B infection among people living with HIV in four sub-Saharan African countries. The data come from the African Cohort Study, which follows patients at twelve clinical sites.

Among 4,241 participants with valid test results, hepatitis B prevalence was 4.7 percent in people with HIV and 4.2 percent in those without. Rates varied sharply by place, reaching 11.1 percent among Nigerian participants with HIV against 2.6 percent in Kenya. Male sex, Nigerian residence, and age over forty each raised the odds of co-infection. The authors recommend routine hepatitis B screening inside HIV programs, especially for older men.
pmc-13215749:
Danilo Pelaes de Almeida, Amanda Maria Picelli, Carolina Romeiro Fernandes Chagas, and Lucio André Viana wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It describes a new species of blood parasite found in green iguanas in the eastern Amazon of Brazil.

The parasite belongs to Lankesterella, a group of coccidian blood dwellers in reptiles. Under the microscope, the new species showed a strange flexible nucleus that changes shape and packing depending on where it sits in the host cell. It infects red blood cells and two kinds of white cells, warping their nuclei in the process. Gene sequencing placed it among other lizard Lankesterella, and a second, unnamed relative turned up in the same iguanas. The authors argue that pairing microscopy with DNA work is essential for sorting out these neglected parasites.
pmc-13217449:
Daniella A. Spittle and Alice M. Turner present a 2026 review of alpha-1 antitrypsin, a blood protein best known for shielding the lungs from digestive enzymes released by immune cells. When the protein is missing or overwhelmed, that protection fails and lung tissue is slowly destroyed.

The review covers the protein's wider talents beyond enzyme blocking: calming inflammation, steering immune cells, and resisting cell death and oxidative stress. Deficiency-driven emphysema is the proven indication for replacement therapy, which is already in clinical use. The authors then examine whether the same treatment could help in bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, and interstitial lung diseases, where protease burden runs high even without the genetic defect. They weigh the emerging evidence for widening its use.
pmc-13217849:
Jonathan Brutti and co-authors present a 2026 surgical study asking whether adding a nerve block to the standard painkilling injection cocktail improves the first day after knee replacement. The design is a natural experiment: one surgeon's patients received injection alone in year one and injection plus adductor canal block in year two.

The final sample held 188 patients, 104 with the block and 84 without. The block group used less opioid in the first twenty-four hours, averaging 31.6 morphine milligram equivalents against 42.5, and reported lower average and peak pain scores, with a summed pain measure of 40 against 54. Differences survived adjustment for age, sex, body size, and anaesthetic risk class. The authors conclude the block earns its place in the regimen.
pmc-13217949:
Yaning Shi and colleagues report in 2026 that celastrol, a compound from the root of the thunder god vine, slows atherosclerosis in mice. The disease builds fatty plaques inside arteries, and one driver is pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death in macrophages, the immune cells inside plaques. The study tests whether celastrol can quiet that process.

The team combined a mouse model of atherosclerosis with cultured macrophages exposed to oxidized LDL, the cholesterol form that triggers pyroptosis. Celastrol reduced cell death in the dishes and eased plaque growth and instability in the animals. Tests of binding and signaling showed that celastrol blocks the receptor TLR4, which lowers STAT3 activation and in turn switches off the NLRP3 inflammasome that drives pyroptosis. The authors propose celastrol as a candidate drug for atherosclerosis, though all findings so far are preclinical.
pmc-13218149:
Qindan Du and colleagues report a 2026 study uncovering a second, non-burning role for the protein gasdermin D in prostate cancer. The protein's front fragment is known to kill tumor cells by pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death. What the full-length protein does in prostate cancer, particularly for immune evasion, was unexplored.

Using deletion models, the team found removing gasdermin D sped tumor growth, shortened survival, and created an immune-suppressed environment with fewer killer T cells. That state releases a chemokine, switching on growth signals and suppressing T cells. In human tumor samples, gasdermin D levels rose alongside T-cell infiltration and fell as suppressive macrophages rose. Activating the protein, the authors suggest, could thaw cold tumors and help immunotherapy.
pmc-13218249:
An old folk remedy smashes fresh dandelion onto sores, and Shenyu Tan and co-authors rebuild that remedy as a modern wound dressing in a 2026 study. Their film blends bubble-like particles from dandelion juice with fibers spun from the plant's own leftovers. The aim is the stubborn wounds of diabetes, which stall in inflamed tissue.

The film nudged immune cells from attack mode to repair mode and spurred new blood vessels. Loaded densely into the film, the juice particles released on demand. Treated wounds in animals closed almost fully within two weeks, far ahead of untreated ones, with better collagen layout and vessel regrowth.
pmc-13218349:
Siyu Long, Marie-Hélène Boudrias, and Georgios D. Mitsis examine bursts of beta brain waves and the blood-flow responses that follow them, in a 2026 neuroscience study. Beta oscillations are rhythms in brain activity tied to holding back movement, arriving in short bursts rather than a steady hum. Where these bursts occur during movement, and how they relate to the blood oxygen signals seen in brain scans, was unmapped.

Eleven adults performed a handgrip task at rest and during movement while electroencephalography and MRI recorded. During transitions between phases, the background electrical components and beta bursts grew stronger compared with steady squeezing. Bursts over the motor region were followed by positive responses during movement but negative ones at rest, while other regions showed negative responses. The authors describe this flip as a new detail in how electrical events become scan signals, calling for larger studies.
pmc-13218649:
Small cysts in the brain's fluid factory may mark the failing cleanup system of liver driven brain disease, suggests a 2026 scan study by Li Chen and co-authors. The team imaged three groups: patients with hepatic encephalopathy, patients with cirrhosis but clear minds, and healthy controls.

Every encephalopathy patient carried the cysts, against six in ten with cirrhosis and about a quarter of controls. A scan index of the brain's waste flow fell step by step across the groups, and cyst load tracked worse thinking and more shrinkage. The authors propose the cysts as a visible sign of a deeper drainage failure.
pmc-13219549:
Michal Paret and co-authors review infections caused by a family of bacteria called Fusobacterium, in a paper from 2026. These germs live without oxygen and colonize the mouth, gut, and other sites. Illness ranges from throat and soft tissue infections to blood poisoning with no clear source. One species can trigger a grave clotting infection of the neck vein.

The review walks through the germ's traits, the syndromes it causes, and how each is treated. Blood infections are rare but carry a high death rate. One species strikes the young and healthy after neck infections, while another hits older patients with cancer. Most strains still yield to common antibiotics, though resistance to two drugs is rising. Since labs rarely test these germs, strong first-choice drugs are the norm for severe cases.
pmc-13220349: The Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation issued this short correction in 2026 for a case series by Andrea Demofonti and co-authors on tailored rehabilitation after lower limb soft tissue sarcoma reconstruction. The notice is a correction only. In the original version, one author's given and family names, Marco Morelli Coppola, were wrongly ordered, though the name was right in all versions when published. The original article has now been corrected. Its results and conclusions stand.
pmc-13222049:
Zirong Liu and colleagues survey patients with venous thromboembolism about long-term blood thinner use, in a 2026 cross-sectional study at a Shandong hospital. Three hundred eighty-nine patients completed a questionnaire covering knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice around anticoagulation. Younger patients made up a large share, with a mean age near forty-six.

About half of respondents met the preset bar for adequate knowledge, while majorities showed positive attitudes and proactive habits. Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores all rose together in correlation analysis. Patients under forty-five scored higher on knowledge and attitude than older groups. The gaps suggest education should target older patients, whose understanding lagged despite years of potential treatment ahead.
pmc-13222949:
Xu Jia, Jun Xie, Fang Chai, HaoBo Jiang, and Rui Shi offer a two thousand twenty-six case study of digital prescription review in Sanya, China. Irrational drug use wastes money and harms care quality. Small clinics often lack the pharmacy expertise of big hospitals.

A centralized electronic review platform linked the region's facilities into one checking system. Artificial intelligence with retrieval support backed the reviewers. Over four hundred thousand prescriptions from one year were analyzed. Trend tests tracked safety, cost efficiency, and consistency of service over time. The Sanya model is offered as a route to fairer pharmaceutical care.
pmc-13223349:
Sarah Søgaard Jakobsen and co-authors run a post hoc quality-of-life analysis of fecal microbiota transplantation for chronic pouchitis, in a 2026 report from the MicroPouch trial. Pouchitis inflames the surgical pouch built after colon removal for ulcerative colitis, and antibiotics often fail in chronic cases. Thirty patients were randomized evenly to transplant enemas or placebo over four weeks, then followed for a year.

At thirty days, transplant patients reported significantly worse quality of life on an inflammatory bowel questionnaire than at baseline. Placebo patients scored higher on a general health survey at both checks. No questionnaire showed improvement from the transplant. The authors conclude fecal transfer may temporarily worsen symptoms in this setting, a caution against assuming benefit.
pmc-13223949:
Manish J Barvaliya and co-authors publish a protocol for testing an Ayurvedic preparation alongside iron tablets for anemia in women, in a 2026 trial protocol. Half receive standard iron and folic acid tablets twice daily for three months. The other half add six grams of Drakshavaleha twice daily before food. Monthly visits will track blood counts and iron profiles, with kidney, liver, and blood sugar checks at the end. The registered trial will judge whether the integrative pairing raises hemoglobin safely.
pmc-13224049:
Rongfen Feng and co-authors study why sodium battery anodes fail at temperature extremes in this 2026 paper. Sodium-ion batteries promise cheap storage, but their hard carbon anodes degrade in cold and heat. The team ran charge tests and multi-scale imaging at deep cold and at high heat.

In the cold, sluggish chemistry grew metal spikes and thickened the surface film, wasting sodium and blocking flow. At high heat, the film turned crystalline for the first time on record. That dense layer blocked sodium movement and fed more side reactions, in a self-worsening cycle. The authors show the failure sits at the surface, not inside the carbon, which guides future designs.
pmc-13225449:
The authors review cases from China of a rare inherited disease in children in a paper from 2026. Faults in the gene SUCLG1 drain cells of mitochondrial DNA, the small genome inside the cell's power plants. The team gathered thirteen child cases from nine reports in a Chinese database and summed up their gene faults and clinical traits.

Common traits were floppy muscles, slow mental and motor growth, feeding trouble, and liver strain. Brain scans often showed deep brain lesions or shrinkage. Fourteen gene variants were found, with no clear link between variant and severity. All children got vitamin support; two died and the rest improved somewhat.
pmc-13226249:
Kellie McGlynn, a solo author, writes on police response to family violence. The paper from twenty twenty-six calls such response a second violence. It sits in a wider survivor led research program.

One police station visit is studied in close detail. The author went to report breaks of a court order. Notes and memos from a four year study form the data. She uses her own lived account as the research base. Rules, tasks, and work splits shaped how safe she was. Police contact is framed as a health risk.
pmc-13226849:
Zahra Tahmasebi Ashtiani and colleagues searched for Bartonella infection in immune-weakened patients in Iran in 2026. Bartonella bacteria spread through biting insects or contact with animals and can cause severe illness when the immune system is weak. Blood samples from several hundred such patients were tested with molecular methods in a cross-sectional study.

Evidence pointed to infection with one Bartonella species, reported as the first molecular proof of that species in this patient group in Iran. Cases were notably present among people living with HIV. Apparent risk links did not hold up as independent factors in stricter analysis, so the authors urge careful reading and greater clinical awareness.
pmc-13228849:
Ebraheam Aljazei reviews a 2026 literature on AI as a diagnostic aid for benign prostatic hyperplasia, the non-cancerous prostate growth that burdens many ageing men. Several also helped distinguish benign growth from prostate cancer, supporting treatment decisions. Persistent problems temper the promise: small and varied datasets, scarce testing outside the development setting, possible bias in the models, and no shared standard for judging performance.
pmc-13232849:
Elisa Moraga and colleagues report in 2026 a rare case where a multiple sclerosis drug appeared to hold HIV at bay inside one patient. The drug, fingolimod, traps immune cells in lymph nodes and changes the surface of the helper T cells HIV targets. The team compared this patient with untreated-HIV controls, healthy donors, and sclerosis patients on the same drug.

At diagnosis the patient carried a far lower viral load than controls caught at a similar stage. After a year of virus therapy, the hidden reservoir of intact virus ran many times smaller, and after three years none was detectable. Lab infections of the patient cells also took hold poorly. A chance drug overlap has outlined a possible route toward shrinking the reservoir.
pmc-13232949:
Yaojun Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 computer vision study on spotting rice diseases in field images. Finding diseased patches early protects harvests, yet older detection software is slow, misses small lesions, and struggles when light or leaf overlap varies. The group rebuilt a detection model called RT-DETR into a leaner version named ECL-RTDETR.

Their design pairs a lightweight EfficientViT backbone with an upsampling step that preserves fine detail and a dynamic convolution that adapts to changing conditions. Against the original model, the new version raised detection accuracy slightly while running faster and using far fewer parameters and computations. The authors present the model as a practical tool for smart farming equipment.
pmc-13233349:
Yingtong Chen and colleagues reported a 2026 study of retinoblastoma, the most common eye cancer in children. Using single-cell gene data from 189,431 cells across 13 tumors and three normal fetal retina samples, the team mapped the cell types inside these tumors. They focused on a fast-dividing cell group whose cell-cycle genes ran unusually hot.

A gene called BIRC5, which makes the protein survivin, was switched on in nearly all of those aggressive cells and barely present elsewhere. Raising BIRC5 in cultured tumor cells sped growth, invasion, and movement, while silencing it stalled the cell cycle and increased cell death. The authors propose survivin as a drug target aimed squarely at the tumor's most dangerous cell state.
pmc-13233649:
Michael W. Wrucke and colleagues published a 2026 feedback study on a psychosocial screening tool for young adults with cancer. The clinic involved mainly treats blood cancers, including transplant and cellular therapy patients, whose emotional and social needs can be missed in busy adult services. Screening questionnaires were given to patients, and twenty eligible providers were invited to judge the tool, with fourteen responding.

Nearly every responding provider had discussed the screener with a young patient during a visit. Overall views ranged from neutral to positive, suggesting the tool fits clinic workflow acceptably. The authors say provider buy-in is the hinge for routine screening. With that support, they argue, clinics can address young adults' unmet psychosocial needs more consistently.
pmc-13233749:
Habib Hassan, Salman Waheeduddin, and William Macdonald published a 2026 case report of gout appearing in an unexpected place, the larynx. pmc-13264249:
Alba Tomás-Sitjes and colleagues map how brain vessel cells recycle surface proteins in a 2026 proteomics study. The blood-brain barrier depends on specialized endothelial cells whose membrane proteins control nutrient entry, signaling and immune traffic. The team measured turnover for roughly one thousand proteins in rat cells. Turnover means how fast proteins are taken in, recycled and broken down. Rates were taken under healthy and inflamed conditions, comparing brain cells with vessel cells from elsewhere in the body.

Brain cells showed a turnover fingerprint distinct from peripheral cells, beyond simple protein lists. Inflammation shifted that fingerprint toward the peripheral pattern. Abundance changes flagged immune proteins, while turnover changes highlighted vessel remodeling proteins. Turnover itself emerges as a dynamic regulator of barrier identity and of its failure during inflammation.
pmc-13264549:
Irmand Leblond Mikiela Ndzoumbou and co-authors present a 2026 maths paper on networks of evolution equations, the rules that describe how quantities change over space and time. Older models often assumed every node in a network was the same shape and size. Their framework allows nodes that differ and links at edges as well as inside.

For the single-value case, they prove that flow is conserved and that one positive solution exists. For the multi-value case, they prove like results and show the total mass stays bounded when the system conserves mass. They test the theory on a predator-prey model with two nodes. Computer runs match the theory, and the authors offer the framework for spread and transport problems.
pmc-13264849:
Dimple Sushma Alluri and Felix M Pabon-Rodriguez apply machine learning to intensive care outcomes for viral hepatitis patients in a 2026 retrospective study. A large United States critical care database with tens of thousands of admissions supplied social, clinical and resource data. Models including random forest, logistic regression and gradient boosting were compared on three linked predictions. One was how long intensive care would last. The others were the hospital discharge outcome and where the patient would go at discharge.

Hepatitis drives over a million deaths yearly worldwide, and its intensive care course is resource heavy. Disease-specific prediction has lagged behind general intensive care analytics. Accurate forecasts could guide bed planning, family counseling and discharge arrangements. Performance differences among algorithms are the core result readers should weigh, alongside fairness across patient subgroups.
pmc-13264949:
Karoline Louise Imingen Selvik and co-authors wrote a 2026 Norwegian study on family money worries and teen mental distress. They compared what teens feel about family finances with official records of parent income and education. Data came from two waves of the Young-HUNT surveys, in 2006 to 2008 and 2017 to 2019, linked with parent data.

Each wave held more than 8,000 teens aged 13 to 19. Teens who felt their family was worse off than others reported more anxiety and depression symptoms, with the gap a bit larger in girls. Official parent income and education showed little or no link to teen symptoms. Counting parent mental health did not change the pattern, and results were much the same in both waves. The authors say felt financial stress, not recorded wealth, is what tracks teen distress.
pmc-13265049:
Syed Nazeer and co-authors published a 2026 case report on neurocysticercosis, a parasitic infection of the brain, in a young man who had recently moved to Saudi Arabia from South Africa. The infection comes from the larval stage of the pork tapeworm. It is a leading cause of seizures in poor countries. It is rare where he now lives, because pork is prohibited there for religious reasons.

The man, aged thirty-four, came to an emergency department gripped by prolonged seizures. A scan showed cysts in his brain, each with the head of the worm at its center, plus nodules from older cysts. A blood test for antibodies to the worm came back positive. He was given two anti-worm drugs, with a steroid to calm the brain. He recovered fully. The team warns that the infection is rising and must be kept in mind when seizures begin.
pmc-13265649:
Meng Tian and colleagues design bacterial partnerships that fight ginseng root rot while boosting growth, in a 2026 study. The disease, caused by a soil fungus, is the most severe threat to ginseng farming. Helpful bacteria from roots and soil were combined into synthetic communities. Their joint effects and mechanisms were clarified.

Most combined groups inhibited the fungus more strongly than single strains. Several mixes also promoted plant growth. In field tests, six mixes controlled disease by more than half, with the best near two-thirds. Treated roots carried far less fungus, and colonisation exceeded single strains. Soil and defence enzymes also rose.
pmc-13266149:
Jeong-Woong Park and colleagues test dog gum microbes for calming inflammation triggered by a gum disease bacterium, published in 2026. Porphyromonas gingivalis drives gum disease partly through a surface toxin that sparks immune responses. A novel microbe community from dog gums was cultured. Mouse immune cells exposed to the toxin received the candidate microbes.

Nitric oxide, an inflammation marker, fell with microbe treatment. Three inflammatory genes were dialled down compared with toxin-only cells. Toxin alone had raised those same genes. The authors say the calming mechanism remains unknown. Further work should clarify how the candidate microbes reduce inflammation.
pmc-13266849:
Agustina A Pontecorvo and Enrique F Elli discuss in 2026 whether removing the esophagus can help selected patients whose esophageal adenocarcinoma has already spread. Surgery for metastatic disease was long ruled out, but stronger drug treatments have reopened the question. They comment on a study of stage IV patients who had surgery after long courses of systemic therapy.

Matched comparisons showed better survival for operated patients with distant spread than for similar patients managed without surgery. Results were best at experienced centers working in close multidisciplinary teams. Oddly, one stage group fared worse than the metastatic group, a pattern the authors link to hidden spread missed by scans. They frame surgery as targeted disease control for carefully chosen patients.
pmc-13267549:
Dhathri Priya Bandi and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of gum bacteria in pregnant women with diabetes of pregnancy. Both gestational diabetes and gum disease involve lasting inflammation and may worsen outcomes for mother and baby. The team studied 80 pregnant women, all with gum disease: 40 with diabetes of pregnancy and 40 without.

Samples of plaque from under the gum line were tested for seven known gum pathogens. Women with diabetes carried higher loads of five of them, including Porphyromonas gingivalis. That species tracked closely with deeper gum pockets and loss of gum attachment. Gum measures and blood sugar test results both helped predict pathogen levels. The authors call the link between blood sugar control and gum microbes a two-way street worth clinical attention.
pmc-13267749:
Derrick Bennett and colleagues wrote a 2026 summary of a workshop on statistical reviewing for medical journals. Statistics in medical papers have grown more complex, yet journals struggle to find trained statistical reviewers. A national research group ran an online workshop to close that gap, aimed at people new to the task.

Statistical review checks whether a paper's methods fit its question, were carried out correctly, and are openly reported. The summary shares the workshop's key lessons and practical advice for new reviewers. It covers what to look for, how to write a useful review, and why this work matters for trust in medical research. The authors hope more statisticians and clinicians will take up reviewing.
pmc-13268349:
Hye Seung Kang published a 2025 study of health coaching for older adults with diabetes in Korea. The eight-week program combined group coaching, health education, stress management, and monitoring, and was built on a nursing model that emphasizes the interaction between patient and coach. Fifty-nine adults aged sixty-five and older took part, split between coaching and a comparison group.

The coached group improved more on blood sugar control, cholesterol, and blood pressure, and also reported better self-care habits and less diabetes-related distress. Structured coaching of this kind offers clinics a way to support the daily behavior changes that diabetes demands beyond prescribing medicine.
pmc-13269049:
Natalia Quintero Serrano and Olga Lucía Melo Trujillo published a case report in 2026 about a 76-year-old man with gout. Soon after he gave himself one 75 milligram shot of diclofenac, a pain and swelling drug, he developed a severe skin reaction. The reaction, toxic epidermal necrolysis, makes large areas of skin blister and peel away.

At the hospital, sores covered 40.5 percent of his body surface, with severe mouth and organ damage. His risk score of 5 meant an estimated death rate of about 85 percent. He died soon after arrival despite strong supportive care. A scoring method rated the drug link as only possible, since other drugs were also in his history.
pmc-13269349:
Thomas Gough and colleagues review whether eating while distracted changes how much adults eat. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in twenty twenty-six. Screens and phones now accompany many meals daily. An older small review suggested distraction raises intake.

Fifty studies qualified for the updated analysis. Most measured intake during the distracted meal itself. A smaller set measured eating later the same day. Statistical pooling combined results across all the studies. Searches covered databases, citations, and the earlier review set. The authors weigh effects at the meal and afterwards separately. Readers get the most complete summary yet of a common daily habit.
pmc-13269649:
Yair Alvarez-Ricardo and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on three new vanadium compounds built with ring-shaped partner molecules, tested against cancer cells. Their structures were checked with standard lab methods, and one was mapped exactly by X-ray crystallography, a method that reveals atomic layout.

Across six human cancer cell lines, the compounds beat the common drug cisplatin in five, needing lower doses to halve cell growth. One compound was strongest against a lung cancer line, and another against a colon cancer line. Unlike cisplatin, they barely harmed healthy fiber cells. One compound pushed lung cancer cells into late-stage programmed death without tissue-rotting death. Computer studies also showed the compounds stick to DNA.
pmc-13269849:
Luisa Di Paola and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on recovering a pigment protein complex from shellfish waste. Shells of European lobster and Atlantic blue crab hold astaxanthin, a pigment with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Computer models examined how the complex could carry the pigment for drug and cosmetic use.

Simulations suggested astaxanthin would compete with a cell defender protein at its binding site. Freeing that defender would switch on the cell's own antioxidant machinery. Early lab evidence supported the modeling. The authors propose shell waste as a source of a bioactive agent for diseases tied to cell stress, including cancer. They stress that animal and human studies must first confirm the promise.
pmc-13270249:
Mariana Bastos-Oreiro and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on real-world use of bispecific antibodies in B-cell lymphoma across Spain's GELTAMO network. These drugs grab both a T cell and a cancer B cell to redirect the attack. Thirty-eight centers treated patients whose lymphoma had returned or resisted earlier care.

The study included 168 patients with a median age of 64, split 58 percent large B-cell lymphoma and 42 percent follicular lymphoma. Most, 86 percent, had a planned hospital admission during dose step-up, with a median stay of four days. Unplanned admissions hit 32 percent, led by infections in half of urgent cases. Twenty-nine percent of patients would not have qualified for the pivotal drug trials.
pmc-13270549:
Brandon A Ally, Paul A Mentele, and Scott A Wylie measure in 2026 how much game-speed thinking college football players regain after a year away from cannabis. Eighteen NCAA Division I players who had tested positive for THC took a football-specific cognition battery, then retook it after twelve months of verified abstinence. The battery scores nine processes, from perception speed and tracking to impulse control, plus reaction speed and decision accuracy.

At baseline, the players reacted about a fifth slower than their own later scores, a delay near a tenth of a second in decision execution. Composite scores and six individual processes improved significantly after abstinence, and gains held after accounting for raw reaction speed. Chronic use, the authors conclude, taxes split-second decision-making in ways that partly reverse with a year clean.
pmc-13270949:
Vincent L. Sorrell wrote a 2026 editorial titled Sound Waves, Rays, and Magnets, on multimodality cardiovascular imaging, the use of several scan types to study the heart. The title names ultrasound, X-ray based computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging, three tools he has worked with for over two decades.

Sorrell tells how mentors trained him first in ultrasound and nuclear heart imaging, and how he was once advised to pick one specialty rather than master both. Instead, he followed the growth of magnetic resonance and computed tomography, trained in London in cardiac magnetic resonance, and later added computed tomography skills for noninvasive imaging of the heart arteries. The piece is a personal career reflection.
pmc-13271149:
Niek Stevenson is lead author of a 2026 journal article presenting an open-source toolbox for joint modelling of brain scans and behaviour. Joint modelling fits behaviour data and MRI data, which track brain activity, together in one model. It accounts for measurement error and for differences between people.

Built into an R software package called EMC2, the toolbox streamlines building behaviour, brain, and joint models. The authors show it on a perceptual decision task done inside a scanner. They explain how to set up design tables, prior guesses, and brain-behaviour links. Joint fitting steadied weak values and cut a known bias that shrinks brain-behaviour links, they report. Code examples are included.
pmc-13271349:
Yi Zhou is lead author of a 2026 review on Fusarium oxysporum forma specialis vasinfectum race 4, shortened to Fov4. That is a highly damaging fungus that causes wilt disease in cotton, especially in the United States. The review gathers what is known from field disease through to the pathogen's genome.

Fov4 genomes are larger and richer in repeated DNA than those of related races, the authors note, though their chromosome layout is still unresolved. Studies have flagged candidate attack factors, including race-specific effector proteins and chemical-making genes. Because the fungus persists in soil and adapts genetically, control relies on mixing resistant cotton varieties, farming practices, and close monitoring, they conclude.
pmc-13271549:
Nakul Verma and coauthors describe in 2026 the features and outcomes of cavitary retinoblastoma, a child eye cancer that forms hollow spaces inside the tumor. Retinoblastoma is the most common eye cancer in young children. The cavitary form is less often described, so its behavior under treatment matters to care teams.

Records covered 40 children with 43 affected eyes, most diagnosed near age two. White pupil reflex was the most common first sign, and nearly all eyes received chemotherapy through a vein. Every eye achieved tumor control at final follow-up, with no spread or deaths. The results support standard chemotherapy for this tumor form.
pmc-13271949:
Rong-rong Zhang and coauthors follow in 2026 wound healing in people with diabetic kidney disease who take SGLT2 inhibitor drugs. These drugs protect heart and kidneys, yet sugar in the urine raised worry that wounds might heal more slowly. Clinicians lacked direct evidence for patients with active wounds.

The study enrolled 247 adults at a wound care center and matched 102 drug users with 102 similar non-users. Median healing time was nearly identical, at about thirty-three days in both groups. Infection and kidney outcomes at six months also showed no clear difference. The results ease concern about continuing these drugs during wound care.
pmc-13272149:
Heng Chen and coauthors estimate in 2026 how emergency policy changes affected regional emergency logistics capacity across China. Contingency plans are meant to make disaster response faster and better stocked, but hard evidence of their effect is scarce. The 2006 national master plan for public health emergencies serves as a natural experiment.

Panel data from thirty provinces between 2005 and 2022 fed a difference-in-differences analysis. Provinces whose plans matched the national text closely gained a measurable rise in response capacity, about forty-seven percent on the study's scale. Matching the text alone did not guarantee strength, though; weak alignment reliably went with weak capacity.
pmc-13272249:
Lena Marie Süß is lead author of a 2026 journal article on blocking P2Y6 receptors to slow kidney fibrosis. Fibrosis is the scarring that drives chronic kidney disease. That disease affects over 850 million people worldwide. Signals from released nucleotides through P2 receptors help activate the fibroblast cells that lay down scar tissue, but their role was poorly understood.

Using precise RNA staining, the team found P2Y1 and P2Y6 receptors in kidney interstitial fibroblasts, with P2Y6 sharply raised in several mouse fibrosis models. Cultured fibroblasts moved more when stimulated by a nucleotide signal. In a mouse kidney disease model, a selective P2Y6 blocker cut expression of a scar-cell marker and of collagen I, a main scar protein. They propose P2Y6 blockade as a new anti-fibrosis strategy.
pmc-13272349:
Chen Yuhang and coauthors sort in 2026 older adults in two Chengdu districts by how well their basic mental needs are met or blocked. Needs for choice, skill, and close ties shape mental health late in life, yet people mix met and blocked needs in distinct ways. Grouping those mixes can help aim support where it fits.

Surveys from 430 residents, gathered in late 2025, supported four groups. The largest group, near half the sample, had its needs well met, while a small group had them broadly unmet. Life satisfaction, distress scores, and social support helped explain who fell in each group. The authors use the groups to guide local mental health work with older adults.
pmc-13272449:
Ran Meng and coauthors review in 2026 hydrogel therapies that deliver healing cargo directly into heart muscle damaged by heart attack. About seven million heart attacks occur yearly, and surviving muscle often scars into heart failure that drugs and devices cannot reverse. Injectable gels suit the heart because they are water-rich, body-friendly, and can carry living cargo.

The review traces the path from blocked artery to scarred, failing heart, then compares gels loaded with drugs, bioactive molecules, cells, or exosomes. Each cargo class attacks a different step, from calming inflammation to growing vessels. The authors judge hydrogels a promising repair platform still proving itself clinically.
pmc-13272549:
Ellis Eikenboom, Helena van Doorn, and Anja Wagner wrote a 2026 authors' reply about womb surveillance in Lynch syndrome in the Netherlands. Lynch syndrome raises cancer risk, and their earlier paper questioned whether regular checks of the womb lining help Dutch carriers. The reply answers comments on that paper.

They explain why the subtype of overgrown womb lining did not change their advice, since surgery is advised for any such growth. They note that more growths and cancers were found in the checked group, yet cancers were not less advanced in a way that cut later treatment or improved survival. A much larger study is needed, they argue.
pmc-13272749:
Fang Zhang leads a 2026 study of a protein called SEMA6A in colorectal cancer, cancer of the colon and rectum. The protein was lower in cancer tissue than normal, and low levels linked to more aggressive tumors and a poorer outlook. The team tested what raising SEMA6A does in cells and in animals.

Raising SEMA6A slowed tumors and boosted killing by CD8 T cells, the immune cells that attack cancer. It acted by lowering a protein called ISG15, which otherwise helps stabilize TGF-beta, a signal that shields tumors. Patients with high SEMA6A and low ISG15 responded better to immunotherapy, and raising SEMA6A improved anti-PD-1 treatment in mice.
pmc-13273349:
Santi Poungcharean and colleagues described early life development in seven wild mouth-brooding fighting fish in a 2026 study from Thailand. These small air breathing fish hold eggs and young in the father's mouth for protection. Knowing how each species grows helps tell them apart while young.

The team bred fish gathered from type localities and followed their young through larval and juvenile stages. Most species released their young at a set stage about eleven days after fertilization, though one took up to twenty days. Young then reached the juvenile stage within a month of release. Counts of body segments and fin rays differed by species, as did pigment bands on the head and stripes along the body. A step by step identification key with illustrations sums up the differences.
pmc-13274149:
Yujie Chen and co-authors study why bowel growths return after removal, and how gut microbes differ in those cases, in work from two thousand twenty-six. Such growths can turn into bowel cancer, so spotting return risk matters. Thirty people with returned growths were compared with fifteen without.

More growths at first and a smoking history stood out as lone risk factors for return. Overall microbe variety was much the same in both groups. Some harmful bacteria ran higher in the return group, while two helpful types ran lower. Fat-linked pathways were more active in the group without returns. The authors link return to a skewed gut mix.
pmc-13274349:
Dattesh Bala Saranga and a large team engineer a soil bacterium to make plant scent compounds. Their twenty twenty-six study uses Azospirillum brasilense Sp7. Sesquiterpenes serve in many commercial products, but plant extraction has limits. Microbes could make them if yields were high enough.

The chosen bacterium already moves much material through a pigment pathway. That flow passes a shared building block for sesquiterpenes. The team improved strains and growth media step by step. Pigment output rose sharply, and cells tolerated the target compounds well. Adding the needed enzymes produced two model compounds at low levels. Further pathway and export changes raised output more than tenfold.
pmc-13274549:
Xiaocui Ma and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on what shapes bird diversity in a small Chinese nature reserve.
