HuiLing Xu and coauthors report a 2026 laboratory study of synovial sarcoma, a rare and aggressive cancer of soft tissue. The work asks how a small RNA molecule, miR-29b-5p, affects tumor growth and stem-like behavior in this cancer through a signaling route involving TGF-beta and the gene EP300.

The team predicted a link between miR-29b-5p and EP300 with computer tools, then tested it in cell experiments. Tumor spheres grown in the lab showed low miR-29b-5p and high EP300, along with stronger growth, movement, and invasion. Raising miR-29b-5p curbed sphere formation, which points to a possible control point for future treatment research.
pmc-13393949:
Jingjing Liu and coauthors test whether folic acid in pregnancy affects mothers' later thinking skills in a 2026 cohort study. Folic acid supports nervous system function at all ages, but its long-term effect on postnatal maternal cognition had never been tested.

From the Ma'anshan Birth Cohort follow-up, 182 women with prenatal supplement records completed Stroop, digit-symbol, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment tests after birth. Supplement use in each trimester was recorded prospectively by questionnaire. The paper offers early evidence that pregnancy nutrition may shape maternal brain health well beyond delivery.
pmc-13394449:
Adrien Robin leads a 2026 study of how the heart and blood vessels cope when gravity shifts and blood volume drops. Sixteen healthy adults lay on a tilting table, from head-down to head-up in small steps. They repeated the test after a drug made them pass more urine and lose fluid. The team tracked heart rate, output, and vessel tone at each angle.

With less fluid, heart rate and vessel tone rose while each beat moved less blood. Pressure stayed steady, and heart rhythm signals shifted toward stress patterns. The tilt curve let the team place Moon and Mars gravity levels on one chart. Space crews and doctors may both use the map.
pmc-13394849:
Sabrina Atha Shania and co-authors design, in 2026, a phone app to guide stroke recovery in Indonesia. The country carries one of the heaviest stroke loads in its region, with too few therapists for home care. The team spoke with ten experts and eight stroke survivors, then built the app in three rounds of design and testing. Each round sharpened the prototype.

The app offers training plans for movement, speech, and daily tasks, with progress tracking. It adds video lessons, reminders, targets, games, and links to staff for chats and home visits. Test users rated the design as good overall. The authors offer the plan as a guide for clinics and rule makers.
pmc-13395749:
Yuwei Li and co-authors find, in 2026, a guard that keeps myelin-making cells safe from rust-like death. Cells that wrap nerves face heavy strain as they build fatty sheaths. A tagging enzyme named RLIM marks a cystine porter for keeping at the cell surface. That porter feeds production of glutathione, a master shield.

Mice lacking RLIM in these cells lost porter from the surface, made fewer cells, and formed poor myelin. Their movement, social acts, and thinking slipped in ways that echo human cases. Most harmful human variants broke the porter grip. Extra glutathione rescued mice in the tests. The authors pitch the shield as a therapy lead.
pmc-13395949:
Stylianos Kapetanakis and co-authors reviewed records of older patients who needed repeat vertebroplasty, a procedure that injects cement into broken spinal bones, in a study published in 2026. The patients were 75 to 85 years old and had osteoporosis-related fractures in the chest and lower back.

All had earlier vertebroplasty and came back for repair at three or four levels in a single session, between August 2019 and November 2023, at one center. Pain scores and a disability index were recorded before surgery and at one, three, six, and twelve months after. The authors set out to judge pain relief, daily function, and safety for a group that earlier reports rarely covered.
pmc-13396349:
Geethamani Rajamani and Jaganathan Subramani offer a map-based graph net for city food safety under climate strain in a 2026 study. Climate shocks and soil wear threaten soil-free farms, and food-juice wobble in water-grown and mist-grown crops needs early flags.

A Pi-based sensor web tracked sky traits, plant health, and food-juice levels as map points, while a tuned multi-scale graph net forecast growth from lettuce trials. Plant color signs flagged strain early, before crops failed. City growers gain a watch frame for tough soil-free farms in a hot, rough climate.
pmc-13396449:
Yuchen Lin and colleagues build a textile interface that decodes silent speech for people who cannot speak aloud in a 2026 study. People with impaired vocal organs face profound communication barriers, yet subtle multi-muscle activity remains even when audible speech is absent.

The team created a scarf interface that imperceptibly captures those muscle signals and decodes silent speech robustly, fusing electromagnetic physiological communication with metamaterial embroidery. The design reconciles spatial selectivity with fidelity in noisy environments. The paper offers a wearable path back to conversation for people with speech loss.
pmc-13396649:
Abdalrahman G. Al-Gamal and co-authors decorated graphene and carbon nanotubes with extra atoms and measured how the decorations change the materials, in a 2026 study aimed at cleaner energy devices. Three additions were tried: fluorine, bromine in a carrier compound, and lithium fluoride.

Graphene oxide was fluorinated with hydrofluoric acid and brominated through a salt treatment, while multi-walled nanotubes took up lithium fluoride. A battery of imaging and spectroscopy tools confirmed each structure, and light-based and electrical tests tracked the changes. Because each dopant altered conductivity and light behavior differently, the comparison guides which decoration suits which energy job.
pmc-13396849:
Alexandre Araujo Pereira and co-authors borrowed a heart procedure to fix a leg artery fork, and report the first such use in a 2026 case. A 46-year-old man had lifestyle-limiting leg pain on walking from a heavily calcified narrowing where the iliac artery splits toward the pelvis and the leg.

The double-kissing double-crush method, routine for coronary forks, stents both branches of a split in a choreographed sequence that keeps each branch open. Applied here across the common, internal, and external iliac arteries, it restored flow. At twelve months the man remained free of symptoms with the stents open, evidence that heart-born techniques can travel to the pelvis.
pmc-13397949:
Yash Jawale and team projected how many skilled health workers rural India will need by 2030 and what closing the gap would cost. Their 2026 study tracks doctors, nurses, and midwives at rural primary-care and community clinics, using national Rural Health Statistics from 2009 to 2019. India already faces a shortage, and rural shortfalls had not been weighed against global development targets.

Skilled worker density grew about 2.59 percent per year and is set to rise from 8.85 per 10,000 people in 2019 to 11.47 per 10,000 people in 2030. Even so, India would still face a shortfall of roughly half a million workers at the low end and 1.83 million at the high end, costing an estimated 1.46 trillion rupees at the low end and 4.96 trillion at the high end to close. The authors argue that cost equals about 15 percent of government health spending, making scale-up feasible. The result is a state-aware planning baseline, not a hiring plan.
pmc-13398249:
Francesco Liuzza and colleagues report results of cement-free hip replacement in patients whose hip sockets formed poorly from birth. Their 2026 study reviews eight women, mean age near 53.9 years, treated at one centre between 2019 and 2025. Developmental dysplasia warps the joint's anatomy, making it hard to restore leg length, stability and natural mechanics.

Alongside the cementless implant, surgeons balanced soft tissues and, where needed, rebuilt the socket using bone from the patient's own femoral head. Hip scores including the Harris Hip Score and the WOMAC index tracked pain and function, while X-rays checked implant position and healing. The series offers ground-level evidence for tackling moderate to severe dysplasia in one operation.
pmc-13398749:
R. J. Lowes and colleagues tested how much digital joint-motion results depend on choices made while building the starting pose. Their 2026 paper concerns range-of-motion analysis for extinct vertebrates, where joint mobility limits which limb poses are biologically plausible. Digital workflows are growing, yet no thorough sensitivity study had checked how subjective setup steps change the viable poses.

The team ran a complete six-degree-of-freedom automated workflow on guinea fowl ankle and foot joints, varying each stage of reference pose assembly. Outputs proved sensitive to variation, especially the choice of joint surfaces and the shape used to define the joint center. Single-study conclusions based on maximum rotations may survive, but cross-study and cross-species comparisons could mislead. The authors urge future studies to publish full joint models.
pmc-13399049:
Martínková and Trnka review, in 2026, tunnelling nanotubes, the hair-thin membrane bridges that let cells pass cargo between their interiors, with a focus on cancer. Found a little over two decades ago, these bridges have since been found across body function and disease. The review sums up their structural and molecular features and the cytoskeletal machinery that builds them. It covers the striking range of freight they carry, from nucleic acids and proteins to organelles, pathogens, and drugs.

Mitochondria transfer gets attention: in a classic experiment, healthy pheochromocytoma cells donated mitochondria through nanotubes to ultraviolet-stressed sister cells, rescuing them from early apoptosis. The authors also weigh newer evidence for mRNA transfer changing recipient cell behavior and ribosome transfer implying cells can share protein-making capacity. In tumors, such cooperation supports metabolic sharing, stress adaptation, and treatment resistance, making them both a biological curiosity and a therapeutic target.
pmc-13399149:
Ashish Heerani, Muskan Bai, and Noor Un Nisa wrote this 2026 letter questioning a proposal to screen everyone with Hashimoto's thyroiditis for a diabetes antibody. The discussed article suggested routine testing for glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies, called GADA, so latent autoimmune diabetes in adults might be caught early. The letter writers accept the link between the two autoimmune conditions but dispute the screening logic.

Their first objection is that no prospective evidence shows screening changes the course of this diabetes; the drug data cited come from relatives at risk of type 1 diabetes, a different group. Second, a positive antibody result in thyroid patients has not been shown to predict who later develops autoimmune diabetes. Third, without prevalence and test-performance figures for the actual screening population, the value of routine testing cannot be judged. The authors ask for long-term studies before such screening is adopted.
pmc-13399349:
Marwa S. Ibrahim, Ibrahim A. Naqid, and Ghadeer Suaifan surveyed Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in the wounds of diabetic patients in Duhok Province, Iraq, in a 2026 study. This bacterium is a frequent wound invader in diabetes and often resists many drugs. Between June 2024 and July 2025 the team collected 141 wound swabs from adult diabetic patients.

The bacterium grew from 44.68 percent of the samples, as the laboratory results showed. Most patient traits showed no clear link to infection. Wound location did matter. Infections in the leg region carried nearly four times the odds, with an adjusted figure of 3.94 reported by the authors. Resistance testing found high multidrug resistance, especially against aztreonam and ceftazidime. Colistin kept the best activity against the isolates, followed by the carbapenem antibiotics. The authors urge early testing and careful drug choice.
pmc-13399449:
Alfonso Trinidad and colleagues reviewed a quarter century of research on teaching swimming in schools, in a 2026 systematic review. School programs are the main route to aquatic literacy, the mix of knowledge, skill, and confidence that keeps children safe in water. The team searched PubMed, Scopus, SportDiscus, and Web of Science following PRISMA guidance, covering programs from early childhood through secondary school.

Sixteen studies met their criteria and were quality-checked. Most programs took a technical, utilitarian approach, drilling specific strokes and skills with little connection to the wider curriculum. Research clustered in infant and primary years and thinned out sharply at secondary level. Program length, session frequency, content, and assessment tools varied so widely that comparisons were difficult. The authors conclude that school swimming has progressed but still lacks systematic implementation. They call for stronger backing, better teacher training, and stage-appropriate teaching.
pmc-13399649:
Cheng-Wei Kuo and co-authors published a 2026 study on whether nutrition scores predict survival in advanced liver cancer. The scores combine blood protein levels, immune cell counts, and body weight into one number. Patients with better nutrition tend to withstand treatment better. The team tested two such scores in people receiving a standard first drug, lenvatinib.

The study covered 276 patients with advanced disease. Those with high scores lived much longer without their cancer growing: about seven and a half months versus four. Overall survival roughly doubled as well, near nineteen to twenty-one months against under ten. High-score patients also responded more often and had fewer severe side effects. They were more likely to receive further treatment after the first drug. Both scores predicted death risk on their own, and together they did slightly better.
pmc-13399749:
Ayu Hidaka and co-authors evaluated a shortcut test for lupus anticoagulant, a clotting-related antibody central to diagnosing antiphospholipid syndrome, in a 2026 laboratory study. Their proposed method takes one ratio: clotting time with a high-sensitivity reagent divided by clotting time with a low-sensitivity reagent, both from the familiar APTT test family.

The team checked the ratio against guideline-based testing in plasma from 57 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and 74 patients with prolonged clotting times. They also used samples deliberately spiked with anticoagulant drugs. Agreement with the standard pathway was good overall. Five patients whom the guideline route called negative showed elevated ratios, a discrepancy the authors flag for cautious follow-up rather than dismissal. They position the method as a screening sieve: a negative result makes lupus anticoagulant unlikely, while positives still require the full confirmatory workup.
pmc-13400249:
Ran Svirsky and colleagues mapped germline genetic findings among men with prostate cancer in a real-world, multicenter study. Their 2026 paper asks whether broad next-generation sequencing adds value beyond testing for known founder variants, inherited changes common in a population. Genetic results can guide treatment and family screening, yet testing patterns in routine care had been unclear.

Among 293 tested men, 39, or 13.3 percent, carried a positive finding, including 18 with high-penetrance genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, and ATM, and 21 with risk variants. One third of disease-causing variants found by sequencing were unique rather than founder variants. Family history of cancer was the only demographic or clinical factor tied to positive results. The authors argue for broad sequencing regardless of ethnicity or stage.
pmc-13400549:
João Victor dos Anjos Almeida and co-authors review, in 2026, prebiotics and probiotics in animal nutrition and what they mean for food safety and greener farming. Prebiotics feed helpful gut microbes, while probiotics supply live beneficial microbes directly. Interest has grown as producers seek alternatives to routine antibiotics.

Across poultry, pigs, cattle, fish and shrimp, these additives can improve digestion, gut wall health and immune strength while suppressing harmful germs such as E coli and Salmonella. Trials link them to better growth, feed efficiency and carcass quality, plus less reliance on antibiotics. The review also highlights turning farm waste streams, like fruit pomace and cereal bran, into useful feed substrates within circular production systems.
pmc-13400649:
Anthony W Sali and colleagues issue, in 2026, a correction to their 2025 study of how sustained attention affects readiness to move the eyes. A stimulus error had cut the last trial of each run short for some people. For others, the response was not recorded. A few worked-out measures also held mistakes.

The team cut the faulty trials and fixed the counts, then ran the tests again. One key interaction, between shift likelihood and attention state, kept the same direction but weakened. It no longer cleared the usual threshold for a firm finding. The results and discussion text was softened to match. The authors say the overall pattern and conclusions stand.
pmc-13400749:
Calvo-Sánchez and colleagues studied liver cancer risk after hepatitis C cure in a multicentre cohort study published in 2026. Clearing the virus lowers risk, but some patients still develop hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. The team asked whether longer use of metformin, a common diabetes drug, was linked to lower risk after cure.

They followed 1,531 patients who had cleared the virus with direct-acting antiviral drugs, and 50 developed liver cancer over a median follow-up of about six years. With models that track metformin use as it builds up, each extra year of use was linked to about half the cancer risk. The pattern held in patients with type 2 diabetes. Portal hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and a high fibrosis score each raised risk. The findings support trials of metformin as a cheap preventive after hepatitis C cure.
pmc-13401649:
Davis Ngarashi and co-authors carried out a 2026 cross-sectional study of noncontact infrared thermometers in healthy Black African adults, asking how much the body site and room temperature shift the readings. These forehead-style devices screen quickly at a distance, a virtue during infectious emergencies, but their accuracy varies and evidence from African populations was thin.

In an environmental chamber, 216 adults were measured at the forehead, neck, temple, and wrist. Readings came first at a cooler setting and then at a warmer one, in a fixed order. Statistical tests compared sites and conditions, while Bland-Altman plots and kappa statistics judged agreement between readings. The repeated-measures design isolates how much of a thermometer's answer comes from where it points and how warm the room is, rather than from the person being measured.
pmc-13401749: Andrés Fernando Montalvo Vásquez and co-authors are named in a 2026 correction notice in AIDS Research and Treatment for their 2025 article. It covers how migration movements shape the epidemiology and clinical profile of HIV infection in Quito, Ecuador. The notice is a correction only: the article was first published with the wrong article type, labelled a Review Article when it should have been a Research Article. The first author's name was stated incompletely. The article has been updated and the publisher apologises.
pmc-13401949:
Ram B Basany and colleagues describe making silicone finger prostheses for people who have lost fingers, in a 2026 case series. Traumatic hand injuries damage far more than grip: dexterity, work capacity, social ease, and psychological well-being all suffer, and losses can also follow birth defects, infection, or disease.

The team presents their work designing and fabricating custom hand prostheses tailored to each patient. A well-made silicone prosthesis restores appearance convincingly and can support some function, though it cannot fully replace a natural hand. Their reported gains centre on aesthetics, confidence, independence, and reintegration into daily and social life. Success, they argue, rests on clinical expertise, careful treatment planning, and a compassionate approach as much as on materials. The series documents their fabrication efforts and what the devices meant to the patients fitted with them.
pmc-13402249:
Akhilesh M Wodeyar and co-authors review how glowing dyes could sharpen robot surgery done through the mouth for head and neck cancers. The robot route, called TORS, cuts harm and preserves function, yet the surgeon loses touch and depth sense, which makes judging tumor edges hard. Fluorescence imaging, where tissue lights up under special light, offers real-time sight of the tumor instead.

The review weighs a general dye, indocyanine green, against tumor-targeted agents such as panitumumab-IRDye800CW, checking fit with the da Vinci Firefly camera system. Targeted tracers gave the strongest contrast in the sensitive imaging mode, but results hinged on settings: camera angle, light output, field evenness, and autoscaling all mattered. The authors add lessons from their own operating rooms and call for shared protocols and stronger trials before the method becomes routine.
pmc-13402649:
Pritam Bera, Rajesh Raju, and Debodipta Das compare lung tumors with the lung cancer cell lines labs use to model them, working at pathway level rather than gene by gene. They set 513 lung adenocarcinoma tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas against 45 cell lines from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia. Each sample was scored across hallmark gene sets, and a penalized model hunted for separating patterns.

Five pathways split the two groups cleanly: E2F targets, interferon-gamma response, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, coagulation, and the G2M checkpoint. Cell lines ran hot on growth pathways and carried higher mutation loads, with more TP53 and STK11 changes, while true tumors kept immune and surrounding-tissue programs that lines have lost. The same split held in lung squamous cancer. The authors offer the five-pathway test as a yardstick for picking cell models honestly.
pmc-13402849:
Muhammad Usman and co-authors report a 20-year-old Marshallese man whose tuberculosis had spread body-wide, striking skin, brain vessels, and clotting at once despite a healthy immune system. He arrived with trouble swallowing, weight loss, and confusion after a fall, and imaging found disease in lungs, pleura, and the skin by his left ear. He tested negative for HIV, and clotting workups found no inherited cause.

His course worsened with a large stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory, with mild bleeding into it, plus a pulmonary embolism in the left lung. Pleural fluid markers strongly supported tuberculous pleuritis, yet PCR tests on lung washings and blood stayed negative, deepening the puzzle. The authors blame a tuberculosis-driven clotting state and urge suspicion for spread disease in young patients from high-burden regions.
pmc-13403149:
Vishwadeepak Rajput, Vishavdeep Kaur, and Ankalayya Bobbara compare heart rate variability at rest and after step exercise in 200 young adults split evenly between normal weight and overweight. Extra fat in youth can tilt the autonomic balance before heart disease declares itself, and variability in beat timing reads that balance noninvasively. Volunteers aged 17 to 25 stepped on a 23 centimeter stool at 40 steps a minute for up to five minutes.

At rest the overweight group already showed lower variability across time-domain measures and higher heart rate, all with p values below 0.001 in the reported tests. After exercise their recovery values, including SDNN, RMSSD, and high-frequency power, stayed lower, and adjusted models tied overweight status to lower fitness index scores too. The authors read early autonomic strain in overweight youth, detectable with a stool, a stopwatch, and an ECG.
pmc-13404149:
Anna Szlachcic and Nadinath B. Nillegoda probed in 2026 how mixed helper proteins team up to dissolve toxic protein clumps in animal cells. Clumps threaten cell health and build up with age and disease. The clearing machine pairs a workhorse protein, Hsp70, with helper proteins from two classes.

The team muted each helper's grip on the workhorse in turn, while keeping the helpers paired. Teamwork gains vanished when either partner could not engage the workhorse. Size-sorted tests showed the mixed pair handled clump types that neither class managed alone. Both helpers thus pull workhorses in together, widening what the machine can clear.
pmc-13404249:
Shiinoki and colleagues teach a model to read lung function from moving chest X-rays. The aim is patients who cannot do the forced breathing tests demand. Spirometry, the reference test, fails with children, frail elders, and people with poor cognition. Their 2026 study reuses chest radiography, a low dose image sequence taken while a patient breathes, in 151 patients. It extracts image features at breath phases and from a motion map. Models are trained to predict standard lung values.

Models built on the multiphase images and motion map beat the formula that estimates lung function from age, sex, and height alone. The approach predicted both breathing volumes and sorted patients by the ratio used to flag high risk obstruction. Because the study is one center and looks backward, the authors call for validation elsewhere before clinics trust it. An X-ray that reports function could reach patients spirometry leaves untested.
pmc-13404849:
Huayue Zeng and colleagues built a single test that finds three chicken viruses at once, reporting in 2026. Avian leukosis virus, chicken infectious anaemia virus and fowl adenovirus cause tumours, weak immunity and heavy losses on poultry farms. Testing for each separately costs time during outbreaks.

Their triplex crystal digital RT-PCR copies and counts genetic material from all three viruses in one run. After tuning reaction settings, the test showed strong specificity, sensitivity and repeatability. On 1,211 farm samples it agreed with reference methods in at least 98.18 percent of cases in the reported checks. The team offers the assay for routine flock screening where the three viruses circulate.
pmc-13405449:
Ali Ijaz, Kin Mun Lau and Andrew CF Hui write in 2026 with two objections to a recent study of dermatomyositis diagnosis in 14 patients. The original authors concluded that electromyography, a test of electrical activity in muscle, can exclude the disease. They also proposed that every suspected patient should receive the test.

Both claims overreach the data, the letter argues. Abnormal results appear in 70 to 90 percent of inflammatory muscle disease, yet some classic cases with raised muscle enzymes showed no such pattern in the study itself. A test that misses real cases cannot rule the disease out. The correspondents ask for the conclusions to be softened to match the small, real-world series.
pmc-13405649:
Serena Stigliano and co-authors compare two scope routes for draining the gallbladder in patients too frail for surgery, in a 2026 Italian series. Ultrasound-guided drainage through a metal stent serves people with gallbladder inflammation or blocked bile ducts from cancer. The scope can pass through the stomach wall or the duodenum, and which is better is debated.

Seventy consecutive patients treated between 2020 and 2026 were reviewed, with an average age of 77. Technical success reached 98.5 percent in the reported results. The stomach route was used in 48.5 percent of cases. Success, complications, readmissions and repeat procedures are compared between the two routes to guide route choice.
pmc-13407349:
Zhaoxi Wang and co-authors survey, in 2026, heat shock proteins and protein housekeeping in worn spinal discs, a leading source of low back pain. Heat shock proteins act as chaperones that refold stressed proteins, and in disc tissue they can protect cells or, in other settings, feed the damage process.

The review tracks members such as HSP70, HSP90, and HSP27 across the disc. They appear in its gel-like centre and its fibrous outer ring. The authors tie them to inflammation, cell death, and matrix turnover. Tuning these chaperones could pair with biomaterials, physical stimulation, or regenerative approaches. Direct disc-specific evidence for some family members is still scarce, a gap the authors flag for future work.
pmc-13407449:
Laura Valentina Klüner and co-authors, in 2026, scanned child-sized head models to compare two CT detector technologies for children's brain imaging. Photon-counting detectors are newer than standard energy-integrating ones, and the team varied image quality settings on models representing ages one, five, and ten, recording dose, noise, and signal clarity.

Photon-counting scans needed lower radiation dose at every age, with the biggest saving, about 9 percent, in the ten-year-old model at clinically used settings. Signal clarity ran higher for both brain tissue and bone, by up to roughly 20 and 50 percent across the full range tested, and image noise was lower in the younger models. Organ doses were highest in the smallest model under both systems. The results support gentler, clearer paediatric head scanning.
pmc-13407849:
Yan Wei and co-authors report, in 2026, turning a water pollutant into a recoverable polymer without gumming up the catalyst. Oxidation-driven linking can convert pollutants into useful products. Reactions on solid surfaces coat catalysts with polymer and stall, though. The team moved the key bond-forming steps out into the water itself. A facet-cut bismuth oxyiodide catalyst with peroxide did the work.

The catalyst steers peroxide activation toward freely diffusing iodine, a moderate oxidiser that polymerised the target chlorophenol mainly in solution. A record 73 percent of polymer product stayed in the aqueous phase for recovery. Specialised microscopy watched iodine form and react in place, and calculations showed one crystal facet's hydrogen-bonding arrangement favours iodine generation while another favours radical routes. Fouling-resistant cleanup coupled to resource recovery is the promise.
pmc-13408049:
Alexander R. Markes and James P. Bradley describe, in 2026, a combined arthroscopic operation for massive rotator cuff tears that cannot be sewn back. Two fixes are paired. The first rebuilds the cuff's cable, the load-spreading structure along the tear's edge, with heavy non-absorbable suture anchored at the bone. The second resurfaces the bone knob, tuberoplasty, capped with a dermal graft from donated tissue.

The operation suits multi-tendon tears with heavy retraction where complete repair is impossible and pain persists despite conservative care. Published results for the components separately show fewer re-tears, better shoulder mechanics, and pain relief. Combining them aims to restore partial biomechanics and soothe pain through the biological interposition graft. Joint replacement is avoided. Portal placement, graft rolling for insertion, and anchor choice by bone quality are covered as key technical points.
pmc-13408149:
Simone Nascimento Santos Ribeiro and co-authors build, in 2026, a camera-based system that counts newborn breathing without touching the baby. Contact sensors and subjective observation limit neonatal monitoring, especially for preterm infants. The team therefore trained a vision model to segment the chest-abdomen region in video. It then extracted the breathing signal from motion between frames, counting peaks only while a pose tracker judged the infant still.

Twenty-three recordings of spontaneously breathing newborns, three to fifteen days old, supplied 3,387 hand-labelled frames. Segmentation precision exceeded 94 percent on the reported metric, and estimated breathing rate missed the simultaneous clinical reference by an average of 2.1 breaths per minute. The single-centre sample was small, so the authors present technical feasibility and call for multicentre prospective validation.
pmc-13408349:
Seenivasan Subramani and Muthu Chidambaram discuss in 2026 why everyday care for bronchiolitis, a viral chest infection of infants, still drifts away from published guidance. The illness fills paediatric wards every season, respiratory syncytial virus causes most cases, and care is supportive only: fluids and oxygen, with no drug proven to help much.

Drawing on a survey of practitioners, the authors catalogue how often inhalers, steroids, adrenaline, antibiotics, and scans are still used despite guidance advising against most of them. Premature babies face several times the risk of severe disease, which may encourage intervention. Readers get a clear map of the gap between guidance and habit, and a reference point for audits aiming to standardise supportive care in busy children's hospitals.
pmc-13408949:
Yangxiang Zhou and team propose 6HAN, a graph attention network algorithm to make IPv6 scanning targets for prefixes with no seed addresses. Their 2026 work takes on a core web measurement snag: the IPv6 space is vast and sparse, and past generators lean on seed patterns, failing on nonseed prefixes. Prior nonseed methods used single traits, underused Whois data, and could not handle missing Whois fields.

6HAN builds a mixed graph from IPv6 prefixes and Whois metadata. It learns prefix codes by joining Whois traits with structural traits, and fills missing Whois fields by graph guessing before moving patterns from like seed prefixes. Sending 50 million probes, it lifted hit rates by 13.81 to 201.05 percent and prefix coverage by 17.41 to 233.58 percent over two rival methods. The work offers a stronger tool for IPv6 measurement, with scanning ethics and authorization still required.
pmc-13410549:

pmc-13412149:

pmc-13412549:

pmc-13417649:

pmc-13418249:

pmc-13418549:

pmc-13418749:

pmc-13418849:

pmc-13421349:

pmc-13427749:

pmc-13431349:

pmc-13432849:

pmc-13433749:

pmc-13433949:

pmc-13434149:

pmc-13434249:

pmc-13434449:

pmc-13441949:

pmc-13455249:

pmc-13457149:

pmc-13457449:
Luiz Gustavo de Quadros and colleagues pool the studies on pairing stomach-shrinking endoscopy with weight-loss drugs. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty reshapes the stomach from inside, and clinics increasingly add anti-obesity medications, yet the extra benefit was unproven. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered comparative studies of the combination against the procedure alone in adults with overweight or obesity.

Ten studies with 578 participants qualified. At roughly seven months, the combination held a small edge in total weight loss, a mean difference of 1.9 percentage points, but the gap was not statistically significant and the studies disagreed sharply with one another. Blood sugar results were essentially a wash, with a pooled HbA1c difference of minus 0.04 percent and inconsistent findings across individual reports. The authors suggest combined therapy may suit selected patients rather than everyone, and they call for multicenter randomized trials with standard drug protocols and longer follow-up.
pmc-13457649:
Chunyan Wang and Congli Yuan propose a fresh lens for how bacterial weapons plug into human cell signaling. Many pathogens inject effector proteins carrying EPIYA motifs; host enzymes phosphorylate them, and host SH2-domain proteins then dock and reroute the cell. Their 2026 perspective builds a sequence-informed, three-layer convergence model comparing the bacterial motifs with the host's braking signals, ITIM and ITSM.

Convergence, they argue, happens at three levels: the sequence grammar around the tyrosine, compatibility with host kinases writing the mark, and recognition by SH2 readers interpreting it. Effectors such as Helicobacter's CagA, Bartonella's BepD, and E. coli's Tir show pathogens installing look-alike docking sites without copying host motifs; a logo-based comparison makes the pattern visible. The authors stress this is analogy, not homology. Their framework shifts attention to whether host machinery can write and read a motif, a prediction tool for new effectors.
pmc-13458249:
Yi W. Chen and colleagues track blood sugar changes after adults with cystic fibrosis start the triple modulator therapy ETI, which transforms lung outcomes and may also ease the diabetes that stalks this disease. Their 2026 single-center retrospective study includes 61 adults carrying at least one F508del mutation: 23 with cystic fibrosis-related diabetes and 38 without, followed for a year on treatment.

In the diabetes group, HbA1c drifted from 6.6 to 6.1 percent and insulin doses eased, neither change reaching statistical significance. The non-diabetic group showed clearer movement. Glucose at one and two hours after a glucose drink fell significantly, 13 of 38 people improved their tolerance category, and nobody progressed to diabetes during follow-up. Lung function improved in both groups, as expected. The authors read the pattern as a favorable metabolic bonus atop the known respiratory gains, supporting more dynamic, individualized management of blood sugar in cystic fibrosis clinics.
pmc-13458349:
Jane Koerner and colleagues try to bring order to Australia's thicket of digital mental health navigation tools, the apps and sites meant to guide people to the right service. Proliferation without shared definitions has produced confusion, with navigation and navigator swapped freely. As part of building the MChart tool for planners, their 2026 study convened 28 experts, from psychiatrists and GPs to funders, community groups, and consumers, for two structured co-design sessions.

The panel agreed a consensus definition of what these tools are, whom they target, and what falls inside their scope. It then listed 157 traits, sorted into five domains: type, management, content, design, and quality. Working within an implementation-science readiness framework, the group produced a typology meant to serve as a shared frame. The authors argue the definition and list lay the groundwork for quality standards, letting developers, users, and officials judge competing tools on common terms.
pmc-13458549:
Jack H DeLap and colleagues track birds across 12 years of edge building near Puget Sound in a 2026 study. Fringe building reshapes habitat, yet whether low-intensity green layouts beat dense planned estates for birds was untested at group scale. Presence models for single birds and whole bird groups compared green developments with planned estates in the central Puget Sound region of Washington.

More of the overall bird group, plus forest-shy birds and flexible birds, lived in green developments than planned estates, matching forecasts. Built-area birds showed no overall building effect and varied on their own. Guild best forecast single-bird results for shy birds at 87 percent, then flexible birds at 63 percent and built-area birds at only 44 percent. Planners gain proof that building layout, not just density, shapes bird groups, above all for fragile birds.
pmc-13459249:
Osman Faruk Bayramlar and Selma Karabey price device-linked bugs in a Turkish ICU in a 2026 matched study. Care-linked bugs lengthen stays and drain budgets, yet clean cost figures need careful matching for patient differences. Data from 700 stays between 2016 and 2018 at an Istanbul ICU were studied, with 81 bug cases matched to controls.

Bugs hit 14.1 percent of stays. Extra costs ran to 6,781 dollars for ventilator-linked pneumonia, 2,037 dollars for central line blood bug, 5,320 dollars for tube bladder bug, and 4,213 dollars for all bugs combined. Bug rates ranked highest by US NHSN rules. Hospital leaders gain matched, per-device cost figures to justify spending on stopping them, above all against breathing-machine pneumonia.
pmc-13459749:
Bourdeau-Brien and colleagues modeled in 2026 how to shape Canada's new flood cover plan so the public gains the most from it. Flood cover in high risk zones fights two pulls: bills must stay fair, yet only the most at risk sign up. The team set three aims: fair bills, full pay outs, and wide take up. A fresh loss bank, built from seven hundred thousand fake flood scenes, fed the tests. Fee parts were mixed and matched: aid, caps, first loss sums, top pay lines, and shut outs.

One blend won the trade offs. Aid that grows as means shrink did the heavy lift on fair bills. Fee caps and a mid first loss sum held costs in check. A top pay line kept the plan sound, and shut outs for the worst risk homes kept take up broad. The team holds the blend up for peer lands too.
pmc-13460649:
Amit R. T. Joshi, Adrian Anthony, Dara O'Keeffe, April Roslani, and David O'Regan argue in a 2026 essay that surgical education needs a genuinely global structure. Workforce shortages, competency-based training, tangled regulation, and fast-moving technology now cross every border, yet training governance stays national or local. Colleges, specialty societies, and certifying bodies each contribute strengths, the authors concede, although none was built as a worldwide platform.

Their proposed answer is a federation of societies, modeled on the participating society structure of the International Society of Surgery, where national and specialty groups co-create programs while keeping local control. They present ICOSET, an international collaborative begun in the mid-2000s by surgical educators from major colleges, as the vehicle for that shared venture.
pmc-13461349:
F. Chassot leads a physics team that demonstrated in 2026 a fleeting topological state in the semiconductor tin telluride, created only while intense light pulses strike the crystal. Such Floquet states, where a periodic electric field reshapes the material's bands, had never before produced a confirmed topological phase in such a material. Using ultrafast snapshots with momentum resolution, the team watched the bands while femtosecond pulses were applied.

When the light's energy sat near the material's bandgap, the bands inverted, the signature move that creates topological behavior, and the band shapes warped in ways revealing the light-dressed states themselves. The state vanishes with the pulse, yet its existence proves that optical control can switch these properties on demand, a prospect for spin-based and quantum devices.
pmc-13461849:
Shuangyue Wang and colleagues pool trial results, in a 2026 review, on liver harm from a combined treatment for liver tumors that cannot be removed by surgery. The combination joins an immune checkpoint drug, which frees immune cells to attack cancer, with a targeted one. The rival is a single targeted drug from the kinase blocker family. Eight randomized trials with 4,379 patients came from three databases.

Liver-related serious side effects were more common with the combination than with the single drug. Fatal side effects occurred at similar rates in both groups. One liver blood marker, total bilirubin, rose more often with the combination. Other liver markers and problems, including two key enzymes, fluid in the belly, and a bile enzyme, showed no clear difference. The authors say the pairing raises liver risk in specific ways rather than across the board. They advise close watching of liver tests during treatment.
pmc-13461949:
Sahira Chaiben and colleagues propose, in a 2026 methods paper, a blood-based way to detect whether patients take their long-term oral drugs. Self-reports, pill monitors, and single drug-level checks often miss hidden missed doses. Their approach uses population drug modeling with two measures: the drug itself and a breakdown product that leaves the body at a different speed.

The team picked the blood pressure drug spironolactone and its product canrenone, which suit the method. Virtual patients were simulated under steady dosing, then pushed through varied patterns of missed or extra doses. A sampling algorithm estimated each patient's drug traits and dose history, producing an adherence probability. Using both measures beat either alone, above all for missed doses. Low-point blood samples worked better than peak samples. The authors say the approach can extend to other drugs where two measures behave distinctly.
pmc-13462049:
Michela Dell'Alma and a large team track, in a 2026 study, the microbes and chemistry of spontaneous fermentation in Picolit, a wine grape from northeast Italy. Picolit grapes often form uneven berries and carry high sugar. Unlike guided fermentations, the spontaneous kind relies on microbes from the vineyard itself. Grapes came from an organic winery in the Savorgnano area of Friuli. Five fermentation stages were sampled.

Gene sequencing and chemical profiling followed the handover between microbe sets. Starting juice held a mix led by non-Saccharomyces yeasts, oxygen-using bacteria, and the gray mold fungus. That fungus oddly persisted and grew, hinting at a tight tie to the grape's traits. Early stages featured varied yeasts linked to acid balance and aroma building. From mid-fermentation, several Saccharomyces species took over as bacterial variety shrank. The authors describe a local path shaped by grape traits, place, and native microbes.
pmc-13463249:
Abedi Koupai and colleagues report a 2026 study of a two-layer dressing for full-thickness skin wounds. The lower layer is 3D-printed from natural gels and loaded with G-CSF, a growth factor that calls in repair cells. The upper layer is a mat of electrospun nanofibers carrying abietic acid, a plant compound with anti-inflammatory action.

The team tuned the mix of polymers to balance strength, swelling, and breakdown behavior, the properties that decide how a dressing handles wound fluid and stays intact. Splitting jobs between layers mirrors skin itself: a regenerative base against the wound and a protective top facing the world.  A bioprinted growth layer under an anti-inflammatory shield is a concrete design others can build on and test in animals next.
pmc-13463649:
Herrera-Ramírez and co-authors traced in 2026 how Helicobacter pylori switches on a chain of signals inside gastric cells. The bacterium is linked to ulcers and gastric cancer. The team worked with two gastric cancer cell lines. They also used tumor organoids grown from patients. Their focus was a low-oxygen sensor protein, HIF-1 alpha, and the traffic-control machinery it activates.

Infection raised levels of ALS2, a protein that switches on another protein, Rab5. Rab5 manages the cell's internal shipping compartments. The activation depended entirely on HIF-1 alpha. Blocking the sensor stopped the whole chain. With Rab5 active, a growth signal called beta-catenin stayed switched on. Its off-switch was locked away inside those compartments. Silencing ALS2 prevented Rab5 activation, compartment swelling, and the growth signal alike. Patient organoids repeated the pattern, confirming a new route toward cancer.
pmc-13465049:
Xijie Zhao and five co-authors build a near-infrared method that reads three quality marks in lycopene drinks at once. Lycopene gives tomatoes their red color and antioxidant fame, yet drink makers lack a fast joint check for acidity, moisture, and lycopene itself. Light scans paired with math modeling fill that gap.

A smoothing and scatter-fix pairing cleaned the light signals best across all three targets. Explanation tools pointed to the light zones tied to each mark, keeping the models chemically sensible. Trimming to a few key signals helped acidity and moisture forecasts, while lycopene scored best with the full cleaned signal. The setup stayed lab-bound, so the authors frame it as groundwork for line-side quality tools.
pmc-13465149:
Núñez-Rodríguez and colleagues studied body makeup and skin heat patterns in older adults in Burgos, Spain. Their one-time snapshot study enrolled 127 people who lived in the community. The team measured body fat and muscle mass with a mild electric signal test. They also took heat images of the skin and compared left and right sides.

Women had more body fat than men and showed larger left-right heat gaps. Higher body fat went with wider heat gaps in the arms and higher heat balance scores. Muscle mass, in contrast, showed no clear link to any heat gap measure. Even the best model explained only a small share of the heat differences between people. The authors treat these results as early clues and call for larger studies before heat imaging guides care for older adults.
pmc-13465349:
Fu and colleagues report a 2026 survey of what patients with type 2 diabetes in Nanjing, China, know and feel about art therapy.  The team surveyed patients at one hospital's endocrine department in early 2025 on knowledge, attitudes, art habits, and willingness to try the therapy.

Responses were analyzed item by item, and statistical models searched for what predicts willingness to try. Knowing which patient groups lean in, by age, education, or prior art experience, decides whether a hospital should offer group sessions, taster formats, or none at all.  A baseline map is the first step before any program can be fairly tested.
pmc-13465549:
Jiro Kikuchi and Hiroshi Yasui compare two CD38 antibodies for multiple myeloma, daratumumab and isatuximab, and argue they are not interchangeable. Both hit the same surface target, yet their grip points and side talents differ. The review assembles mechanism studies and clinic patterns side by side.

Isatuximab clamps the target's enzyme mouth, killing partly through oxidative bursts and a growth switch shutdown. A chromosome gain common in myeloma may mark tumors that answer it best. Daratumumab leans on immune muscle, stripping target levels and loosening drug resistance glue. Each drug also reshapes leftover disease and the immune scene differently. Picking by tumor biology, the authors propose, beats picking by habit.
pmc-13465649:
Roya Khanmohammadi and colleagues compared balance tests in 2026 for athletes with chronic ankle instability, a wobbly ankle that undermines dynamic control. Clinicians debate whether a simple reach test or a lab force plate better spots the deficit. Sixty-two athletes with instability and 31 healthy controls took the Y-balance reach test and force plate measures during gait start.

Backward reaches fell sharply in both instability groups, while only the more unstable group lost forward reach, and sideways pressure shifts also dropped. Backward-outward reach diagnosed instability best, at 95.7% area under the curve with 90.5% sensitivity and 90.0% specificity. Neither test separated high from low instability, so the reach test offers a cheap screen while plates add mechanism detail.
pmc-13465749:
Jay Sakore and Suman Ray wrote a 2026 letter commenting on a Riyadh study of parents' views on HPV infection and shots. Cervical cancer ranks fourth among women's cancers worldwide and stems mostly from persistent HPV infection, while vaccines plus screening have cut HPV cases sharply. The letter praises the original study's call for targeted education, then probes the limits of vaccine shield.

Cancer takes decades to follow HPV, so firm proof of cancer prevention is only now emerging. Current vaccines cover types 16 and 18, about 70% of cervical cancers, leaving other oncogenic types to screening. Shield also peaks before sex starts and grows less sure with age or prior contact, with cover past nine years still unknown. The comment thus argues screening must continue alongside the shots, even for vaccinated women.
pmc-13466149:
Hannes Hagström and colleagues studied socioeconomic gaps in 2026 among Swedish patients whose liver cancer was found through surveillance. Screening aims to catch liver cancer early enough for curative treatment, yet poorer patients may still fare worse even after detection. The nationwide cohort covered 1,514 adults with cirrhosis and surveillance-found liver cancer from 2012 to 2022.

Early-stage diagnosis reached 56% and curative treatment reached 64%, but low socioeconomic status independently cut treatment odds to 0.42 against high status after full adjustment. Among treated patients, low status also raised death risk by half, at a hazard ratio of 1.50. Surveillance alone cannot close gaps in a universal system, the authors argue, without people-centred support across the whole care path.
pmc-13466449:
Aiswarya Mukundan Nair and Helen Piontkivska compare RNA editing patterns in blood from patients with critical versus milder COVID-19, in a 2026 study. Editing enzymes called ADARs, switched on by interferon, rewrite RNA letters and shape immune responses. Patients were matched on age, sex, and other illnesses so severity stood out as the main contrast.

Critical cases showed many gene activity differences, including pathways tied to neutrophil granule release, and higher levels of one editing enzyme and its shorter form. Editing sites unique to each severity group appeared, some changing the protein a gene builds. The authors read these patterns as part of why similar people can fare so differently in this infection.
pmc-13466549:
Giulia Del Duca and colleagues argue that a simple fatigue questionnaire may help grade long COVID severity, in a 2026 article. Patient-reported measures are often treated as softer than lab markers, yet the authors push back: a blood value means little without knowing how a given patient responds to it. Long COVID still has no validated diagnostic marker.

The Fatigue Assessment Scale, a short standardized questionnaire, captures the illness's impact in a repeatable way. In a condition defined largely by symptoms, such a tool could sort patients by severity where molecules cannot yet. The piece makes a broader case for patient reports inside precision medicine.
pmc-13467049:
Wasim Iyad Alghoul and nine colleagues published this 2026 review on why urinary tract infections keep returning after menopause. Low estrogen alone does not explain why some women relapse and others do not. The authors gathered evidence on how hormone loss, microbes living in the urinary and genital tracts, diabetes and obesity interact. They also covered hidden reservoirs of bacteria in the gut, rectum and bladder wall.

Searching PubMed and Scopus, the team structured 62 original reports published from 2021 to mid-2026. Menopause was linked with fewer protective Lactobacillus bacteria and a higher vaginal pH, though results varied. Vaginal estrogen cut recurrence and improved the local environment. Diabetes was tied to disturbed microbes and weaker bladder-lining defences, while evidence for obesity was less direct. Bladder emptying problems and catheter use added further risk. The authors present their framework as a useful lens, not a proven causal model.
pmc-13467549:
Nikolina Rijavec and Željka Večerić-Haler review in 2026 how lithium, a cornerstone mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, can harm the kidneys. They also review how psychiatric and kidney care can be shared safely. Lithium prevents relapses and is uniquely tied to lower suicide risk. Yet long use can leave the kidneys unable to concentrate urine. It can also cause a form of diabetes insipidus where water handling fails, or slowly scar the kidney tissue in a minority of users.

The review explains how lithium enters kidney collecting duct cells and disrupts the water channel system. It then lists what raises the risk: past lithium poisoning, dehydration, interacting drugs, long treatment, and existing kidney disease. The authors finish with a practical shared-care pathway for patients who develop heavy urination, kidney injury, or chronic kidney disease while staying on a drug many still need.
pmc-13468449:
Zou and colleagues present a 2026 review of MXene-based catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction, the slow half of splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen. MXenes are flat sheets of metal carbides and related compounds with high conductivity and water-loving surfaces. The review first lays out the three accepted reaction pathways, then organizes design strategies for making MXenes perform.

Bare MXenes have too few active sites, restack into useless piles, and oxidize under the harsh conditions of oxygen making. The strategies surveyed attack each flaw: adding active partners, spacing the sheets, and shielding surfaces. Mechanistic grounding is the review's spine: knowing which pathway a catalyst follows tells chemists which intermediate to stabilize. Better oxygen catalysts decide the economics of green hydrogen, since this reaction wastes the most energy in electrolysis today.
pmc-13468749:
Yuqi Li and co-authors solve in 2026 a practical fatigue problem for wheel loaders. The load spectrum at the bucket edge decides how the working arm fatigues. It cannot be measured directly, because sensors cannot be mounted there. Their data-driven method learns the machine nonlinear input-output behavior with a NARX model, a neural-style predictor that uses past inputs and outputs. A genetic algorithm then runs the model backwards, searching for the input spectrum that reproduces the structural responses engineers can measure.

That inverted spectrum becomes the load program for bench fatigue tests, standing in for expensive field campaigns. The authors frame the payoff plainly: fatigue-resistant design of loader working devices without direct testing at the unmeasurable point, and a much shorter development loop. Construction machinery lives under random punishing loads, so a cheap, credible load history is valuable intellectual infrastructure for every redesign.
pmc-13469249:
Jerez-Henríquez and co-authors document how communities in Chile's Biobío region respond to climate change, in this 2026 study. The region is also marked by extractive industry. It has a long history of conflict between the Mapuche people and the Chilean state. The team calls the local responses climatic pluriverses. These are initiatives rooted in local knowledge and ways of life. They offer alternatives to one-size-fits-all climate policy.

The team built a mapped inventory of community initiatives. They also carried out fieldwork across Andean foothill, dryland, and coastal areas. They found resilience grounded in deep attachment to place. Local people also depend closely on nearby ecosystems. Groups defended their land through varied strategies against combined climate and extraction pressures. The authors present these experiences as co-produced with nature. They argue the cases offer decolonial lessons for climate strategy in diverse, damaged regions.
pmc-13470349:
Hadi Karimipour Fard and co-authors model in 2026 the tangle of worm and soil factors behind citrus decline in southern Iran. Orchards in Fars and Kohgiluyeh Boyerahmad provinces suffer a slow decline driven by living and nonliving stresses together. Eighty soil and root collections from 2020 to 2022 measured the citrus nematode, a microscopic root feeding worm, alongside soil texture, salt, acidity, and lime content.

Three statistical approaches linked worm density to how severe the decline was. Light textured soils with moderate salt held the most worms. Alkaline soil, high lime, and dense worm populations combined to worsen shortages of micronutrients in the trees. The authors recommend joined up responses: tolerant rootstocks, worm control, and soil improvement together rather than any single fix.
pmc-13470449:
Man-Xi Ge and co-authors identify in 2026 a helper protein that links the cell main folding crews to the making of membrane proteins. Membrane proteins fold partly inside a compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum and partly in the cell fluid, and how those halves coordinate is poorly understood. A genome wide gene knockout screen flagged the anchored protein FKBP8 as essential for folding and assembling such proteins.

Working with transporter proteins as test cases, the team showed FKBP8 partners with the Hsp70 and Hsp90 chaperone systems to reshape unfinished domains. Electron microscope images revealed a roomy client holding cavity formed with Hsp90. Cells missing FKBP8, or carrying its disease linked mutations, trapped the test proteins for destruction instead. A rebuilt mixture of purified parts restored correct folding, defining a minimal folding machine.
pmc-13470649:
Tao and colleagues report in 2026 a split-neck study comparing low-energy and high-energy microplasma radiofrequency for mild to moderate neck wrinkles. This skin-resurfacing treatment was tested to see which energy protocol gives the better trade of results against pain and visits.

Seventeen patients had one side of the neck treated gently in six sessions and the other side at high energy in three sessions, with 3D imaging follow-up to six months. Both sides improved significantly, and the degree of improvement never differed significantly between protocols at any checkpoint. At six months the low-energy side actually showed the higher improvement rate, about twenty-four percent against fifteen on their reported figures. Pain separated the protocols clearly: mild on the low-energy side, moderate on the high-energy side. Redness and swelling settled within six hours, and no scarring or pigmentation problems occurred.
pmc-13470849:
Balabram and colleagues studied in 2026 how to protect annatto seed extract, a natural coloring rich in protective carotenoid compounds, inside potato starch packaging films. They trapped the extract, made with a natural solvent blend, inside a double emulsion, meaning droplets nested inside droplets, before adding it to the film.

The double emulsion captured about 96 percent of the extract and kept much of its antioxidant power. Films carrying it held about 47 percent less moisture and let about half as much water vapor through as plain films. The best film also stayed strong in tension tests and blocked ultraviolet light better. Microscopy and X-ray checks showed the emulsion changed the film's internal structure without stopping it from forming, supporting biodegradable active packaging uses.
pmc-13470949:
Braggio and a clinical team exercised patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia in 2026, hunting hidden heart and muscle problems before iron overload damages the heart. Nine patients without cardiac iron and nine healthy controls took exercise tests with lung ultrasound, and blood markers of vessel activation and muscle metabolism were measured. Grip strength and body composition completed the picture; at rest, everyone's heart measures looked alike.

Exercise exposed the gap: patients reached lower peak oxygen uptake, pumped less oxygen per heartbeat, and raised heart rate less. Ultrasound showed more lung fluid lines during effort, a sign the heart's filling side stiffens under load, and patients carried less lean mass and gripped more weakly. A growth factor tied to metabolic stress ran high, a small muscle RNA ran low, and a vessel activation marker spiked after exercise. The authors propose exercise ultrasound as an early warning tool for this blood disorder.
pmc-13471249:
Mehrjoei and colleagues tested a tiny RNA regulator, miR-32, as a blood signal for colorectal cancer in 2026, where early detection transforms outcomes. The team measured PTEN, the target gene of miR-32, alongside the RNA itself in tumor tissue, nearby healthy tissue, and blood plasma. Samples came from 55 patients and 55 matched controls, and statistical curves judged how well the marker separates the groups.

The pattern was clean and mirrored: miR-32 ran significantly high in both tumors and plasma. PTEN, a tumor suppressor the RNA helps silence, ran low in tumors, the two moving in opposite directions as biology predicts. As a diagnostic test, tissue miR-32 scored 0.94 accuracy on a scale where 1.0 is perfect, and plasma scored a still-good level near the mid-eighties in percentage terms. Higher miR-32 also tracked with more advanced tumor stage. The authors propose it as a non-invasive detection candidate, pending larger validation.
pmc-13471449:
Gou and colleagues investigated why ovarian cancers stop responding to PARP inhibitors, drugs that block a DNA-repair enzyme, focusing on how the drug reshapes chromosome folding. Their 2026 study built a genome-wide contact map of cells treated with olaparib and bred an olaparib-resistant ovarian cancer cell line for comparison.

The team traced resistance to RAD21, a cohesin protein that holds chromosome loops together, which kept the repair gene RAD51 switched on through an enhancer loop. High RAD21 expression in patients was significantly associated with shorter overall and progression-free survival. About half of high-grade serous ovarian cancers carry inherited faults in repair genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, the group notes, making resistance mechanisms like this one a central clinical problem.
pmc-13471549:
Ceyhun and Ceyhun tested whether smartwatch data can flag healthy adults who are quietly heading toward high blood pressure. Their 2026 prospective study followed 230 normotensive adults aged 30 to 60 for 12 months. The predictors came from the first 30 days of watch data: heart rate variability, resting heart rate, and active minutes.

Twenty-eight participants, 12.2% of the cohort, developed hypertension during the year, and most were caught by office readings, with 85.7% of cases meeting guideline thresholds. Those who converted had shown lower heart rate variability and less moderate-to-vigorous activity at baseline, and both stayed independent predictors alongside higher body mass index. Most participants, 84.3% of them, wore an Apple Watch Series 9.
pmc-13472149:
Rui Xue and co-authors watch in 2026 two bacterial species divide the work of destroying a common antibiotic in a built ecosystem. One Microbacterium strain cracks sulfadiazine but leaves a fragment, 2-aminopyrimidine, behind, while its Terrabacter partner cannot touch the parent drug at all. Fed labeled drug as their only carbon source, the pair together cleared it completely with no fragment accumulating.

Single cell Raman light scattering told the two species apart and counted their ratio over time, matching the chemistry measurements. Isotope tracing proved the partner assimilated the fragment into its own biomass, with under half its cells actively degrading it at any moment. The release of the fragment by the first species is the trigger for the second. The authors present the pairing as tidy commensalism, one species waste feeding the other.
pmc-13472849:
Rosenstock and co-authors report the ACCESS phase 2b trial of aleniglipron, a once-daily oral GLP-1 pill for obesity, against placebo over 36 weeks. Their 2026 randomized double-blind study enrolled 230 adults with a mean body mass index of 39.5 across 38 United States sites, escalating doses every four weeks to 45, 90, or 120 milligrams.

Every dose beat placebo on the primary endpoint: placebo-adjusted weight change reached −8.2% at 45 mg, −9.8% at 90 mg, and −11.3% at the 120 mg dose by week 36, all highly significant. Weight was still falling when the blinded phase ended, with no plateau in sight. Gut side effects were mostly mild to moderate and faded over time, and treatment-related discontinuations ran at 10.4% across the drug arms.
pmc-13473449:
Yan and co-authors uncovered a three-link chain that helps bladder cancer grow and spread to lymph nodes, centered on the enzyme ZRANB1. Their 2026 study screened ubiquitin-system genes across bladder cancer datasets, confirmed ZRANB1 elevation in patient tissue, and tested its effects in cell and mouse models, including a 110-patient survival cohort.

High ZRANB1 tracked with deeper tumor stage, node metastasis, and poorer survival. Mechanistically, ZRANB1 rescues the splicing factor SF3B3 from destruction, and SF3B3 in turn blocks skipping of exon 4 in the checkpoint gene CHEK2, suppressing a tumor-suppressing variant of it. The stakes are plain: about 75% of patients present with non-muscle-invasive disease, and 15 to 20% of those progress to the muscle-invasive form.
pmc-13473549:
Katarina E. Goodge and three colleagues released in 2026 a reference dataset to help sort textiles by fibre type with near-infrared light. Near-infrared spectroscopy reads chemical bonds quickly and without damage, making it attractive for identifying feedstock in recycling. Data with known provenance for textile fibres and fabrics have been scarce. Existing models usually rest on private libraries or home-built databases, so results across the industry cannot be compared.

The new dataset covers textile specimens for fibre content checks, system and software development, and testing of sorting systems. Its repository holds benchtop near-infrared spectra, handheld near-infrared spectra, and fabric-scale microscopy images, giving researchers matched measurements at different scales. For recyclers, instrument makers, and model builders, the value is a shared benchmark: methods can now be tested on the same known materials. Claims about sorting accuracy can be checked rather than asserted.
pmc-13474249:
Hosna Hajati and co-authors test coated lysine feed for meat chickens in 2026. Lysine is a key building block that chickens must get from feed, and coated forms may release it more slowly. Six hundred day-old chicks were split into six diets, from full standard lysine to diets where coated lysine supplied as little as three fifths of that amount. Lab checks first confirmed the coating wrapped the core well.

Final weight and feed intake did not differ across diets. Chicks on coated lysine at eighty to one hundred percent converted feed to growth more efficiently in the first four weeks. Some blood fat measures also rose at mid-level doses. Farms may cut lysine waste while holding growth steady.
pmc-13474549:
Alvin Santoso Kalim and five colleagues reported in 2026 two children with umbilical cord hernia accompanied by a patent omphalomesenteric duct, a leftover foetal channel. Umbilical cord hernia is rare, affecting about 1 in 5,000 births, and is sometimes mistaken for a small omphalocele. Both children had surgery to remove the duct and reconnect the bowel.

In the first child the duct was found by chance during closure, and recovery was smooth, with discharge on day 21. In the second, the duct had prolapsed, and the child developed breathing-related blood acidity and died on day 7. The contrast shows why surgeons should search for hidden defects alongside abdominal wall defects, since they can change the outcome.
pmc-13474849:
Atri and colleagues describe seven adults treated in 2026 for a blocked small bowel caused by a congenital band, a fibrous strap left over from development before birth. Most bowel blockages come from scar tissue after surgery, so a band in an adult who never had abdominal surgery is easy to miss. The series comes from one tertiary center's admissions between 2010 and 2022, paired with a review of published cases.

The seven patients formed 2.6 percent of the 269 blockage admissions in that period, and all arrived with abdominal pain and vomiting as their main symptoms. Scans found the blockage point in every case but never showed the band itself, so diagnosis came during surgery for all seven patients. Six needed only the band cut, one needed a damaged bowel segment removed, and patients stayed 3.7 days on average, with no complications afterward.
pmc-13475349:
Fengqing Chao and co-authors estimate teen birth rates in 2026 for 201 states and areas from 1950 to 2023. Girls aged ten to fourteen and fifteen to nineteen were modeled apart. A Bayesian time model used total fertility and girls schooling as guides while correcting bias and undercounts. Rates were then turned into birth counts using population data.

Global rates for the younger group fell by about three quarters between 1990 and 2023. Rates for older teens fell by about half over the same span. Births to older teens in sub-Saharan Africa still rose, driven by population growth. Sound counts help track a global health goal on teen care access.
pmc-13475449:
Shunsuke Kidani and three co-authors published a 2026 mouse study testing a new falling-trap assay for anxiety. Behavioral tests for anxiety often replicate poorly, so the team built a simple elevated path where falls are the measure, on the theory that calmer mice fall more. Male mice received either a dummy treatment or chlordiazepoxide, a known anti-anxiety drug, and were tested both in the new trap and in the classic elevated plus maze.

In the trap, drugged mice did not fall significantly more than controls. In the maze, the drug clearly increased time spent on open arms, as expected. The authors conclude the falling-trap count, as tested, does not measure anxiety-like behavior. They call for work on the conditions under which the assay might work, and for checks of its reliability.
pmc-13475549:
María José Ferreira Díaz maps the global health workforce shortfall toward 2030 in a 2026 review. Literature, global data sets, and policy papers from 2014 to 2024 were screened and blended. Numbers work sat beside theme analysis of drivers and system effects. The goal was a policy frame that treats workforce strain as a whole-system problem.

Projections point to a gap near eleven million health workers by 2030. Nursing gaps run deepest, with millions more needed once retirements and demand growth count in. Five drivers recur: poor work conditions, weak retention, aging staff, governance faults, and unmanaged migration. The frame ties local fixes to national and global action.
pmc-13476449:
Gowhar Iqbal and co-authors build gene-editing tools in 2026 for the myostatin gene in rohu, a major farmed carp. Myostatin brakes muscle growth, so editing it could raise yields. Guide RNAs for the first gene segment were built into a glowing editor plasmid. Sanger reading confirmed the guides sat in the right place and direction.

Muscle cells from the fish glowed at three culture ages, showing the editor entered and switched on each time. Entry held steady from early to late passages of the cell line. The groundwork supports later edits in live fish and eggs. Muscle gene editing in aquaculture gains a tested starter kit.
pmc-13478049:
Md Ikbal Hossain and colleagues present a 2026 survey of mental health among nursing students on clinical placement in Sylhet, Bangladesh. Placement work is required for graduation but exposes students to heavy workloads and difficult ward relationships. Data were collected over about three weeks in mid-2025 at one nursing college, using the DASS-21 symptom screening scale.

The survey covered 382 students with an average age near 22 years. Symptoms rated mild or worse were reported by about 75 percent for depression, about 78 percent for anxiety, and about 53 percent for stress. Female sex, poor peer relationships, lack of rest chances, and dissatisfaction with staff nurse behavior were tied to worse scores. The authors stress that the scale screens symptoms rather than diagnosing illness, and they point to rest and ward culture as practical targets.
pmc-13478749: Harkins and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their 2020 methods study on reading the native ends of broken DNA strands. The fix swaps back the color codes in two figures, which had been flipped in revision: blue marks the three prime overhangs, and red marks the five prime ones. Fresh copies of both figures are printed with their full captions. The authors state plainly that the slip touched the legends alone. No result, claim, or finding of the study changes.
pmc-13479449:
Hao Xu and colleagues published a 2026 genome study of Peganum, a genus of hardy desert plants from arid Central Asia known for hybrid forms. Untangling which species mothered each hybrid requires the maternally inherited organelle genomes, and few were available for this genus. The team assembled both chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes using three sequencing technologies.

Mitochondrial genomes ran from about 427,000 to 447,000 letters, each closing into a single circle holding 33 to 35 protein-coding genes. Chloroplast genomes were about 160,000 letters with 86 protein-coding genes. Comparing structures across species lets the authors trace maternal lineages inside the hybrid forms. The work supplies reference genomes for a model genus in hybrid speciation research.
pmc-13479549:
Hongrui Cui, Qingli Tan, and Xiaoshan Liu published a 2026 numbers-based study of gaps in health care across China's regions. Stories about rich coasts and poor inland areas are common, but fair yardsticks are rare. The team gathered province data from 2012 to 2021 and chose eighteen medical service gauges for a close look in 2021.

Factor math boiled the gauges down into service scores, cluster math grouped provinces by level, and gap indexes tracked how lopsided the spread of staff and gear was. Large gaps appeared, with the lowest service levels in poorer regions and the west and center of China shortest on supplies. The authors offer the rankings as a guide for reforms that aim to place staff, beds, and gear where need is greatest.
pmc-13480049:
Cheng Liu and colleagues present a 2026 study of how people with eating disorders view one-to-one peer support. Since 2023 a London specialist unit has paired patients with trained peers who have lived through an eating disorder. The team spoke in depth with twelve adults who had taken part and sorted their accounts into shared themes.

Seven themes stood out, covering shared understanding, an informal tone with equal footing, and a sense of safety without judgment. Peers helped patients place the illness within a wider life and picture recovery through a real example. Daily tips gained weight because they came from lived experience. The main gripe was that the help ended too soon, with many wanting more sessions. Findings fed into a new feedback tool built for this type of support.
pmc-13480249:
Tuba Metin and co-authors present a 2026 study of how patient and caregiver needs intertwine in home-based cancer care. The team surveyed 124 patients and their 124 family caregivers at one home palliative unit. Caregivers rated their own unmet support needs and quality of life, while patients rated theirs, and a chained model traced how each side shaped the other.

Caregivers reported hefty unmet needs and middling quality of life on average. The chained path held: patient unmet needs and patient symptom load together carried the link between caregiver quality of life and caregiver support needs. In plain terms, a struggling patient and a struggling caregiver feed each other's strain. Services that treat the pair as one unit, rather than two cases, may ease both sides.
pmc-13480749:
El-Setouhy and a large team in Saudi Arabia surveyed in 2026 aches among staff at Jazan University, and what ties to them. Desk work with poor desk setups and poor sleep are known strain loads. The team gave 460 staff three set forms: one on body aches, one that scored each desk setup, and one that graded sleep. Staff came from all parts of the school, picked by a staged draw.

Aches were the norm, not the rare case. Low back and neck pain each struck about two in three staff. Seats, hips, and knees hurt the fewest. Poor sleep stood on its own as a tie to neck, upper back, and knee pain. Poor desk setups tied to aches in most zones as well. The authors urge desk fixes and sleep health drives on campus, with long term checks to prove the gains.
pmc-13481949:
